title: Hiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue sky | Air transport | The Guardian
description: As the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastened
Author: Patrick Keneally
Headline: As the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastened
Content: Turbulence is the leading cause of injuries to aircraft passengers and crew in non-fatal accidentsAir transportHiding in plane sight: the invisible turbulence that can strike out of a clear blue skyAs the planet warms, airlines are grappling with what this means for air travel – and for the passengers who simply refuse to keep their seatbelts fastenedPatrick KeneallySat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.41 EDTShareIt was a swelteringly hot afternoon in south-west Myanmar on 21 May 2024. Tropical thunderstorms, showers and highs of 36C were forecast for the area around the Irrawaddy Basin. High above, monsoonal heat and humidity were building into a vast convective column of water vapour, a towering cumulonimbus cloud soaring up to 35,000ft (more than 10,500 metres) into the air. From the ground, it would have looked like something from a children’s picture book – a soft, fluffy white mass. But for Singapore Airlines flight SQ321 passing just above, it was anything but benign.In the cabin of the Boeing 777, passengers were being woken up for breakfast with three hours to go on the journey from London to Singapore. For the 210 travellers on board, the past 10 hours had been uneventful. The seatbelt signs were off. Some were milling around, others were using the toilets, and cabin staff were preparing trolleys for service. At 2.19pm and 23 seconds local time, moderate turbulence shook the plane for 17 seconds and the seatbelt sign was switched on. Then, as one passenger described it, it was “like a grenade had gone off”. In just 4.6 seconds, any passenger not strapped in hit the roof with 1.5 times the force of gravity and was thrown back on the floor in an instant.Passengers reported hearing people screaming in agony, blood streaming down faces, with overhead panels broken by the force of bodies hitting them. One person was left dead and 79 were seriously injured. The turbulence had lasted just over 21 seconds.WhileSQ321 was an extreme case that made global headlines, turbulence is the leading cause of injuries to passengers and crew in non-fatal accidents, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA). Figures from the Federal Aviation Administration record about a dozen serious injuries a year from turbulence across the US alone.It can be caused by a multitude of factors, including geographic features such as mountains – thetop 10 most turbulent routesare all over either the Andes or the Himalayas. Some forms, such as the typecaused by mountainsand wake turbulence, which is caused by other aircraft, are fairly well understood and avoided. Pilots have always had to contend with the sky’s speed bumps as part of the job.double quotation markThere’s more energy in a typical thunderstorm than there is in a nuclear weaponRichard Woodward, former RAAF and Qantas pilotBut the threat of turbulence across the world is increasing due to the climate crisis. Not only will pilots need to contend with the frequency and severity of these episodes rising, they’re facing a future that includes a large surge in clear-air turbulence – an invisible, largely undetectable turbulence that comes, quite literally, out of the blue.Flying over the top of a cycloneRichard Woodward is a former Royal Australian Air Force test pilot andQantasA380 captain who served the airline for 32 years. He hasflown routes all around the world and has seen more than his fair share of difficult conditions, including flying over a cyclone (it was surprisingly smooth and the radar “painted it beautifully”).But Woodward says airlines and the aviation industry are increasingly aware of the threat posed by global heating.“There’ll be an increase in the severity of thunderstorms and storms in general because, as the planet warms, the amount of energy inputting into these events will become massively greater,” he says.Thunderstorm or convective turbulence – the cause of the SQ321 incident – creates strong updrafts, then strong downdrafts as the air and water vapour cool. It may be encountered several thousand feet above clouds and as far as 20 miles (more than 30km) on either side. This can be particularly dangerous, Woodward says, given that “there’s more energy in a typical thunderstorm than there is in a nuclear weapon”.That massive amount of energy can be seen in lightning – which sometimes even reaches into space, Woodward says – but it also manifests in turbulence. More heat, and greater differences between hot and cold areas, will supercharge already powerful thunderstorms.2:32‘Going completely horizontal’: passengers on Singapore Airlines flight hit by turbulence – videoIt’s a problem that pilots and passengers have encountered in Australia. In the same month as the SQ321 episode, a Qantas Boeing 737encountered severe turbulencewhile on approach to Brisbane airport after entering a storm cloud at 11,400ft. Three cabin crew, who were not seated at the time, were injured; one was left with a broken ankle. Another crew member with an undiagnosed concussion returned to work on several subsequent flights without medical attention. The Australian Transport Safety Board report was highly critical of the airline’s response, saying the crew member “returning to work with an undiagnosed concussion likely compromised [their] ability to perform safety-critical tasks”. Qantas has since overhauled its safety protocols for crew injuries.Sign up for a weekly email featuring our best reads“In eastern Australia in a typical warm season we get lots of thunderstorms – warm air below, cooler air above, gives you the instability,” says Dr Milton Speer, a forecasting meteorologist and a fellow in the school of mathematical and physical sciences at the University of Technology Sydney. He has conducted research that found atmospheric conditions in eastern Australia are increasingly resulting in stronger, more frequent thunderstorm microbursts that can be hard to predict.Brisbane to Sydney consistently ranks as the most turbulent route in Australia due to these fast-developing and dynamic storm systems.‘The fuel of thunderstorms’The physical science behind the rise in atmospheric turbulence from global heating is both simple and incredibly complex.“The science is pretty clear on this: for every degree of warming, the atmosphere can hold 7% more water vapour,” says Todd Lane, a professor of atmospheric science at the University of Melbourne. “And water vapour is the fuel of thunderstorms.’”There’s also a strong relationship between the severity of the thunderstorm and the amount of turbulence inside. “So if we have more severe thunderstorms, we expect more turbulence within them,” he says. “And also that leads to more turbulence around the storms as well.”What causes air turbulence and is the climate crisis making it worse?Read moreMostonboard injuries caused by turbulenceare linked to thunderstorms but storms and bad weather are at least to some extent visible via radar and can be forecast.That’s not true for invisible turbulence. Clear-air turbulence is usually found in the upper atmosphere, at cruising altitude, often at the edges of jet streams. While it can be modelled or reported by other aircraft, it can’t be detected in advance using radar.Ananalysis by scientists at the University of Readingof four decades of atmospheric data collected between 1979 and 2020 found that severe clear-air turbulence increased by 55% and moderate and light turbulence had increased 37% and 17% over the same period.Clear-air turbulence will increase even under the most optimistic scenarios of global heating – a 1.5C increase above preindustrial levelswill lead to a 27% increase; with a 2.75C increase in global temperatures that figure jumps to 56%.Lane, who has worked on problems associated with clear-air turbulence for 25 years, calls it a “particular hazard for commercial aircraft” and says it occurs when there’s an increase in wind shear – a change in wind speed or direction over a relatively short distance, often at the edge of jet streams, the fast-moving air currents that flow around the Earth.With global heating, changes in temperature differences between the equator and the poles can intensify the wind shear from jet streams, Lane says.In 2017 Ignacio Gallego-Marcos was sitting on a plane on the tarmac awaiting takeoff for a flight from Madrid to Stockholm. It was a calm day but the engineer searched for a forecast out of curiosity and realised there was nothing available for the public. It prompted Gallego-Marcos – who has a PhD in fluid dynamics, the study of how liquids (or gases) move and respond to physical forces – to buildturbli.com, a publicly accessible turbulence forecasting site.Anyone can use Turbli to get a read on an upcoming flight. Aviation enthusiasts are among the 300,000 monthly users of the site, alongside nervous flyers.Gallego-Marcos says turbulence is, to some extent, predictable. And even though global heating may increase its frequency and severity, some types are easier to model than others.1:31Passengers carried off Singapore Airlines plane after severe turbulence – video report“Clear air turbulence can be very easily predicted when it comes to the jet stream, which are very large flowing masses, so the resolution of the current forecasts can predict them,” Gallego-Marcos says. “But clear turbulence is also found in the vicinity of thunderstorm clouds and there it becomes difficult to predict because a thunderstorm is very small – it has a lot of features that you cannot predict in weather models.”‘The ones you’re going to drive into the ceiling’Stuart Fox, IATA’s director of flight and technical operations, says the traditional approach of pilots relying on reports from other pilots and weather advisories to help avoid turbulence has some limitations given “information may not be available at the right time and can vary in quality”.In 2018 IATA began collecting turbulence observations from about 30 airlines running more than 3,700 aircraft and sharing them with participating airlines, which include United Airlines, Qatar, Etihad, ANA and Lufthansa.The project uses onboard sensors to record turbulence information and share that instantaneously. The data, modelled using AI tools, is now providing near-time predictions of turbulence.double quotation markStructurally, the aircraft are built to withstand far more than they would ever be expected to encounterSteve Lieb, aviation lecturerSome manufacturers are looking at aircraft design and sophisticated sensors includingLidar, which uses lasers to detect atmospheric density ahead of an aircraft.And some airlines are becoming more risk-averse. After the SQ321 injuries, Singapore Airlines enforces much stricter rules in the cabin when turbulence is expected, with meal services stopped and crew members seated. On some flights along the same route, it’s routine to have the seatbelt sign on for most of the flight.But this approach has one particular flaw.“No matter how many times you tell people to put their seatbelts on, there’s a chunk of them in the back who find it uncomfortable to have a loosely fitted seatbelt, for some stupid reason,” Woodward says.Why the climate crisis is especially bad news for frightened flyersRead more“People still need to go to the toilet, they get bored, and once the seatbelt sign’s been on for a small period of time … they’ll get up and go to the toilet anyway.“And they’re the ones you’re going to drive into the ceiling if you get a sudden event.”For nervous flyers, there’s a reassuring fact to hold tight to, along with your armrests: there hasn’t been a crash of a passenger airliner attributed solely to turbulence since flight HN431, a Dutch plane that lost control after entering a tornado in 1981.“The reality is, structurally, the aircraft are built to withstand far more than they would ever be expected to encounter in the normal line of operations,” says Steve Lieb, a senior lecturer in aviation at Central Queensland University.The real problem lies not in the plane itself but what’s inside. Airlines will have to continue to tweak guidelines and protocol for pilots, cabin crew and passengers when it comes to the ding of that seatbelt light.“The single biggest limitation I will say in modern airplanes is not the reliability of the engines or anything in it,” Woodward says. “It’s the humans on board.”

title: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators
Author: Linda Geddes
Headline: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators
Content: Linda Geddes: ‘Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me.’Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLinda Geddes: ‘Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me.’Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianCybercrimeFake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my bylineHow a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonatorsLinda GeddesSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them.I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing asCaroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicinecontacted me to ask whetherI’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.I donned my sleuthing cap and discovered a potential link between Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Entering my impersonator’s email address into Outlook.com’s account recovery system revealed a partially obscured Gmail recovery address. An editor at Science had independently discovered the same address pattern associated with Fake Caroline’s email.View image in fullscreenLinda Geddes: ‘As someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling.’Photograph: Haybooks-May/AlamyAs someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling. Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me, while putting my professional credibility at risk. Apart from one interview conducted by email, the quotes in the New York Post article were lifted from previously published features, without attribution. Many of Fake Linda’s pitches also bear the hallmarks of AI-assisted writing. Even unsuccessful pitches could damage relationships with editors.The New York Post has since removed the article, conducted an internal review and referred the matter to the appropriate authorities, a spokesperson said.What I find particularly baffling is the motive. Freelance science journalism is hardly a lucrative profession, and is quite niche. My best guess is that a struggling freelancer is impersonating more established peers to boost their earnings, perhaps using AI to make the process more efficient. But how would they receive payment without revealing their identity?Other possibilities have crossed my mind. Could it be a PR professional trying to secure coverage for a client, or someone testing how easily publishers can be fooled? Perhaps it is someone with a personal grudge. But as Caroline put it: “Why us? We’re nice!”Dr Simon Miller, the director of policy, strategy and communications at the UK fraud prevention service Cifas, is equally bemused. “Ordinarily, if you’re seeking to defraud, you’re seeking to do it at scale, in a relatively light-touch way, using mechanised, industrialised processes,” he said. “This is tantalisingly unusual. It’s almost the stuff of Agatha Christie, but with 21st-century technology.”Journalists are far from the only people finding their names attached to work they didn’t produce. In April, Prof Eric Topol, of the Scripps Institute in California, discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about.Four of his five supposed co-authors were similarly unaware of the paper, while the fifth could not be identified. Within hours of Topol flagging the incident on X, the journal’s website had disappeared.View image in fullscreenIn April, Prof Eric Topol discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTopol, who is a bestselling author, said he has discovered at least 12 books on Amazon with his name on that he didn’t write, including several cookbooks. “I don’t even know how to cook,” he said. Particularly upsetting was when a patient told him he’d read his supposed memoir. “They said: ‘I was reading it, and a lot of those things don’t seem to be accurate.’ That’s how I found out about it.”Dr Leslie McIntosh, a vice-president of research integrity and security at Digital Science, said someone might add a respected name to a scientific paper without permission to make the work appear more credible. Fraudsters also sometimes added respected researchers as editors to make bogus journals appear legitimate and attract publication fees.Even more nightmarish would be someone deliberately publishing misleading information under someone else’s name to damage their reputation. “If their name ended up on a retracted paper, they would then have to explain that retraction,” she said.Employers are encountering yet another form of impersonation. Jamie Collier, a researcher at Google Threat Intelligence, said criminals had used stolen personal information to secure remote jobs under other people’s names, sometimes without the victim’s knowledge.Generative AI is making such deception easier, “mainly by stripping away the usual tell-tale red flags that hiring managers relied on to spot fraud,” Collier said. Large language models can generate convincing CVs, tailored cover letters and fabricated evidence of professional experience.“Real-time video filters and voice-cloning tools are the next step. While live deepfakes are still relatively nascent … threat actors are already testing them to bypass quick video screenings and mask regional accents,” Collier said.TheSociety of Authors and the Writers’ Guild of Great Britainhave warned of increasingly sophisticated scams involving people impersonating literary agents and publishers, in an attempt to get writers to part with money or sign away their rights.The Society of Authors’ chief executive, Anna Ganley, said she personally received between five and 10 scam emails a day, supposedly from book festivals, literary agents, publishers and others. Some writers had lost thousands of pounds after responding to genuine-sounding offers. “It’s incredibly difficult for writers, because you are often looking for opportunities to market your books,” she said.Unlike those scams, Fake Linda’s activities seem like a lot of work for relatively small financial gain. But the latest technology could make such impersonations easier. Miller said: “AI is allowing criminals to create sophisticated impersonations at unprecedented speed and scale.”Or multiple impersonations. I’ve since identified a third science journalist,Sara Novak, with a potential link to Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Fake Sara apparently pitched a story to Chemical and Engineering News in August, which was declined. When Real Sara shared her impersonator’s email address with me, I discovered it links to the same masked recovery address.View image in fullscreenThe real Sara Novak.The consequences extend beyond those being impersonated. “The risk for journals and publishers is huge,” said Dr Ben Johnson, the chief editor at Nature Health,who turned down a pitch by Fake Linda. “People trust the Nature brand as a source of evidence-based quality information. If an AI-generated story from a fake journalist is submitted then I will likely spend hours editing it from AI slop into Nature prose, including all the fake quotes from people never interviewed.”All of this raises uncomfortable questions about how you can be sure you know who you’re dealing with when communicating online. When I emailed the New York Post about my impersonator, it agreed to help rectify the situation, then asked: “I see that you’re emailing me from a Guardian email address. Is there any other info you can provide to verify who you are?”After discovering that Science had inadvertently published a news story by Fake Caroline, its managing news editor, John Travis, said his team had started running all pitches and drafts through AI detectors, “though they are not perfect”. “We also require Zoom calls for any new writers,” he said.The experience has also put editors at Nature on higher alert. “Sadly, for early career freelancers, this makes me less likely to commission news stories from journalists that I haven’t worked with before,” Johnson said. “I will also have to try to find the time to have a call with new freelancers before they write, to check they are who they say they are.”Even video calls are no guarantee of identity. Google Threat Intelligence recently documentedNorth Korea-linked hackersusing real-time deepfakes to lure executives into Zoom calls with trusted peers. “They faked video and audio glitches to get the target to download a ‘troubleshooting tool’ that wiped out their credentials and wallets,” Collier said.Miller advises independently checking unexpected approaches through an established email address or telephone number. McIntosh advocates several layers of verification, like the multiple identity checks at airports. “You have to have multiple ways to ensure and triangulate that you’re speaking to the person you think you’re speaking to,” she said.For people whose identities have been hijacked, Miller advises warning professional networks and monitoring for further impersonation attempts.There may also be legal remedies. Rupert Earle, senior counsel at the London law firm Bates Wells, said that under UK law, impersonating someone to secure paid work could constitute fraud. Victims could also have civil claims for “passing off” – misleading people into believing that work or services come from an established person or business – or false attribution, if work they didn’t create was published under their name.However, identifying the perpetrator and taking legal action can be difficult, particularly when the publications are overseas and the impersonator’s location is unknown. Despite uncovering several clues linking Fake Linda and Fake Caroline, we still don’t know who is behind the accounts.But the hunt for Fake Linda continues. I’ll be reporting the incident to the UK’sReport Fraudservice. I’ve also sent a cease-and-desist email to my impersonator, demanding they stop.For such a prolific writer, they’ve gone surprisingly quiet.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeIdentity fraudDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)The GuardianNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Digger disaster: what an epic movie flop means for Tom Cruise and Hollywood | Digger | The Guardian
description: Unprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris is predicted to lose $245m. How did this happen?
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Unprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris is predicted to lose $245m. How did this happen?
Content: The world premiere turned out to be the high point of Digger’s theatrical runComposite: Alex Mellon/Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe world premiere turned out to be the high point of Digger’s theatrical runComposite: Alex Mellon/Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesThe Saturday readDiggerThe Digger disaster: what an epic movie flop means for Tom Cruise and HollywoodUnprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris is predicted to lose $245m. How did this happen?Catherine ShoardSat 17 Oct 2026 04.12 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTShareThe fanfare at Digger’s world premiere in London four weeks ago was literal. As the Prince and Princess of Wales took to the stage, their arrival was heralded by the band of the Irish guards’ fanfare team – bugles gleaming, epaulets shining, bearskin bonnets rippling under the lights.Given the occasion, the band were not overdressed. Joining William (velvet tux) and Kate (chiffon gown, the late Diana’s earrings) to introduce the film was cinema’s longest-reigning monarch, Tom Cruise (Armani), along with a retinue including directorAlejandro González Iñárrituand co-stars Sandra Hüller, Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Jesse Plemons and Michael Stuhlbarg. Loyal courtiers filled the front rows: Salma Hayek, Hannah Waddingham and no fewer than three Beckhams (David, Cruz and Romeo).The film itself started two hours late, thanks to Cruise’s trademark completism with red carpet selfies and autographs. But no one minded, much. If anyone has earned the right to keep 800 people waiting as the babysitter fees mount and they lose all feeling in their legs, it is surely the one remaining unassailable movie star, that most grinning and irresistible enigma, the man who “saved Hollywood’s ass” when Top Gun: Maverick tempted people back to multiplexes after two years of Covid.View image in fullscreenPrince William, Catherine, Princess of Wales and Tom Cruise attend the Digger world premiere in London.Photograph: Chris Jackson/Getty Images for Warner BrosAt 11pm, when the lights came up, the mood was different. There was disquiet. Applause, too, of course, but also murmurings and scurries for the exit, only slightly hobbled by pins and needles. Could it be that this hottest of tickets was actually a stone cold turkey?The world premiere turned out to be the high point of Digger’s theatrical run. When the film opened worldwide a week later, reeling from almost universally horrified reviews, the box office was appalling – and things went downhill from there. Digger made $8m over its first weekend in the US, before dropping 60% for its second. Its international opening was yet worse: $12m across 74 territories, for a per country average of $162k. So far, Digger has made $37.7m. Estimates suggest a final haul of $50m.Its costs were … higher. Originally budgeted at $125m, production on the six-month shoot spiralled to about $175m. A further $100m was spent on marketing. Given that cinemas retain around half of the revenue of ticket sales, the film would appear to need to make $350m to break even (thoughWarner Brosputs the number at closer to $300m). These numbers are complicated further by Cruise’s “first-dollar” deal, which means initial takings are diverted straight to him, rather than the studio.Digger’s predicted $245m loss catapults it straight into the upper echelons of the most costly flops of all time, alongside 1995 swashbuckler Cutthroat Island ($222m loss, adjusted for inflation), 2018 steampunk dud Mortal Engines ($224m adjusted) and doomed Captain America spin-off The Marvels (whose estimated adjusted losses range between $205m and $250m). In some sense, Digger has already performed worse than all three. Pre-release, no one had high hopes for any of them – yet they still managed to make at least double the amount Digger is expected to take in. No one anticipated Cutthroat Island upending our ideas about what big swing satire could be. Or that Hugo Weaving’s turn in Mortal Engines would make him an Oscars shoo-in. But Digger is unique: an unprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris.View image in fullscreenDigger’s predicted loss catapults it into the upper echelons of the most costly flops of all time.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros PicturesTo excavate Digger’s fatal flaw, it is helpful to return to its roots. The idea for its central character – a boorish billionaire oil magnate, whose drilling in the arctic triggers eco-catastrophe – came to Iñárritu, the Mexican film-maker who broke through with Amores Perros, in 2015. Then, he was working on The Revenant – another expensive ($165m) epic centred on a big gamey performance, in that case from Leonardo DiCaprio, who, playing a frontiersman on the run, waded through a frozen river, ate raw bison liver, climbed inside a horse’s carcass – and duly won an Oscar. At the same ceremony, Iñárritu also won best director, making him the third person ever to do so in consecutive years, having triumphed in 2014 with the splashy theatrics of Birdman.Iñárritu has said he didn’t initially pursue Digger because, despite developing an obsession with the character, he “wasn’t looking for a story” (ominous words, in hindsight). But after The Revenant’s success, he began to develop the concept with Netflix as a vehicle for DiCaprio, under the working title Blah, Blah, Blah (ominous klaxon #2). Then someone at the streamer noticed they already had a pricey eco-dramedy with Leonardo DiCaprio in the works in the form of Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up – the failure of which completes a quick ominous hat-trick – and Digger was ditched. So Iñárritu busied himself instead with Bardo, False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths: an almost three-hour, black-and-white, existential semi-autographical vanity project of the type only the most recently gilded of directors would have the indulgence to realise. Few people saw it, fewer still liked it.Meanwhile, Cruise, glowing from his recent canonisation as the saviour of cinema, was on the hunt for films to broaden his portfolio beyond action franchises such as Top Gun and Mission: Impossible. Perhaps recalling the delighted horror that met his fat-suited cameo in Tropic Thunder as repellant studio head Les Grossman, he reached out to Iñárritu, and they began work in 2022. The shoot began in late 2024, on 35mm, filmed in Vista Vision – which is, for the avoidance of doubt, magnificently expensive.This time last year, the film was in post-production, and Cruise was in Los Angeles receiving an honorary Oscar – his first ever Academy Award. His emotional speech detailed a lifetime devoted to the craft. “Making films is not what I do, it is who I am,” he told the crowd. The man to give him the statuette? Iñárritu. The auguries were obvious: if ever a movie were to win Cruise his first Oscar proper, this would be the man who would hand it to him.View image in fullscreenAlejandro González Iñárritu is only the third person ever to win the Oscar for best director in consecutive years.Photograph: Rodrigo Reyes Marin/AFLO/ShutterstockDid anyone notice during production that Digger was awful? Or that sufficient numbers of people were likely to loathe it that the film would be a fiasco? If so, they were either cowed or buoyed by the confidence of the two men at its helm. Plus, says Steven Gaydos, former executive editor of Variety, for the past decade or so, this kind of reckless endeavour has been standard industry practice: “Digger is just the latest Hollywood supertanker art film to go down.”He tracks the origins of that trend to the pre-pandemic eagerness of streamers to write blank cheques for directors who might confer credibility on them. Auteurs were quick to sign up, but the lack of oversight or guardrails – exactly the terms that sweetened the deal – meant their movies often pleased only themselves.Sometimes the strategy (sincebinnedat Netflix) sort of worked. Neither Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma nor Noah Baumbach’s Marriage Story, Jane Campion’s The Power of the Dog or David Fincher’s Mank secured Netflix that coveted best picture Oscar, but they came pretty close. Often, it was more obviously unsuccessful. Gaydos highlights the $175m Netflix sunk into Martin Scorsese’s The Irishman in 2019, and then the $200m Apple handed him in 2022 for Killers of the Flower Moon. “Again,” says Gaydos, “beaucoup Oscar nominations, no wins”.View image in fullscreenBabylon was a critical flop that ‘missed recoupment by $135m’.Photograph: Scott Garfield/APMeanwhile traditional studios, spooked by streamers’ dominance, copied the playbook – including the fallout. After awards glory with Whiplash and La La Land, Damien Chazelle saddled Paramount with Babylon, a critical flop, which, says Gaydos, “missed recoupment by $135m”. After sweeping the Oscars with Parasite, Bong Joon-ho’s Mickey 17 repeated the trick at Warner Bros, sinking $200m.That studio’s form with the Hollywood supertanker art film isn’t all bad: last year they lost $150m on another VistaVision whopper, but at least Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another won them lots of Oscars, including best picture. And at that stage Warners could sustain the hit, with the coffers swamped from the likes of Sinners, The Minecraft Movie and F1.This time round, there was no blockbuster safety net – hence, says Gaydos, “this supertanker might have sunk the studio’s chiefs Michael de Luca and Pam Abdy.” The final release from the studio before its Paramount Skydance takeover was such an unqualified calamity that the first move of incoming owner David Ellison was to axe them both.Pre-merger, many had voiced concerns about the sorts of projects that might be greenlit by the new super-studio. Now they know: Ellison’s appetite for new ideas and original IP will have been diminished yet further. “Overspending on art has never been a winning strategy in Hollywood,” says Gaydos. “But no one’s ever seen the scale of these recent maydays and the oceans of red ink the supertanker art films have left in their wake.”View image in fullscreenTom Cruise, left, and Riz Ahmed in a scene from Digger.Photograph: Warner Bros Pictures/APOf all the injured parties emerging from the wreckage of Digger – save perhaps for De Luca and Abdy – Cruise is the most mortally wounded. He’s had misfires before: 2017’s The Mummy lost $95m, but still grossed over $400m. The only conclusions to be drawn will be chastening for a man who would have assumed he was appreciated as much as an artist as a preternaturally-youthful pensioner with a fierce commitment to near fatal stunts and taking his top off.Yet clearly, it seems, people do not go to aTom Cruisemovie to see him act. They go to see a movie star. Yes, he sported prosthetics in Tropic Thunder, but you could still see the man beneath the mask, and he wasn’t in it for long anyway. In Digger, so thick are the layers of rubber it might as well be anyone beneath them.Aside from riding a motorbike off a cliff, Cruise’s fans do not want him to take risks, nor to indulge in the level of belligerent insanity both he and his character display here, which serves as an uncomfortable reminder of the Oprah sofa-jumping years. They also want him to be the good guy. In Top Gun and, especially, Mission: Impossible, he’s a quasi-Messiah: the only man able save the world. In Digger, he plays the only man able to destroy it. That’s the opposite of what Cruise’s fanbase wants.Yet beyond Cruise’s usual acolytes, there are plenty of people who might well have been keen to see Digger if they’d known what it really was: an ambitious, meta-textual liberal satire that seeks to address collective culpability for ecological collapse. Unfortunately all of the promotion for the film has sought to suppress this – in part because explaining how necessitates revealing a key plot spoiler.Instead, the push focused on its star’s transformation, on teases and reveals of Digger’s colossal tum and obnoxious hectoring. So confident were the makers of Digger in their film’s pre-sold allure they forgot to actually sell it.By the time the reviews were out, the marketing had no choice but to scramble. A new campaign was launched quoting negative and positive reviews, before urging audiences to ignore the critics and judge for themselves. Retrospectively positioning a movie’s divisiveness as intentional isn’t necessarily a bad plan. But the strategy inevitably recalled that taken by Francis Ford Coppola’s $125m disaster Megalopolis in 2024 – which further self-sabotaged by attributing made-up quotes to real-life critics. This was an unhappy association, and within days Digger’s ads had pivoted again, suddenly telling punters they should take note of the critics after all, because although US reviewers were iffy, the French really liked it.View image in fullscreenTom Cruise attends the premiere of Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, May 15, 2025.Photograph: Kate Green/Getty Images for Paramount PicturesBy then, the muddle didn’t matter. Only the morbidly curious could be tempted to the cinema. Word of mouth did its own work, too: Digger’s CinemaScore (which records exiting audience reaction on US opening night) was C+. That’s considerably less than the new Paw Patrol movie (A) and worse even than new Mark Zuckerberg drama The Social Reckoning (B+), whose own duff box office further suggests people aren’t automatically eager to spend their weekends gazing at supersized billionaires doing dreadful things.Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpieceRead moreCruise may still discreetly campaign for an Oscar nomination – the cost of doing so would be small change compared with the losses already incurred. In a year of standout performances from the likes of Andrew Scott (Elsinore) and John Malkovich (Wild Horse Nine), victory is all but impossible, yet Cruise and co may yet calculate that some such acknowledgment from his peers might help lessen the blow – and vindicate everyone’s decision-making.And, in fact, there are early signs that the scale of Digger’s disaster may work in its favour. After all, this is no Bardo-ish damp squib, destined to be a footnote in a book no one ever reads. This is a movie whose title is already synonymous with gobsmacking folly. An apparently grassroots lobby is building a compelling case for Digger being a cult classic in the making. Celebrities have put their heads above the parapet to champion it – and not only partisan ones such as Anne Hathaway, set to star with Cruise in the upcoming Days of Thunder sequel, who gave it 10/10 on Letterboxd, or Glen Powell – whom Cruise mentored on Top Gun: Maverick – and who called it “pure cinematic joy”.Jane Fonda cheerled at length for the film on Instagram, calling Cruise “very good and very brave”. “Daring, bold and cinematically complex,” chipped in Guillermo del Toro. Neil Young named it “the best film I have ever seen”. Meanwhile, commemorative programmes from that world premiere – still less than a month ago – are already fetching considerable sums on eBay, onelistingproudly describing the “highly sought-after collectable” as “brand new and unread”. Digger, it seems, is unlikely to stay buried for ever.This article was amended on 17 October to correct the average per country first weekend take of Digger outside the US to $162k.

title: Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad) | Men | The Guardian
description: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power
Author: Gabrielle Schwarz
Headline: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power
Content: A Frenchman weeps as historic French battle flags are taken out of Marseille for safekeeping in 1941.Photograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Frenchman weeps as historic French battle flags are taken out of Marseille for safekeeping in 1941.Photograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty ImagesMenMuscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad)From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power. Introduction by Luke KennardCaptions byGabrielle Schwarzand Felix BazalgetteSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 04.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion. As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration. Daft that it should be a remarkable sight, I thought, but there we go. Probably I’d have felt less self-conscious if I’d followed David Bowie’s example and – as in one of the images showcased here – worn what looks like a dress.On depictions of men and women in art history, John Berger famously stated that “men act, women appear”.Menwere portrayed demonstrating their physical power and readiness for action; to assert their dominance. Just turning that gaze around and using the lens to capture masculinity feels subversive, maybe even a little undermining.It is odd that a quarter of the way through the 21st century images of men crying–see the “weeping Frenchman” during the second world war and Paul Gascoigne’s tears during the 1990 World Cup – could still be seen as remarkable. Judith Butler describes masculinity as aphantasm, a haunting fiction of invulnerability and toughness that is all the more potent because it’s such a lie. We know this, but we’ve probably all had a part in enforcing it, knowingly or obliviously. Boys are still told they shouldn’t be sensitive, that it’s somehow shameful.These photographs are proof that masculinity has strong connotations, histories and counter-histories; a lot of baggage. We stand in some relation to that baggage however we choose to express ourselves, and an image can either reinforce or challenge those associations.Anyone with half a mind must feel a certain amount of pity for a man who feels the need to be depicted in his finery, or in a manner that expresses his prowess or authority – see Karen Knorr’s photographs satirising the privileged postures of men in gentlemen’s clubs – but we’re still surrounded by them, like it or not.Despite the wonderful range here, it’s interesting how normatively hench many of the men depicted are, from Eugen Sandow, the father of bodybuilding, to Arnie to Hulk Hogan. There’s an absence of the body type enjoyed by roughly 80% of men: basically OK, a bit lumpy, sporadically hairy. We might run a 3k every couple of weeks and feel so pleased with ourselves that we down a bottle of wine and a box of cheese straws the same night.double quotation markIt’s interesting how normatively hench many of the men depicted are. There’s an absence of the body type enjoyed by roughly 80% of men: basically OK, a bit lumpy, sporadically hairyTo judge from our media, one would think we were either waifs or muscle-men. Of course, the super-jacked male form is ubiquitous in film and television now, from Hollywood movies (where you expect it) to depressing ITV crime dramas (where you’d hope for a few more noodle arms and football-shaped tummies). Even the bang-average is barely represented; I feel like cheering when an even slightly flabby man takes his top off.If there’s no body positivity movement for average men, that’s because men’s bodies are less likely to be scrutinised and judged. Certainly we don’t talk about body image much unless it’s in the context of the gym. It has only occurred to me in my 40s that I can marginally improve my appearance through exercise (I’m still not fully convinced and suspect I’m wearing myself out for no reason). We can say, “What do you bench?” but can’t say, “I’m feeling insecure about my jowls today.”There’s a powerful defiance to the camp and the performative, of casually putting on a dress or a sarong as a straight man, already aware of the tedious reactions and thinking: “Yeah, and what of it?” There’s also a terrible self-consciousness to masculinity. I find the giant fake Warhammer-figurine shoulders of American football kits absolutely adorable. I’d feel the same about dictators on horseback if they weren’t dictators.Depictions of queer masculinity offer an alternative here, from Leigh Bowery’s magnificently confrontational surrealist portraits to Rotimi Fani-Kayode’s beautiful, sculptural compositions of black queer men. Deliberately rougher round the edges, Sunil Gupta’s Exilesseries depicts the underground (then illegal) culture of gay male life in India in the 80s: a furtive glance, a shy smile, the position of a cigarette, a palpable sense of risk.Protesters, pop stars and pioneers: 38 images that changed the way we see women (for better and for worse)Read moreThe current resurgence of the crassest form of strongman masculinity feels overwhelming; a dictatorship of the most dysfunctional, damaged, spiteful elements of the male ego, emotionally dysregulated and outright evil. It’s pervasive in the manosphere, but also in government and political administrations. I’ve heard it described as a death-rattle before it finally goes extinct. That may be wishful thinking.So many current manifestations of masculinity feel beneath contempt, but maybe they’re not. Maybe we should loudly express our contempt for them and hopefully speed their decline. Every significant photograph that enters the collective unconsciousness shifts our reality a little – the power of an image to either bolster or subvert machismo is still profound.Luke Kennard is the author ofBlack BagArnold Schwarzenegger,1976ByRobert MapplethorpeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Robert Mapplethorpe Foundation. Used by permission.“He made no effort to seem overpowering,” wrote a Gay Times correspondent of Arnold Schwarzenegger in 1978, “but, rather, radiated a mild – nay – sunny, disposition.” In the 1970s, Schwarzenegger turned body-building from a niche subculture into a national obsession. He combined an exaggeratedly masculine body with a sense that he was secure in himself. “He accepts the inevitable attention of gay men as a compliment,” concluded Gay Times.Robert Mapplethorpe took this portrait of Schwarzenegger in 1976, a year before the release of Pumping Iron, the hit docudrama that led to his Hollywood stardom. Mapplethorpe, who was celebrated for his images of queer and S&M subcultures, was particularly fond of this photograph, using it for postcards and party invitations. “Hot Dirty Man,” went the text over Schwarzenegger’s torso on one invitation from 1979. “You are invited to … ”FBMarlon Brando,1950ByWarner BrosView image in fullscreenPhotograph: John Kobal Foundation/Getty Images“When Marlon Brando appeared on stage in a torn, sweaty T-shirt,” wrote Gore Vidal in 1985, “there was an earthquake.” Before Brando’s breakout performance in A Streetcar Named Desire in 1947, Hollywood leading men had been “nothing but a suit of clothes”, Vidal argued. Brando made it OK for a man to be a sex object.Many of the actor’s performances eschewed the buttoned-up vision of masculinity in the films of the 1930s and 1940s. He was emotional, violent and physical. “I’d never seen anything as visceral,” wrote the critic Pauline Kael, remembering her first glimpse of Brando on stage in the late 1940s.FBOscar Wilde, 1882By Napoleon SaronyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sepia Times/Universal Images Group/Getty Images“Great success here,” wrote Oscar Wilde of the American speaking tour on which this photograph was taken. “Nothing like it since Dickens, they tell me.” Though the 27-year-old had not yet written famous works such as The Importance of Being Earnest and The Picture of Dorian Gray, he was already a society sensation. His tightly controlled performance of a queer, urbane form of masculinity made him famous, but came with great risks. He was later imprisoned for gross indecency with men, and polite society turned on him – perhaps prefigured by newspaper digs at the time about the “effeminate” figure in this portrait.FBSessue Hayakawa, 1918By Fred HartsookView image in fullscreenPhotograph: AlamyYou may not recognise him now, butSessue Hayakawawas one of Hollywood’s first heart-throbs. Born in Japan, he moved to the US in early adulthood and broke out as a major matinée idol with a star-making turn as the villainous lead in Cecil B DeMille’sThe Cheat(1915). He was then one of LA’s highest-paid actors. One photographer recalled Hayakawa arriving at a premiere to a horde of female fans who “spread their fur coats at his feet” so he could avoid stepping in a puddle.As an Asian leading man, Hayakawa had to put up with a lot of racialised typecasting, and anti-miscegenation laws meant his characters never got the girl; when anti-Japanese sentiment rose in the 1920s, his star faded. He did get a late-career comeback, however, with his Oscar-nominated role as the tyrannical Colonel Saito in 1957’s The Bridge on the River Kwai.GSThe Wrestlers, Kordofan, Sudan, 1949By George RodgerView image in fullscreenPhotograph: George Rodger/Magnum PhotosNuba mountain communities in the Kordofan region of Sudan have faced violence from outsiders for centuries, from British colonial authorities to the Khartoum central government. Against this backdrop, a renowned tradition of wrestling tournaments has developed.This image by Magnum co-founder George Rodger, of a wrestler hoisted on a supporter’s shoulders, brought global, and unwelcome, attention to the area. Former Nazi photographer Leni Riefenstahl produced controversial and exoticising work there. “When they found out what was going on, people felt exploited,” said Sudanese professor Guma Kunda Komey.FBLivingWith theEnemy, 1987By Donna FerratoView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Donna FerratoIt’s estimated that aroundone in four women worldwidehave experienced physical or sexual violence by a male partner. Since the early 1980s, the photojournalist Donna Ferrato has dedicated her career to documenting the devastating impacts of these relationships.This photo is from Ferrato’s 1991 book Living With the Enemy, which includes texts based on conversations with victims and perpetrators. Over the course of the project, she spent time in women’s shelters as well as riding in police cars and staying in people’s homes. Here, an eight-year-old boy, Diamond, shouts at his father as he is being arrested at their home in Minneapolis: “I hate you for hitting my mother.”“I’d never seen a child stand up to his abusive father,”Ferrato later recalled. “That blew my mind. The mom hadn’t called the cops – the boy called the cops. He had just shown the police where his father had hidden the screwdriver.”GSTeddy Roosevelt on a horse,1898Photographer unknownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Buyenlarge/Getty Images“The most masculine president in the American memory,” according to one recent biographer of Theodore “Teddy” Roosevelt. He is pictured here on horseback when he was a lieutenant colonel in an army unit known as the Rough Riders.His carefully crafted butch image was, on closer inspection, a jumble of contradictions. Raised in extreme wealth, he was fond of being photographed in suspiciously pristine working-class clothing. And, plagued by physical infirmities since childhood, he was sensitive to any hint of weakness.FBRepose in agentlemen’s club, 1982By Karen KnorrView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Karen KnorrKaren Knorr’s languid photograph, part of a series of 26 images she took in gentlemen’s clubs in Mayfair, London, captures how comfortable certain men feel luxuriating in hereditary privilege – “an archetypal image of aristocratic power”, in Knorr’s words.Each photograph is paired with a satirical text written by Knorr, who was inspired by parliamentary speeches and books about the British empire. “I wanted to make work that used irony and parody to explore attitudes prevalent amongst the English establishment in the 1980s,” she said.FBPutin on a horse,2009By Alexei DruzhininView image in fullscreenPhotograph: RIA Novosti/ReutersRussian presidentVladimir Putinhas a penchant for staging topless photo ops – always while partaking in a macho outdoor activity such as horse-riding or hunting. “It is easy to laugh at,” says Ruth Ben-Ghiat, author ofa book on the political figure of the strongmanfrom Mussolini (who also liked to pose shirtless) to the present. “But the use of masculinity as an authoritarian tool is deadly serious. Strongmen use their bodies to proclaim themselves the defenders of the nation, and yet they often pose as victims as well.”GSJohn F Kennedywith baby Caroline, 1958ByEd ClarkView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Life Picture Collection/Shutterstock“A vital element has been added to the well-planned and generously financed campaign to make Senator Jack Kennedy president of the United States,” reported the North American Newspaper Alliance in 1957: the Kennedys were expecting their first child, Caroline.A year later, Life magazine staff photographer Ed Clark visited the couple’s family home in Georgetown. Clark later recalled that when asked if he could take a photo of the senator with the baby, “Jackie said no, that she was upstairs asleep. But Jack bounded up the stairs, and I followed.”Jackie ended up asking for 75 copies of “that marvellous picture” to give to family and friends. And after JFK became president in 1961, the framed photo was hung in the Oval Office. His identity as a father of small children had become a key part of his public image as a novel breed of male politician: the youthful and vigorous leader of – to borrow his well-known phrase – “a new generation of Americans”.GSThe naked gunner,1944By Horace BristolView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Horace and Masako Bristol EstateThis famous shot of a naked aeroplane gunner was captured by Horace Bristol, who was part of a group of photographers recruited to promote US naval aviation during the second world war. The aircraft had been sent to rescue a US marine pilot shot down while attacking Japanese forces at Rabaul Bay in the Pacific.“One of our crew stripped off his clothes and jumped in … He couldn’t have swum very well wearing his boots and clothes,” Bristol later recalled. “As soon as we could, we took off.” Though the soldier has never been identified, his image quickly became a symbol of male valour and heroism in wartime.GSLeigh Bowery,1988ByFergus GreerView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Fergus Greer. Courtesy Michael Hoppen Gallery“He was a dandy and a great eccentric,” rememberedLeigh Bowery’s friend Donald Urquart in 2004, “in the tradition of Curricle Coates, Bunny Roger, Barbara Cartland, Edith Sitwell, and Quentin Crisp.” As a performance artist and “club kid” of the 1980s, Bowery’s intricately constructed – and sometimes controversial – outfits and costumes exploded traditional ideas of what a man could look like and what he could do.In one famous performance, he birthed his friend and later wife, Nicola Bateman, out of a “vagina”, with an umbilical string of sausages trailing behind. Another was seen by painter Lucian Freud, who immediately asked Bowery to sit for him.Bowery died in 1994 at 33 of an Aids-related illness. “I miss him,” friend and film-maker John Maybury said last year. “He was like a kinetic beacon, vibrating.”FBAdrian Street with his coalminer father,1974By Dennis HutchinsonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Mirrorpix/Getty ImagesAdrian Streetwent by many nicknames, including “the Exotic one”, “the Sadist in Sequins” and “the queen bitch of pro wrestling”. His catchphrase was, “Imagine what I could do to you,” finished with a suggestive, moaning, “Mmm…”In the 70s, the Welsh former coalminer became famous for his taunting, butch, queer-coded persona. For a profile in a national tabloid in 1974, he arranged this striking photograph – much reprinted over the years – down his former pit with his miner father, who had disapproved of his career.“That look, even though it’s outrageous, he would have said it was super-masculine,” says artistJeremy Deller, whomade a filmwith Street before his death in 2023. “It’s a challenge, isn’t it? You’re challenging other people as well as society, so you have to back it up.”FBGun 1, New York, 1954By William KleinView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © William Klein Estate/Courtesy of HackelBury Fine Art, London“It’s fake violence, a parody,” said William Klein of his 1954 photograph. “I asked the boy to point the gun at me and look tough. He did, and then we both laughed.” Klein saw the image as a “double self-portrait”; he himself was a mix of “the street kid trying to look tough, and the timid good little boy on the right”.Klein saw it as playful, but the twisted face of the child retains a threatening power.FBThe weeping Frenchman, 1940ByMarcel de RenzisView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty ImagesThis photograph – actually a still froma newsreel– was first published in Life magazine in 1941, to illustrate the fall of France after the Nazi invasion. As the Germans advanced, the French government decided to send the historic regimental flags of its armies to safety in Africa. Before they were put on ships out of Marseille, a parade was held through the streets of the town. It was here that cameraman Marcel de Renzis caught footage of a French citizen called Jerôme Barzetti weeping as they passed by.The image is often cited as a rare example of public tears from a man, as taboos around male emotional expression have softened in recent years. A2016 studyfound that modern men cry in public more than twice as often as their fathers. Barzetti’s tears, however, fit into a long history of martial crying, with roots in Homeric epics. According to one count, men are depicted weeping in the Odyssey more than 30 times.FBEugenSandow,bodybuilder, 1895Photographer unknownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Hulton Archive/Getty Images“The most wonderful specimen of man I have ever seen” is how a Harvard professor described Eugen Sandow upon taking his measurements in the 1890s. By then, the Prussian-born athlete was a global fitness star. Today, he is remembered as the father of modern bodybuilding, having organised the world’s first major “physique” competition in London in 1901. “He’sArnold Schwarzeneggerbefore Arnold Schwarzenegger,” says sports historian Conor Heffernan.As Heffernan explains, Sandow’s “lean and muscular physique” – still aspirational now – had previously been more associated with farmers and sailors than the perfect man. Images such as this helped to reinforce what modern bodybuilders refer to as the “Grecian ideal”: a physical type based on statues from the ancient world. (Although appearances can be deceiving, as Heffernan points out: the dumbbell Sandow is lifting is probably empty.)GSThe Invisible Man,1952By Gordon ParksView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Gordon Parks/The Gordon Parks FoundationIn Ralph Ellison’s novel Invisible Man, the unnamed narrator, an African-American man, hides out in a basement in New York, which he lights with 1,369 bulbs. “Before that I lived in the darkness into which I was chased, but now I see. I’ve illuminated the blackness of my invisibility – and vice versa,” he says, before telling the story of a life that had, until then, been defined by ideas projected on to him due to his race and gender.Gordon Parks collaborated with Ellison on A Man Becomes Invisible, a photo essay published in Life magazine to promote the book. The striking images recreate key scenes from the narrative; this one shows the final passage, in which the protagonist (played by John Bates, an actor friend of Ellison’s) emerges from his underground retreat through a manhole – a reclamation of his place in society.GSThe Cock (kiss), 2002By Wolfgang TillmansView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Wolfgang Tillmans, courtesy Maureen Paley, London, Galerie Buchholz, Berlin, David Zwirner, New York“You can show two men killing each other at three in the afternoon in any country in the world on public television,” said photographer Wolfgang Tillmansin an interview in 2022. “But you can’t show two men kissing each other.” Ghetto was a cult London venue of the noughties; at a club night there called The Cock, Tillmans captured a tender, passionate moment between two men. When the photograph was exhibited in Washington DC in 2007, one visitor reacted by slashing it with a key. It’s since become a symbol of solidarity and resistance: after the shooting at Orlando’s gay nightclub Pulse in 2016, many posted Tillmans’ photograph as a defiant act of protest.FBDavid Bowie pushing a pram, 1971Photographer unknownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Trinity Mirror/Mirrorpix/AlamyIn this photograph, David Bowie is captured pushing a pram with his baby, Zowie, alongside then wife Angie. Laura King, a historian of modern Britain, explains its significance: “In the decades after the second world war, there was a real movement towards what I call family-oriented masculinity. Men often weren’t doing anything like what women were doing in terms of looking after children, but fatherhood was very much aligned with masculinity.” Pushing a pram became a way to signal your identity as an involved family man.Bowie – the famously gender-bending icon – wasn’t exactly a typical dad of his time. “I don’t feel very paternal,”he told an interviewer in 1976.GSJuan Pablo Rodríguez, 2023BySantiago BarreiroView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Santiago Barreiro“Ballet is woman,” proclaimed the choreographer George Balanchine. The idea that it’s a dance form for girls persists today, especially in cultures where machismo is dominant.Against this backdrop, Uruguayan photographerSantiago Barreirodocuments the diversity of men’s ballet in Latin America. For Barreiro, his subjects offer an example of how traditional gender roles – which he has observed as deeply ingrained in Latin societies – can be deconstructed through art.This portrait depicts Juan Pablo Rodríguez, a Colombian-born choreographer and principal soloist with the Ballet Nacional del Perú. Rodríguez told Barreiro that he sees freedom of expression as an act of resistance.GSHugh HefnerwithPlayboy bunnies,1966Photographer unknownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Keystone/Getty ImagesHugh Hefner’s urbane, sex-obsessed vision of masculinity “became central to what it meant to be a modern man” in the 1960s, says historian Amber Batura. Hefner would spin Playboy magazine – first published in 1953 thanks to a loan from his mother, among others – into a global empire of clubs, staffed by women wearing distinctive “bunny” uniforms.Like Ian Fleming’s James Bond, Hefner modelled a fantasy of masculinity “as gratifying, masterly play”, in the writer Esther Allen’s words, “in which women were seen as a sort of consumer product”. As Hefner put it himself in 1992: “Much of my life has been like an adolescent dream of an adult life.”FBUntitled,1988By Rotimi Fani-KayodeView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Rotimi Fani-Kayode/Autograph“Black men from the third world have not previously revealed either to their own peoples or to the west a certain shocking fact,” wrote the Nigerian photographer Rotimi Fani-Kayode in 1988. “They can desire each other.”After training with the US photographer Robert Mapplethorpe in New York, Fani-Kayode moved to London and produced a stunning body of work from his Brixton home studio, before his death from Aids-related complications in 1989.Mark Sealy, co-editor of a new book of Fani-Kayode’s work released this month, calls it a “radical transformation of Black male subjectivity”, made at a time when “the Black male subject was wrapped up in violent hostility via the press as muggers and bad guys”. Fani-Kayode’s work presented a subversive and playful vision of queer Black masculinity “at the height of Aids, in a very, very homophobic society”.FBHulk HoganvAndré the Giant,1987Photographer unknownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: WWE/Getty Images“The virtue of all-in wrestling is that it is the spectacle of excess,” wroteRoland Barthes; wrestlers are performers in a pantomime of rivalry and aggression. This photo depicts one of the most celebrated bouts of all time: the hotly anticipated face-off betweenHulk HoganandAndré the Giant(also known as Fezzik fromThe Princess Bride) at WrestleMania III in 1987. Pro wrestling had boomed in popularity and the stakes were raised by a much-publicised feud between the superstars, who were actually good friends. Hogan defeated a 520-pound (37 stone) André with his legendary “bodyslam that was heard around the world”.GSGB. England. Wolverhampton. Wolves fans celebrate,2012By Martin ParrView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Martin Parr/Magnum PhotosOver the course ofhis 50-year career, Martin Parr repeatedly trained his camera on the football stadium – though, as a committed chronicler of ordinary British life, he was less interested in the players and more in the fans. In this photograph from 2012, we witness a moment of unbridled euphoria for the supporters of Wolverhampton Wanderers, who have just scored in a home match at Molineux stadium.“[Football fandom is] a way of people accessing emotions. It’s very tribal,” Parr saidwhen interviewed in 2022. “It’s an important aspect of creating your own identity. Especially for men; it’s a very welcome way of letting your emotions go.”There is a dark side, too; recent statistics show thatracist and homophobic abuse are on the riseat matches, and there was once againa spike in domestic violence reports during this year’s World Cup.GSBilly Porter at the Oscars, 2019By Frazer HarrisonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Frazer Harrison/Getty ImagesThe actor Billy Porter is known for his audacious, gender-fluid red carpet fashion. “This look was interesting because it’s not drag,” he told Vogue of this gown, which he famously wore to the Oscars. “I’m not a drag queen. I’m a man in a dress.” Inspired by a Renoir painting, and made at short notice in over a week of 18-hour days by designer Christian Siriano, Porter’s tuxedo dress garnered huge attention, coming just a month after he wore a bright pink cape to the Globes, which in his words “changed everything for me”. The dress was later displayed in theVictoria and Albert Museum, and has its own (extensive)Wikipedia page.FBMan With a Box. Fully Automated Nikon, 1973By Laurie AndersonView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Laurie Anderson“I decided to shoot pictures of men who made comments to me on the street,” Anderson wrote of her 1973 series titled Fully Automated Nikon (Object/Objection/Objectivity). The artist displayed the images with white strips over catcallers’ eyes, granting them anonymity while also symbolically taking away their ability to objectify her.GSOur Motherland Collective, 2023ByHassan HajjajView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Hassan Hajjaj/Courtesy of Our Motherland Collective crew, Vigo Gallery, London and Hassan Hajjaj“Growing up in Morocco, we were definitely not scared of colour,” Moroccan-British photographer Hassan Hajjaj has said. His playful portraits blend north African textiles with markers of global consumerism; his sitters often wear clothes designed by him.This image was part of Hajjaj’s recent My London Rockstars series featuring portraits of artists in the capital, including Our Motherland Collective, a skateboarding crew that has transformed into an arts group.“The people in the pictures come from all different parts of the world, and when you start putting them next to each other, it becomes a positive image,” Hajjaj has said of his work that explores identity and multiculturalism. If his photos make a young person think, “Oh I can be that person,” or, “I can be the person taking that picture,” he says, “that’s the greatest feeling you can have as an artist”.FBIndia Gate from the series Exiles, 1987By Sunil GuptaView image in fullscreenPhotograph: © Sunil Gupta. All Rights Reserved, DACS 2025.“I had a personal motivation to establish an Indian gay presence in art history,” says theartist and photographer Sunil Gupta, who was born in New Delhi in 1953; he later settled in London in the 1970s. “It was hard for me to be postmodern because I had no references. So I decided to make the references.” He wanted to “visualise” the experience of gay men in Delhi.Initially, “nobody wanted to be in the picture” –homosexuality in India wasn’t decriminalised until 2018. Eventually, Gupta was introduced to a network of gay men who agreed to model for the project Exiles (1986–87). The accompanying texts came from interviews he’d conducted at cruising sites around the city.GSL’Enfant (man and baby), 1986BySpencer RowellView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Dr Spencer RowellThis year marks the 40th anniversary of one of the bestselling posters of all time: a photograph of a hunky man cradling a baby. Paul Rodriguez, art director of the poster retailer Athena, conceived the idea and recruited photographer Spencer Rowell. The image tapped into the archetype of masculinity that emerged in western culture in the 1980s: the New Man, who rejected sexist ideas around domesticity.The model is Adam Perry, who later claimed to have leveraged the poster’s fame to sleep with more than 3,000 women – not quite a New Man, after all.GSPregnant man,1970ByAlan BrookingView image in fullscreenPhotograph: The Advertising Archives“Ever since that picture of a pregnant man was sprung on an astonished nation,” wrote a Daily Mirrorcolumnist in 1970, “we men haven’t been able to stop wondering what would happen if we really did become pregnant.”The public information poster, dreamed up by ad company Cramer Saatchi, caused a storm when it was released, aimed at increasing the “sexual responsibility of the male”.Photographer Alan Brooking, now 98, remembers an extended search for the perfect model – a man in possession of “the subtle kind of embarrassment that one might expect in that situation”.FBCongo’s sapeurs,2019By Tariq ZaidiView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Tariq Zaidi“It is like a resistance movement for peace,” journalist and photographer Justin Makangara says of the sapeurs. “They are fighting with clothes.” The sapeurs of the twin Congolese capitals of Brazzaville and Kinshasa have become famous for their style.Until recently, many regarded the sapeurs as “foolish, hooligans, idiot people” for spending so much money on flashy clothes. Recently, however, Makangara has seen a change in their public perception. Most sapeurs – like Celestin Moundounga, the 48-year-old technician here – hold down respectable jobs and are “responsible to the needs of their families”. And as the civil war grinds on in the east of the Democratic Republic of Congo, their way of life suggests that “even in conflict, we can try to be in joy”.FB* * *David Beckham’s ‘sarong-gate’, 1998By Harry PageView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Harry Page/News Group40 outrageous photos that changed fashion, from teenage Kate Moss to Twiggy in a mini and Lady Gaga’s meat dressRead moreIt was the 1998 World Cup in France, a peak moment for British lad culture. Then David Beckham was photographed wearing a Jean Paul Gaultier wrap. The Sun ran the photo alongside the headline “Beckham has got his Posh frock on”.The footballer has stood by the look. “Sarongs are great,”he said in 2014. “I would still wear it now.” Today his bold outfit is recognised for cementing Beckham’s role as the poster boy for a new type of heterosexual male ideal: the fashion-forward metrosexual of the 2000s.GSPortraits of the Taliban,2001UnknownphotographersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Collection T Dworzak/MagnumThomas Dworzak was on a photographic assignment covering the fall of the Taliban when he stumbled on a set of highly stylised studio portraits of soldiers of the former regime in a photo shop. The fighters had probably died before they could pick them up.“I was very surprised, of course,” he says. The Taliban had famously banned all photography of living beings. He bought the prints – the beginning of a collection eventually published in the2003 photobook Taliban.In the secretly commissioned portraits, the fighters pose against pastel-coloured and scenic backdrops and hold props such as flowers and guns. Here, two men clasp hands. The unmistakably “camp aesthetic”, Dworzak explains, was “not specific to the Taliban” – such images can be found across the region. But they also couldn’t be further from what we expect a militant soldier to look like.GSDaniel Craig with baby carrier, 2018ByElder OrdonezView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Elder Ordonez/SplashNews.comThe sight of a man with a baby strapped to him was too much forPiers Morgan in 2018, who posted this picture with the hashtag #emasculatedBond. Men responded in their thousands with photographs of themselves similarly “emasculated” – including wrestling star Adam Copeland holding his child while dressed as Elsa from Frozen. “Any man who wastes time quantifying masculinity,” tweeted actor Chris Evans at the time, “is terrified on the inside.”FB* * *Mods vrockers, 1964Photographer unknownView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Bentley Archive/Popperfoto/Getty ImagesThe clashes that arise between differing factions of masculinity could be summed up by this photograph of a brawl between mods and rockers in Brighton in 1964. That summer, long-standing tensions between the competing youth subcultures erupted in a series of confrontations during bank holiday weekends in seaside towns across the south of England.It’s now thought that the extent of the fighting was overplayed at the time – a moral panic stirred up by the establishment about the youth of the day. But the rivalry was real enough.The rockers, who rode high-speed customised motorcycles known as “cafe racers”, mockingly compared the Italian scooters of the “sissy” mods to their “mums’ hairdryers”. As one mod put it to a BBC interviewer at the time: “You can’t just stand and let a load of kids take the mick out of you, can you?”GSHells Angels,1965By Bill RayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Bill Ray/The Life Picture Collection/ShutterstockHells Angels – the motorcycle gang founded in California – haunted the US psyche in the 1960s. They modelled a rebellious, hyper-masculine image, but were also – for the time – provocatively homoerotic, frequently giving each other “a sloppy wet kiss”, in writer Hunter S Thompson’s words. “It blows their minds,” said one Hells Angel of the effect on “squares” – “especially the tongue bit”.FBRusty, 2008By Catherine OpieView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Catherine Opie/© Catherine Opie, Courtesy Regen Projects, Los Angeles; Lehmann Maupin, New York, Hong Kong, London, and Seoul; and Thomas Dane Gallery.An interest in “performing masculinity” – which she first explored in San Francisco’s butch lesbian community in the 1990s – eventually led photographer Catherine Opie to high school football. Her portraits of star players, taken just after practice, show “adolescent boys beginning to form and perform for the first time an image-ideal of manhood”, in the words of one critic.Opie also linked the series to the various wars that the US was involved in at the time. “So many young men were having to make very interesting choices between sports scholarships and becoming a soldier,” she has said. “It was actually very emotional.”FBA Scottish Pub,1968By Jürgen SchadebergView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jürgen SchadebergHistorically, pubs and other drinking places were considered a “masculine republic”, somewhere for the menfolk to gather while their wives stayed at home. The notion of the watering hole as an almost exclusively male space – with notable exceptions granted to barmaids, landladies and loose women – is summed up in this image of an establishment in the working-class Gorbals district of Glasgow in 1968.German-bornSchadeberg, best-known for his portraits oflife in South Africaunder apartheid, had been sent to the Gorbals to document an area in rapid transition: the old tenements were being pulled down and replaced by modernist housing.GSPaul Gascoigne crying at the World Cup, 1990By Billy SticklandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Inpho Photography/Getty Images“I had let down the fans, my team-mates, the manager, everybody,” remembered Paul Gascoigne in 2020. “I cried because I thought it was the end of my career.”In 1990, 23-year-old Gazza had already captured the hearts of the public for his skill in the World Cup. When he burst into tears after receiving a yellow card for tackling a West German player, the nation erupted with a mixture of sympathy and, eventually, mockery.Today, public male tears are a relatively uncontroversial part of major sports tournaments, with everyone from Tiger Woods to Roger Federer having a good sob.FBThese 39 images are a snapshot of men’s lives – which other landmark pictures come to mind for you? title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges? | France | The Guardian
description: Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers
