Content: Packages of perished goods piled outside an Intermarché store in Paris the day after a cyber-attack targeted refrigeration and freezer systems.Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersView image in fullscreenPackages of perished goods piled outside an Intermarché store in Paris the day after a cyber-attack targeted refrigeration and freezer systems.Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersFranceNot cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezersKim Willsherin ParisSat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles acrossFrancebegan to flicker and rise.In a“bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack,hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux inParis. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”View image in fullscreenSupermarket staff had to remove tons of spoiled food and work late to reorder and restock shelves.Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersAfter removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country inEurope.Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.View image in fullscreenA woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France.Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centreANSSI confirmedsupermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.1:05French supermarket director apologises after cyber-attack spoils fresh and frozen food - video“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went intounscheduled defrost cycles overnightcausing massive food loss.France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management companyUpguard.In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.View image in fullscreenSupermarket employees restock goods in Nancy, north-east France.Photograph: Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu/GettyBillois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case | EditorialRead moreRybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”Explore more on these topicsFranceCybercrimeSupermarketsFoodRetail industryEuropeParisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women
Content: This photo provided by police in Cologne, Germany, shows a robot that was seized as evidence, on 11 October.Photograph: Polizei Koeln/Cologne Police/APView image in fullscreenThis photo provided by police in Cologne, Germany, shows a robot that was seized as evidence, on 11 October.Photograph: Polizei Koeln/Cologne Police/APThe Week in PatriarchyRobotsMove over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogropingArwa MahdawiWhenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and womenSat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTShareYou may be familiar withrule 34of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women.See, for example, Meta’s “pervert glasses”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers havefilmed themselvestrying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they areharassedby strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg didnot feel the needto apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology.Then there is the Flock license plate tracking system, which has been abused by anextraordinary numberof law enforcement officers totrack the locationsof their exes or other women they are sexually interested in. And, of course, there are the AI image generators, which have been used to create deepfake pornography of women and girls. According to a2023 report, “deepfake pornography made up 98 per cent of all deepfake videos online, and 99 per cent depicted women”.Now, there’s a new toxic tech trend to worry about: livestreamed robogroping. Police in Cologne, Germany, are currentlyinvestigating an incidentin which a humanoid robot controlled by two teenage males touched a 16-year-old girl’s buttocks and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Footage of the groping robot, which was wearing human clothes and a fake mustache, was reportedly livestreamed by the two males online.The robot in question has now been confiscated by the local police, who seem a little befuddled by the whole thing. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” a police spokesperson told the Associated Press, adding it was “new territory for us”.It may be new territory but I can guarantee you that this won’t be the last time we hear about an incident like this. Getting your hands on an AI-powered humanoid robot is still a lot more expensive than buying a pair of smartglasses, but the technology is rapidly becoming a lot more accessible. Earlier this year, a school in New York made headlines after announcing its new teaching assistant would be ahumanoid robotcalled Sally, made by a company that makes realistic sex dolls. Outrage over the announcement forced the school district tohalt its plans, but it’s only a matter of time before we see humanoid robots in schools. Indeed, in a report published last year,Bank of Americapredicted that, as costs go down, we will see mass adoption of humanoid robots from 2035 onwards. By 2060, they expect there to be 3bn humanoid robots, which will replace 20% of the workforce in the industrial sector and 50% of the workforce in the service sector.As the industry develops, expect corporations to ensure that their profit-maximizing robots have more legal protections than the humans they may harm. This week in Philadelphia, for example, awoman was arrestedafter allegedly blocking the path of one of the annoying Uber delivery robots that are now ubiquitous in the city. (The fact the police intervened is absolutely wild to me as a Philadelphia resident, considering they rarely seem interested in doing their jobs.) A growing body of case law has found that police officers arenot under anylegal obligation to protect citizens who are not in their custody. Yet they seem surprisingly keen on protecting robots.Our brave new world, everyone! I’m afraid pervert glasses are just a small glimpse of what’s to come. By 2060, robogroping may be as commonplace as catcalling is today.You can pay $7,500 to take dating lessons from a man accused of rapeBraden Eric Peters, who goes by the nom-de-influencer Clavicular, shot to fame for smashing his facewith a hammerin order to beautify himself. Bonesmashing, as it’s called, is part of a toxic trend calledlooksmaxxing, which involves people (largely young men) going to extremes to increase their “sexual market value”. When not bonesmashing, Peters gets into regular trouble with the law. Most lately, he was charged withrape and drug offensesin Massachusetts last month; his attorneys have denied the allegations. Nevertheless, it seems that there are people out therewilling to pay $7,500for a week at Camp Looksmax, a new venture in which Peters coaches attendees on confidence and dating.Katie Miller blames the fall of the Roman Empire on women“If more women put the same energy into their marriages and into finding a spouse that they do into their careers, you would see society have a lot more babies because, ultimately, that’s what led to the downfall of Rome – when women stopped having babies, and you started putting energy elsewhere,” Stephen Miller’s influential wife said onFox News this week. Someone buy the Millers a history book please.Tradwife influencer Nara Smith says she is ‘getting her tubes tied’Smith, 25, and her husband, 28, havefour kidscalled Slim Easy, Rumble Honey, Whimsy Lou and Fawnie Golden. Speaking on theAspire podcastrecently, Smith said she didn’t think she could handle having another kid. Sounds sensible to me, but I’m not sure Katie Miller’s going to approve of that decision.Women up to 74% more likely than men to be told autoimmune condition symptoms are psychological“The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem,” the lead author of theUK-based study said.A Palestinian toddler watched her mother get burned alive in Gaza CityReem Asaad Awad was killed when an Israeli airstrike hit her home. Her young daughter, Maryam Ahmed Ghanem, was pulledout of the burning building. Maryam’s father was reportedlykilled earlierin the ongoing genocide, and it’s unclear whether she has surviving family or will become one of Gaza’smany WCNSFs: wounded child, no surviving family.Sally Rooney is unable to sell her books in the UK because of Palestine Action supportThe bestselling author said last July that royalties from her book would be used to support direct action group Palestine Action, which has been proscribed as a terrorist organization in the UK, despite the fact that it hasnever killed anyoneor attempted to do so. Rooney has now said she canno longer sell her workin the UK and can’t visit because she risks imprisonment. A round of applause, please, for the brave British government for arresting thousands of people, many ofwhom are pensioners, for their Palestine Action support and protecting us from dangerous people like Rooney. Meanwhile, the British Museum is rolling out the red carpet forIgor Tulchinsky, a billionaire who reportedly funded an illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank.Iranian woman given death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media postTwenty-three-year-old Najmeh Amini has beensentenced to deathon charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet). Death sentences for blasphemy are relatively rare, but rights groups have warned that Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to quash dissent.Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary after five daysOh, dear!She didn’t even get her 15 minutes of fame; her disastrous first press briefing only lasted 14 minutes. Maybe Trump should replace her with a humanoid robot.The week in pawtriarchyIf you desperately need a palate cleanser now, I recommend the Guardian’s week inwildlife photographs. I particularly enjoyed the photo of the black crested gibbon and its thousand-yard stare, which pretty much mirrors my expression all week. Hope you ape-preciate it.Explore more on these topicsRobotsThe Week in PatriarchyWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: French mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olives
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: French mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olives
Content: Footage shows attacked French mayor in occupied West BankWest BankIsraeli settlers attack European diplomats in West BankFrench mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olivesEmma Graham-Harrisonin TaybehSat 17 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupiedWest Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.View image in fullscreenThe smashed window of mayor Badoux’s car.Photograph: Emma Graham-Harrison/The GuardianMaxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September,Israeli militants have used violenceto stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”On Friday, Israeli militantsattacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levineas she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.US Secretary ⁠of ​State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that America wants Israel ⁠to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers. “We’re very disturbed by those images and ⁠what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack ⁠down on that stuff.”Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the international criminal court to intervene.Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupiedPalestinebut wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’ | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British
Content: Speaking earlier in the week, Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, said that while his party carries out vetting, ‘you can’t vet people for what they say in the future’.Photograph: SOPA Images Limited/AlamyView image in fullscreenSpeaking earlier in the week, Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, said that while his party carries out vetting, ‘you can’t vet people for what they say in the future’.Photograph: SOPA Images Limited/AlamyReform UKReform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be BritishNadeem Badshahand agencySat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA would-beReform UKMP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”.The comments were recorded as part of the undercover investigation byITVthat has already seen Reform accused of “appalling behaviour” and “extreme racism”.Reform has said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding there was “no room for racism” in the party.In footage due to be broadcast on Sunday, a Reform activist and aspiring MP, who has yet to be publicly identified, described himself as “pretty hardline about Islam”.He said: “If a Muslim’s prepared to de-convert, I’m happy.View image in fullscreenZia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson has described himself as a ‘British Muslim patriot’.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy“But if they want to remain faithful to Islam, then this would be, I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, [Reform home affairs spokesperson] Zia Yusuf is a Muslim … to me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.”Discussing people crossing the Channel in small boats, the same activist said: “In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there.”Excerpts from the investigation released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates within Reform using racist language.In one excerpt, black children were referred to as “animals”, while in another a Reform member said his area had become “infested” with Asian families.Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said Nigel Farage’s response to the revelations showed he was “completely unfit to lead”.She said: “Bad apples don’t fall far from the tree. The sleaze, scandals and appalling revelations of racism and rank misogyny piling up by the day go right to the top of Reform UK.“Nigel Farage is incapable of taking responsibility and getting his house in order because he himself shares culpability.”Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting, “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”.In a statement to ITV, the party said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting.“This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment.“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”On Friday,Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillorfor Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments he had made were uncovered in the investigation.View image in fullscreenAlan Feeney resigned as Reform councillor on Friday.Photograph: ITVITV revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.In a subsequent Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”He added: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKIslamophobiaITVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Fifteen NHS staff sacked after accessing medical records of Valdo Calocane victims | NHS | The Guardian
description: Healthcare professionals retrieved files belonging to 19-year old students and a caretaker killed in Nottingham attack
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Healthcare professionals retrieved files belonging to 19-year old students and a caretaker killed in Nottingham attack
Content: Nottingham university hospitals NHS trust also issued 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenNottingham university hospitals NHS trust also issued 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPANHSFifteen NHS staff sacked after accessing medical records of Valdo Calocane victimsHealthcare professionals retrieved files belonging to 19-year old students and a caretaker killed in Nottingham attackNadeem BadshahSat 17 Oct 2026 18.39 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 18.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA total of 15 NHS staff have now been sacked after accessing medical records belonging to the victims of a 2023Nottinghamattack, a trust said.Valdo Calocane killed two 19-year-old students, Barnaby Webber and Grace O’Malley-Kumar, and Ian Coates, a 65-year-old caretaker, and attempted to kill three other people in the city in June 2023.During its investigation, Nottingham university hospitalsNHStrust (NUH) has so far dismissed 15 staff, issued 15 final written warnings and two first written warnings.Doctors, nurses, registered healthcare professionals and other staff have been included in the investigation. The victims’ families were told about the latest update this week.Dr Manjeet Shehmar, the medical director at NUH, said: “There is simply no excuse for accessing the records of a patient without a legitimate reason, and I hope this sends a really clear message – we will investigate and we will take action.“To lose a loved one in the way that the families of Ian, Grace and Barnaby have is heartbreaking enough. I am so sorry that they have had this further compounded by the actions of these staff members.“We will continue to investigate inappropriate access to these records and take action as and where necessary.“Alongside this, we are doing all we can to educate our staff on appropriate access and how to keep the records of our patients safe. We are also introducing a new system which acts to detect possible data breaches.”In May, the trust said it had sacked 11 staff members who illegally accessed the medical records of the victims.Calocane was sentenced to an indefinite hospital order in January 2024 after admitting manslaughter by diminished responsibility and attempted murder.The head of NHSEnglandannounced last month that NHS staff suspected of inappropriately accessing patient medical records will be suspended immediately and have their access to health service computer systems cut off.Sir Jim Mackey said there had been “too many cases” of workers “abusing” trust. He warned that “snooping” could cost staff their careers and they could end up with a criminal record.Launching the crackdown, Mackey wrote to all NHS trusts demanding the new approach is implemented in an effort to protect patients from further breaches. It follows a number of high-profile cases in recent months.In May, it emerged that dozens of staff at University Hospitals of Liverpool Group had looked at the records of victims of the 2024 Southport attack, which left three girls dead and 10 others injured.The records of a three-year-old boy hurt after falling into a crocodile pit in Cambridgeshire in June were also viewed by about 40 hospital staff.Explore more on these topicsNHSHealthEnglandNottinghamnewsShareReuse this content

title: All the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory on Trump’s team | Trump administration | The Guardian
description: Half of the women on Trump’s team have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remain
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Half of the women on Trump’s team have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remain
Content: During Donald Trump’s second term, there has been one common characteristic among most of those who departed his administration.Composite: AFP, Getty Images, ZUMA, Rex, Shutterstock, AP, ReutersView image in fullscreenDuring Donald Trump’s second term, there has been one common characteristic among most of those who departed his administration.Composite: AFP, Getty Images, ZUMA, Rex, Shutterstock, AP, ReutersTrump administrationAnalysisAll the president’s women: a familiar downward trajectory on Trump’s teamLucy CampbellHalf of the women on Trump’s team have been replaced by men, while men facing misconduct allegations remainSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 19.26 EDTShareDonald Trump is not, by any measure, a feminist. He hassaid sohimself. But the president has often pointed to his hiring and promoting of women in an attempt to stave off criticism of both his policies and personal conduct over the years.During his second term, however, there is one common characteristic among most of those who have departed theTrump administration.In the space of just a few months, half of his eight high-level female officials have either resigned or been fired. All have been replaced by men. Several other women in his administration have also departed, whether voluntarily or involuntarily.On Friday, Trump was forced to deny reports that he was considering replacing Susie Wiles, his White House chief of staff, and thefirst woman to do the job. “She’s gonna be here for a long time,” he claimed.Numerous top male officials, meanwhile, from Trump’s defense secretary Pete Hegseth, who has on multiple occasionscourtedglobalcondemnation, to thewidelyridiculedFBI director Kash Patel, have survived intense scrutiny and repeated calls for their resignation – and yet remain in post.Katie ZachariaThe latest female casualty was White House press secretary Katie Zacharia, who wasfiredon Friday just five days into the role. After a rocky start to her tenure, sparked by a widelypannedfirst White House press briefing on Tuesday, she had also faced questions over her legal credentials after admitting she did not pass the bar exam. The ensuing semantics battle over whether or not she is a lawyer, or an attorney,placedher in apickle– even with the rightwing cable network Fox News.Zacharia had taken over from Karoline Leavitt, whosaidin August that she had chosen to resign from the role after 20 months so she could spend more time with her young family.Kristi NoemIn terms of firings, the first domino to fall was former homeland security secretaryKristi Noem, who was the face of Trump’s mass deportation campaign until she was unceremoniously sacked on 5 March. Her tenure was plagued by controversy, in large part amid national uproar over federal immigration enforcement operations that killed two US citizens in Minneapolis (one of whom Noem called a “domestic terrorist”, with no evidence), and coincided with a sharp decline in national support for Trump’s immigration agenda.Her suggestion at a congressional hearing in March that Trump had known about her decision to approve a contract for a $220m ad campaign to encourage immigrants to “self-deport” – which prominentlyfeaturedNoem on horseback – reportedly left Trump “pissed” and appeared to be the straw that broke the camel’s back. There had also been scrutiny of general leadership failures under Noem, as well as questions the influence of her adviser, Corey Lewandowski, who also left his role when she was ousted.Noem was repurposed as special envoy to the so-called “Shield of the Americas” coalition and, after that arrangementexpiredlast month, is now serving in a vaguely defined advisory role. She wassucceededas DHS secretary by Markwayne Mullin.Pam BondiNext fell former attorney general and Trump loyalist Pam Bondi, who waspushed outin April after a turbulent 14 months that saw the president increasingly frustrated over her mishandling of the Department of Justice’s long-awaited release of the Epstein files. The Epstein issue became a huge political liability for Trump andinfuriatedhis Maga base, and he also felt that Bondi had failed to sufficiently prosecute his political enemies.Bondi revealed a month after she was ousted that she had been diagnosed with thyroid cancer. Her deputy, Todd Blanche,assumedthe role in August.It’s worth noting that commerce secretary Howard Lutnick faced public scrutiny after details emerged surrounding hispast tiesto Jeffrey Epstein and visits to his private island. By contrast, the White House supported him after Democrats called for his resignation.Lori Chavez-DeRemerAlso in April, former labor secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer stepped down after a Department of Labor inspector general investigation led to a series ofallegationsofmisconduct, including having an affair with a subordinate and drinking alcohol on the job. She was replaced by Keith Sonderling.Kash Patel has also beenallegedto have been intoxicated or absent on the job. He has denied these allegations, and remains FBI director.Tulsi GabbardA month later, in May, Tulsi Gabbardresignedfrom her position as Trump’s national intelligence director.While she officially cited her husband’s rare cancer diagnosis, Gabbard wasreportedlyforced out after a tumultuous stint in which she was largely sidelined as Trump launched attacks on Venezuela and Iran. She had previously testified to Congress that Iran was not building a nuclear weapon.Gabbard wasreplaced on an acting basis by Bill Pulte, a Trump loyalist with no previous experience in the intelligence sphere, and eventually byJay Clayton.Kimberly GuilfoyleEarlier this week, the Trump administrationaskedlongtime Trump ally Kimberly Guilfoyle to step down from her position as US ambassador to Greece after weeks ofreportsthat she sought payment from a Trump donor in exchange for access to administration officials.The only senior male official to have been somewhat punished by Trump since his return to office is Mike Waltz. The then-national security adviser was fired in May last year after inadvertently adding a journalist to a Signal group chat in which Pete Hegsethdisclosedsecret war plans.Waltz had been on thin ice with Trump for a while, and the president wasreportedlyannoyed by Waltz’s hawkish stance on Iran. Signalgate merely sealed his fate.But he didn’t disappear to some obscure advisory role; Waltz was nominated to the position of US ambassador to the United Nations. Hegseth, meanwhile, was allowed to ride out the controversy and –severalcontroversieslater, including allegations of war crimes – remains in post.Democrats have highlightedthedoublestandardthat Trump only seems to fire women in his administration – even those who are ultra-loyal to him, and decidedly less incompetent than some of their male colleagues.“If you’re a man in the Trump administration, it seems that they reward misconduct,” Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, the Democratic congresswoman, observed in April.“I wouldn’t say I’m a feminist,” Trumpsaid in a 2018 interview. “I mean, I think that would be, maybe, going too far. I’m for women. I’m for men. I’m for everyone.”But not everyone gets to stick around.Explore more on these topicsTrump administrationWomenUS politicsDonald TrumpGenderKristi NoemPam BondianalysisShareReuse this content

title: Yvette Cooper pledges £140m to boost urgent care as NHS faces ‘tough’ winter | NHS | The Guardian
description: Health secretary says government has been preparing early and will spend money on ambulances and A&E upgrades
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Health secretary says government has been preparing early and will spend money on ambulances and A&E upgrades
Content: The NHS’s medical director said hospital admissions for flu were the ‘highest’ she could remember for the time of year.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe NHS’s medical director said hospital admissions for flu were the ‘highest’ she could remember for the time of year.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNHSYvette Cooper pledges £140m to boost urgent care as NHS faces ‘tough’ winterHealth secretary says government has been preparing early and will spend money on ambulances and A&E upgradesPress AssociationSat 17 Oct 2026 19.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe NHS faces a more challenging winter than normal, the health secretary has warned, as she announced a £140m increase for urgent care inEngland.Yvette Cooper said the money would help increase capacity, and that the NHS has been preparing since July to deal with the impact of seasonal illnesses.She said: “Winter will be more challenging for ourNHSthis year, after such a heavy summer.“That’s why we have been preparing early and investing in extra urgent care capacity to help get patients the care they need.”The money will be spent on 14 schemes across the country, including new urgent care centres, ambulance fleets and upgrades to emergency departments.It comes after a summer of extreme heat placed additional strain on the NHS. Almost 7.3 million people attended A&E between June and August, the highest figure for a summer period.In September, experts warned of a “twin crisis” facing the NHS with the impact of record temperatures in the summer combined with seasonal winter illnesses such as flu and norovirus.The NHS’s national medical director warned earlier this month that hospitals were showing “ominous” signs of an early flu season.Prof Frankie Swords said hospital admissions for the virus were the “highest” she could remember for the time of year, coinciding with an expected increase in Covid admissions.Emma Rowland, the NHS England executive director for performance and delivery, said: “We know this winter will be tough for the NHS and we’re doing everything we can to reduce pressure on our emergency departments and make sure patients get the care they need, while protecting our staff.“Investment in same-day emergency care and urgent treatment centres will help more patients get the right care in the right place, at the right time.”She also urged the public to make sure they get vaccinated against flu and other winter viruses if they are eligible.Patricia Marquis, the executive director of the Royal College of Nursing England, said the extra money was welcome in the short term but would still only provide “just another sticking plaster on a system that is at breaking point”.She said: “The nursing workforce needed to deliver these services goes into winter already running on empty and short of staff.“With the budget just weeks away, ministers have the opportunity to provide the real investment needed to grow a nursing workforce fit for the future and ensure patient care is protected all year round.”Explore more on these topicsNHSHealth policyHealthPublic services policyEnglandYvette CooperHospitalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plants
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Ukrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plants
Content: ‘The lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the “diesel deal” is the first step,’ said Zelenskyy.Photograph: Thierry Monasse/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the “diesel deal” is the first step,’ said Zelenskyy.Photograph: Thierry Monasse/Getty ImagesUkraineTrump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy saysUkrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plantsPower plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivableAndrew Rothin KyivSat 17 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has describedDonald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russiaas a “reward” for Vladimir Putin and warned it will embolden the Russian leader and intensify the Kremlin’s war, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.The Ukrainian president also said he expected theTrump administrationto lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”In a social media message, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground.“We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”View image in fullscreenA policeman helps an elderly woman to walk out from a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine.Photograph: Kateryna Klochko/APIn the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions withRussia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.The act, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham,who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourageVladimir Putinto intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Saturday said Trump’s sanctions waiver would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.View image in fullscreenA car burns after a Russian airstrike on a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Kateryna Klochko/APThe move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.Zelenskyy also said themilitary-grade Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forcesstill had limited functionality, and would disconnect from the network when travelling at more than 161km/h (100mph), interfering with drone operations.The service was throttled insideUkrainewithout warning on Tuesday, and Zelenskyy said his government had determined that the restrictions were a “deliberate operation … to prevent us from defending ourselves”.By sending vehicles with the terminals into EU countries, the Ukrainians found they operated at speeds of more than 180km/h, in effect proving that the terminals were only experiencing restrictions in Ukraine.“The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union,” he said. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump’s announcement that he would pause US sanctions came a week after he said Washington hadagreed to purchase diesel from Russiato try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.View image in fullscreenA protest calling for the resignation of Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko, amid anger over increasing cost of  public transport, the destruction of Kyiv’s green spaces and handing them over for development, and insufficient funding for the Ukrainian army from the city budget.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAThe Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, in addition to the White House reportedly ordering the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces.“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.View image in fullscreenA mobile blast shelter installed in Kyiv for emergency protection during air raid alerts.Photograph: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/Getty ImagesZelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpRussiaVladimir PutinUS foreign policyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days | UK news | The Guardian
description: Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’
Content: The plaque being unveiled on 9 October.Photograph: English HeritageThe plaque being unveiled on 9 October.Photograph: English HeritageUK newsPlaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within daysDescendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’Natricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentSat 17 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and IndigenousCaribbeanpeople, their descendants say.Ronald Raymond McDonald, a professional drummer, was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle near Portsmouth last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors fromSt Vincent and the Grenadineswere among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … it’s very sad,” he said.The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by theSt Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.View image in fullscreenThe unveiling was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.Photograph: English HeritageBut days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia Gorden said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said.In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.Emilio “Sásamu” Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s sentiments, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised.His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”Once a site of horror, a tiny Caribbean island could become a Garifuna shrineRead moreThe missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those onboard losing their lives.Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.The vandalism came duringBlack History Monthand amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories.“Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”.He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsRaceSt Vincent and the GrenadinesCaribbeanBlack History MonthCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym | Isabel Allende | The Guardian
description: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits
Content: Allende on stage with King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain at the award ceremony in Barcelona.Photograph: Pau de la Calle/GTRES/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAllende on stage with King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain at the award ceremony in Barcelona.Photograph: Pau de la Calle/GTRES/ShutterstockIsabel AllendeIsabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonymChilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the SpiritsEmma LoffhagenandElla CreamerSat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Chilean-American authorIsabel Allendehas won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday withLa hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired byChile.The newstory follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional titleLos que faltan.However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”Isabel Allende: ‘I have been displaced most of my life’Read moreThe prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded toLa bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Molawas in fact three male writers– Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.Explore more on these topicsIsabel AllendeFictionAwards and prizesSpainChileEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off | Devon | The Guardian
description: School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments
Content: The Friends of Lower Field protesting against the sale of playing fields in Totnes, South Devon.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Friends of Lower Field protesting against the sale of playing fields in Totnes, South Devon.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianDevon‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-offSchool looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishmentsSteven MorrisSat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historicDevonmarket town.The local comprehensive,King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC),has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field– and it is likely houses will be built on it.School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.View image in fullscreenAnna Ali said there was ‘hidden impoverishment’ in the area.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealingalmost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign groupFriends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”Lewis Winks, a leading member of theRight to Roamgroup, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known forprogressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.View image in fullscreenCampaigner Lewis Winks said Lower Field had been shared by the school and community for about a century.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianA key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to themare unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.Matthew Shanks, chief executive ofEducation South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”Explore more on these topicsDevonAccess to green spaceSchoolsSchool fundingLand rightsCommunitiesPublic landsnewsShareReuse this content

title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’  | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors
Content: It is not so much ‘killer robots’ keeping one cabinet minister awake as the idea of concentrated, super-intelligent power ending up in the hands of bad actors.Photograph: Master/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt is not so much ‘killer robots’ keeping one cabinet minister awake as the idea of concentrated, super-intelligent power ending up in the hands of bad actors.Photograph: Master/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actorsRowena MasonandDan MilmoSat 17 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.It wasLabourconference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband was strident about the dangers of AI at the Labour party conference.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesIn his conference speech,Ed Milibandwas the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was“likely, if not inevitable”that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.View image in fullscreenKanishka Narayan said it was ‘likely, if not inevitable’ that rogue agents would hack the British state.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesIt was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He saidthe biggest threat was extremist groupsusing the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.View image in fullscreenKen McCallum, the director general of MI5, warned of extremist groups using AI to unleash bioweapons.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/WPA/Getty ImagesByrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies –Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”View image in fullscreenLiam Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation.Photograph: House of CommonsThe UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI whospoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing, believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.“It’s very likely that open source models are alreadypowerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?Read moreThe business committee heard this week thatAI-enabled bioweaponscould become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat.“There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said.View image in fullscreenThere is said to be concern over the cancellation last year of the AI programme at Porton Down.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Getty ImagesIn the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks.Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks.This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”.
