They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”.Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists.The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails.Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)UK security and counter-terrorismDefence policyData and computer securityComputingLabourEd MilibandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Charlie Vickers: ‘Tom Cruise cheated at freediving – that’s the headline’ | The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power | The Guardian
description: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power star on his muddy marriage proposal, controversial cheese opinions, memories of Sam Neill and having a good evil face
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power star on his muddy marriage proposal, controversial cheese opinions, memories of Sam Neill and having a good evil face
Content: Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power star Charlie Vickers: ‘When I proposed, I thought, “Love of my life and all that, but I’m not going to kneel in the mud.”’Photograph: Photo Image Press/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLord of the Rings: The Rings of Power star Charlie Vickers: ‘When I proposed, I thought, “Love of my life and all that, but I’m not going to kneel in the mud.”’Photograph: Photo Image Press/Rex/Shutterstock10 Chaotic QuestionsThe Lord of the Rings: The Rings of PowerCharlie Vickers: ‘Tom Cruise cheated at freediving – that’s the headline’The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power star on his muddy marriage proposal, controversial cheese opinions, memories of Sam Neill and having a good evil faceRich PelleySat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou once played Basil Fawlty in an amateur student production of Fawlty Towers at Queen’s College in Melbourne. How amateur was your Basil Fawlty moustache?It was terrible. It was real but it was definitely coloured in – I still have holes in my beard. I’d also shaved my head, so if you look at the early promo posters, you can clearly see I’m wearing a wig. Our theatre was closed so we had to perform in a circus tent in the middle of winter, on an oval in the university grounds, which was all very Fawlty Towers.I’ve always loved comedy. I didn’t really do anything serious until drama school. I always thought there might be a good spin-off with Sauron and Celebrimbor as an odd-couple situation.You play Sauron inThe Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power. Tolkien wrote that Sauron “represents as near an approach to the wholly evil will as is possible”. What do you consider wholly evil?A complete disregard for the feelings and wellbeing of other people, to put it simply. It’s the intention, I think. I have horrible flashbacks to playing Aussie rules when I was about 17. I thought people were being quite evil to me at the time. I felt like I was being bullied because I wasn’t being aggressive or manly enough, and people were just trying to make me feel bad and dent my confidence for no reason.That’s the only thing that pops into my head, which I think is probably a good sign!View image in fullscreenVickers as Sauron in season three of The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power.Photograph: Ben Rothstein/PrimeWhat was the mostSam Neillthing Sam Neill did when you were making Palm Beach?The most Sam Neill thing was just beingunbelievably kind to everyone. Hedidre-enact a Jurassic Park dinosaur sequence with one of our cast mates, because she wanted to send some photographs to her friends. From memory, he was the dinosaur and she was playing him.What’s the strangest thing you’ve done for love?Juliet Stevenson: ‘Do I have a nemesis? Where do we start? Putin, Musk, Trump, Erdoğan, Modi, Netanyahu’Read moreWhen I proposed to my wife, we were in the woods in Hampshire, near where she grew up. She used to go there when she was little and her parents would leave letters from fairies for her. Now the woods are full of little fairy figurines. It was also really muddy so when I proposed I thought, “Oh shit, this is the bit where you’ve got to get down on one knee.” But I was in jeans, so I thought, “Love of my life and all that, but I’m not going to kneel in the mud.” I ended up doing quite a deep lunge, trying to simulate kneeling. If someone was watching it probably would have looked quite strange.What’s been your most cringeworthy encounter with another celebrity?I once waved at Mo Farah from across the room, thinking he was looking at me. He wasn’t, so he didn’t respond at all. I was with one of my friends who saw everything.Who would win in a freediving competition between you andTom Cruise?This is quite controversial but I think a lot of actors who do freediving talk about these ridiculous numbers. I think he’s done six or seven minutes or something like that.I could get to four, so he would win in a straight-up fight. But I’m pretty sure on Mission: Impossible and on Avatar and stuff they used oxygen beforehand. I’m sort of butchering the explanation, but they would breathe oxygen through a mask before freediving, to saturate their blood. Whereas we didn’t do that. We just breathed normal air, which I think means you can’t hold your breath for as long.So you’re saying Tom Cruise cheated?Yeah, exactly. That’s the headline. Tom Cruise cheated at freediving.View image in fullscreenVickers with Morfydd Clark on set.Photograph: APWhat’s the ideal length of men’s shorts?I have quite long thin legs so this is actually quite a sore spot for me. I used to be – and still am – quite sensitive about my knees and ankles. No matter how much I go to the gym, I’ve never been able to put any muscle on my knees. I was going to say 90cm but that’s really long, isn’t it? That’s like three-quarter length for me.I used to say over the knee, so I could cover mine up. But because it’s been so hot this summer, I’ve got into shorts that are quite short.Like Harry Styles?Yeah, I guess he wears quite short shorts. But I feel like Harry Styles has much more muscular legs than me. There’s your second headline.What are you secretly really good at?Ella Hooper: ‘Most embarrassing celebrity encounter? I said the classic thing you don’t ever say to Billy Bragg’Read moreI can play the drums, although I haven’t played properly in a while. I was in a rock band in year six called No Name Yet, and we’d play Green Day and the Doors covers, with Hitchin’ a Ride by Vanity Fare as our encore. Then I was in a jazz band called Over the Limit. There’s actually a bit in The Silmarillion where Sauron has a sing-off with Finrod. It’s not quite in the right time period but they could do some kind of homage and have Sauron in a drum-off, maybe.What’s your most controversial pop culture opinion?I’m not a huge fan of cheese. I know that’s not really a pop culture thing. Is cheese a pop culture reference? But everyone loves cheese for some reason, and I don’t really like it. Pretty much cheese across the board. Strong cheese? No chance.Charcuterie boards are quite a big thing in England. Growing up in Australia, we didn’t have this thing where people would have a bunch of cheese. Is it before dinner? Is it after dinner? Whatever it is: cheese. And you can throw cold meat into that. That’s gross as well.How can someone with such a pretty face be so evil?I actually think it’s because my eyes are – this is a very anatomical description – quite deep in my head. So I think if I move my head in any direction, my eyes are literally quite hard to see. So perhaps that is why. It’s just an anatomical thing. It’s got nothing to do with my existence.The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power season three premieres on Prime Video on 11 NovemberExplore more on these topicsThe Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power10 Chaotic QuestionsTelevisionJRR TolkienAmazon Prime VideoSam NeillTom CruisefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 7 Miles Out review – Carol Morley’s funny-poignant self-portrait of teenage kicks in Stockport | Movies | The Guardian
description: A daring, rich and funny study of the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self amid confounding changes
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: A daring, rich and funny study of the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self amid confounding changes
Content: Tender … 7 Miles Out.Photograph: Cannon and Morley ProductionsView image in fullscreenTender … 7 Miles Out.Photograph: Cannon and Morley ProductionsMoviesReview7 Miles Out review – Carol Morley’s funny-poignant self-portrait of teenage kicks in StockportA daring, rich and funny study of the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self amid confounding changesPeter BradshawSat 17 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCarol Morley’s self-portrait of the artist as a young woman is rich, tender and terribly funny and sad: a study in the chaos of being young and a triptych of childhood, girlhood and youth, with some daring touches of Terence Davies. It is about the ordeal of having to invent and reinvent your own teenage sense of self, even as the things you thought permanent suddenly collapse – including the background stability of your poor old mum and dad. And it’s also about the untold, unacknowledged story of sadness that lay behind the angry blaze of punk and new wave. Watching this I thought of something I’d assumed lost for ever: my own feelings, aged 17, on hearing Buzzcocks’ Sixteen: “… I wish I was 16 again / Then things would be such fun / All the things I’d do would be the same / But they’re much more fun / Than when you’re 21.” Could it be, I thought, that I’m already sad about not being 16?7 Miles Out is based onMorley’s autobiographical novel of the same title, the once-upon-a-time-in-Stockport story of Ann, played with charm and zing by Lucy Halliday, and as a sweetly innocent young girl by Amelie Hughes. Young Ann pretends to be making a radio programme with her cassette recorder the way so many did in the 1970s, and hero-worships her would-be rock journalist elder brother Scott (Kasper Hilton-Hille) – based onMorley’s brother Paul– who is already plugged into the burgeoning post-punk and new wave scene.Ann’s mum Bryn, wonderfully played by Gemma Whelan, is capable and good-humoured in a no-nonsense sort of way, but later to be beset with anger and mercurial depression. She has however found something to smile about now in the news that her husband and Ann’s dad Ronald, played by Aidan Gillen, has found a prestigious new job inManchester– seven miles out. So to get to work, he has apparently been supplied with a handsome, though not brand-new car.Ronald exudes a dangerous and almost radioactive aura of angry discontent that Gillen knows how to project. Sitting on his armchair, smoking and watching TV still dressed in suit and slightly loosened tie, Gillen’s Ronald plays along with Ann’s artless requests for a radio interview on the subject of his exciting new professional future. He is capable of romantic gestures and gentleness, which perhaps baffle and unnerve his family. What exactly has got into him? What has he decided upon?Ronald’s terrible fate is to govern the rest of Ann’s life, even as she gets bullied and then thrown out of school (a place as brutally uncaring as anything in Kes); she later has to live in a grisly boarding house that her mum hates. Ann tries to start a band with her best mate Hel (Leila Entwistle) – perhaps more than best mate – in imitation of her heroes,Joy Division. She yearns for the musical scene in Manchester, to escape her pain, to cauterise the agony of what happened to her dad, and nullify her own wretchedness in never being able to tell anyone. There are three people who take their own lives in this movie, but the only one without a shame-filled cover-up is Ian Curtis, lead singer of Joy Division.Ann’s attempts to get tickets to see Joy Division, and then to see Joy Division without tickets, are gripping in themselves and bring us to that figure who somehow looms inevitably large in any representation of this subject: TV presenter, Factory Records owner and co-founder of the Haçienda club,Tony Wilson(played here by Jim English); he is one of the many supercilious individuals who let Ann down and won’t let her and her mates in to see the band. Later when Ann descends into depression and drinking, she ringingly denounces the pompous Wilson: “I’ve shagged him; he gave me my first croissant!” It’s a line so surreal that it has to be taken from life.And so Ann gets further and further into the music scene, closer and closer to a reckoning with her own pain – but then mysteriously goes away from it, or through it or past it. Is it something she has dealt with or simply found a way of burying? There is a tricky encounter with a London music promoter, played in cameo by Claire Grogan; Ann can’t forgive her for something she says about Curtis. This poignant, smart film is such a pleasure.7 Miles Out screened at the London film festivalExplore more on these topicsFilmDrama filmsPeriod and historical filmsManchesterJoy DivisionTony WilsonLondon film festivalreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works’: film-maker Charles Burnett on his chronicling of Black working-class life | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: A restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audience
Author: Adria R Walker
Headline: A restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audience
Content: Actors Dennis Kemper and Everette Silas on set of Charles Burnett’s My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveView image in fullscreenActors Dennis Kemper and Everette Silas on set of Charles Burnett’s My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveBlack US culture‘Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works’: film-maker Charles Burnett on his chronicling of Black working-class lifeA restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audienceAdria R WalkerSat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTShareCharles Burnett had a dilemma. He had agreed to attend the wedding of a co-worker, but the wedding was scheduled for the same day and time as a funeral for a childhood friend.Initially, the film-maker – a landmark chronicler of Black working-class lives – decided he’d go to the funeral. But when he tried to break the news to the co-worker, she was so dejected that he couldn’t go through with it. He tried asking the bride to change the wedding – which was “ridiculous to think of trying to do”, he says decades later – but that didn’t work either. He decided he’d go to both events.But when the day came, he got trapped at the wedding. He “suffered through that” and, in the process, missed the funeral.This dilemma is at the heart of My Brother’s Wedding, Burnett’s tragicomic 1983 film. Like Burnett, character Pierce Mundy has committed to going to a wedding when a childhood friend suddenly dies. Like Burnett, Pierce feels an obligation to be at both places, though the wedding and funeral were scheduled for the same time. Like Burnett, Pierce even, unsuccessfully, tries to change the wedding.The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable review – Netflix doc on ‘secret album’ is strictly for super fansRead more“The idea was the fact that if you want to be someone’s brother’s keeper, you have to have principles and you have to be mature enough to make decisions and say, yes or no,” Burnett says. “You may have good thoughts and be a decent person, but you have to have more than that. If you’re going to be responsible for someone, you have to have a certain amount of maturity. It means making just decisions, proper decisions in your life.”View image in fullscreenEverette Silas (as Pierce Mundy) and Jessie Holmes (his mother, Mrs Mundy) in Charles Burnett’s 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: A film by Charles Burnett/Milestone FilmsMy Brother’s Wedding was beset with production problems that limited the film’s release. The main actor disappeared from set after demanding more pay (when Burnett tracked the actor down, he had reinvented himself as a pastor).In post-production, a German broadcaster asked Burnett for a finished cut of the film. He rushed through a rough cut, which the production company accepted as the final cut against his wishes. That longer, unfinished version of the film was shown to mixed reviews at the New Directors/NewFilms festival in New York City in 1983, and was essentially impossible to view for many years.“It would have been better just to say, start all over again,” Burnett said. “The days were gone by that time. Rather than re-edit the film, I had to make terms with the material I had. That’s what film-making is about. You run into all these problems, and in each one, you have a whole set of different problems. Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works, it works.”At 82, Burnett, once called “the nation’s least-known great film-maker” by the New York Times, is enjoying a resurgence of interest in and celebration of his career. In 2025, his 1978 debut filmKiller of Sheep, considered a masterpiece, was restored, introducing the director and his oeuvre to newer audiences. And this year, after several decades, My Brother’s Wedding, the director’s sophomore film, was digitally restored and remastered by Milestone Films, the largest Black-owned film distributor in the US, UCLA Film & Television Archive, the Berkeley Art Museum & Pacific Film Archive, and Kino Lorber.Burnett supervised the restoration of My Brother’s Keeper in consultation with Maya S Cade, president of Milestone Films, and Jillian Borders, head of preservation at the UCLA Film & Television Archive. The restored film has enjoyed sold-out screenings at New York’s Film Forum, is being shown at theatres across the country and is available to stream on the Criterion Channel. The film is also slated to be screened across the United Kingdom and Europe later this year.View image in fullscreenOn the set of My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveCade said that the restorations of both films “feel like resurrections”. Both Burnett’s debut and sophomore films are, decades after their initial release, able to be presented as originally intended. “We’re trying to use the tools available to ensure that Charles’s vision lasts not only our lifetimes, but many other lifetimes to come,” Cade said. “The goal of restoration is to use every tool in our arsenal to make the song that you may be familiar with, if you will, sing anew.”Groundbreaking director Reginald Hudlin: ‘It’s taken a lot of effort but the reward is always worth it’Read moreCade, who also runsBlack Film Archive, an online database of Black films made between 1898 and 1999, has been Burnett’s archivist for more than one and a half years. Recently, while sorting through his materials, she uncovered never-before-seen images made on the set of My Brother’s Keeper. The images, printed here, are raw and intimate. They’re testaments, Cade said, to the number of people required to make a film and “its own kind of archival repair”.They are also ways for the non-professional actors and everyday people who participated in the making of the film to be honored. For Burnett, the restorations and the images allow him to reminisce about his experiences with old friends, many of whom are now dead. It’s both a painful and joyous experience for the auteur. “It’s nice to see them again,” he said. “I do appreciate what they’ve done because most of the independent films I made were done with non-actors, and I’m always so guilty about not having the money to pay them. But I’m glad [about] the restoration because I’m sure they see it and they can see it again in a positive way. It looks good and it’s their story.”View image in fullscreenOn set of My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveBurnett wrote, directed and produced My Brother’s Wedding on location in south central Los Angeles, where he grew up. His realism frankly depicts Black life in LA, using non-professional actors who, like the director, are firmly rooted in a time and place. In his original treatment for the film, Burnett wrote that “the story communicates to all persons.”Making the film allowed Burnett to explore his feelings about class differences that he saw and experienced while growing up in Watts, a neighborhood in south LA. In the film, Pierce’s brother, Wendell, is engaged to Sonia, an upper-middle-class woman whose “sweetness”, Pierce thinks, is “about as fake as a $3 bill”.In one scene, Wendell and Sonia’s families share dinner together. Sonia’s family’s wealth is on display – “signifying”, Pierce calls it, elsewhere in the film – from their fine wine to a maid who serves the family dinner. Pierce, who “has a romantic view of the ‘have-nots’”, is over it.He lists various jobs he’s held, from driving a cement truck, working as a brakeman at the railroad and driving explosives and “all sorts of dangerous materials”. Pierce’s mother says that she wishes her sons were a doctor and lawyer, like Sonia’s parents’ children, instead. The scene culminates in a fiery exchange between Pierce, Wendell and Sonia.“When we were growing up in LA, there was this class difference. We had this romantic notion about the poor and the middle class,” Burnett says. He said that class limited the opportunities available to lower-income people in his community.Burnett, who was born in Vicksburg, Mississippi, said there was a “porch life”, when he was growing up, where people talked and told stories about their lives in the south. Like him, most of his neighbors were southerners – from Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas – who moved to California.“My grandmother and mother and them would always be talking about their experiences in Mississippi,” he said. “They were from Natchez and Vicksburg … It was this vision of the south. It was so mystical, in a way, because of the way they told it and their relationships with people … It was like this story of this place that had this magical quality about it.”In his films, Burnett maintains this culture of storytelling, and an intrinsic understanding of the importance of the mundane, translating it to the screen. The characters in My Brother’s Wedding are just people. They have wants and desires; they are not caricatures of good or evil, even if they are in conflict with each other. The film’s humor is found in the simple moments, much like it is in real life.View image in fullscreenOn the set of My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveMuch of the film follows Pierce as he lives his life. Burnett’s decision to focus on a narrative about a young Black man and his experiences in south central LA was revolutionary. Pierce isn’t a larger-than-life character from a Blaxploitation film, nor is he a caricature. He is just a young man with a difficult decision.Burnett was a central figure in the LA Rebellion film movement, in which several Black film-makers, including Julie Dash, Haile Gerima and others, rejected Hollywood norms and instead prioritized realism and a focus on Black life. “The whole idea was telling stories about Black experience,” Burnett said. The directors were pushing back against racist films that shaped American cinema, like DW Griffith’s 1915 filmThe Birth of a Nation, which led to a resurgence of the Ku Klux Klan and anti-Black violence. “[In the] LA Rebellion, we’re responding to the negative images of Hollywood, particularly Birth of a Nation and things like that, that really destroy who we are … We were fighting against those negative images and Blackface and things like that.”It’s worth considering how Burnett’s career might have developed differently had his sophomore film received the distribution it deserved. His first film inspired generations of artists, such as Ava DuVernay, Sean Baker, Yasiin Bey and Barry Jenkins. Though his career was not allowed to flourish as it should have, in many ways, Burnett is responsible for generations of film-makers, though he speaks about himself and his career with a humbleness that doesn’t hint at the weight of his impact. Arthur Jafa and Dash, both of whom would go on to shape cinema in their own right, first met while working as assistants on My Brother’s Wedding. Jafa was first assistant camera, on his first-ever film set, while Dash was first assistant director. Years ago, while he was casting for a professional acting crew, Burnett said that he ran into many older Black actors. When they walked into the room, he asked, “Where have you been?”View image in fullscreenEverette Silas (as Pierce Mundy) and Dennis Kemper (as Mr Mundy) in My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: A film by Charles Burnett/Milestone Films“It’s a dumb question to ask, because you know where they’ve been,” he said. “Not given an opportunity to express themselves [even though they] are so talented. That was one of the most difficult experiences, realizing this wasted talent.”But, in some cases, their stories are preserved in the archives. They’re in photos, like the ones from the set of My Brother’s Wedding, or in other documents Cade has found in Burnett’s archive.Burnett was always focused on telling stories, on being a director – he eschewed any notion that he himself was or should be a brand. And yet, he subconsciously created an archive, allowing himself and others to step back in time and appreciate the largely under-sung work he and other Black artists did for American cinema.

title: ‘If AI were asked to make miso, it would taste like this’: the best (and worst) supermarket miso, tasted and rated | Food | The Guardian
description: We ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thing
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: We ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thing
Content: The least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenThe least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFoodReview‘If AI were asked to make miso, it would taste like this’: the best (and worst) supermarket miso, tasted and ratedWe ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thingThe best supermarket kimchiTom HuntSat 17 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiso is a simple product that’s traditionally made by fermenting pulses (usually soya beans) with salt andkoji, typically a grain (rice or barley, and more recently oats, say) inoculated withAspergillus oryzaemould. Bar one fabulous exception, however, our supermarkets seem to have flipped the “you get what you pay for” adage on its head when it comes to miso: the least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive, even though they’re little more than synthetic imitations cut with thickeners, colourants, acidulants and preservatives.I asked my friend Jono Hope fromSlow Sauce, a miso and shoyu brewery in Scotland, for advice, and he told me not to taste it straight from the jar; its intense, salty flavour would ruin my palate. Instead, he advised mixing a teaspoon with warm water, then drinking it – “the soup test”.The best supermarket miso pastesBest overall:Hikari Maru-Yu additive-free koji misoView image in fullscreen£5.49 for 375g at the Japan Centre (£1.46/100g)★★★★★A glossy, burnt sienna paste with a granular texture and rich, floral, sweet and earthy aroma. Soup test: fresh, sweet on the nose, with a salty, fruity flavour. Made simply.Best bargain:Yutaka organic miso pasteView image in fullscreen£3.30 for 300g at Sainsbury’s (£1.10/100g)★★★★★A very smooth, sienna-coloured caramel paste with a velvety texture and yeasty, umami aroma. The soup is mild and very sweet, with notes of barley. Great Taste two-star winner in 2024. A perfectly simple recipe formula (34% soya beans, rice, 11.9% salt) and incredible value.And the rest …Slow Sauce organic pink misoView image in fullscreen£13 for 200g at Slow Sauce (£6.50/100g)★★★★★A coarse yellow paste with a sweet and fruity aroma. Soup test: a soft, sweet lactic aroma and a clean taste. Made with Scottish oat koji, flamingo peas and sea salt, all magnified through the slow fermentation. Sweet, young, funky and alive – and this week’s best splurge.Clearspring organic brown rice misoView image in fullscreen£5 for 300g at Waitrose (£1.67/100g)£5.10 for 300g at Ocado (£1.70/100g)★★★★☆A shiny, dark chocolate brown paste with an unfathomably rich and mature soy sauce aroma. Soup test: a sweet, subtle aroma, and a deep, meaty, mushroom flavour with an underlying sour twang. Made from brown rice koji.Miso Tasty red misoView image in fullscreen£3.10 for 200g at Tesco (£1.55/100g)£3.10 for 200g at Amazon (£1.55/100g)★★★☆☆A matt, umber-violet paste with a smooth texture and deep, rich and floral aroma. Soup test: a sweet, fruity scent and a rich but mildly astringent taste. Made to a simple formula. Great Taste one star in 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarukome miso with dashiView image in fullscreen£5.99 for 375g at Japan Centre (£1.60/100g)★★★☆☆A glossy, yellow paste with a super-smooth texture and a deep, smoky, fishy aroma. Soup test: a smoked bonito and fruity, sweet sake lees aroma, perfect for instant miso soups and noodles. An ultra-processed recipe, though, including MSG, bonito, disodium inosinate and disodium guanylate.Itsu traditional Miso’easyView image in fullscreen£2 for 105g (5 x 21g sachets) at Asda (£1.90/100g)£2 for 105g (5 x 21g sachets) at Ocado (£1.90/100g)★★☆☆☆Thin, glossy, caramel-coloured paste with the aroma of ethanol, acetic acid and soy sauce. Soup test: mild, sweet and simple in flavour. Made with 53% miso cut with water, alcohol and yeast extract.Blue Dragon miso pasteView image in fullscreen£2 for 135g at Morrisons (£1.48/100g)£2.50 for 135g at Asda (£1.85/100g)★☆☆☆☆A thin, glossy, brown sugar-coloured paste with a sour but rounded umami aroma. Soup test: an acidic aroma and intensely salty taste with rich umami notes in the background. It’s 55% miso paste cut with salt, sugar, acidity regulators and preservatives.Sainsbury’s Inspired to Cook miso pasteView image in fullscreen£1.90 for 100g at Sainsbury’s (£1.90/100g)★☆☆☆☆A thin, ochre paste with an acidic umami aroma. Soup test: sour-forward with a rounded, earthy flavour. Made with 45% miso paste cut with cornflour, acidity regulator and preservative potassium sorbate.Tesco miso pasteView image in fullscreen£1.80 for 100g at Tesco (£1.80/100g)☆☆☆☆☆A thin, shiny, yellow paste with an odd sour but still umami aroma. Soup test: unexpectedly sour. If AI were asked to make miso, I expect it would taste like this synthetic impression of miso that’s nothing like the real thing. Contains citric acid, colour (plain caramel) and potassium sorbate.For more, read thebest (and worst) supermarket sushi, tasted and ratedExplore more on these topicsFoodThe FilterJapanese food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From little acorns … to his 1,000th article for the Guardian country diary | Wildlife | The Guardian
description: As Mark Cocker approaches a landmark for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, he is still inspired by powerful encounters with nature
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: As Mark Cocker approaches a landmark for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, he is still inspired by powerful encounters with nature
Content: Mark Cocker: ‘It’s that connection between … the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.’Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMark Cocker: ‘It’s that connection between … the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.’Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The GuardianCountry diaryWildlifeFrom little acorns … to his 1,000th article for the Guardian country diaryAs Mark Cocker approaches a landmark for the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, he is still inspired by powerful encounters with naturePatrick BarkhamSat 17 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the autumn of 1987, Mark Cocker sat in a field near Norwich and watched a jay burying acorns for the long winter ahead. He described the scene in his firstcountry diaryfor the Guardian. Thirty-nine years on, some of those jay-planted acorns will be mature oaks now, and Cocker is completing his1,000th diaryfor the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper.In his next diary, he will reflect on the changing birdlife around Flint Clough, in the Peak District, where he first marvelled at rare birds aged 12 after devouring bird books in his bedroom. As a boy, he would find cuckoo, golden plover, ring ouzel and twite, a once-common bird which isnow virtually extinct in England.On his latest visit a few weeks ago, he saw raptors he would have only dreamed of as a boy, “a whole slew of buzzards, two peregrines, two marsh harriers – the first I’ve ever seen inDerbyshire– and several red kites”.View image in fullscreenMark Cocker standing on Flint Clough in Derbyshire.Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The GuardianThe Guardian country diary began in 1904 with the nature-loving dispatches of Thomas Coward, a retired textile bleacher from Cheshire. Today there is a diverse roster of about 30 diarists spread from Cornwall to the Cairngorms who include farmers, scientists, conservationists, a vicar, a thatcher and a forager, as well as writer-naturalists such as Cocker, who pens a fortnightly dispatch, usually from his local patch in Derbyshire.Despite honing his skills by working as a warden at Holkham national nature reserve in north Norfolk, while also becoming the first member of his family to attend university, where he studied English, Cocker says it took him 10 years to master the deceptively difficult craft of the diary – a compelling story about rural life in just 360 words.“You need quite a long apprenticeship to get it right because it’s so short,” he said. “It’s like a haiku. You’ve got to awaken the subject from its dormancy and get straight into the theme. And then the best diaries link it to something else.“You have a single shaft of light and, if you can, you excavate its relationship to the other parts. You have to often imply or adumbrate rather than specify. And it’s that connection between the part and the whole, the moment and the universal, which is the trick of the diary.”View image in fullscreenCocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come.Photograph: Fabio de Paola/The GuardianFor Cocker, who earlier this month publishedThe Nature of Seeing, a collection of recent diaries alongside new essays exploring how we might experience nature more fully, the close observation required for appreciating nature is a discipline that benefits all writing. He points to the surprising number of literary greats who have also kindled a passion for wildlife, from Margaret Atwood to Vladimir Nabokov.Before he began writing, Cocker worked as a refuse collector, a road sweeper, a potato picker and, as a penniless student, posed nude for the local art college.His big break came after a conservationist friend wrote to the Guardian to complain about the surfeit of inconsequential diaries about cricket matches. “She said: ‘The Guardian needs to get its boots and hat and coat on, and get out into the wild,’” remembered Cocker.View image in fullscreenThe country diary of 21 March 1904.Photograph: The GuardianCocker did that, writing early columns on chiffchaffs, silver-studded blue butterflies and sparrowhawks, before becoming a regular when the legendary Lakeland diarist Enid Wilson fell ill. Between them, Wilson and Cocker have covered a span of 76 years.Cocker shrugs off his own skills as a naturalist, which he says would be completely normal in another culture or era. In The Nature of Seeing, he writes about Inuit fishers who navigated home through the fog by recognising the subtly different patterns of snow bunting songs which corresponded to particular sections of the (invisible) coastline. “That is the level of attention to the living world which we’ve lost and need to recapture,” he said.He never steps outside with a preordained list of subjects to write about but seeks powerful encounters. “I have to feel the article viscerally. I have to feel that it moved me. That’s really where the experience begins and ends. If it doesn’t engage you personally, if you aren’t affected by it, the diary is a cheat.”AfterPhil Gatesretired recently following nearly 40 years on the diary, Cocker is now the longest-serving diarist.Country diary: The wasps’ nest in our shed is a work of art, a family saga | Mark CockerRead moreThe country diary editor, Paul Fleckney, said: “Mark is a gift to the diary. What you get from him is hyper-detailed knowledge with one eye on the bigger picture, and all written with such persuasion. Beneath it is a deep, deep love for the natural world, but also a rare kind of indefatigability. It’s as if all he wants to do is open people’s eyes and ears to the wonders around us, and it is infectious.”In a time of climate and biodiversity crises, as overconsumption imperils humanity, Cocker is convinced that, for all its modesty, the country diary’s time has come.“Meaning has been poured on to the diary because it is a repository now for a sense of the impending crisis which assails all life,” he said. “We’re now recognising that the intensifying nature of capitalism, the rise of the right, migration, climate change, drought, starvation, overpopulation – everything is to do with one meta-story, and that is our relationship with the rest of life. The diary’s become a valuable philosophical place for big ideas to be shared.”Mark’s new book,The Nature of Seeing, is out now, published by Jonathan CapeExplore more on these topicsWildlifeCountry diaryBirdsDerbyshireThe GuardianNational newspapersNewspapersnewsShareReuse this content

title: From 3,000 feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom craze | Rolls-Royce | The Guardian
description: In our second in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the artists and artisans working on bespoke versions of Britain’s luxury car brand
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: In our second in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the artists and artisans working on bespoke versions of Britain’s luxury car brand
Content: A nearly-completed Rolls-Royce Spectre.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA nearly-completed Rolls-Royce Spectre.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianRolls-RoyceFrom 3,000 feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom crazeIn our second in a series on high-end UK manufacturing, we visit the artisans producing rich clients’ bespoke luxury cars‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in WalesAlex DanielSat 17 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey are the plaything of kings, presidents and A-listers, with Rolls-Royce enthusiasts ranging from the Sultan of Brunei to Rowan Atkinson, from King Charles III toKermit the frog.And at the carmaker’s factory in Goodwood, West Sussex, special requests from customers get more indulgent every year. An interior lined with 3,000 iridescent feathers, or abuilt-in champagne cooler, or a car built in homage to its owners’ dog, have all become part of the job.Even with a fast-growing team of artisans and engineers, the company is stretched, and soon it will nearly double the size of its factory as part of a £300m investment by its owner, BMW, which it said at thetime of the announcementwas part of “securing our future here in the UK”.View image in fullscreenDetail of a Rolls-Royce phantom dashboard covered in iridescent feathers.Photograph: Wassim Raslan @weesography/Wassim RaslanBehind much of the demand is a new kind of client, who is younger than ever and with a fortune built in technology, says Julian Jenkins, Rolls-Royce’s director of sales and brand. The average buyer is now just 43 – down from 56 in 2010. “Never has there been so much wealth created so quickly at such a young age,” he says.Bespoke, high-value customisation is becoming an increasingly valuable pillar of UK manufacturing, which still makes up about 9% of the UK economy despite the years of deindustrialisation that Andy Burnham hasvowed to reverse. This week, the wider sector helped drive asurprise expansion of GDPin August, after growing 0.8% month on month.View image in fullscreenA Rolls-Royce craftsperson holds a carbon-fibre panel etched with a bitcoin symbol.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianOn a tour of the Goodwood factory, an inner door panel is emblazoned with a bitcoin symbol, hinting at changing tastes. “The industries – cryptocurrency, AI and tech – are where we see some of these young entrepreneurs finding their way very quickly to Rolls-Royce,” Jenkins says. “They are very specific about what they want.”Another car, built for a wealthy American couple, was devoted to their Labrador, Bailey. The dog’s face was pieced together on a rear panel using more than 180 individual slivers of wood, which was a four-month project, with paw prints engraved in the doors for good measure. Clients nowadays, Jenkins says, “are creating something in their image”.Four models make up the current Rolls-Royce range: the Phantom, starting at £441,000, the nearly three-tonne Cullinan SUV, from £345,000, the Spectre electric car, from £333,000, and the cheaper Ghost, from £290,000.View image in fullscreenThe wooden panel engraved with Bailey’s portrait.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianBut the average Rolls-Royce sells for about £500,000, up from about £300,000 a decade ago, driven largely by customisation work. A heavily personalised car can cost 25% more than the standard price, and seven-figure sums are “not unusual”, a spokesperson says.“The limits are set by the client,” Jenkins says. “We’ve seen some extremely complex and intricate commissions, and some of those can take multiple years. With that, there is value that comes as a consequence.”It is a vision Rolls-Royce’s founders could scarcely have imagined for a company that staked its early reputation on reliability. The business dates back to 1904, when Charles Rolls, an aristocrat and racing driver, met Henry Royce, an engineer, at the Midland Hotel in Manchester, and agreed to sell every car the latter could build.By 1907, Autocar magazine called the Silver Ghost, an early model, the “best car in the world” after completing the gruelling Scottish Reliability Trial without a single mechanical fault. Now, Rolls-Royce has its own entry in the Collins dictionary, as a byword for “anything considered to be the very best of its kind”. Its longest-running model, the Phantom, celebrated its centenary last year.An expansion into aero engines during the world wars made it a manufacturing powerhouse, but later financial collapse forced the government of the time to nationalise the company in 1971. The car business was split off and sold to the engineering firm Vickers. Rolls-Royce,the FTSE 100 aerospace giant, still shares the same logo.View image in fullscreenA white Rolls-Royce Phantom parked outside the Rolls-Royce factory.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianIn 1998, BMW bought the right to put the Rolls-Royce name on cars, and in 2003 opened the Goodwood factory, promising to triple annual production from about 2,000 cars a year. Two decades later it succeeded, whenoutput peaked at 6,032 cars,falling back to 5,664 last year.Would the Rolls-Royce engineers whose Merlin engines powered the second world war Spitfire have guessed the company name would end up in German hands?“Rolls-Royce motorcars is very much a British company at heart,” says Chris Brownridge, its chief executive. However, he admits it benefits from “synergies” with BMW, such as “battery technology research and development, access to wind-tunnels and other major facilities”.The expansion at Goodwood comes as carmakers are under significant strain from Chinese competition, soaring industrial energy costs and US tariffs. Jaguar Land Roverrecently said it would cut 4,000 jobs, while Volkswagen, which owns Rolls-Royce’s arch rival Bentley, iscutting 100,000 jobs by 2030.Shrinking demand in China, a key export market for luxury goods, has “obviously been significant”, Jenkins admits, pointing to Rolls-Royce clients “who made their wealth through the [Chinese] property market … which has been adversely affected.”View image in fullscreenAn artisan installs individual starlights into the ceiling of a Rolls-Royce.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianElectrification has been part of that story, too. Rolls-Royce’s first electric vehicle, the Spectre, launched in 2022, alongside a pledge from the company to sell only EVs by the end of the decade. The model sold briskly at first but deliveries nearly halved in 2025, and earlier this year Rolls-Roycescrapped its 2030 target.Jenkins says the company is “not immune to the shifts that have happened, and some of the resistance that we’ve seen [to EVs]”. A revamped version, the Spectre Series Two, recently launched with a longer range and more power.The latest factory upgrade, Jenkins says, is less about pumping out more cars, but rather about meeting the “ever more complex” demands of clients. Every car is made to order and assembled at Goodwood, where 2,500 people work across a production line with 45 stations. A single car can take up to 600 hours to build, passing through more than 100 pairs of hands.Those include 14 artisans finishing personalised vehicles. Artists hand-paint designs on bodywork and inner panels, while embroiderers are on hand to make the ceilings of cars look like the night sky. A standard sky contains up to 1,600 fibre-optic stars and takes around nine hours to thread by hand, while the most elaborate commissions can take two full days.A trio of innovation specialists work on novel techniques. One dragon design used a method borrowed from fine furniture called sand shading, in which each individual scale is burned at the edges in a hot pan to create a shadow effect across the creature’s body.View image in fullscreenA panel customised with a dragon using sand shading.Photograph: Peter Flude/The GuardianAndrew Hopkins, a lead craftsperson, studied furniture making before joining Goodwood when it opened in 2003. Does he ever think a request is a bit much? “Whether you like it personally, you don’t really take it into account,” he says. “You learn quite fast not to be the taste police.”But who is paying for it? Well-documented owners include Tyson Fury, David Beckham and members of the Kardashian family. Kylie Jenner had her Rolls-Royce Cullinan finished with a pink interior and a plaque reading “Stormi’s Mom” in honour of her daughter.Despite its slowdown, many of the youngest, tech-rich buyers are still coming from China. Jenkins was recently in Beijing, opening a new dealership and presenting a car to a 26-year-old woman who had “fallen in love” with a custom design.“They are individuals that are very much on the way up in terms of their wealth creation,” he says, “but doing so at an incredible pace.”Is the growing concentration of wealth among fewer and younger people a good thing for society? Whatever the answer, it has certainly helped Rolls-Royce. “It’s a fact, isn’t it?” says Jenkins.Explore more on these topicsRolls-RoyceAutomotive industryMotoringfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jonathan Glazer was ‘shocked into silence’ by NAZA documentary | NAZA | The Guardian
description: Film’s executive producer talks about first time he watched film detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Film’s executive producer talks about first time he watched film detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza
Content: Jonathan Glazer said NAZA was ‘clearly in dialogue’ with his Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJonathan Glazer said NAZA was ‘clearly in dialogue’ with his Oscar-winning film The Zone of Interest.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNAZAJonathan Glazer was ‘shocked into silence’ by NAZA documentaryFilm’s executive producer talks about first time he watched film detailing Israel’s mass killing of civilians in GazaSammy GecsoylerSat 17 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTFirst published on Fri 16 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe director Jonathan Glazer has called Israel’s retaliation against NAZA’s film-makers and the military figures interviewed in theaward-winning documentary“much more venal” than anticipated.Since the film’s release, the Israeli government has denounced it and pursued those involved,announcing plans aimed at stripping citizenshipfrom people who “smear” Israeli soldiers; accused NAZA’s co-directors, Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, of treason; and ordered top legal and security officials to find and prosecute soldiers and officers interviewed in the documentary for causing “harm to Israel’s diplomatic and security interests”.Calling the shots: what NAZA says about perpetrator cinemaRead moreSpeaking to the Guardian’s editor-in-chief, Katharine Viner, at NAZA’s UK premiere in London on Thursday night, Glazer, who is an executive producer on the film, said he was “shocked into silence” the first time he watched NAZA, which is produced by the Guardian and details Israel’s mass killing of civilians in Gaza.He noted that it was “clearly in dialogue” with and “deals with very similar themes” to The Zone of Interest, the 2023 historical drama he directed and that depicted the mundane daily lives of Nazi officers overseeing the extermination of Jews at Auschwitz.“Both films deal with dehumanisation,” Glazer said. “And how we get to where we do as a species by othering and dehumanising, and what that then leads to.”The Israeli government has promoted an online film project that mimics the style ofNAZAin an attempt to counter the film’s findings. When asked whether he was surprised by the intense reaction of the Israeli government to NAZA, Glazer said some of it was expected but that, “in my point of view, it was much more venal” than anticipated.Abraham said the film allows viewers to look at the “mechanisms that allow human beings to do this to other human beings”, and Szor said the idea to shoot footage looking inside Tel Aviv citizens’ apartments was to focus on the “ritual” of people gathering around the TV to watch the “news and to see the absence or justification” of the devastation happening inGaza.View image in fullscreenYuval Abraham speaking at the panel event.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianNAZA is in UK cinemas and will be shown in more than 50 countries. As well as its global cinema releases, NAZA will be available free on the Guardian’s website from late November. When the film opened in Italy last month, it surpassed the Marvel movie Avengers Endgame: Encore to open at No 1.The film contains 24 interviews with Israeli military insiders who detail how an AI-assisted apparatus of mass surveillance was activated during theGazawar, revealing the systems that were used to target Hamas operatives in the knowledge that large numbers of Palestinian civilians would also die.Various bodies, including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based, have said Israel is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.The film premiered at the Venice film festival, where it was met with a 25-minute standing ovation – a festival record. The documentary went onto win the special jury prize.Israeli government officials have attempted to discredit NAZA’s content, while far-right activists have threatened to hunt down the directors.The Israel Defense Forces’ chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, has said they will use “every tool at our disposal” against the film, while themilitary has issueda 10-page response to NAZA, which was based on interviews with more than 100 sources with knowledge of the military systems used in the war.View image in fullscreenA mural depicting Israeli filmmakers Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, initially painted by an artist accusing the filmmakers of being ‘traitors,’ the text on the mural was subsequently modified by another artist to read ‘heroes.’Photograph: Mostafa Alkharouf/Anadolu/Getty ImagesDemonstrators have gathered outside the home of Szor’s parents, demanding that she face the death penalty, and a mural depicting the film-makers through the sights of a gun appeared in the Israeli city of Ashdod.Szor and Abrahamaddressed the backlashto their documentary at a Q&A after its New York premiere. “Our country is doing so much to hide these systems,” Szor told the audience. “It’s not a world that is open even to the Israeli public.”The Zone of Interest won the Oscar for best international film in 2024.Explore more on these topicsNAZAJonathan GlazerIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaDocumentary filmsIsrael-Gaza warWar crimesShareReuse this content

title: The Influencer Project to Melanie C: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: A social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tour
Content: Doom scroll … The Influencer Project.Photograph: -View image in fullscreenDoom scroll … The Influencer Project.Photograph: -Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Going out, staying inCultureThe Influencer Project to Melanie C: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadA social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tourSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaThe Influencer ProjectOut nowWhen your career involves constantly posting footage of everything you do to social media, it makes things a cakewalk for stalkers. And lo, the influencer-in-peril horror subgenre was born. British social media star Chiara King plays herself in this chilling iteration, set in Copenhagen.NazaOut nowThe ongoing genocide in Gaza has proven an urgent subject for documentaries and drama alike. Here, directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (two of the four film-makers behind the 2025 Oscar winner No Other Land) construct a doc made up of interviews with Israeli Intelligence Corps agents, who map out the details of targeted airstrikes in civilian areas.WhalefallOut nowWhat if you were swallowed by a whale but survived? That’s the vivid premise of this – what to call it? Eco horror? Monster movie? Survival thriller? Maybe all three? – in which scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams) has one hour to find a way to escape before his oxygen runs out. Also starring Josh Brolin (sadly not as the whale).Street FighterOut nowThis reboot marks the third live-action movie based on the hit video game to make it to the big screen, and features Jason Momoa as Blanka, 50 Cent as Balrog, and Callina Liang as Chun-Li. Ready… set… fight!Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenThe Spice of life … Melanie C.Photograph: Taylor Jewell/Invision/APMelanie C18 to 24 October; tour starts DublinThe seemingly indefatigable Melanie C, whose dancefloor-focused ninth solo album Sweat peaked at No 3 earlier in the year, takes her solo oeuvre for a spin around a collection of mid-sized venues. As well as the raft of recent bangers, there should be space for some Northern Star-era pop gems, too.Michael CraggJ Cole19 October to 2 November; tour starts LondonThe US rapper heads out on his first solo headline tour in five years in support of seventh, and apparently final album, The Fall-Off. A star-studded, 24-track behemoth, it’s quite the swansong, so chances are these arena shows will carry a similar sense of celebratory closure.MCMingus Big BandRonnie Scott’s, London, 19 to 24 OctoberCharles Mingus, one of the most soulfully creative jazz composers, died in 1979, but the powerful legacy band bearing his name has cherished his repertoire for three decades. The classy lineup includes saxists Wayne Escoffery and Craig Handy, trumpter Alex Sipiagin, and uncannily Mingus-echoing bassist Boris Kozlov.John FordhamRoyal Liverpool PhilharmonicLiverpool Philharmonic Hall, 17OctoberRising-star conductor Adam Hickox takes to the podium for the world premiere of a new clarinet concerto by Gavin Higgins, performed by outgoing RLPO artist in residence Mark Simpson. The programme culminates in Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring – still thrilling, more than a century after its own premiere provoked a riot.Flora WillsonGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenAl smiles … Sturtevant’s Haring Tag, 1986.Photograph: Fredrik Nilsen StudioSturtevantRaven Row, London, to 20 DecemberSturtevant was the ultimate appropriator, a satirical copycat who had been mimicking the work of other artists since the 1960s. This first UK institutional show since her death in 2014 is a celebration of her radical take on conceptualism.Hokusai: 36 Views of Mount FujiDulwich Picture Gallery, London, 13 October to 17 JanuaryHokusai’s iconic depiction of Mount Fuji, one of the most famous images in the history of art, wasn’t a one-off. It was part of a series, and this exhibition brings the full set together.Joy GregoryArnolfini, Bristol, 17 October to 7 FebruaryA celebration of four decades of experimental photography by this leading voice in Black and feminist art, working across historic photographic processes and digital manipulation.Larry AchiampongKarst, Plymouth, to 12 DecemberUsing the visual language of science fiction, this British Ghanaian artist tackles big ideas of colonialism, class, diaspora and displacement in this continuation of his ambitious film project.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenCruise control … Olga Koch.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOlga KochWhere Else?, Margate, 15 October; touring to 4 DecemberNot all standups ooze confidence like Koch – and not all have such good reason to. In her meticulously crafted new show Fat Tom Cruise, the Russian-British comedian (and PhD student) explores the masculinity crisis via routines delivered with vim, vigour and flair.Rachel AroestiSome WomanNational Theatre: Dorfman, London,to 21 NovemberAnne-Marie Duff stars as an overlooked woman who, after a troubling encounter on a train platform, decides to take a stand in this new play from Helen Edmundson.Miriam GillinsonNorthern Ballet: CinderellaNottingham Theatre Royal, Friday to 24 October; touringto 15 DecemberA new Cinderella for Northern Ballet. Created by choreographer Michael Pink for Milwaukee Ballet, this is the show’s UK premiere, with all the trappings – pumpkin carriage, fairy godmother, comic stepsisters – as well as a great live Prokofiev score.Lyndsey WinshipLannyBristol Old Vic,to 7 NovemberMax Porter’s acclaimed novel is adapted for the stage by Bea Roberts, with a cast drawn largely from the south-west. It’s a blurred and beguiling tale about a young boy who goes missing: is it foul play, the work of an ancient shape-shifting figure or something else?MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenReich here, Reich now … It Gets Worse.Photograph: Channel 4It Gets WorseChannel 4, 15 October, 10pmLeo Reich has created the first good gen Z hangout comedy with this London-set tale of three university friends struggling to self-actualise in their mid-20s. From Lena Dunham to Zadie Smith, celebrity cameos abound – but Reich’s winningly bratty protagonist is the real star attraction.The AudacityHBO Max, 15 OctoberWriter Jonathan Glatzer (Succession, Better Call Saul) mines frantic comedy from the dark heart of Silicon Valley in a series about a megalomaniacal tech boss (Billy Magnussen). Industry’s Sarah Goldberg plays his therapist, Motherland’s Lucy Punch is his wife and Zach Galifianakis guests as another unhinged billionaire.The New Stanford Prison ExperimentNetflix, 14 OctoberThe 1971 psychological study which saw male college students randomly split into guards and prisoners in a mock jail remains one of the most fascinating and notorious of all time. Will Netflix’s new reality show version have the same results – and, crucially, the same grim appeal?Last One Laughing: HalloweenPrime Video, 16 OctoberThe spectacular success of our version of the Japanese gameshow means it’s already entered seasonal spin-off territory. Phil Wang and Reece Shearsmith (plus old faves Lou Sanders and Daisy May Cooper) are among the comics trying desperately not to laugh or – spooky twist alert! – scream in this latest edition.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenNintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoNintendo Switch Sports ResortSwitch 2; out 15 OctoberTake up boxing, bowling, archery, basketball, tennis, skating and more in this latest game in the fine controller-waggling lineage of Wii Sports. Parents of competitive siblings: remember to use the controller straps to stop a Joy-Con from flying through a window.Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4PC, Switch 2, PS5, Xbox; out FridayActivision’s theatre of war goes on tour to Korea, where an invasion threatens the stability of the rest of the world. The multiplayer offers the usual cornucopia of ways to play soldiers, where the campaign follows a Korean private and returning character Captain Price, on the run after an assassination.Keza MacDonaldStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenSongs for the ages … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelRachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too SoonOut nowLyrically influenced by a mid-20s existential crisis, the second album by London singer-songwriter Chinouriri sweetens those fears with vibrant musical touches. On Broken Chair and One Song Away from Crying she dabbles in bubbling 80s synthpop, while the murkier Make Believe grows slowly overcast.Angèle – InstinctOut nowFive years after her second album, Nonante-Cinq, the Belgian superstar returns with more gleaming dance-pop. With production from French knob twiddlers Justice and SebastiAn, plus assistance from Caroline Polachek on the slinky Love Triangle, it’s a play for the big leagues.Florrie – Magic for a WhileOut nowAs part of production hothouse Xenomania, Florrie played drums on hits by Kylie and Girls Aloud. Since stepping up to the mic she’s released her own collection of decadent bops, with this second album expanding into indie pop (The Times) and pensive balladry (Catch You If You Fall).Fontaines DC – Dopamine ChamberOut nowAfter hitting their creative and commercial stride on 2024’s Grammy-nominated Romance, the Irish rock experimentalists are back with this swaggering fifth album. As with Romance it’s been produced by James Ford, who peppers the undulating Tongue with twitchy electronic effects.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenThe LRB PodcastPodcastIntellectuals’ favourite the London Review of Books makes the big questions of our time slightly more digestible in this audio series. Writers, thinkers and experts discuss everything from the worth of criticism to the German far right.TED-Ed:Public Speaking 101YouTubeThis ongoing and insightful series of lectures on public speaking is sure to give even the shyest person confidence to talk to a crowd. The most recent episode covers succinct ways to explain complex ideas.Illuminated: FaithlessBBC Sounds, out nowJournalist May Robson’s expertly reported and deeply moving documentary follows four people who were raised in religious devotion and who have since chosen to leave their faith. Testimony comes from former Jehovah’s Witnesses, Mormons and others.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Daniel Dubois delivers devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain WBO title | Boxing | The Guardian
description: Daniel Dubois overwhelmed Fabio Wardley in the second round of their WBO world title fight as he continued his quest to become the most authoritative heavyweight fighter on the planet
Author: Donald McRae
Headline: Daniel Dubois overwhelmed Fabio Wardley in the second round of their WBO world title fight as he continued his quest to become the most authoritative heavyweight fighter on the planet
Content: Daniel Dubois lands a blow on Fabio Wardley at the O2 Arena.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenDaniel Dubois lands a blow on Fabio Wardley at the O2 Arena.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersBoxingDaniel Dubois delivers devastating second-round stoppage of Fabio Wardley to retain WBO titleDubois underlines status as Britain’s leading heavyweightWardley’s corner throw in the towel in second roundDonald McRaeat the O2 ArenaSat 17 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDaniel Dubois overwhelmed Fabio Wardley in their WBO world title fight on Saturday night as he continued his quest to become the most authoritative heavyweight fighter on the planet with this crushing victory. This was the second time in five months that Dubois has defeated Wardley but, after theirfight of the year contender in May, he unleashed a shockingly one-sided shellacking.Daniel Dubois knocks out Fabio Wardley to retain WBO heavyweight title – live reactionRead moreAfter two minutes and 21 seconds of round two, Wardley was rescued from the bludgeoning fists of Dubois by the referee, just as the fluttering white towel of his trainer, Ben Davison, sailed over the ropes in surrender. Davison had been on the brink of throwing in the towel at the very end of the opening round but the bell sounded to end a disastrous first three minutes for Wardley. He was dropped heavily after just 17 seconds as Dubois landed a left cross followed by a pulverising right hand.It was the first time Wardley had been forced to take a count in 23 fights as a professional and he looked suitably stunned. He seemed helpless as Dubois pummelled him around the ring with a thunderous array of mostly unanswered punches. In the last 15 seconds of the round Wardley was pinned in Dubois’ corner as the punishing blows intensified.View image in fullscreenDaniel Dubois overpowers Fabio Wardley in their much-anticipated clash in London.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/ReutersHe came out for the second round and, while he threw some wild haymakers and wayward uppercuts, Wardley could not stem the dark tide of punches engulfing him. The end was merciful.Wardley had walked to the ring in a sombre yet purposeful manner but the bridge of his nose still carried a red scar of the deep gash he had suffered when he last shared a ring with Dubois. But he raised his right hand high as soon as he ducked through the ropes. Dubois followed at a much quicker lick as Salt-N-Pepa’s Whatta Man boomed around him. The two men were brought face to face for their final instructions – and carnage ensued soon afterwards.Dubois’ boxing fundamentals are far superior to Wardley’s more crude technique, which lacks a proper grounding in amateur boxing. Wardley used to be a white-collar boxer and his rise to becoming a respected world champion is an unlikely but hugely admirable sporting story. He lost his title and unbeaten record to Dubois in their gripping but also harrowing first fight; and this devastating defeat confirmed the limits of Wardley’s talent.“I had bad intentions from the beginning,” Dubois said. “Our back was against the wall last time – this time we had to go out and show we mean business from the start.”The contest in May took chunks out of Wardley because, despite knocking down Dubois twice in the early rounds, he suffered a horrible pounding for the rest of the bout, which ended in the 11th. He would have been better advised to take a far longer break from boxing than rushing back into a rematch. It can only be hoped that the salutary lessons doled out by Dubois persuade him to change course.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenDaniel Dubois celebrates retaining his WBO title.Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/Reuters“It’s never fun to lose – but it is what it is, it’s the name of the game,” Wardley said in his conversational way. “I’ve always taken on the biggest challenges … I tried to adjust some things but it didn’t work tonight.Boxingis a game of fine margins. I didn’t touch the canvas, so there’s a little bit of pride in that.”Wardley is an engaging and intelligent man and he would carve out an impressive career as a boxing analyst on television. It would be far better for his health if he could do his best work in the years to come on the safe side of the ropes.The future for Dubois, in contrast, is much more straightforward. This clinical and decisive performance will propel him towards a potential series of unification contests against Filip Hrgovic and Agit Kabayel, who hold rival versions of the world title. But, as he proved with this utterly dominant performance, Dubois looks a cut above the rest of the heavyweight pack.Explore more on these topicsBoxingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Haaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat Ipswich  | Premier League | The Guardian
description: An Erling Haaland double helped extend City’s winning start to seven – a Premier League record for Enzo Maresca – in their 3-2 victory over Ipswich
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: An Erling Haaland double helped extend City’s winning start to seven – a Premier League record for Enzo Maresca – in their 3-2 victory over Ipswich
Content: Erling Haaland slots home Manchester City’s third goal against Ipswich.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APView image in fullscreenErling Haaland slots home Manchester City’s third goal against Ipswich.Photograph: Dave Thompson/APPremier LeagueHaaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat IpswichWill Unwinat the Etihad StadiumSat 17 Oct 2026 12.08 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 17.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere have been few winners in Manchester City’s guilty verdict, except highly paid lawyers and the inflatable fruit industry. The fans have suffered, being forced to question everything they have been told, while being labelled “cheats”, but they were able to forget the cacophony of noise around the club as Enzo Maresca became the first Premier League manager to win his first seven games.Ipswich were the latest victims, but they put up a fight in City’s first home Premier League game since being foundto have breached financial rules. Defiance has fortified most of the City fanbase, who were able to see local boy Phil Foden instigate the triumph with a kiss of the badge, before an emblem of their wealth, Erling Haaland, secured the points to move six clear, albeit with a few scares between, courtesy of Daizen Maeda and Zian Flemming.Isak completes Liverpool’s comeback win as Brentford finish with nineRead more“I didn’t expect to win seven out of seven, but we are working well,” Maresca said. “This is the most important thing.”Victory came at a cost as Haaland and AntoineSemenyo limped off at full-time, in addition to Mateo Kovacic, Matheus Nunes and Nico O’Reilly suffering injuries, although Maresca was left unsure of the severity as City prepare to host AEK Athens on Tuesday.If City have felt like it has been their backs against the wall for the past few weeks, it was Ipswich’s turn. Gary O’Neil put 11 men behind the ball whenever the hosts ventured over the halfway line as City enjoyed 90% possession in the opening quarter-hour, but without truly threatening as they struggled to find space in the lowest of blocks, expertly organised and fully disciplined.Maresca had made six changes to refresh the side and it took time to understand one another’s rhythm, with Ayyoub Bouaddi creating it from defensive midfield in another mature performance from the teenager making his firstPremier Leaguestart.View image in fullscreenEnzo Maresca has guided Manchester City a record seven-match winning start in the Premier League.Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty ImagesIt was inevitable what was coming as there was irrefutable evidence that City were dominant.As at Anfield, Jérémy Doku was a key instigator, showing mesmeric skill on the left of the area before finding Foden to sweep home for his first goal since mid-December.“I know him from years ago, for me he’s one of the best Premier League players,” Maresca said. “Since day one, it’s my duty to help him to be again one of the best players. I’m very happy for his goal and hopefully it can be just the beginning of many goals and many good performances.”There was an element of pantomime around the ground from the booing of the Premier League anthem, the singalongs and inflatables. It was fitting Marc Guéhi did not know Maeda was behind him, allowing the Ipswich man to latch on to a sublime curved through ball from Abdoul Ouattara and equalise two minutes after the opener.Quick GuideManchester City 3-2 Ipswich key factsShow• With Manchester City maintaining their 100% record, Enzo Maresca isthe first manager to win his first sevenPremier League games in charge of a team.• Manchester City are  the third team to wintheir opening seven gamesof a Premier League season, afterLiverpool in 2019-20(first 8) andChelsea in 2005-06(first 9).• Erling Haaland (pictured) has now scored100 non-penalty goalsin the Premier League, reaching this milestonein fewer appearancesthan any other player (139). The previous fewest was 150 appearances, by Alan Shearer in 1996.OptaPhotograph: Martin Rickett/PAWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.After a missed chance, Haaland showed it is possible to get a better result second time around, making the most of Kovacic becoming an auxiliary winger. The header lacked power, but Christian Walton could not keep it out, palming the ball from one hand to the other and into the net before Haaland was serenaded with the clap of bananas.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCity found themselves stuck in a lull, unable to prise open Ipswich, instead having to bide their time. It was a test of patience and a sweeping move upfield concluded with a precision pass from Iliman Ndiaye and an aggressive finish from Haaland, who was later denied a hat-trick by the video assistant referee.View image in fullscreenManchester City fans have gone back to more innocent times with their inflatable bananas.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesFarai Hallam reviewed footage of Guéhi taking out Abdul Fatawu in the area and Flemming did the rest in the 90th minute, as reward for an impressive team performance, leaving O’Neil upset Ipswich departed with nothing.“They’re an incredible group,” he said. “Players giving everything. It’s a privilege to stand there and represent them because they’re an incredible group.”City were left to complain about a Premier League official’s decision when 12 minutes was added on, with few knowing why, but this result will not be questioned.Maresca called on his team to make their own noise while a cacophony swirls around them, but on-pitch success will not speak louder while what is happening off it is unresolved. The fans sang about relegation and trips to Stockport, embracing a dark situation with humour to match.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester CityIpswich Townmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Isak completes Liverpool’s comeback win as Brentford finish with nine | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Alexander Isak scored Liverpool’s winner in their 2-1 victory at Brentford, who had Yehor Yarmolyuk sent off at 1-0 up and Vitaly Janelt later saw red
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Alexander Isak scored Liverpool’s winner in their 2-1 victory at Brentford, who had Yehor Yarmolyuk sent off at 1-0 up and Vitaly Janelt later saw red
Content: Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola celebrate Liverpool’s winner.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAlexander Isak and Bradley Barcola celebrate Liverpool’s winner.Photograph: Marc Atkins/Getty ImagesPremier LeagueIsak completes Liverpool’s comeback win as Brentford finish with nineJacob Steinbergat the Gtech Community StadiumSat 17 Oct 2026 12.21 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 14.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf Liverpool’s spluttering forwards end up remembering this as the day when their luck turned then they will owe a big debt of gratitude to Yehor Yarmolyuk.
