This was a game with a very clear before and after.Andoni Iraola will hope surviving one of the toughest tests thePremier Leaguehas to offer is a sign his methods are starting to work, but Liverpool’s manager will not forget it was a very different contest after Yarmolyuk’s red card for a butt on Jérémy Jacquet left Brentford trying to defend a 1-0 lead with 10 men for the entire second half.Haaland helps extend record start for Maresca as Manchester City defeat IpswichRead moreBrentford, who later lost Vitaly Janelt to a second yellow card, could not hold out. They raged at John Brooks’s officiating after their unbeaten start ended, but they had only themselves to blame after tumbling out of the top four.Brentfordpressed the self-destruct button when they had Liverpool on the ropes. Yarmolyuk was never going to get away it in the video assistant referee era and Liverpool made the midfielder pay.Iraola was delighted with how an attack worth close to £400m made the numerical advantage count after half-time. Most important was a telling contribution from Florian Wirtz. The £100m signing has struggled withthe responsibility of playing as Liverpool’s No 10since joining from Bayer Leverkusen, but this time he was decisive. The clever pass to release Victor Muñoz for a sharp equaliser was his second assist of the season and was followed by Bradley Barcola creating a goal for the first time sincehis move for an initial £106mfrom Paris Saint-Germain, the French winger’s header teeing up Alexander Isak to complete the turnaround in the 70th minute and lift Liverpool into fifth place.The challenge is to push on. Isak’s Liverpool career has been stop-start since his£125m move from Newcastle, injuries holding the forward back. The Spaniard was critical of some sloppy finishing from Barcola, but was readier to dish out the praise for Wirtz’s intelligence in tight spaces in the second half. It feels significant that both of Wirtz’s assists have come for Muñoz.“A good battle today,” Iraola said before switching focus to Barcola and Wirtz. “Both had a lot of influence. Bradley and Flo, they are players that against 10 men are lovely to have.”There was not much between the sides before Yarmolyuk’s rush of blood to the head. Isak returned after missinglast week’s defeat to Manchester Cityand Liverpool shaded the early openings. Barcola almost punished an error from Janelt, only to miss a chance to build onhis midweek hat-trick against LASK. Isak nodded over from a good position.Pressure on Arbeloa lifted after Alex Iwobi sinks Hull for Fulham’s first winRead moreBrentford responded with a series of fast breaks and Liverpool had to be strong. They looked readier for the threat posed by Brentford than whenthey folded in this fixtureunder Arne Slot 12 months ago. Jacquet, quietly impressive in central defence, made a crucial tackle to deny Igor Thiago. The initial problem for Liverpool was more their expensive attack was yet to gel.Michael Kayode was keeping Barcola in check and Keane Lewis-Potter was edging his battle with Muñoz. Wirtz was timid and Liverpool’s worries grew when they lost Dominik Szoboszlai to injury.With Ryan Gravenberch suspended, Liverpool were light on midfield options. Trey Nyoni replaced Szoboszali and the 19-year-old’s introduction was followed by a whirlwind spell. Iraola was unhappy when Liverpool had a penalty overturned as replays showed Dango Outtara got a clear touch on the ball before colliding with Alexis Mac Allister.View image in fullscreenYehor Yarmolyuk leaves the pitch after being shown the red card.Photograph: Adam Davy/PABrentford were pumped up after the VAR intervention and soon made Liverpool rue a failure to clear their lines. The ball came back too easily, Mac Allister backed off Thiago, who crossed for Lewis-Potter to run in from left-back and head into the top corner.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We were edging it,” Keith Andrews said. Brentford’s manager wants his team “to play on the edge”, but felt too many decisions went Liverpool’s way. However, he had no complaints about the first red. He said Liverpool were “cute and clever” during the incident, but promised that Yarmolyuk would learn from his mistake.They were into six added minutes at the end of the first half when the midfielder clashed with Jacquet before a Liverpool corner. It was more of a jut than a proper blow, but it was enough to justify the sending off. Brooks checked the pitchside monitor and his decision was not a surprise.Liverpool took a while to adjust in the second half. They encountered further complications when injury forced Jeremie Frimpong off seven minutes after replacing Ronald Araújo at right-back. Mac Allister let fly from distance, but Caoimhín Kelleher saved and Rio Ngumoha, on for Frimpong, crossed for Virgil van Dijk to volley wide.Quick GuideBrentford 1-2 Liverpool key factsShow• Florian Wirtz is the first player to createnine or more chances from open playin a Premier League game since Sadio Mané against Burnley in January 2021 (9), also for Liverpool, and first in an away match since Samir Nasri for Manchester City v Spurs in August 2011 (10). Victor Muñoz (pictured centre, with Wirtz and Trey Nyoni) scored from one of them.• Liverpool’s Alexander Isakhas scored in all fiveof his Premier League appearances against Brentford (5 goals); only Erling Haaland v Crystal Palace (6) has a better 100% rate in the competition.• Brentford received two red cards in the same league game for the first time since April 2013 against Sheffield United in League One.OptaPhotograph: Peter Cziborra/REUTERSWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Brentford began to wobble and they were caught on the counterattack in the 62nd minute. Wirtz dropped back and played a clever pass inside Lewis-Potter. Muñoz raced clear, cut back and drilled a low shot into the far corner with his left foot.The change in mood was dramatic. Barcola sliced a volley just wide, but the winner was coming. Mac Allister took a pass from Wirtz and crossed. Barcola headed down and Isak finished from close range.Iraola was not happy with Liverpool’s play once they led. Brentford threatened an equaliser through Thiago and Liverpool were too rushed. There are flaws to iron out, but this was a positive week for Iraola.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueBrentfordLiverpoolmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Champions Cup roundup: La Rochelle beat Lions after emotional tribute to Andrews | Champions Cup | The Guardian
description: After both team remembered the Lions lock Hyron Andrews, who was found dead on Friday, La Rochelle beat the Johannesburg side 31-14
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After both team remembered the Lions lock Hyron Andrews, who was found dead on Friday, La Rochelle beat the Johannesburg side 31-14
Content: Players from both teams observed a minute of silence in tribute to Hyron Andrews, who died on Friday, at his hotel.Photograph: Yohan Bonnet/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPlayers from both teams observed a minute of silence in tribute to Hyron Andrews, who died on Friday, at his hotel.Photograph: Yohan Bonnet/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockChampions CupChampions Cup roundup: La Rochelle beat Lions after emotional tribute to AndrewsLions lock Hyron Andrews, 31, found dead on FridayConnacht 45-36 Saracens; Sale 27-47 GlasgowAgence France-Press and Press AssociationSat 17 Oct 2026 17.33 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Johannesburg-basedLionsput up a gritty fight on an emotionalChampions Cupdebut but came up short 31-14 atLa Rochelleas both sides paid tribute to the South African lock Hyron Andrews, who died suddenly at the team’s hotel in western France.The whole stadium observed a minute’s silence while Andrews’s No 5 shirt was laid on the pitch before kick-off. La Rochelle’s three South African players presented a jersey to their visitors in memory of the player, who died on Friday at Lions’ hotel on the nearby Ile de Ré. A source close to the investigation said thatAndrews, who was 31, was found in cardiac arrestin a shower cubicle that was locked from the inside.The wingers Tevita Ofa and Davit Niniashvili were on the scoresheet in the first half for hostsLa Rochelle, who led 19-14 as Lions replied through Henco van Wyk and Morné Brandon. Second-half scores from Australia hooker Silatolu Latu and Fijian winger Avakuki Niusalelekitoga earned La Rochelle a bonus point.In the other game in Pool 2, Cian Prendergast and Ciaran Frawley scored two tries apiece asConnachtdefeatedSaracens45-36 in a thriller. Saracens made the better start and opened up a 12-0 lead through tries from Sione Vaenuku and Noah Caluori but the Irish side came storming back.View image in fullscreenSaracens’ Noah Caluori (centre) is tackled by Connacht’s Daniel Ryan.Photograph: Brian Lawless/PAThree tries in 12 minutes from Prendergast, Cathal Forde and Shamus Hurley-Langton put them in front, but the latter was sent to the sin-bin just before half-time and Nick Tompkins capitalised to make it 19-19 at the break. It remained nip and tuck as Prendergast went over for his second only for Rotimi Segun to find a swift reply. Frawley was next to cross before Vaenuku grabbed his second but tries from Caolin Blade and Frawley’s second helped Connacht open up a 14-point gap.That was reduced to nine when Elliot Daly scored Saracens’ sixth try following a yellow card for Prendergast but Owen Farrell missed the conversion to deny them a bonus point.Glasgow Warriorsextended their unbeaten start to the new season by pulling away to claim an impressive 47-27 win atSalein Pool 1. Glasgow’s winning score looked convincing, but they secured victory in the final 20 minutes after Rekeiti Ma’asi-White had temporarily reduced Sale’s deficit to four.View image in fullscreenRekeiti Ma’asi-White of Sale Sharks points to the sky in celebration after scoring a try.Photograph: Jan Kruger/Getty Images for Sale SharksThe hosts had made all the running in the early stages and were 12 points up inside the first 10 minutes thanks to tries from Ben Curry and Arron Reed. The visitors hit back through a penalty try and further efforts from Kyle Steyn and Jamie Dobie to carve out a 21-15 lead at the interval.The game looked in the balance until late tries from Rory Darge, Ollie Smith and debutant Tavi Tuipulotu helped Glasgow pull away and wrap up a bonus-point win. Glasgow host Pau in their next Champions Cup encounter while Sale travel toLeinsterfor a tricky test in mid-December.Also in Pool 1,Leinsterproduced a fine second-half display as the Irish side recorded a bonus-point 48-23 win againstClermontat the Stade Marcel-Michelin.Tadhg Furlong and Dan Sheehan both scored tries for Leinster in the opening period, but the visitors trailed 16-15 at the interval after a Joris Jurand try and 11 points from Harry Plummer’s boot. Sam Prendergast crossed for Leinster moments after the half-time break and they took full control when Clermont collapsed a scrum which handed the visitors a penalty try and led to Nohem Ez Zahouany being sent to the sin-bin.Leinster quickly took advantage of their numerical superiority as Sheehan touched down for his second try of the afternoon. Mathys Belaubre crossed for Clermont’s second try of the day, Jack Conan quickly responded with a converted score that gave Leinster a 20-point advantage when the penalty expired. Tommy O’Brien’s 76th-minute try then added gloss to the score as the Irish side wrapped up an impressive victory on French soil.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn Pool 3, theStormersran in seven tries in a 49-12 thumping ofBristolin their Champions Cup opener. The home side were on top from the start in Cape Town, with Seabelo Senatla scoring their first try in the seventh minute before Leolin Zas added a second eight minutes later.Joe Owen broke away down the wing for a solo try for Bristol in the 22nd minute but Jonny Roche restored Stormers’ advantage before the half-hour mark. JJ Kotze was shown a 20-minute red card for head-to-head contact before the break, while a yellow card for Zas – resulting in a disallowed try – gave the Bears a significant numerical advantage that they took advantage of through a first try for the club from Sol Moody.However, Roche then scored his second and the final 10 minutes was a horror show for Bristol as they conceded three more tries. First, Warrick Gelant crossed, then Andre-Hugo Venter got in on the act before Vas ended an eventful game with his second – with all seven tries converted by Sacha Feinberg-Mngomezulu.Also in Pool 3, Brian Gleeson paid the perfect tribute to the late Anthony Foley, relinquishing the No 8 jersey then scoringMunster’sopening try in a 33-25 win overRacing 92. The No 8 jersey was retired for the night at Supervalu Pairc ui Chaoimh in honour of the club’s former captain and head coach, who died aged 42 on the eve of a clash between the same teams in 2016.Gleeson instead wore No 24 and gave the Irish side a seventh-minute lead when he powered over the line. That helped his side take a 14-6 half-time lead, Shay McCarthy adding a second score. Both teams touched down three times in an expansive second half, Tadhg Beirne, Fineen Wychereley and Craig Casey for the hosts, who never surrendered the lead, while Wilfried Hulleu, Maxime Machenaud and Joey Manu responded for the French team. Charlie O’Shea converted three times on debut and Antoine Gibert kicked 10 points in a losing cause.In Pool 4, theBullsbeatStadeFrançais21-6, whileBathwere dealt a second-half lesson byMontpellieras they fell to a 32-14 defeat at The Rec. The home side led 14-10 at the interval after Ollie Lawrence and Arthur Green both scored tries following Stuart Hogg’s opener.However, Joe Cokanasiga then wasted a golden opportunity to extend Bath’s advantage after the interval and the French side capitalised. Donovan Taofifenua crossed in the corner to give Montpellier the lead before he then intercepted Finn Russell’s pass to deliver a quickfire double. Alex Becognee made the points safe for the visiting side after Josh Bayliss’s try forBathwas ruled out because of an earlier infringement.Explore more on these topicsChampions CupSaleGlasgow RugbyStade FrançaisBullsRugby unionLeinsternewsShareReuse this content

title: Europe is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a  super-club | Europa League | The Guardian
description: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: The four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domestically
Content: Sunderland’s Noah Sadiki celebrates scoring against Torreense. Bournemouth and Sunderland are prospering in the Europa League but the price for lively adventures abroad is high domestically.Photograph: Octávio Passos/UEFA/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSunderland’s Noah Sadiki celebrates scoring against Torreense. Bournemouth and Sunderland are prospering in the Europa League but the price for lively adventures abroad is high domestically.Photograph: Octávio Passos/UEFA/Getty ImagesInside footballEuropa LeagueEurope is a blast – but more a curse than a blessing if you are not a  super-clubJonathan WilsonThe four Premier League clubs playing in the lesser continental competitions face each other on Sunday – but three are struggling domesticallySat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.02 EDTShareThe sun shone. The temperature was in the high 20s. There was a mood of great conviviality. If you were struggling with the official allocation, it turned out you could just email the president of Torreense and he’d sort you out. Were these “Nuno-tickets” real? It turned out they were. Not only that, but you could sit anywhere you wanted in a stadium too big for the game and, if you happened to have gravitated to the comfortable hospitality seating at the back of the lower tier, the beer was inexplicably free.Locals in Leiria seemed bewildered but could hardly have been more accommodating. A beer pump had been installed outside a patisserie on the Praça Francisco Rodrigues Lobo, whose owner soon found fans happy to help stack empty barrels if that facilitated the free flow of Sagres. “There was a meeting at the town hall to explain these are not hooligans,” said the owner of a radical leftist flammkuchen restaurant between the square and the cathedral. “They told us the club comes from the labour movement and I found that very interesting.” And how had she found the fans? “Noisy, but with a quirky sense of humour.”Do Premier League teams really need to run more to win matches?Read moreThis was everything Sunderland fans could have wished for from their first European away game in 53 years and more. They had seen other fans experience these things, and now they could tick off the checklist: complicated travel to a pretty foreign town they would otherwise never visit, a fussy Albanian referee and a great sense of togetherness and community. There was evenan injury-time winnerfrom, miracle of miracles, Noah Sadiki.Ask any of the 5,000 or so Wearsiders who made the trip to Portugal if the Europa League was worth it and the answer would be unanimous. Bournemouth,Crystal Palaceand Brighton fans would surely say something similar: European football, especially for clubs who are unfamiliar with it, is a joy and an adventure. It generates experiences that will be remembered for ever, and if the cost is that the risk of relegation goes up, that’s a price worth paying. Others at those clubs may see things differently.View image in fullscreenSunderland fans enjoyed a trip they will remember for ever when they played TorreensePhotograph: Paulo Cunha/EPAThe four Premier League clubs involved in the lesser two European competitions play each other on Sunday.Brighton are thriving; the other three are not. Palace were 12th before the weekend fixtures but not playing well. Bournemouth against Sunderland is a battle of third- and fourth-bottom. Whether the Europa League football can yet be blamed is debatable.Brighton surely can’t be bucking the trendjust because of the lesser demands of the Conference League. Thursday’s was only the second round of Europa League league games, and the clubs involved bypassed a round of the Carabao Cup; fatigue may come but it shouldn’t be an issue yet.There are other factors at play. Sunderland have already played Manchester City, Arsenal, Brighton and Brentford, the top four going into this weekend. They could easily have been a couple of goals up by half-time at Brentford. They missed a penalty to go ahead against Arsenal. They registered an xG of 2.72 inlosing 5-3 at Manchester City. Only in thedefeat to Brightonlast weekend have they really disappointed. In the equivalent six games last season (substituting Ipswich for Burnley), Sunderland took only one point; in that sense, they are actually three points better off this campaign.But that can’t alter the fact that four points from six games leaves them beginning to fret. There is pressure on this next run of fixtures: afterBournemouth, they are home to Leeds, then away to Coventry. Sunderland’s transfer business left a major question on the right of the forward line that has yet to be resolved. A lack of depth in certain areas has been exposed by injuries to Brian Brobbey and Habib Diarra, although both players were on the bench on Thursday.Bournemouth have also lost key players to injury. Eli JuniorKroupi, who scored 13 league goals last season, has not played this campaign. Neither has Amine Adli, although he came off the bench on Thursday, as did Justin Kluivert, who had been out for a month. Most damagingly of all, perhaps, after impressing for England against Croatia,Alex Scott has been ruled outwith a thigh injury.The transition away from Andoni Iraola was always likely to be disruptive and, while Saturday’s5-1 defeat at Chelseawas a jolt, their other losses this season wereto Manchester CityandLiverpool. There has been a sense of margins going against them, of draws that might have been wins. The concern, as with Sunderland, comes if that affects morale, and decent displays that have yielded disappointing results curdle into disappointing performances.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenÁlvaro Rodríguez scores Bournemouth’s third goal against Sturm Graz, but they have found domestic assignments tougher.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersPalace are in a slightly different position. Other than City, their fixture list has been relatively kind. Seven points from six games would constitute comfortable survival if extrapolated over the season as a whole, but Opta’s expected points table, which has Bournemouth ninth andSunderland10th, has them 18th. A new manager is settling in, Maxence Lacroix and Daniel Múñoz were sold over the summer, while Jean-Philippe Mateta hasn’t played since the opening weekend.For none of those three sides can unsettled starts be blamed entirely or even primarily on Europe. That said, the evidence is clear: over the past five years, teams who did not play in Europe the previous season see their league position fall when they do play in Europe: Palace dropped from 12th to 15th, Nottingham Forest from seventh to 16th, Newcastle from fifth to 12th, Brighton from sixth to 11th, West Ham from sixth to seventh. Of those examples, only Forest even came vaguely close to relegation, but the fear nags away.Although winning theEuropa Leaguewould bring the vast rewards of Champions League football, losing in the final would probably bring in not much more than £20m for a Premier League club, plus gate receipts and whatever intangible benefits there might be from increased exposure. To put that in context, that’s roughly the difference between finishing ninth and 14th in the Premier League.Which is to say that while fans revel in trips to Milan, Prague or Lyon, for club executives a few nice mini-breaks do not balance out the potential financial headaches.Explore more on these topicsEuropa LeagueInside footballSunderlandCrystal PalaceBournemouthConference LeagueBrighton & Hove AlbioncommentShareReuse this content

title: Ombudsman shines in Champion Stakes for Gosden team at Ascot: Champions Day – as it happened | Horse racing | The Guardian
description: Ombudsman emphatically reversed the form from last year’s Champion Stakes with a defeat of Calandagan in the feature race on Champions Day at Ascot
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Ombudsman emphatically reversed the form from last year’s Champion Stakes with a defeat of Calandagan in the feature race on Champions Day at Ascot
Content: 9h ago12.00 EDTOMBUDSMAN THE HIGHLIGHT OF GODOLPHIN'S CHAMPIONS DAY TREBLEGreg WoodOmbudsman,the 5-4 favourite, emphatically reversed the form from last year’sChampion Stakeswith a three-and-three-quarter length defeat ofCalandaganin the feature race onChampions Dayat Ascot on Saturday.William Buickwas always travelling well aboard the favourite as his pacemaker, Devil’s Advocate, cut out the early running, andOmbudsmanresponded instantly when his rider asked for a finishing kick.Calandagan,who was slow from the stalls, made some inroads into his lead from the rear approaching the furlong pole but Ombudsman then kicked again to put the result beyond doubt.Ombudsmanmay now retire to stud as one of the top-rated horses in world racing although John Gosden, who trains the five-year-old with his son, Thady, also floated a possibility afterwards that he could have a swansong in theBreeders’ Cup Turfat Keeneland in two weeks’ time.“He’s the right type of horse and I think the track would suit him,” Gosden said, “so it’s a possibility. We don’t have to make a rapid decision.”Ombudsman’s success completed a double for the Godolphin operation in the two most valuable races on the card, following a win for Charlie Appleby’sTalk Of New Yorkin the preceding Queen Elizabeth II Stakes.“It’s exciting,” Appleby said. “He’s a three-year-old, he’s not done too much wrong in his career apart from immaturity early on, but thankfully that looks like it has been ironed out and he’s progressing with age.“That will be him finished for this year, he’ll head into winter quarters and you’ll see him again next spring.”Aidan O’Brien’s two fancied runners in the feature events,Constitution River(Champion Stakes) andGstaad(QEII), both failed to fire, but the reigning champion trainer had earlier swapped Group One wins with his big rival for this year’s championship, Andrew Balding.O’Brien’sMinnie Hauk took theFillies & Mares Stakes, a race in which Balding’s mareKalpanawas the well-beaten favourite, whileMount Atlassprang a 33-1 shock for the Balding stable in theLong Distance Cup.As a result,Baldingis less than £80k behindO’Brienin the title race, which runs until 31 December, and while O’Brien may have runners only at Doncaster’sFuturity Trophymeeting between now and the end of the year, Balding can target the extensive all-weather programme to close the gap.O’Brien,who would have been almost unbackable had he taken out one of the feature events, is quoted at around 4-7 to win a third consecutive title, while Balding can be backed at around 5-4.ShareUpdated at12.10 EDT

title: England stunned as Tonga tonking leaves Rugby League World Cup hopes in shreds | Rugby League World Cup 2026 | The Guardian
description: England men’s prospects of reaching the knockout stages of the Rugby League World Cup are hanging by a thread already after a 30-12 loss to Tonga
Author: Aaron Bower
Headline: England men’s prospects of reaching the knockout stages of the Rugby League World Cup are hanging by a thread already after a 30-12 loss to Tonga
Content: England’s Victor Radley is brought down to earth by Jason Taumalolo as Tonga sprung a surprise in Perth.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPView image in fullscreenEngland’s Victor Radley is brought down to earth by Jason Taumalolo as Tonga sprung a surprise in Perth.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAPRugby League World Cup 2026England stunned as Tonga tonking leaves Rugby League World Cup hopes in shredsPool B + C: England 12-30 TongaEngland Women thump Wales 70-6Aaron BowerSat 17 Oct 2026 07.35 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Rugby League World Cup began with a sense of mission improbable for England, but after one game, it already represents something more like mission impossible.The talk pre-tournament from Brian McDermott had been about being different. Going against the grain of how the national team has played against the world’s best and falling short; having a creative spark that would be significant in crucial moments. For all the talk of change, the most important thing of all remained the same in Perth on Saturday: the result.Australia cruise past Samoa in women’s Rugby League World Cup openerRead moreWhoever lost this game was always going to be a victim of the farcical format this reduced World Cup has in place. The six nations from Groups B and C will be put into a combined league table with the top two joining the winners and runners-up of Group A in the semi-finals.This defeat, arguably of England’s own making given their profligacy in attack and critical disciplinary lapses, means they are now relying on favours elsewhere. England need Tonga to beat Samoa on 1 November while they pile on the points against Papua New Guinea and France to stand any chance.The most plausible outcome, though, is that England are heading home in a fortnight and it would be the first time they have not made at least the final four. A damning indictment on the English game, at a time when its administrators are once again stalling over a deal to sanctionmuch-needed NRL investment.This contest could have been different. For half an hour England were excellent, pushing Tonga on to the back foot with intuitive and entertaining second-phase rugby. But when they found themselves in Tonga territory, just like in last year’s Ashes, England did not have the creative capability to find a decisive play.That meant Tonga could absorb a lot of what England threw their way and responded with Stefano Utoikamanu’s try somewhat against the run of play. The outstanding Isaiya Katoa converted the try and added two penalties to put Tonga ahead by 10 at half-time. Harsh? Perhaps. But this is international rugby: where the margins are fine.View image in fullscreenHaumole Olakau’atu celebrates a try for Tonga.Photograph: Janelle St Pierre/Getty Images“We opened them up in that first 20 and found ourselves in good positions, but we had some scrappy finishes,” McDermott said. “It was too erratic. Our gameplan doesn’t need to change, we just need to be patient.“It was a really good contest and I thought we stood toe to toe with them for nearly all the game. They’re a big, strong team and they’ve got some tremendous players. There’s tonnes of positives to take. There’s one or two glaring things that we need to get rid of, such as losing possession, but we’ll be chasing the good stuff.”However, the format means patience will be in short supply. In contrast, Tonga remain in control of their own destiny. Roared on by a passionate Mate Ma’a fanbase, they won the crucial moments and showed greater composure on their opponents’ line. AJ Brimson’s early second-half try looked as though it had swung momentum back England’s way, but penalties relieved the pressure for Tonga and they took advantage.Quick GuideEngland 12-30 Tonga: teams and scorersShowEnglandBrimson; Young, Savala, Farnworth, Eckersley; Williams, Smith; King, O’Neill, Thompson, Nsemba, Pearce-Paul, Radley.InterchangeCurrie, Litten, Havard, Walters.TriesBrimson, Young.GoalsSavala 2.TongaHopoate; Watene-Zelezniak, Koula, Toia, Fifita; Fainu, Katoa; Fonua-Blake, Foketi, Taumalolo, Olakau’atu, Wong, Frizell.InterchangeLolohea, Utoikamanu, Vaimauga, Halasima.TriesUtoikamanu, Olakau'atu 2, Koula.GoalsKatoa 7.RefereeG Sutton (Aus).Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Katoa’s clever kick caught England out and allowed Haumole Olakau’atu the space to score. Three minutes later, Tonga struck a devastating blow as Tui Lolohea cut the English defence open with the boot, Toluta’u Koula reacting fastest. England were in big trouble.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSport in FocusOur picture editors select their favourite sporting images from the past week, from the spectacular to the powerful, and with a little bit of fun thrown inEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThey threatened a grandstand finale when Dom Young finished a slick move in the corner, but with 10 minutes left, Tonga re-established control through Olaka’atu’s second and another wonderful move in the final moments meant Koula claim his second late on.Some of England’s problems, as McDermott admitted, were indeed of their own making. With time, they can be cleaned up. But here is the thing: England don’t have time. It might have already run out.View image in fullscreenAmelia Brown surges towards the try line to touch down for England against Wales.Photograph: Joel Carrett/EPAMeanwhile, England’s women warmed up for next Saturday’s game against the reigning world champions, Australia, with an eye-catching 70-6 win over Wales in their opening match.All eyes are on the English to see whether they can provide a competitive challenge to the all-conquering Jillaroos when they meet in Perth next Saturday to decide who wins Group A.Australia beat Samoa 40-0on Friday.Anna Davies and the debutant Connie Boyd scored hat-tricks for England, with Izzy Rowe scoring twice and finishing with a points haul of 26.Explore more on these topicsRugby League World Cup 2026England rugby league teamTongarugbyleagueteamRugby leagueEngland women's rugby league teamAustralia sportmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Boos for Arsenal as draw with Birmingham extends winless WSL run | Women's Super League | The Guardian
description: Olivia Smith’s strike for Arsenal followed Oceane Hurte’s solo goal in the 1-1 draw to make it five WSL matches without a win for Arsenal
Author: John Brewin
Headline: Olivia Smith’s strike for Arsenal followed Oceane Hurte’s solo goal in the 1-1 draw to make it five WSL matches without a win for Arsenal
Content: Renée Slegers said: ‘I don’t think we created enough in the first half.’Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRenée Slegers said: ‘I don’t think we created enough in the first half.’Photograph: Alex Burstow/Arsenal FC/Getty ImagesWomen's Super LeagueBoos for Arsenal as draw with Birmingham extends winless WSL runJohn BrewinSat 17 Oct 2026 11.44 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn equaliser from Olivia Smith averted defeat for Arsenal, but a home draw with Birmingham did little to calm fears for Renée Slegers’s future as Gunners coach. Boos accompanied the final whistle at the Emirates Stadium, as the result left Arsenal on six points from six matches and without a win in five Women’s Super League matches,the club’s longest winless runin WSL history. They are eighth in the table, nine points behind the leaders, Manchester City, who have played one game fewer.Birmingham opened the scoring at the start of the second half when Océane Hurtré coolly tapped in after her run from the halfway line went unchecked. Alessia Russo had hit the woodwork in the first half with a diving header, among a slew of Arsenal chances as Sophie Baggaley was kept the busier of the goalkeepers.The WSL so far: goal-shy Arsenal, underrated Brighton and more data pointersRead more“I don’t think we created enough in the first half,” said Slegers. “Second half is different. There was one player we needed to stop and that was Hurtré. But she came through in a fast break and a counter, we don’t defend that well enough.”After Smith’s spectacular strike, in the 66th minute, curled from outside the area, Arsenal would not find the winning goal that might ease pressure on Slegers. Baggaley’s goalkeeping and slack finishing meant Birmingham secured their point. “We are in a scenario we’ve had too many times season,” said Slegers.Next week for Arsenal is a north London derby with Tottenham, who kick off at Chelsea in fourth on Sunday. Slegers said: “The next game is always the next opportunity. [It’s good] we always keep going and we rise after setbacks.“We just need to put ourselves in better positions earlier so that’s not necessary every time because it takes energy from the team having to play those scenarios. But yes, the team has been brilliant. The urgency, the willingness, the desire in the second half was really good.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDespite those boos at the final whistle, Smith said of the home fans: “They always bring out great support, [we’re] so happy to have them here. Again, disappointed not to get the result, must be frustrating for them, but they stay with us and support us.”Explore more on these topicsWomen's Super LeagueArsenal WomenBirmingham City WomenWomen's footballmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Kartal battles past Ostapenko in Wuhan to secure spot in first WTA 1000 final | Tennis | The Guardian
description: Sonay Kartal’s dream comeback continued as the Briton beat Jelena Ostapenko 7-6 (9), 7-6 (5) to advance to the biggest final of her career at the Wuhan Open
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Sonay Kartal’s dream comeback continued as the Briton beat Jelena Ostapenko 7-6 (9), 7-6 (5) to advance to the biggest final of her career at the Wuhan Open
Content: Sonay Kartal becomes the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final since the format began in 2009.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersView image in fullscreenSonay Kartal becomes the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final since the format began in 2009.Photograph: Maxim Shemetov/ReutersTennisKartal battles past Ostapenko in Wuhan to secure spot in first WTA 1000 finalThe 24-year-old becomes new British No 1Biggest final of career after six months out with injuryPress AssociationSat 17 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSonay Kartal’s dream comeback continues as the Briton beat Jelena Ostapenko in straight sets on Saturday to advance to the biggest final of her career at the Wuhan Open. Kartal was behind in both sets and fought off six set points to claim a 7-6 (9), 7-6 (5) win over the former French Open champion in her second tour-level tournament back after injury.The 24-year-old, who started this week ranked world No 170 due to her recent inactivity, becomes the lowest-ranked player to reach a WTA 1000 final since the format began in 2009. The victory means Kartal is guaranteed to jump into the world’s top 50 in the WTA rankings next week, overtaking Katie Boulter to become the British No 1.“That was probably one of the toughest matches I’ve played in,” Kartal said. “At times [Ostapenko] is unplayable and sometimes you have to ride that wave. Mentally, this is one of the best performances I’ve had.”Kartal clawed back a double break in the opening set and rode her luck on serve before forcing a marathon tie-break, which she edged 11-9 after saving two set points. She also had to dig deep in the second set, recovering another break and saving two more set points on serve at 6-5, forcing a second tie-break that she took to complete the win.It extends a remarkable series of wins against the former Olympic champion Belinda Bencic, two-time slam finalist Jasmine Paolini and the world No 6, Elina Svitolina.Kartal made her breakthrough by reaching thefourth round of last year’s Wimbledon, but her career stalled after sustaining a back injury that kept her out of action for six months. She showed positive signs by winning two matches on her return at the China Open this month.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the other semi-final, a left-leg ⁠injury derailed Iga Swiatek as she ⁠went down ⁠fighting ​to Polish compatriot and childhood friend Maja ⁠Chwalinska 7-5, 6-1. Swiatek, a six-time grand slam ‌winner, ‌had to take a medical ‌timeout while trailing 6-5 in the first set and continued the match with a bandaged ‌left thigh, but found it difficult to ​put pressure on her leg and struggled to chase returns across the ⁠court.Explore more on these topicsTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty |  Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Michael Gove , produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke John Smith ; the executive producers are Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale | The Guardian
description: In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam
Author: Aditya Chakrabortty
Headline: In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam
Content: 58:18Radical Thinking with Aditya ChakraborttyPoliticsWhy Michael Gove worries about Britishness | Radical Thinking with Aditya ChakraborttyFor more than three decades, Michael Gove has been a leading figure in British Conservatism. As a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Tory bible, the Spectator, he has helped shape the right even as it has moved further rightwards. In the latest episode of Radical Thinking, Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s position on Islam.Aditya’s suggested reading:To read the fruits of Michael Gove’s dalliance with the Marxism Today gang, look up his essay in a 1998 collection called The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair.For a slalom ride through Michael Gove’s years in power, readThe Demented Dalekby the historian Richard J Evans in the London Review of Books.To learn more about what’s become of the British right, there’s acolumn by mefor the Guardian.Phil Burton-Cartledge examines why Britain's most successful political party is now failing in his bookThe Party’s Over: The Rise and Fall of the Conservatives from Thatcher to Sunak.Phil also writes a very good blog on British politics, which keeps a close eye on how each party is trying to marshal a coalition of voters.Herehe is on Kemi Badenoch.Geoffrey Wheatcroft offers an entertaining short narrative inBloody Panico!: or, Whatever Happened to The Tory PartyFor more on the economics of the Cameron years,this paperexamines how the Tories failed to move the UK away from being a country of renters towards a country of makers. Two of its authors will join us for a podcast later in the series.And if you want to read how Brexit may have cost the UK 8% of GDP, readthis paperbased on data from the Bank of England.Finally, on the Spectator, read Nesrine Malik’s recent column in the Guardian:Why has Britain’s oldest political magazine become such a rabid cheerleader for Islamophobia?Presented byAditya ChakraborttywithMichael Gove, produced byFrankie TobiandLuke John Smith; the executive producers areMaz Ebtehaj,Kirsty MajorandJames TindaleSat 17 Oct 2026 02.50 EDTShareExplore more on these topicsPoliticsRadical Thinking with Aditya ChakraborttyPolitics booksMichael GoveConservativesPodcastsThe SpectatorMagazines

title: Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and  scary – Chinese AI | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China
Content: Models such as DeepSeek  allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.Photograph: GK Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenModels such as DeepSeek  allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.Photograph: GK Images/AlamyViewpoint columnInternational tradeWhy Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and  scary – Chinese AIPhillip InmanIn the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from ChinaSat 17 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTShareThere is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed inChinaand handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They arecheaper than other EVs sold in the UKand, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries.Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level.It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again.Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last centuryin Tiananmen Square.A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule.Then came AI and the state discovered complete control.Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to.Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished.For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world.Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigoratedbelt and road initiativecreates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology.Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions.Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights.Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents.There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need.Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, asmany AI experts have documented. But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option.As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of theCentre for Information Resilience(CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation.He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.”Anevaluation reportby the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship.“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says.The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities.Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assumedata inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state.The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers.Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeViewpoint columnAI (artificial intelligence)EconomicsChinaAsia PacificAutomotive industryUK security and counter-terrorismcommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time | Jeffrey Ingold | The Guardian
description: If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …, says culture writer Jeffrey Ingold
Author: Jeffrey Ingold
Headline: If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …, says culture writer Jeffrey Ingold
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onMoviesThe hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on timeJeffrey IngoldIf cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …Sat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.43 EDTShareDo you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm.I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas. We are all the victims of their predatory time-wasting system.If you went to see a play and the ticket said the show started at 7.30pm, you’d rightly be annoyed if after 20 minutes the performance still hadn’t started. Yet when it comes to watching movies, we’ve collectively accepted that it’s fine for them to start later than advertised. Which also means we all put up with people coming in late, shining their phone torches and bumping into you because they tried to show up when the film actually starts.Now thatalmost a third of wide releases run over two hoursand pre-show advertising and trailers last for 20-30 minutes, something’s gotta give. I say films should start on time. I know a better moviegoing experience is possible. I grew up in Canada, where our cinemas played their films at the ticketed time and the ads started earlier. When my family showed up 10 minutes late to The Fellowship of the Ring, we missed the entire opening sequence explaining the history of the rings of power. We deserved that!A brave senator in Connecticut tried to tackle this injustice in 2025 with a bill that would “require the disclosure of accurate movie start times in advertisements and listings”. However, it was watered down to a mere “working group” after pushback from cinema operators. They warned they’d lose vital revenue if advertisers pulled back because people started skipping the pre-show entirely. Erin Brockovich wouldn’t have given in so easily.How can we succeed where the Connecticut senator failed? Simple: we also get rid of assigned seating. Say goodbye to paying£26 for an Ultra Lux reclinerif you want the best view. It’s a flat fee no matter where you sit. Welcome to the Hunger Games of cinema seating.If you want a “good” seat for a film, you have to earn it by showing up early. Exactly like when I was young, the ads and trailers will play before the start time so the film can begin promptly. Arrive on time, after the trailers, and you might be stuck in the front row, but that’s on you for avoiding the ads.I’m just a cinephile, standing in front of a movie theatre, asking it to respect me and my time. Why is that so hard?Jeffrey Ingold is a freelance journalist covering LGBTQ+ issues, music and cultureExplore more on these topicsFilmThe hill I will die onAdvertisingcommentShareReuse this content

title: As King Charles heads to the Caribbean, he should know what Winston Churchill admitted to 90 years ago | Kenneth Mohammed | The Guardian
description: Modern politicians play on tales of empire to exaggerate what Britain left behind, but the monarch should consider a historical speech on imperial plunder
Author: Kenneth Mohammed
Headline: Modern politicians play on tales of empire to exaggerate what Britain left behind, but the monarch should consider a historical speech on imperial plunder
Content: A flag being flown in Windrush Square calling for reparations during the fifth anniversary of remembering those impacted by the Windrush scandal.Photograph: Thabo Jaiyesimi/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA flag being flown in Windrush Square calling for reparations during the fifth anniversary of remembering those impacted by the Windrush scandal.Photograph: Thabo Jaiyesimi/SOPA Images/LightRocket/Getty ImagesOpinionGlobal developmentAs King Charles heads to the Caribbean, he should know what Winston Churchill admitted to 90 years agoKenneth MohammedModern politicians play on tales of empire to exaggerate what Britain left behind, but the monarch should consider a historical speech on imperial plunderSupported byAbout this contentSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 08.33 EDTShareFor us in the Caribbean, there is something surreal about Britain’s renewed nostalgia over empire. As Britain’s monarch prepares tovisit the Caribbean, and at a time when we in the former colonies are demanding to have a serious reckoning withslavery and reparations, UK politicians are invoking a dumbed-down distortion of history.Rewriting the facts: the Reform MP Robert Jenrick has argued that colonies owed Britain a “debt of gratitude” for the institutions empire bequeathed them. Jacob Rees-Mogg, a former minister in a Conservative government, hasdescribed British colonialismas “one of the greatest civilising, prosperity-creating forces the world has ever seen”. The opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch,has disputedcolonialism’s contribution to Britain’s prosperity. Then there is Suella Braverman. The Reform MP suggested in July that rather than Britain paying reparations,former colonies should repay Britainfor the investment and infrastructure provided under empire. This prompted Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, to call that proposition “asinine”. At best it is historical amnesia. At its worse it is an insidious misrepresentation of facts.The question from a global development perspective is: who developed whom? We can askEric Williams,Walter Rodney,George Padmoreor generations of African, Caribbean and Indian scholars. But there is one inconvenient witness that stands as a testimony to the truth. Winston Churchill.On 20 July 1937,Churchill addressedthe West India committee dinner at London’s Dorchester Hotel. Peter Hulme, emeritus professor of literature at the University of Essex, painstakingly reconstructed the provenanceof that speech.In it, Churchill reflected on how Britain became a global economic power. His words seem stark when placed alongside today’s politically sanitised recounts of empire. Britain’s possession of the West Indies and India, Churchill explained, provided “the strength, the support, but especially the capital, the wealth” that allowed Britain to survive its wars, dominate international commerce and establish its global commercial and financial leadership. Churchill was acknowledging that colonial wealth had financed the development of Britain.Churchill’s surviving notes contained an even more revealing phrase: Britain’sCaribbeanpossessions had provided “that unexpected margin of capital”, an advantage Hulme describes as arising from two centuries of Caribbean slavery.The conventional imperial story begins with what Britain left behind: railways, ports, courts, schools, parliamentary institutions, the English language and Christianity. It rarely begins with what Britain and Europe took away, or rather extracted, through exploitation and genocide. Railways and ports were integral to transporting colonial commodities to overseas markets.Colonialismwas an exploitative and violent system designed solely for the benefit of the coloniser.The Caribbean provides the clearest illustration. For generations, extraordinary wealth was produced through sugar by enslaved Africans and their descendants. Yet when slavery was abolished, Britain compensated not the enslaved but the enslavers.Hulme’s reconstruction of Churchill’s dinner provides an almost grotesquely appropriate snapshot of that political economy. Among those present was Lord Hailsham, whose family fortune was connected to Caribbean sugar and enslavement; his ancestor Charles McGarel received £129,464 in compensation following abolition for 2,489 enslaved people. About £101m in today’s money, by Hulme’s calculation. TheRegister of British Slave Traderspresents data on the13,000 investorsin the transatlantic trafficking of enslaved Africans. It reveals the impact on Britain’s development during its formative era. So, while the slave trade built generational wealth in Europe, it kidnapped and displaced about 13 million Africans, stealing and destroying their generational wealth.While Churchill celebrated imperial achievement at the Dorchester, Caribbean workers were rebelling against their economic conditions. The 1930s saw strikes and disturbances across the British Caribbean. Movements demanding political representation and self-government were gathering strength. These must seem strange expressions of gratitude to the rehabilitators of colonialism. They ask what Britain built rather than what Britain extracted. They count railways but not resources. They celebrate institutions while ignoring who those institutions were originally designed to govern and whose interests they protected. That is the part of the “gratitude” argument that is so troubling. It asks us to judge colonialism through the eyes of the coloniser.Most importantly, they treat development as something Britain bestowed upon the rest of humanity rather than a global historical process in which the labour, resources and markets of colonised peoples contributed heavily to Britain’s transformation. That is why the question of who developed who is consequential.Which brings us to King Charles. From 27 October to 4 November, he will visit the Bahamas, Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, culminating in the Commonwealth heads of government meeting. Buckingham Palace describes the visit in terms of community and a shared future. But is this royal diplomacy an attempt to contain or dissuadeCaribbean demandsfor reparatory justice and constitutional independence?View image in fullscreenThe then Prince of Wales, now King Charles, and Duchess of Cornwall with a group of musicians at Bob Marley’s former home in Kingston, Jamaica, 2008.Photograph: Anwar Hussein/WireImageBritain faces growing demands to confront its colonial responsibilities. Jamaica is pursuing alegal routenow. However, in 2014, several Caribbean countries attempted to sue the British government for reparations. Britain then used jurisdiction issues arising from the Commonwealth toblock the claim. Caribbean and some African governments continue to press for dialogue yet several, seemingly suffering from Stockholm syndrome, persist in retaining the British monarch as head of state: Antigua and Barbuda, Bahamas, Belize, Grenada, Jamaica, St Kitts and Nevis, St Lucia, and St Vincent and the Grenadines.Buckingham Palace has already confirmed that Charles will not formally apologise for Britain’s involvement in slavery. Apparently, apologies and reparations are matters for government, which opposes paying reparations. Charles has expressed personal sorrow over slavery and described it as an atrocity. But sorrow without accountability is a meaningless attempt at appeasing the “natives”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Commonwealth presents itself as an association of equal, independent nations, committed to democracy, development and cooperation. Its supporters point to diplomatic access, technical assistance, educational opportunities, election observation and collective influence on the climate crisis, debt and development. But membership must be judged by outcomes, not colonial sentiment.If Commonwealth countries cannot secure meaningful engagement from Britain on one of their most consequential historical grievances, how equal is the relationship in practice? What influence do smaller members genuinely exercise over the priorities of the organisation’s wealthiest and most powerful states? And does membership provide sufficient economic and diplomatic benefits to justify its continued symbolic association with an empire whose historical injustices remain unresolved?These questions are particularly relevant to Caribbean states confronting climate vulnerability, high debt burdens and persistent structural economic disadvantage. The Commonwealth cannot remain an instrument of British soft power, where royal receptions and appeals to shared history substitute for substantive economic justice. Therefore, proposals on reparations warrant serious negotiation, even where governments disagree about legal liability and historical responsibility.As King Charles arrives in the Caribbean, there will be welcoming ceremonies and speeches about friendship and solidarity. But these crucial questions remain unanswered.Churchill concluded, on that now-forgotten evening in London: “We could never forget the patriotism and loyalty of the West Indies in those historic times to the mother country.”The Caribbean should welcome genuine partnership. It need not accept neocolonialism and historical amnesia as its price.Kenneth Mohammed is a freelance writer and Caribbean analyst with a focus on corruptionExplore more on these topicsGlobal developmentOpinionColonialismKing Charles IIICaribbeanReparations and reparative justiceWinston ChurchillSlaverycommentShareReuse this content

title: Women just want to work out in peace. Why all the thigh-rubbing lechery? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: On Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also pernicious, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: On Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also pernicious, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Shane Gillis during his appearance on Saturday Night Live.Photograph: NBC/Will Heath/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenShane Gillis during his appearance on Saturday Night Live.Photograph: NBC/Will Heath/Getty ImagesOpinionFitnessWomen just want to work out in peace. Why all the thigh-rubbing lechery?Emma BeddingtonOn Saturday Night Live last week, comedian Shane Gillis made a pathetic ‘joke’ about the clothes women wear to the gym. It was puerile – but also perniciousSat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTShareI’ve spent the morning doing Shane Gillis’s work: checking out women in the gym. If you’ve avoided Gillis thus far, apologies for enlightening you – he’s a “comedian” who recently told a“joke” on Saturday Night Livethat began: “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dressed like whores now.”Well, reporting for duty from the weight room, here’s the clothing tally: eight women in leggings and T-shirts; six in T-shirts and trackie bottoms; five in shorts and vest tops; one in a crop top and leggings. It’s not exactly the Folies Bergère – there’s not much, I would have thought, to cause Gillis to blush. But maybe I’m wrong – how undressed, exactly, constitutes whorish? Is a glimpse of a female forearm a distracting provocation? Should we pull up our socks to avoid inflaming male passions with our slutty ankles when we’re doing step-ups?There’s a long, grim history of women trying to do physical activity in appropriate clothes and not being allowed, or feeling able to. We might not be sweating in floor-length dresses and corsets likeearly Olympian women, but bros are still complaining about girls doing squats in shorts in their eyeline, staring, propositioning and commenting (the#gymcreep hashtagis a veritable rogues’ gallery of them). Even Gillis’s language isn’t, unfortunately, exceptional: after his monologue, fitness writer Mikala Jamison shared a message on herSubstackfrom a man she considered a friend, saying a gym had “whores everywhere”.Thigh-rubbing lechery around women’s workout gear, however jokey, is gross and infuriating, but it’s more pernicious than that. Women get alienated from sport and fitness when they’re not allowed to feel comfortable in their bodies and clothes:research by the England hockey player Tess Howardfound that many girls were put off sport because of clothing requirements and concerns around sexualisation, whileWomen in Sportfound more than 1 million girls in the UK “fall out of love” with sport in their teenage years. Women are less active than men, with38% still not doing 150 minutes of exercise a week. When girls and women are deprived of, or never allowed to develop, a sense of ease and enjoyment around having a body in public, this is the result.I say “enjoyment” specifically because that’s something I think gets left aside in making the inarguable, entirely correct, case that what women wear to work out for comfort, practicality or ease of movement, is nobody’s business but their own. But what about pleasure? Gyms are many things – a refuge, a third space, a repository of crimes against music – but they’re also a place toenjoyyour body, including how it looks.I know, because going to the gym made me feel good about (bits of) mine for the first time since puberty. I was the one in the crop top this morning, flaunting my stretchmarks, hernia and distended belly button, yes, but also the results of two years’ hard work. I’m proud I can lift a wardrobe now, but I’m also proud to look a bit pumped. It gives me confidence: enough to walk into strange weight rooms full of men wherever I happen to be and do my thing. Those experiences in turn have shown me that most gym-goers of both sexes aren’t remotely interested in what anyone else is doing, or wearing – they’re working on (maybe admiring!) themselves.But I’m 51, and my experience of the gym isn’t the same as it is for younger women.Sport England researchpublished this summer found 19% of women aged 16-34 felt uncomfortable or unsafe in fitness centres because of the possibility of harassment or intimidation; 86% reported experiencing physical, verbal, non-verbal or online harassment or intimidation in a fitness or leisure centre in the last three years. This kind of comment feeds the fear, and emboldens aggressors, making it not just unfunny, but depressing and enraging. Everyone should be able to enjoy moving their body unmolested, that’s a given. But dammit, we should also get to enjoy wearing short shorts, second-skin leggings and spaghetti-strap tops. To look safely and happily in a gym mirror and find ourselves, yeah, a bit fit.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Letby public inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safe | Mark McDonald | The Guardian
description: I fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyone, says Lucy Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald
Author: Mark McDonald
Headline: I fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyone, says Lucy Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald
Content: ‘The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreen‘The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAOpinionLucy LetbyThe Letby public inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safeMark McDonaldI fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyoneMark McDonald is a barrister representing Lucy LetbySat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 03.31 EDTShareIhave been Lucy Letby’s barrister for the past two years. I have spent thousands of hours going through the evidence, speaking to experts and examining what happened to the babies who died or became seriously unwell on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. I have worked with nearly 30 experts, including internationally recognised specialists in neonatology, pathology, insulin, statistics and other fields. It may be to some an inconvenient truth, but I am convinced that Letby is innocent, and her convictions represent one of the most serious miscarriages of justice in modern British legal history. That means she was failed by the police, the NHS, the criminal justice system and, importantly, a plethora of experts who simply got it wrong.My work on the case has also raised wider concerns about the evidence and conclusions surrounding the deaths on the neonatal unit, and what the lessons being drawn fromthis casewill mean for doctors and nurses in neonatal medicine.Neonatal units are among the most demanding environments in theNHS. These are tiny, desperately ill babies. Their condition can change within minutes, and doctors and nurses make difficult decisions under enormous pressure, often with incomplete information.Sometimes, despite the best care, babies die. That is an uncomfortable truth, but any serious discussion about neonatal safety has to acknowledge it. What worries me is that we risk creating a culture in which clinicians become frightened to work in these environments.Imagine being a doctor working a night shift in a neonatal unit. A baby’s condition suddenly deteriorates and you have to make decisions quickly, but despite your efforts they die. Then, years later, the circumstances of those decisions are reconstructed with the benefit of hindsight. Every action is examined. Every decision is questioned. And the possibility of a criminal investigation hangs over the process. Who would still want to work in neonatal medicine?This is not only atheoretical question. The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions. We need them to be able to say: “I don’t know”. We need them to admit mistakes, report near misses and challenge colleagues and managers. Above all, we need them to tell the truth.For many years, the NHS has tried to develop what is often described as a learning or “no-blame” culture. The idea behind this was never that there should be no accountability. What it means is that when something goes wrong, the first questions should be: what happened? Why did it happen? And what can we learn?A public inquiry set up after Letby’s convictions, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall,delivered its reportin mid-September. The report placed great emphasis on monitoring and surveillance, and specifically stated a needto move away from the no-blame culture. These recommendations risk creating a surveillance society within the NHS, where clinicians fear that every adverse outcome may lead to scrutiny and blame. Patient safety depends on openness, trust and learning from mistakes, not a culture of suspicion in which clinical error, systemic failure and deliberate criminal conduct become dangerously blurred.That would be a terrible unintended consequence. The safest NHS is not one in which staff are frightened of making mistakes and practise defensively. It is one in which staff feel safe enough to admit mistakes.Thirlwall’s is not the first major inquiry into failures in maternity and neonatal care. Over the past two decades, there have been major investigations into trusts inMorecambe Bay,Shrewsbury and Telford,East KentandNottingham, among others. Again and again, inquiries have found problems with leadership, communication, escalation, teamwork and listening. Again and again, recommendations have been made and promises given that the NHS will learn. So perhaps we need to ask a more difficult question: why hasn’t it?The answer cannot simply be that we need another set of rules, another layer of monitoring, or another system for identifying individual responsibility. We need to listen to the people who actually work in these units. This is where I am particularly critical of the government, of successive governments.Who is asking what these changes will feel like to a nurse working a 12-hour shift in an understaffed neonatal intensive care unit? Who is asking what it will feel like to a doctor knowing that an unexpected clinical outcome could result in years of scrutiny? The government has a responsibility to protect patients. But it also has a responsibility to protect the workforce on whom patient safety depends. The two things are inseparable.I think trade unions also have a responsibility here. They should defend patients, but they should also defend their members. This does not mean defending wrongdoing. It means defending fairness, and making sure that a doctor or nurse is judged in the circumstances in which they actually made a decision, rather than simply with the benefit of hindsight. It means recognising that an adverse clinical outcome is not evidence of criminal conduct.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere has been remarkably little public debate about the possibility that the response to Thirlwall’s inquiry could create fear among NHS workers. Furthermore, no Labour MP has spoken up, and that silence matters.The Thirlwall recommendations risk creating an environment in which a disgruntled healthcare professional can point the finger at another, triggering investigations that can quickly become criminal investigations.The doctors and nurses caring for vulnerable newborns deserve protection from unfair hindsight, disproportionate suspicion and a culture in which every adverse outcome becomes a potential question of individual blame. Because if the lesson we take from the Thirlwall inquiry is that we need more blame, more surveillance and more fear, then I worry that we will have learned the wrong lesson.We will not have made the NHS safer. We will simply have made it harder for the NHS to care for the babies who need it most.Mark McDonald is a criminal defence and human rights barrister specialising in miscarriages of justiceDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
