title: French schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truth | Rokhaya Diallo | The Guardian
description: To protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not, says Guardian Europe columnist Rokhaya Diallo
Author: Rokhaya Diallo
Headline: To protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not, says Guardian Europe columnist Rokhaya Diallo
Content: Police preparing to charge against pupils and students in Paris, France, on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Tonny Linke/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice preparing to charge against pupils and students in Paris, France, on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Tonny Linke/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionFranceFrench schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truthRokhaya DialloTo protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is notSat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 04.53 EDTShareAs a secondary school pupil in 1994, I took part inprotestsagainst a reform that would have allowed French employers to pay young people below the minimum wage. Our campaign was successful, but if we had had to face the terrifying police responseunleashed on student protestersin France over recent weeks, I would have stayed at home.A 14-year-old boy, Eden, suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out after a police teargas grenade struck him in the face. Sixteen-year-old Maëllostthe sight in one eye allegedly after being struck by a shot from an LBD, a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Evan, 15, had his hand blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. And in Dunkirk, a police SUV is alleged to have driven repeatedlyat groupsof secondary school pupils, as an officer could be heard saying: “Come closer, we’ll smash their fucking faces in.”Accountsfrom children left terrified by brutal treatment in police custody describe traumatic experiences with severe psychological and physical consequences.France, the self-styled home of human rights, is now attracting the kind of international legal scrutiny you would expect if this were an authoritarian regime gone mad. The human rights organisation Ligue des droits de l’Hommehas condemnedthe alarming “brutalisation of young people”, and the threat to their freedom of expression.A UN special rapporteurhas calledon the French authorities to respect the physical safety of protesters. The UN human rights officesaysit is following incidents surrounding the protests in France “with concern”. Amnesty International hascalled for the suspensionof rubber-bullet launchers at school protests, condemned the disproportionate use of force and reminded the authorities of their duty to protect children. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, whose activism increasingly encompasses struggles against oppression and state violence,travelled to Francethis week to support school pupils.View image in fullscreenA student checks her smartphone in front of the Helene Boucher high school during a protest in Paris, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Teresa Suarez)Photograph: Teresa Suárez/APIt is often argued that France is broke, and that crippling debt levels make the student demand for€10bn of investmentto improve their learning conditions a non-starter. But even in our difficult fiscal position, public spending is a political choice: to reduce debt you can cut public spending or you can raise revenue.Economists Élise Huillery and Romane Paris have come up with acredible proposalfor investing an additional €11.8bn a year in education, funded through tax reform targeting large inheritances, raising €12.7bn in 2026 and increasing taxes only for the wealthiest 1% of heirs. This would make money available to raise teachers’ pay, improve support for pupils, student grants and housing, and expand university places.But the debate about public spending does not invalidate the legitimate grievances of pupils, teachers and parents, which are not new. Nor does it justify a vicious law and order response. Learning conditions in some of the most disadvantaged schools have been deteriorating to shockingly poor levels for a long time. I highlighted school conditions in France in the Guardianthree years ago, arguing then that the state education system was among the most unequal in the developed world. The lack of resources assigned to such basic things as teaching vacancies has been glaringly apparent for years, with jobs in some districts sometimes left unfilled for months.More than 20m teaching hours were lost in state secondary schools in 2024-25, equivalent to almost one in 10 lessons. More than 15m of those hours were lost because no replacement teachers were provided. Schools in designated priority education areas, which serve disadvantaged communities, have been particularly affected,according to France’s National Audit Office.In Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest part of mainland France, two-thirds of school doctor posts were vacant in 2023. As early as 2022, the Créteil education authorityreporteda shortfall of 60 school nurses and 20 social workers, with 90% of the unfilled posts in Seine-Saint-Denis. In 2025,49 suicideswere recorded among staff in the national education system. While these deaths cannot all be attributed to work, it is hard to avoid thinking of the severe deterioration in working conditions across the sector.Then there are the schools that are physicallyfalling apart: water that isunsafe to drinkbecause of bacterial contamination, pupilsreporting ratsandcockroaches,filthy toilets, and in one case, a septic tank that overflows when it rains. There are power cuts, missing furniture and some classrooms are sopoorly insulatedthat temperatures fall below 14C in winter and hit 40C during heatwaves.In Mayotte, where protests began, a secondary school built for 900 pupils is accommodating 2,300. The protests then spread to mainlandFrancethrough a school in Créteil that began the academic year short of 13 teachers and other staff, as well as a deputy headteacher.Another issue at the core of pupils’ anger is Parcoursup, the system through which school leavers apply for higher education. Seen as discriminatory, it has left 126,000 applicants – many from disadvantaged backgrounds –without a placethis year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRather than deal with this crisis as justified social protest based on legitimate demands, the government has invoked a doctrine set out in its Operational Guide to Urban Violence. It hastreated school pupils as internal enemiesto be neutralised. This sets up a coercive response, disregarding the possibility of resolving the conflict through constructive measures.By 8 October,6,877 people had been taken into police custody, about 80% of them children. On 1 October alone, police made 1,949 arrests, exceeding the highest single-day total recorded since 1961,saysthe historian Éric Anceau.According tothe Syndicat de la magistrature, a French judges’ leftwing union, the numbers reflect a clear determination to crush the movement. So overwhelming has the police deployment been thatteachersandparentshave had to form human chains to protect children.The police operations are also driven by a focus on arrests, which encourages forceful confrontations and fuels the escalation. This in turn draws more people into rioting. About 700 police officers and a number of teachers have been injured since the start of the unrest.The sociologist Olivier Fillieulepoints outthat policing protests requires an assessment of risk. If the swift break-up a blockade exposes teenagers to serious injury, you have to consider alternatives. Temporarily accepting a degree of disorder when immediate intervention risks creating more of it should remain a guiding principle of policing protests, Filleule says, noting that the French authorities know how to apply restraint when farmers stage blockades.Yet while the police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence, the interior minister Laurent Nuñezsaidhe had given the forces “no instructions to exercise restraint”. This is a shameful and contemptuous way to respond to young people’s healthy expression of dissent. Such violence towards citizens has no place in a democracy.Rokhaya Diallo is a French journalist, film-maker, activist andGuardian EuropecolumnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Plan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in England | Business | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Ministers considering overhaul of apprenticeship funding scheme to tackle youth jobs crisis
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Exclusive: Ministers considering overhaul of apprenticeship funding scheme to tackle youth jobs crisis
Content: Andy Burnham meets an apprentice during a visit to BAE Systems’s submarine skills academy in Barrow-in-Furness.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham meets an apprentice during a visit to BAE Systems’s submarine skills academy in Barrow-in-Furness.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/AFP/Getty ImagesBusinessPlan to make firms pay more to train older workers than youth apprentices in EnglandExclusive: Ministers considering overhaul of apprenticeship funding scheme to tackle youth jobs crisisRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentSat 17 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmployers in England are to be forced to pay more to train an older worker than a youth apprentice under plans being drawn up by the government to tackle the youth jobs crisis.The Guardian understands ministers plan to overhaul Labour’sapprenticeship funding schemeto increase the cost of training by 25% for a worker over the age of 25 in order to encourage businesses to train young people instead.Aiming to reverse a40% drop in youth apprenticeship startsover the past decade, the proposal is being developed as part of the government response to Alan Milburn’s review into why so many young people are out of work.With his final report delayed until after the budget, the former Labour cabinet minister this week signalled thatboosting access to apprenticeshipswould be critical for fixing the first rungs of the career ladder for young people.The chancellor, John Healey, is preparing to include measures to tackle soaring youth unemployment in his highly anticipated tax and spending statement to the Commons in less than a fortnight’s time.After a rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training to almost 1 million, Andy Burnham has made supporting youth job opportunities central to his agenda for power, including sweeping changes toretool technical education and apprenticeships.Ministers have been clear they want to rebalance the apprenticeship system back towards younger people. More than half of new starts are now for over-25s and the number of under-19s enrolling has almost halved in a decade.Under the changes being planned to the growth and skills levy – the £4bn a year tax used to fund the national apprenticeship system – employers in England will face a new “co-investment” rule restricting the funding they can access.Aiming to tip the balance to incentivise youth apprenticeships, the change is controversial because employers have for years been told by successive governments they werefree to spend their levy fundson training as they saw fit.“Employers are not going to like it,” said one senior policy expert close to the government. “They were told ‘it’s your money, you get to decide’. But the system is not working at the moment.”Earlier this year Labourrevamped the apprenticeship levyintroduced by the Conservatives in 2017, with changes handing more flexibility to employers over the types of training the system can be used for – including new foundation apprenticeships and shorter courses.Under the levy, large employers (those with yearly wage costs totalling more than £3m) must pay 0.5% of their total annual pay bill into a dedicated digital pot that they can draw from to fund training and assessment costs.Following the proposed change, money from the pot would still be available to cover eligible training costs for apprentices aged 16 to 24. However, for older apprentices, the funds would cover only 75% of the cost and employers would need to pay for the remainder. It is believed the measure is under consideration for a phased launch from the start of the next academic year, in September 2027.Labour has been warned that its skills strategy to tackle youth unemployment risks failure without a change in course. Official figures show its flagship foundation apprenticeship scheme hasenrolled just 160 young people in the first eight months, against an ambition for 30,000 starts over the course of the parliament.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThis month the Fabian Society thinktank called on ministers to increase the rate of the growth and skills levy to 0.7% to raise an additional £2.5bn, which could be used to target more funding towards youth apprenticeships.However, it is understood that ministers are wary of heaping additional costs on businesses after the backlash suffered overemployer national insurance contributionsand as firms press forbudget supportto help them hire more young people.Alongside tight constraints on the public finances, this has shifted the focus to restricting levy funds as a way to support young people without further adding to the costs for the public purse.A Department for Work and Pensionsspokesperson said: “We remain determined to address the 40% decline in apprenticeship starts among young people and give them the skills they need to succeed.“We are already pivoting the system towards the next generation, including by creating 50,000 additional apprenticeships for young people, and introducing a new hiring payment of £2,000 for SMEs who take on a 16-24-year-old apprentice.“The Milburn review is due in the autumn. We will not pre-empt its findings.”Explore more on these topicsBusinessApprenticeshipsVocational educationYouth unemploymentLabourYoung peopleWork & careersnewsShareReuse this content

title: New York City police seek suspect in fatal subway station shooting | New York | The Guardian
description: Suspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPD
Author: Keely Aouga
Headline: Suspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPD
Content: The 7th Avenue-West 53rd Street subway station in Manhattan, New York City, on Saturday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe 7th Avenue-West 53rd Street subway station in Manhattan, New York City, on Saturday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNew YorkNew York City police seek suspect in fatal subway station shootingSuspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPDKeely AougaSat 17 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenAn image of the suspect provided by the NYPD.Photograph: Courtesy of NYPDView image in fullscreenAn image of the suspect provided by the NYPD.Photograph: Courtesy of NYPDA man was shot and killed in aNew YorkCity subway station Saturday afternoon, and the New York police department is searching for the suspect.The suspect fatally shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to astatement from the NYPD.“On Saturday, October 17, 2026, at approximately 12:21 PM, on the northbound E train platform of the 53rd Street–7th Avenue subway station in Manhattan, this individual shot and killed a man in his 30s,” the NYPD’s statement said.According to the NYPD, the suspect displayed a firearm and discharged it, striking the victim once in the chest. EMS responded and transported the victim to NYC health + hospitals/Bellevue, where he was pronounced deceased.The identity of the victim is not known at this time.The suspect is wanted for homicide within the confines of the Midtown North Precinct/Transit District 1.The NYPD released surveillance photos of the suspect, who fled on foot and headed northbound on 7th Avenue.The images show the suspect dressed in a red tracksuit, a black vest and a black face mask and carrying a backpack.Authorities are urging individuals with information regarding the incident to reach out to itstip lineat 1-800-577-TIPS (8477), or submit tips online at theCrime Stoppers websiteor via X @NYPDTips.The investigation remains ongoing.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkGun crimeUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England  | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use
Content: A protest against the US tech company Palantir outside their UK headquarters in London on 1 October.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protest against the US tech company Palantir outside their UK headquarters in London on 1 October.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesPalantirPalantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in EnglandExclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in useRobert BoothUK technology editorSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”.The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in theNHSof a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.”Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George MonbiotRead moreAccording to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.”Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow.Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson,saying last week: “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP.Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”.But two parliamentary select committees haveurgedthe government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”.“Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.”Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”.“Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said.View image in fullscreenA protest against Palantir’s role in the National Health Service at St Thomas’ hospital in London.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersPalantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”.“The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministersstatingthat it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.”It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP.Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHSEnglandhas, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this weekurgedministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”.Sophie Don, the chief executive of Voror, a patient data company that bid unsuccessfully against Palantir, said: “Of course Palantir isn’t the only company that can do this. It doesn’t surprise me that it is making things harder … If NHS staff are choosing not to use it, it’s a clear sign it’s not creating value. There are many home-grown systems that would release much more value to the NHS than the [Palantir] platform.”A spokesperson for NHS England said: “137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”Explore more on these topicsPalantirNHSEnglandHealthHospitalsShareReuse this content

title: Stinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewer | London | The Guardian
description: Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: Owner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problem
Content: Tamas Polocz’s bike shop faces closure because of an acrid smell from Thames Water sewers that makes it impossible to work.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianView image in fullscreenTamas Polocz’s bike shop faces closure because of an acrid smell from Thames Water sewers that makes it impossible to work.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianLondonStinky business: south London bike shop hit by ‘unbearable’ stench from Thames Water sewerOwner and mechanics fear for their health and future of the Herne Hill shop with no date for fixing problemMatthew WeaverSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe leafy southLondonneighbourhood of Herne Hill is a haven for cyclists who can often be seen lapping the local parks and refuelling at the many cafes that line the suburban streets. But there is something foul in the air of this corner of the capital – and for once it’s not the traffic fumes hitting bicycle riders.A toxic stench thought to be caused by untreated sewage stuck inThames Waterdrains has been emanating from the subterranean depths for months, most likely caused by the summer’s lack of rain.The stink is so acrid that the Bicyclenation shop has had to bar some customers and its mechanics have been forced to work on the pavement outside.The owner of the shop, Tamas Polocz, has repeatedly complained to Thames Water since the smell first hit the shop in June and caused his colleague Nick to vomit.Last week the troubled water company told Polocz it accepted that a mains sewer directly beneath the shop was to blame, but it has yet to offer him and his team of 11 any date for resolving the problem.View image in fullscreenWhen the smell hits, the mechanics at Bicyclenation are forced to evacuate and work outside the shop.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianPolocz and his colleagues have been left fearing for their physical and mental health after repeated exposure to the gassy stench. And the outlook for the business is bleak.The odour comes in putrid wafts that occur at least five times a day, according to a “smell chart” used to log the time and duration of each incident with a description. The words used include “cabbage”, “teargas”, “onions”, “spicy BBQ” and repeated references to “shit”.When the Guardian first arrived at the shop there was a whiff of rotten eggs but not enough to stop mechanics working inside and customers milling about. But within minutes we were overpowered by a repulsive gas that hit the back of the throat and left us scurrying outside, gagging for air.“It’s unbearable,” said Polocz. “You can’t be in the shop when it comes.”He added: “It has a really strong physical presence. This is a smell you take home with you. It’s in your hair, on your skin, sometimes it feels it’s inside your skin. When you go home and cough, you taste it again.”View image in fullscreen‘You can’t be in the shop when it comes,’ Tamas Polocz, the owner, said of the smell.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianThe ordeal comes after record-breaking temperatures and drought prompted calls for aradical overhaul of an outdated sewage system, just as the Great Stink ushered in new sanitation in the Victorian era.Thames Water initially suggested the Herne Hill smell was due to a gas leak. But extensive tests by the local gas supplier ruled that out.Polocz said he had been battling the company every week. “Thames Water have always tried to push me away, or blame others. When they finally accepted liability last week I just broke down. But we still don’t have a date for fixing it.”The exact cause of the stench remains unknown, but a Thames Water engineer told Polocz it was likely to be linked to the lack of rain. The engineer also told him that a cast-iron ventilation pipe that had previously drawn odours away from the shop had not been replaced.Experts warn that during dry periods, untreated sewage builds up in pipes with no rainwater to flush it out. Microbial activity in the sewage causesfoul-smelling gas to be emitted in wafts, in a similar process to the one that causes flatulence in human digestion.Prof Barbara Evans, the chair of public health engineering at Leeds University, said: “It sounds like methane and it’s probably unsafe working conditions. Biological processes are cyclical just like in your digestive system, which is why sewer smells come in wafts.”View image in fullscreenThe shop’s mechanics log the instances of the odour on a ‘smell chart’.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianWhen Polocz woke up to rainfall, he was hopeful it would flush away the stench. “I looked out through the window at home and thought, oh good, but it didn’t make any difference. Even after the rain there was still the smell. Maybe the rain will eventually clear it, but we don’t know. Something is happening down there that is pushing the smell up.”Evans said: “The first flushes of rain will probably make things smell worse because it just stirs things up. It needs a lot of rain to clear. There might be some blockage there but it’s impossible to know without a proper inspection.”Harriet Talbot, a board member of Bicyclenation, said: “You can’t run a business relying on the weather.” She helped set up awebpageasking for customers to sign up for a collect and repair service to help the shop survive.Polocz said the shop was currently unsustainable because staff had to evacuate so frequently. “We have to do half a day in the shop and half outside on the pavement. But now the cold weather is coming, we can’t keep doing that.”And the stress from the stink is taking its toll. Polocz said: “I’m 49, but today I feel 62-ish. We have guys calling in sick. It affects you both physically and mentally.”Polocz said he laid in bed at night worrying how he would be able to keep the shop going. “The last thought of the day and the first thought of the day are now both the same,” he said. “And I wake up at night thinking: what are we going to do about it? I try to listen to a podcast, but I still keep thinking about the smell. Somehow I’m going to get through this and change back to normal.”View image in fullscreen‘It affects you both physically and mentally,’ said Tamas Polocz.Photograph: Lily Renshaw/The GuardianPolocz’s plight is likely to add to calls for an overhaul of London’s Victorian sewage system. Evans said: “This underlines the need for a rethink of our sewers. The system was designed for a climate that we just don’t currently have any more.”The Guardian asked Thames Water when the problem would be fixed, why it had taken so long to resolve, and whether the company would apologise to Polocz.A spokesperson replied: “Our teams are investigating the source of an odour reported at a bike shop. Initial investigations have confirmed there are no blockages in the sewers surrounding the property. Odour monitors are to be installed, which will enable engineers to detect, measure and track odorous gases in real time and help determine the exact cause.”Explore more on these topicsLondonThames WaterWater industryRetail industryEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Is this too little, too late?’: Cornell students on school’s response to gang-rape allegations | US universities | The Guardian
description: Students say the school is more interested in scapegoating fraternities than in committing to institutional change
Author: Sara Braun
Headline: Students say the school is more interested in scapegoating fraternities than in committing to institutional change
Content: Demonstrators protest on the Cornell campus against the school’s handling of the 2024 fraternity-house gang-rape allegations, on 5 October 2026.Photograph: Adrian Kraus/APView image in fullscreenDemonstrators protest on the Cornell campus against the school’s handling of the 2024 fraternity-house gang-rape allegations, on 5 October 2026.Photograph: Adrian Kraus/APUS universities‘Is this too little, too late?’: Cornell students on school’s response to gang-rape allegationsStudents say the school is more interested in scapegoating fraternities than in committing to institutional changeSara BraunSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the wake of a lawsuit over an alleged gang-rape that took place at Cornell University in 2024, the schoolannouncedthis week that it would be suspending parties and social gatherings at fraternity houses for the remainder of the academic year.Last month, a former student, referred to in court documents by the pseudonym “Jane Doe”,filed a civil lawsuitagainst multiple parties, including the university, accusing seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her at a party at their fraternity house on campus in October 2024. All of the men named in the lawsuit have denied wrongdoing, and none have been criminally charged.In a letter to the Cornell community, the school’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, said that the ban on frat parties will be “provide time for a thorough review of fraternity life at Cornell to determine whether and how it can safely continue”.Sexual assault reported at frat house near University of ChicagoRead moreThe Guardian spoke with several undergraduate students at Cornell about the university’s decision, as well as their handling of the alleged assault and its aftermath. The measure, which Kotlikoff referred to as an effort to “strengthen campus safety”, was announced on 13 October in a letter to the Cornell community. While some students welcome the ban on frat parties, others argue that the move is an attempt by the administration to avoid a perception of culpability in the case.When asked for comment, Cornell referred the Guardian to Kotlikoff’s letter to the community from 13 October, in which hesaid: “I have spent the past weeks listening to students, faculty, staff, parents, alumni, and trustees, who have shared their feelings of deep connection and sympathy with Jane Doe, anger and frustration that this could happen at Cornell, and outrage at the broader prevalence of sexual violence against women in our society. These conversations, and campus protests, have underscored my deep conviction that we must do better: that the time for meaningful and lasting change at Cornell, and at campuses across the country, is now.”A sophomore at Cornell’s school of industrial and labor relations, who asked to remain anonymous, supports the school’s latest decision. She acknowledged that Greek life “wasn’t something that really added to my experience at Cornell” and that the ban was “so necessary in light of Jane Doe’s experience”.The student added that while she is not in Greek life herself, many of her friends are. “I think it’s been upsetting for people that are super involved in Greek life,” she said, noting that some members of Greek life feel that they’re being penalized for the actions of others. They “think that [the ban is] somewhat unnecessary because this happened two years ago, and it’s a completely different group of people”.“I have many friends that have opposing viewpoints,” she said.Some students argued that the opposition is the point, and believe that the administration’s decision was intended to further a divide between the student body.“The fact that [the administration] thinks a one-year moratorium will solve this is, I wouldn’t say it’s misguided. I would say it is purposefully manipulative to the student body,” said Jack Huber, a sophomore at the school of industrial and labor relations and member of Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), an independent, student-run organization that advocates for free speech on campus. “I believe it’s a very intentional choice, because what it’s done is create a sentiment that many students are angry, and are blaming protesters for their inability to party.“Cornell is not ready to commit itself to institutional change, and is using this moratorium to essentially scapegoat fraternities when this is a campus-wide issue,” he added. Huber added that issues of sexual assault will remain until the school has implemented an independent judicial system, which was previously in effect from 1969 to 2020.Huber said that school’s current judiciary process operates as “a tool to be used to sweep incidences of sexual violence under the rug because they harm Cornell’s reputation, and persecute protesters because they harm the board of trustees’ investments”.“That’s the system that allowed essays to get written by two of the [Cornell 7]” he said.SDC is demanding that the administration rewrite a portion of its student code of conduct to require independent hearings and minimum sanctions for sexual assault.Darius Pierce, a sophomore at Cornell’s college of architecture, art and planning, remembered hearing about the incident, which had resulted in Chi Phi beingdisbarred and removedfrom campus during his first few weeks of college in 2025.“I was walking past the Chi Phi house, heading back to campus, and a person in my group pointed out [the house] and I asked why I’ve never heard of them, and they explained that there was an issue with ketamine and assault at that house, and that was it,” he said.“No one ever expanded upon that. I hadn’t heard anything about it until the story broke with the Cornell Sun.”Like Huber, Pierce believes that the administration’s decision to ban frat parties is an attempt to “cover up for their own faults and own mistakes”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“They’re trying to make it seem like they’re actually responding to [the alleged assault] and taking action instead of addressing the real issue,” he said.Following the alleged assault, Cornell issued astatementin November 2024 informing the community that there would be an internal investigation while the Cornell University Police Department continued their criminal investigation. Per Jane Doe’s lawsuit, Cornell University Police did not end up pursuing criminal charges. The investigation wasreopenedin September 2026 in response to public outrage. None of the defendants in the civil lawsuit have been charged and all have denied wrongdoing.Pierce, who rushed a fraternity but decided not to join one, also spoke of the endemic culture of drinking and substance use he has witnessed within Greek life at Cornell. He recalled an experience at a fraternity party where “this group of girls kept screaming that it was their first time doing coke at that frat party, and that these frat guys were just handing out lines of coke like candy”.“If you go to a frat, you plan on drinking,” Pierce said. “But it seems like for women specifically who go to these frats, they’re kind of pressured to do more.”The Guardianpreviously reportedon how Jane Doe’s lawsuit has reignited debates over Greek life and the relationship between fraternity parties, drinking culture and sexual assault. A 2019 survey from theAssociation of American Universitiesrevealed that a quarter of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual conduct, with fraternities being the setting where it was most likely to occur.At Cornell, 35% of undergraduate women reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact since arriving at school, according to a2025 surveyconducted by the university.Saya Taylor, a sophomore who is also a member of SDC, believes that the frat ban is a “Band-Aid” solution to a much deeper problem. “They’re trying to give the appearance that they are changing when they are not,” she said. “Cornell University does not want this to [have] a lasting impact.”In addition to the fraternity ban, Kotlikoff also announced that the university would be adding a case manager to Cornell’s office of civil rights to help those who report sexual misconduct at the school navigate the processes. He also pledged that Cornell would work with theNew Yorkstate police and allow their trauma-informed criminal investigators, who are independent of Cornell, to investigate allegations.The sophomore believes that this week’s announcement is a step in the right direction. “For the vast majority, people like me, we want justice and we want the administration to change the structural way that they address sexual assault,” she said.But others need more convincing.“Is this too little, too late? The answer there is a resounding yes,” said Huber. “Jane Doe never got the justice she deserved in the moment.”Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.htmlExplore more on these topicsUS universitiesRape and sexual assaultFraternities and sororitiesUniversity administrationSchoolsViolence against women and girlsUS crimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hope | Birds | The Guardian
description: In an extract from his new book, the nature historian explains how technology could help the seabird survive
Author: Stephen Moss
Headline: In an extract from his new book, the nature historian explains how technology could help the seabird survive
Content: The prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring.Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring.Photograph: Tim Graham/AlamyBirdsHow the quirky puffin became a symbol of the climate crisis – and hopeIn an extract from his new book, the nature historian explains how technology could help the seabird surviveStephen MossSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor centuries human beings have exploited puffins, harvesting them by the thousand on their breeding grounds for their food and feathers. Over time, though, this relationship has changed, so that today we have come to love them, celebrating their quirky character and comical appearance and giving them a central place in our affections – a journey described by the environmental historian Dr Rob Lambert as the shift “from use to delight”.How ironic, then, that just as we have come to truly appreciate them, our own existence now threatens theirs. The climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds, whose life cycle is so intimately connected to the timing and abundance of their food supplies.Warming oceans result in fish such as sand eels shifting their range into cooler waters, and thus either declining or disappearing from the seas around seabird breeding colonies. If puffins need to travel further to their feeding areas, or take longer to find and catch food once they get there, then their chicks have a lower chance of fledging.View image in fullscreenThe climate crisis threatens almost all the world’s roughly 11,000 species of birds, but its consequences have particularly dire significance for seabirds.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEven if they do, they are less likely to survive the following winter. Our changing climate has already led to an increase in the frequency and severity of extreme weather events such as autumn and winter storms, which leads to a higher mortality of birds outside the breeding season.It is often forgotten that the climate crisis is not the only negative factor affecting these birds’ lives. As we have seen, increased marine pollution, especially from oil and plastic, along with less severe yet still serious issues such as disturbance and predation, are already reducing the puffin’s breeding success at many once-thriving colonies.The dire prediction that nine out of 10 puffins could disappear before the middle of this century is hopefully pessimistic, yet we do know that serious declines are already occurring.In early 2026, BBC Newsreportedthat following that winter’s severe storms hundreds of dead and dying puffins, guillemots and razorbills had been washed up on beaches in Cornwall, Scotland and north-east England. Conservation organisations have also reported more than 20,000 stranded birds, mostly puffins, along the Atlantic coasts of France, Spain and Portugal.View image in fullscreenIllustration from The Birds of Great Britain, 1873.Illustration: John Gould/Image courtesy of Biodiversity Heritage LibrarySamuel Wrobel, the RSPB’s senior marine officer, noted that this was the worst wreck for over a decade, since the catastrophic events of winter 2013-14, and warned that “after the impact of avian flu this is the last thing our seabirds need”. Moreover, as most birds are likely to have died at sea, so will never be found, the true death toll is likely to be much higher.Peter Harrison has spent his life watching, painting and studying seabirds, and has a special affection for the puffin. I asked him what he thought about the species’ future, and he began by confirming the many threats the birds face, including a reduction in their prey due to the climate crisis, threats to nest sites and the resulting lower breeding success.Rather to my surprise, however, Harrison feels some optimism for the puffin’s future, pointing to that famous legal victory that stoppedindustrial sand eel fishing in the waters around England and Scotland. He is also enthusiastic about the use of technology to track the movements and survival of all seabirds, including the puffin, since this began in the 1980s.View image in fullscreenAtlantic puffins in Isle of Lunga in the Treshnish Isles, Scotland.Photograph: Nature Picture Library/Alamy“Prior to that time, there was a huge void in our knowledge of what puffins and other seabirds did in their non-breeding period,” he says. “They simply went to sea, only to reappear again in their breeding areas the following season. Rapid technological advances over the last four decades have greatly increased our understanding of their movements, revealing details of seabird distribution and behaviour at sea, including important foraging areas.”And as he points out, this knowledge does not just benefit the puffin. “Auks – including puffins – fulfil a role as important canaries in the cage, indicators of global health and sustainability. If auks are doing well, the oceans will be doing well,” Harrison says.The one thing we have on our side, Harrison believes, is that, unlike landbirds which often only live for a few years, even small seabirds can live for several decades. As he notes, although they might have gone through bad times, seabirds have in the past shown that they can make a rapid comeback, especially if we are able to rid their breeding islands of invasive predators.View image in fullscreenThreats to the birds’ future include a reduction in their prey due to climate breakdown, threats to nest sites and the resulting lower breeding success.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianScientists have a crucial role to play, too. In 2004 BirdLife International developed the BirdLife Seabird Tracking Database (STDB) to collate tracking data using a range of different, and rapidly improving, technologies that can track the presence and movements of seabirds when they are away from their breeding colonies, as they are for most of their lives.The records enabled them to identify six previously unrecognised oceanic routes used by the birds on their journeys: the Atlantic Ocean, North Indian Ocean, East Ocean, West Pacific Ocean, Pacific Ocean, and the Southern Ocean Flyways. The data obtained is also used for seabird research and conservation by BirdLife scientists and their collaborators throughout the world.As Dr Stephen Kress, the scientist who has devoted his life to successfully bringing back puffins to the US, points out: “Seabirds were once abundant along the coastlines of North America and throughout the world, but the declines we’re seeing in their populations are directly related to things humans are doing – they would be fine if we weren’t tampering with their world and messing things up.“And so I feel that we have an ethical responsibility as stewards of the Earth to do something where we can. That’s why we’ve developed these restoration techniques. If we hadn’t done that, we wouldn’t be documenting puffin recovery, we’d be documenting extinction.”Yet perhaps we can maintain at least a small fragment of hope for the future not just of the puffin, but of all the world’s seabirds. They may be outside our day-to-day experience for much of our – and their – lives, yet the huge affection for the puffin, held by millions of people around the world, must surely count for something.This is an edited extract from The Puffin by Stephen Moss published by Vintage at £14.99.
