title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds | Deforestation | The Guardian
description: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation
Content: Deforestation from illegal mining in the Tambopata national reserve near Puerto Maldonado, Peru, in August 2026.Photograph: Angela Ponce/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeforestation from illegal mining in the Tambopata national reserve near Puerto Maldonado, Peru, in August 2026.Photograph: Angela Ponce/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesDeforestationUS corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report findsEnvironmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation RegulationJonathan WattsSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy groupfound.US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber,soyaand wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius,describedit as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has beenin effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous landsRead moreLobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to theEuropean Unionand Cargill.Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission,Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a jointstatementthatpromised the US special treatmentwith regard to the EUDR.The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggestfinancialandtradingcompanies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitalsarguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European marketbecause it would raise costs for US producers. In anopinion piecepublished in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsRead moreThe American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European UnionDeforestationRegulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.Explore more on these topicsDeforestationEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Squash down: smaller pumpkins expected this Halloween after drought in England | Halloween | The Guardian
description: Data shows 2026 could be worst harvest on record, as growers suggest painting faces on vegetables instead of carving
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Data shows 2026 could be worst harvest on record, as growers suggest painting faces on vegetables instead of carving
Content: Pumpkins are relatively drought tolerant but this year’s weather stretched their tolerance to the limit.Photograph: Natalia Ganelin/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPumpkins are relatively drought tolerant but this year’s weather stretched their tolerance to the limit.Photograph: Natalia Ganelin/Getty ImagesHalloweenSquash down: smaller pumpkins expected this Halloween after drought in EnglandData shows 2026 could be worst harvest on record, as growers suggest painting faces on vegetables instead of carvingHelena HortonSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the lead-up toHalloween, front porches across the country feature fat, proudly carved pumpkins, lit from within by tea lights.But this year there is likely to be a shortage due to drought, experts have warned, with the squashes much smaller than usual.Mini pumpkins will have to be used, and some have suggested that those celebrating the spooky festival draw faces on vegetables instead of carving them.England has faced apunishing droughtfor most of this year, which has dramatically affected harvests. Data has found that this year could be the worst harvest on record as farmers struggled to irrigate their crops.Pumpkins are 90% water, and need a lot of it to grow. The vegetables are native to the Americas and were brought over in the Tudor period, during the 16th century.Guy Singh-Watson, the founder of organic veg box company Riverford, said: “After such an extraordinarily hot, dry summer, it’s not surprising that Halloween pumpkins are smaller than usual as they are mostly water. But perhaps it’s time we questioned our obsession with giant carving pumpkins in the first place.”Shunning pumpkins would go some way to bringing the carving of vegetables tradition back to its roots. The custom began in 17th-century Britain while marking the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which was when spirits were thought to roam the Earth.View image in fullscreenOn expert said it may be time to question our obsession with giant carving pumpkins.Photograph: Svitlana Romadina/Getty ImagesRather than pumpkins, root vegetables such as celeriac, turnips and mangelwurzels were carved into grotesque faces, and some believed they could ward off evil spirits.Guy Barter, the chief horticulturalist at the Royal Horticultural Society, said: “Pumpkins are on the small side this year unless heavily watered. Such drought makes watering sufficiently very difficult to accomplish in practice. Pumpkins are relatively drought-tolerant but this year the weather stretched their tolerance to the limit.“The heat later and some drought stress caused fruits to ripen earlier than usual. Their dry matter content and rind hardness are both excellent so the crop should store well, although commercial pumpkins become worthless the day after Halloween. That’s a pity as they make lovely soups until the new year when the much tastier winter squashes take over.”Singh-Watson said the growing of a large, watery squash simply to throw it away after Halloween was wasteful, adding: “I’ve enjoyed growing pumpkins before, they’re a lovely crop, but the idea of growing something that’s going to be thrown away has become increasingly difficult to justify. Growing any crop comes with an environmental cost, and generating a mountain of waste without feeding anyone makes little sense.”The vegetable entrepreneur has been growing a selection of small, colourful squashes and is now selling a box containing a selection including crown prince, red onion, sweet lightning, futsu and stripetti. He said: “This time of the year should be a celebration of the wonderful abundance of seasonal vegetables that see us through autumn and winter. Squash come in an extraordinary variety of shapes, sizes and colours, and offer just as much decorative potential, with considerably more flavour. Let’s paint a face on a squash instead … and then eat it.”Some gardeners have been trying novel methods to try to get the size of pumpkins up.Ali Goding, the garden manager at RHS Harlow Carr in North Yorkshire, said: “Pumpkins struggle to grow in heavy clay soil during drought conditions, so the team at RHS garden Harlow Carr have trialled a new, novel way to grow pumpkins this year – in a compost cake which helps retain moisture, humidity and warmth and the results have been fantastic while also benefiting wildlife.“They have set with hard skins in the heat so should store well and they will also have a good flavour with all that sun.“Normally we are a bit cool, damp and too far north for them to develop a full flavour – so the extra heat worked out well for us. A good year!”Explore more on these topicsHalloweenPumpkinFarmingEnglandVegetablesDroughtnewsShareReuse this content

title: Honeybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study finds | Bees | The Guardian
description: As a surge in beekeepers has led to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers
Author: Rebecca Ratcliffe
Headline: As a surge in beekeepers has led to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowers
Content: Honeybees were more likely to attack and chase rivals – and win – to collect more pollen and nectar, the study found.Photograph: Dr Tom Ings/Anglia Ruskin UniversityView image in fullscreenHoneybees were more likely to attack and chase rivals – and win – to collect more pollen and nectar, the study found.Photograph: Dr Tom Ings/Anglia Ruskin UniversityThe age of extinctionBeesHoneybees are barging aside wild pollinators in hunt for pollen and nectar, study findsAs a surge in beekeepers has led to increased numbers of honeybees, researchers record them pushing bumblebees and other rival species away from flowersSupported byAbout this contentRebecca RatcliffeSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHoneybees are outcompeting wild pollinators for resources by aggressively bumping into them and chasing them away from flowers, research has shown.The study, by researchers from Anglia Ruskin University, found that areas where there were higher concentrations of honeybees had fewer wild pollinators, such as bumblebees, solitary bees and hoverflies.Honeybees were also most likely to instigate, and win, competitive interactions, pushing out rivals to collect more pollen and nectar.The number of managed bees has risen in the UK, as campaigns to “save the bees” resonate with the public, leading to aboom in hobbyists setting up beehives. The number of registered beekeepers has more than doubled, from 19,000 in 2010 to 47,000 in 2025, according to the National Bee Unit.However, there are growing concerns that this growth in managed honeybees isharming other, wild, pollinatorsincluding bumblebees, by increasing competition for food and passing on diseases, especially in areas where there are fewer flowers or an especially high density of hives.To better understand the nature of this competition, the study in Cambridgeshire observed pollinators over a two-year period as they foraged on bramble and ivy in areas close to honeybee colonies. The study documented the outcomes of 300 interactions between flower visitors from five groups: honeybees, bumblebees, solitary bees, hoverflies and “other”, which included types of flower-visiting and pollinating flies, butterflies, beetles and wasps.In each interaction, the study noted where an individual “won”, by gaining access to a resource, “lost”, or if a resource was shared. Honeybees won in most of the encounters across both plant species.Past research has suggested that honeybeesoutcompete other pollinators indirectly, by taking up resources. However, the Cambridgeshire study provides evidence that they are posing a more direct form of competition, known as “interference competition”, where a species might attack or chase others away.“That’s important because, of course, it means that the wild pollinators are facing a challenge from both those types of competition from honeybees,” said Victoria Buckle, lead author of the study and a PhD researcher at Anglia Ruskin University.Honeybees were actively avoided by other flower visitors in 28.4% of interactions on bramble and 35.6% on ivy.In competitive interactions won by a honeybee, the honeybee either displaced other flower visitors – for example, by landing on them or pushing them off flowers – or chased them away, in about 20% of cases.Bumblebees were also observed displacing other pollinators, though Buckle believes this was probably not intentional, and was instead a reflection of their less coordinated movements as they fly through confined spaces.Trill seekers: can scientists use AI and tutors to help birds remember lost songs?Read more“They bumble along the patch and then they’ll mistakenly bump into another pollinator and it just falls off a flower,” Buckle said. “With the honeybees, the aggression was more overt. You could tell that they’re specifically trying to move the other one off the flower.”The reasons for honeybees’ aggressive behaviour is likely to relate to the way in which they organise their social groups, said Buckle, adding: “Some castes of bees can be guard bees, so they have that capacity within them to show threat and aggression, to guard their hives and to look after the brood.”The only pollinator able to hold its own against honeybees was the ivy bee, which was first recorded in the UK in 2001 and feeds mainly on the nectar of ivy flowers. It was seen displacing and chasing honeybees.The study also found that higher temperatures led to an increased number of competitive interactions, probably because nectar was drying up and plants were going into heat stress. Given that mean summer temperatures are predicted to rise by up to 4C in the UK by 2080, such competition is likely to become more frequent, said Buckle.More research is needed to examine how wild pollinators can be better protected, she added.“A lot of beekeepers are environmentally minded and they want to make sure that they’re not impinging or having an impact on other pollinators,” Buckle said. “This research is important because it helps guide our planning and best practices for conservation.”Explore more on these topicsBeesThe age of extinctionInsectsWildlifeBiodiversitynewsShareReuse this content

title: No action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action post | Jonathan Powell | The Guardian
description: Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’
Content: Sarah Helm pictured in 2011. She posted on X on Thursday: ‘God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.’Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSarah Helm pictured in 2011. She posted on X on Thursday: ‘God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.’Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianJonathan PowellNo action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action postTweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’Nadeem BadshahSat 17 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, after she was accused of supporting the banned protest groupPalestine Action.Helm, a journalist and author who is married to Jonathan Powell, posted on X on Thursday: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”The Metropolitan police said on Friday the post was “in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.In an update on Saturday, a force spokesperson said: “On Thursday 15 October, we were made aware of a post on X relating to Palestine Action.“The post was assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold. No further police action will be taken.”Helm was responding on X to a discussion about the Irish authorSally Rooney, who has said she can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.It is understood there was insufficient evidence that the post was capable of encouraging support for a proscribed organisation.The ban, which began in July 2025, made membership or support of the direct action group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.Downing Street has distanced itself from Helm’s remarks.The Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) had called on the police to investigate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe group acknowledged that “spouses are entitled to independent views”, but said Helm’s post “raises extremely serious questions forJonathan Powelland the government.“Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.”Earlier, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”Explore more on these topicsJonathan PowellPalestine ActionSally RooneynewsShareReuse this content

title: SNP says campaign for next referendum on independence ‘has already begun’ | Scottish National party (SNP) | The Guardian
description: John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK
Content: John Swinney after delivering his keynote speech at the Scottish National party conference on Saturday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenJohn Swinney after delivering his keynote speech at the Scottish National party conference on Saturday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAScottish National party (SNP)SNP says campaign for next referendum on independence ‘has already begun’John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UKPatrick GreenfieldSat 17 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Swinney has said that the second referendum campaign for Scottish independence “has already begun”, revealing a nationwide effort to renew the argument for leaving the UK in his keynote address to the SNP party conference.On Saturday, the Scottish first minister said the SNP would launch its “most sophisticated campaign in history” to convince Scottish voters of the benefits of independence, backed by “a six-figure war chest”.Called ChooseScotland, the campaign will aim to build the consensus for leaving the union.Swinney told the SNP party conference in Aberdeen that the “stars were aligning” for the pro-independence cause, arguing that nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland had panicked pro-union parties.“For centuries, people in the Celtic nations have been told that we are not good enough. Our languages were derided, our cultures suppressed, our histories rewritten,” he said.“When I stood on a stage recently with pro-independence leaders from Wales and Ireland, it certainly upset some of our opponents.“From their point of view, they are right to be worried. Watching us pledge to work together and seeing the love and respect we feel for each other’s nations. Never again can they portray us as separatists.”At the conference, leading SNP figures said a hung Westminster parliament is the most realistic path to securing a second independence referendum in Scotland as the nationalists would probably “hold the balance of power” in forming a future progressive government.The party has just eight MPs in parliament, but recent polling indicates that if a vote was held today, that number would surge at the Labour party’s expense in Scotland, although there is uncertainty surrounding how many seats it would gain.Deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth said her party would welcome an early general election to reenergise the push for independence.“The polling, of course, suggests the SNP would hold the balance of power in a hung parliament and really strong support for the SNP across the country allowing us to regain a number of seats,” she said.The sentiment was echoed by Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, whotold a podcastby the pro-independence newspaper the National that they could negotiate another poll if the overall results were tight.“We have a really great opportunity at the next general election to be in a position where that negotiation can seriously start with the next iteration of the Westminster government, whether we have a hung parliament, which is looking very likely, or different coalitions,” she said.“Perhaps now we are talking about a Lib Dem-Labour coalition. The SNP are polled at getting somewhere between 40 and 50 MPs at the general election. That’s huge.“Let’s put it to Westminster and put the onus on them to meet us at the table and set that plan out for us.”The latest MRP polling by Electoral Calculus this weekpredicted a narrow Labour victory, with the SNP winning 28 seats, although previous polls have indicated they could win even more.In a visit to Lanarkshire on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the Scottish government needed to “move beyond” the question of independence while offering to work more closely on devolving power from Holyrood with Swinney’s administration. The Westminster government would have to grant a second vote on Scottish independence.“I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions. In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people. Right now, too much time is wasted on those dramas. It consumes too much energy,” he said, when asked about the issue.Although it is not in Swinney’s power to call a second independence referendum, he told the conference that another vote could happen sooner than expected.“Our independence is very close,” he said. “Our nearest neighbours will always be our closest friends and our strongest allies. I will always want the very best for the people living in England, Wales and across Ireland.“But friends, in the long arc of history, nothing is static. And those that try to hold on to the past fail to grasp the opportunities of the future.“In this period of history, the nations of the United Kingdom are evolving into a new relationship. That is something to welcome.”Explore more on these topicsScottish National party (SNP)John SwinneyScottish politicsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Briton threatened with deportation from Sweden over Brexit rules goes into hiding | UK news | The Guardian
description: Mark Smith, who has severe health issues, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after Brexit
Author: Lisa O’Carroll
Headline: Mark Smith, who has severe health issues, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after Brexit
Content: Mark Smith with his wife, Petra, was told he was an ‘alien’ without permission to stay.Photograph: Annika Karlbom/Hallands NyheterView image in fullscreenMark Smith with his wife, Petra, was told he was an ‘alien’ without permission to stay.Photograph: Annika Karlbom/Hallands NyheterUK newsBriton threatened with deportation from Sweden over Brexit rules goes into hidingMark Smith, who has severe health issues, says he was told three times he needed to do nothing in order to remain after BrexitLisa O’CarrollSenior correspondentSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA seriously ill British man living inSwedenhas been forced into hiding amid fears he will be deported as a result of what he says is a government Brexit residency error.Mark Smith, 60, who has had heart attacks, strokes, severe headaches and chronically high blood pressure that has been difficult to treat, was told on the phone he should leave Sweden by 17 October as he was an “alien” without permission to stay.Terrified of deportation, he and his wife have moved out of their home in Falkenberg, in south-west Sweden, to a caravan park. “We are in hiding, we daren’t go back to our apartment. We are scared to go out as we don’t know if the police will come and take us,” Smith said.A court ruled on 12 October that a decision on deportation would not be suspended but gave him until 20 October to “submit his application for a retrial” in relation to “the grounds for the decision on indefinite deportation”.View image in fullscreenMark Smith and his wife, Petra, have moved out of their apartment in Falkenberg to caravan park.Photograph: Annika Karlbom/Hallands NyheterSmith has been in Sweden since 2017 and says he was told by authorities he did not need to do anything to stay afterBrexitin 2020. He worked, had private health insurance, supported his wife and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority, as required under Swedish rules.He was unaware, however, that Sweden was among 13 of the 27 EU member states that required Britons living in the country before Brexit to make a formal application to remain. Other countries, such as Spain, did not opt for that system and just required Britons to declare they were a resident.Smith said: “I asked the tax authorities three times on different occasions if I had to do anything because of Brexit and they said no, telling me I had to wait for five years to apply for permanent residency.“Because it was the tax authority, a government body, I took it for granted that what they told me was correct,” he added.David Milstead, a British-Swedish volunteer citizens’ rights activist working through the Brits in Sweden group, said Smith’s case was typical of many Britons living in Sweden.View image in fullscreenSmith has been in Sweden since 2017. He worked, had private health insurance, and registered on the population register administered by the national tax authority.Milstead said: “Mark’s experience is far from unusual. I have encountered many British citizens who actively sought information from the Swedish authorities about their residence rights after Brexit, only to receive vague, unhelpful answers, sometimes being told that they needed to do nothing.”They include the78-year-old widow Joyce Thomas, whose husband also inquired about Brexit residency and was told by the tax authorities there was nothing to do, and who is now fighting a removal order.Smith had a minor heart attack on Wednesday night but wanted his situation publicised because he said the British government needed to know what was happening to expats in Sweden, “not just to me but others”.His wife, Petra, said his health conditions had left him so vulnerable she was not sure “if he will last until Christmas”.She said: “He has been told he can’t drive, he can’t fly – what do they expect him to do? Get up and walk to England? Come on, Sweden, we need to step back from all of this and be better.”After 12 years together, she said deportation would be devastating for her and her 15-year-old son who has special needs, who Smith co-parents. “It is wrong what they are doing, I feel ashamed to be Swedish. What they are doing is racist to British people,” Petra said.View image in fullscreenSmith’s troubles began in 2021 when he applied for sickness benefit and was told by officials he should have applied for post-Brexit residency.Milstead said Smith’s case was “depressingly familiar” and should warrant the urgent attention of the European Commission, which has previously said Sweden was not breaking any laws.“A gentleman with Mark’s serious health conditions should not be having to fight deportation. It is difficult to understand how the European Commission has concluded that Sweden’s treatment of late applications under the [Brexit] withdrawal agreement does not warrant a challenge,” he said.“Sweden stands out so starkly from other EU countries, and there are serious questions that remain unanswered, particularly about proportionality and the treatment of vulnerable people. These are precisely the kinds of cases where the protections of the withdrawal agreement ought to matter most.”The Scandinavian country has found itself under mounting pressure over its approach to the withdrawal agreements havingdeported 458 Britons, including one man who had been in the country since he was 10 years old, anda 65-year-old man married to a Swedewith no family or property in the UK.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSweden has also issued removal orders toa man with dementiawho is in 24-hour care and who has been in the country for 25 years.Under the legally binding treaty, it was agreed governments would communicate the Brexit residency rules, consider late applications on reasonable grounds, and exercise “proportionate” decisions including in the case of vulnerable people.Smith’s troubles began in 2021 when he started to get ill and applied for sickness benefit. He was told by officials that he should have applied for post-Brexit residency. The couple immediately did so; they recall making the application at the end of 2021, in time for Sweden’s 31 December 2021 deadline.They waited more than two years to hear back and when they did it was a rejection on the grounds that they were not married and therefore did not have a family connection to merit his residency in Sweden.Mark Smith and Petra on their wedding day in Sweden in 2023.Photograph: SuppliedThey were married in 2023 and had been living together since 2017.It is not clear if Smith applied for the specific Brexit residency or through the usual immigration route, an important difference and one that may not have been made clear to British protected by the withdrawal agreement. Family connections are not a criteria under free movement rights, which apply to any individual regardless of marital status, so campaigners believe they have a strong case.Smith said: “We were so much in love, we lived together, we did everything together, even now we hold hands walking down the streets. We wanted to get married, we wanted to do it the right way. I wanted to ask Petra’s father for permission and have him give her away, but two weeks after he gave me permission to marry his daughter, he passed.“So we were looking into marriage but things just kept happening. But we don’t understand why this matters.”They also said they had not been given the full court paperwork from the first case appealing against the migration agency’s decision, so they appealed to a higher courtwithout the full arguments against them.After speaking to a judge this week, Petra has had assurances that all the paperwork will be sent to them by post, but they feel angry that they were not apprised of the information that the migration agency was arguing before the courts.Sweden’s migration agency has said there is no evidence Sweden has taken an extreme approach to the withdrawal agreement.The UK Foreign Office has raised concerns about Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement with the European Commission on numerous occasions, but has been told Sweden is not breaching the agreement.A spokesperson said: “We are in touch with Mr Smith and are providing consular support. We know this is a distressing and challenging time for those concerned and we are urgently raising the situation with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission.”The Foreign Office welcomed a statement by Sweden’s former migration minister Johan Forssell in August that Sweden would examine “additional measures” that would address the issue of Brexit deportation, and a similar declaration by Magdalena Andersson, who is on track to form the new government.Explore more on these topicsUK newsBrexitSwedenEuropean UnionEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains | Yemen | The Guardian
description: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers
Content: Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a rally to recruit more fighters in Sana’a.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a rally to recruit more fighters in Sana’a.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenUAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gainsUnited Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulersYemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Patrick WintourDiplomatic editorSat 17 Oct 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter theYemenconflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign thatthe deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed– if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations insideYemenin January, cutting off its funding supply line.Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.View image in fullscreenYemeni Southern Giants Brigades fighters celebrate and wave their weapons.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.TheUAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthroughRead moreUAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, theHouthisare determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter. The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisUnited Arab EmiratesSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung
Content: Pope Leo XIV leaves the Gemelli hospital, Rome, four days after lung surgery.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAView image in fullscreenPope Leo XIV leaves the Gemelli hospital, Rome, four days after lung surgery.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAPope Leo XIVPope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operationDoctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lungPope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next?Angela Giuffridain RomeSat 17 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome afterundergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican.He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.View image in fullscreenLeo celebrating Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome.Photograph: Vatican Media/APDoctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged.The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, thatLeo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Squarethat a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October.However, the pope’s surgeon told Vatican media on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to prevent him from traveling to Latin America as scheduled from 6 to 17 November.Dr Stefano Margaritora said that “the Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery” and that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so”.View image in fullscreenThe Gemelli hospital in Rome.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” he told Vatican News.Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVThe papacyReligionCatholicismItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Art dealer who sold forged Warhols sentenced to nearly four years in prison | Art theft | The Guardian
description: Leslie Roberts, 62, who created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, also ordered to repay $2.6m
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Leslie Roberts, 62, who created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, also ordered to repay $2.6m
Content: A visitor snaps a photo of Grace Kelly, 1984, by Andy Warhol in Regents Park, London, on 16 October.Photograph: Stephen Chung/AlamyView image in fullscreenA visitor snaps a photo of Grace Kelly, 1984, by Andy Warhol in Regents Park, London, on 16 October.Photograph: Stephen Chung/AlamyArt theftArt dealer who sold forged Warhols sentenced to nearly four years in prisonLeslie Roberts, 62, who created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, also ordered to repay $2.6mEric BergerSat 17 Oct 2026 16.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 16.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAMiamiart dealer who admitted to selling forgedAndy Warholartwork has been sentenced to nearly four years in prison.Leslie Roberts, 62, created fraudulent invoices and authentication documents, as well as counterfeit stamps to deceive buyers, theUS justice departmentsaid in a statement issued on Thursday.The US district judge Roy Altman sentenced Roberts to three years and 10 months in federal prison on 2 October. TheAssociated Pressreported that Altman also ordered Roberts to repay $2.6m stolen through his scheme centering on artwork falsely attributed to the leader of the pop art movement.Roberts sold the fakes in question through his Miami art gallery, claiming he acquired the artwork from theAndy WarholFoundation for the Visual Arts, according to the justice department. He provided fraudulent invoices that appeared to have been issued by the organization before pleading guilty in June to conspiring to commit wire fraud.He also enlisted Carlos Rodriguez Melendez to pose as an employee of a New York-based auction company and falsely authenticate the work. The accomplice also pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud.A statement from the southern district of Florida’s US attorney, Jason Reding Quiñones, said it was important to prosecute Roberts “because art fraud undermines confidence in the legitimate art market and victimizes buyers who rely on the authenticity of the works they purchase”.Roberts “exploited the trust that collectors place in art dealers and the authenticity of the works they purchase”, Reding Quiñones said.Reding Quiñones said Roberts’ prison sentence “sends a clear message: fraud is fraud, whether it happens on Wall Street or in an art gallery. Those who profit through deception will be held accountable.”Others have also been convicted in recent months of selling fake Warhol work.In April, afather and daughterin New Jersey, Erwin Bankowski and Karolina Bankowska, admitted to commissioning an artist in Poland to create at least 200 Warhol, Banksy and Pablo Picasso fakes and ultimately defrauding buyers of at least $2m.The pair pleaded guilty to running a years-long counterfeiting scheme in which they tricked galleries and auction houses into buying the forgeries. When sentenced, they could face up to 20 years’ imprisonment as well as at least $1.9m in restitution, the US justice departmentsaidin a statement.Explore more on these topicsArt theftUS crimeMiamiAndy WarholnewsShareReuse this content

title: Florida fisher dragged into water and killed by 12ft alligator | Florida | The Guardian
description: Steve Hamilton was fishing in Winter Garden when he was attacked by gator, which was later killed
Author: Eric Berger
Headline: Steve Hamilton was fishing in Winter Garden when he was attacked by gator, which was later killed
Content: Thirty-four people have been killed by alligators in Florida since 1948.Photograph: Bruce Bennett/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThirty-four people have been killed by alligators in Florida since 1948.Photograph: Bruce Bennett/Getty ImagesFloridaFlorida fisher dragged into water and killed by 12ft alligatorSteve Hamilton was fishing in Winter Garden when he was attacked by gator, which was later killedEric BergerSat 17 Oct 2026 11.23 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man fishing at a pond inFloridawas killed on Friday by an alligator that was almost 12ft long in a rare kind of animal attack, according to authorities and media reports.Steve Hamilton, 71, was on the shoreline in the community of Winter Garden when the animal dragged him into the water, the Florida news outlet WOFLreported, citing local police and the state’s fish and wildlife conservation commission.Emergency crews responded to the park where Hamilton was fishing at about 5.20pm on Friday after receiving a 911 call and attempted to rescue him – but they had difficulty doing so because of nearby alligators, the outlet reported.Hamilton’s body was recovered from the water a couple of hours later.Capt Michael Mason of the Winter Garden police department told news media that the alligator hadbeen killedafter the fatal attack on Hamilton.Authorities were not alerted of a gator sighting on Friday at the pond, which is connected to Lake Apopka, Mason said.The body of water has “tons of alligators in it. That is not uncommon to see alligators in this part of town,” Mason said.The chief encouraged people to “be aware of your surroundings”.The gator “looks like it’s docile. It looks like yourFloridaemblem, but it can be dangerous,” Mason said.Alligator attacks are statistically rare. Nonetheless, at least 34 people have been killed by them in Florida since 1948, according to theFlorida fish and wildlife conservation commission, which compiles reports of encounters with the state’s estimated 1.3 million gators.Hamilton’s death came less than four months after a woman namedBrittany Clark was attacked and killedby a 13ft alligator while swimming with her boyfriend in the Econlockhatchee River in Florida’s Seminole county.Autopsy results released in July showed Clark, 31, struggled for her life before dying from the wounds inflicted on her by the alligator, which was removed from the river and euthanized.After Clark’s death, the Republican US House member Greg Steube of Florida introduced a resolution calling for the federal comptroller general and the US Department of the Interior to study how American alligators’ being listed as “threatened due to similarity of appearance” to crocodiles affects his state’s ability to remove nuisance gators from residential and commercial waterways.Steube said the species has been fully recovered since 1987, but it remains protected to prevent the trafficking and hunting of the similar-looking American crocodile.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsFloridaWildlifeAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos? | Global economy | The Guardian
description: Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to last
Content: The IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva (left), speaks with the Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, at an IMF fireside chat in Bangkok.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenThe IMF’s managing director, Kristalina Georgieva (left), speaks with the Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, at an IMF fireside chat in Bangkok.Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/GettyGlobal economy‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?Sky-high oil prices and geopolitical turmoil have made less of a dent than feared … just don’t bank on it to lastHeather Stewartin Bangkok andGraeme WeardenSat 17 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInside the vast, glass-walled Queen Sirikit conference centre in Bangkok, the air-conditioned atmosphere was calm as policymakers from more than 100 countries gathered this week for the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting – and contemplated the surprising strength of the global economy.A small army of smiling, uniformed Thai staff were on hand to explain the baffling geography of the heavily guarded building, where lunch options were as cosmopolitan as the delegates – including, improbably, a Burger King.“Resilience” was the buzzword at one event after another, after six months in which sky-high oil prices and geopolitical chaos have made less of a dent in the global economy than first feared.Growth has not fallen off a cliff, buoyed up by the AI investment boom; stock markets haven’t crashed. “We had Covid, the war in Ukraine, supply-chain shocks, the war in Iran, and the alarm bells go off. And yet we haven’t had that massive synchronised crisis. So I think there’s this feeling that a lot of countries are sort of defying gravity at all income levels,” said Clemence Landers, the vice-president of the Washington-based Center for Global Development.Yet the IMF was also keen to remind delegates that the resilience of the past six months had been bought at a cost and may not last. The message – “Resilience under strain, urgent choices” – leapt out from the front page of its flagship publication, the World Economic Outlook (WEO).According to IMF experts, the cost of the energy support measures governments have put in place to protect their citizens from soaring oil prices, as a result of Donald Trump’s war in Iran, has been an extraordinary 0.5% of global GDP.It said many countries would be unable to sustain support on this scale for much longer – and some had already begun to phase out subsidies, exposing the public to more of the costs of the conflict.The IMF urged governments to limit the costs and let market signals do their work, by sticking to temporary, targeted measures, rather than across-the-board subsidies.View image in fullscreenPeople take part in a protest against the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Group in Bangkok on Friday.Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty ImagesAside from how to cope with the practicalities of a conflict that has persisted far longer than many governments had hoped – and whose end point remains elusive – the IMF was also keen to highlight two pressing risks.The first was what it sees as the unsustainable state of the public finances, particularly in the world’s richest countries. The WEO projected the highest budget deficits this year for advanced economies since the depths of the Covid pandemic.That means government debt in these countries is expected to keep rising – from 108% of GDP last year, to 115% of GDP in five years’ time.“Public debt is high in many economies, and fiscal buffers that could otherwise have helped meet rising spending pressures from ageing populations, climate change and national security needs have instead been used to absorb the repeated shocks,” the WEO said.Anxiety about spendthrift governments appears to have been one factor driving the recent sell-off of government bonds – pushing up yields, or interest rates, to their highest levels in decades; though it also reflects higher expectations for inflation and growth.The IMF’s managing director,Kristalina Georgieva, lamented: “Too many countries, they did not use the post-pandemic recovery to rebuild fiscal buffers, and each new shock has pushed debt levels higher.”Fretting that this leaves governments exposed when the next shock comes, as well as pushing up the share of tax revenues required just to service debt, Georgieva repeatedly implored governments – not least Washington – to tighten their belts. “What is our loudest call to policymakers right now? Make urgent repairs to the fiscal house before the cracks widen,” she said. It seems a message unlikely to land well with voters buffeted by one shock after another.The US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, did not bother to travel to Bangkok to hear it; nor to oversee the meeting ofG20finance ministers, of whom he is formally the chair this year.View image in fullscreenJohn Healey chaired the meeting of G20 finance ministers after the US Treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, failed to turn up.Photograph: Athit Perawongmetha/ReutersThe UK chancellor, John Healey, stepped in to chair the meeting instead. He spent much of his brief time in Bangkok stressing the importance of standing shoulder to shoulder with Ukraine – which the US has notably not been doing of late. Russia’s delegation was allowed to attend the G20 meeting, to the deep discomfort of UK delegates.The UK received a positive review from Georgieva and her colleagues, for setting out a plan to balance the books; though she conceded the bond markets had not rewarded its prudence.“The UK is actually one country where action to reduce the deficit has been taken decisively,” she said. Asked why the UK’s bond yields have not fallen accordingly, Georgieva said London’s status as a global financial centre tended to put the UK under additional scrutiny.“Traditionally we’ve seen more attention, in relative terms in the UK, to what the government is doing. [There is] a bit more sensitivity, and I think the government recognises they need to stay the course.”Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief saysRead moreUnusually, no communique was issued after the G20 meeting: a stark signal of how difficult it has become to reach multilateral agreement in the current fissiparous period.The UK will take over the G20 presidency next year and has ambitious plans, on AI regulation and international development; but Bessent’s no-show was a reminder of the tough task they face in rekindling multilateralism.The other alarming message the IMF was keen to land, concerned the threat of an AI market crash. As Georgieva put it in a blogpost on Friday: “The risk is that expectations may run rapidly ahead of productivity gains, setting the stage for near-term disappointment.”The Federal Reserve chair, Kevin Warsh, while professing himself an optimist about the long-term gains of “superintelligence”, as he insisted on calling it, put it another way: “We really don’t know what the market structure is going to be of these new technologies. Who’s going to get to make the money? What are the consequences for those that bet that they were going to make money, but the market structure doesn’t allow it?”And AI is not just a stock market phenomenon but a huge driver of real-world exports, of the hardware and infrastructure necessary – albeit the benefits are heavily concentrated in a small number of economies, including Taiwan and South Korea. The knock-on effects, then, would be significant.View image in fullscreenSouth Korea’s Kospi share index recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, tumbling by 14.5% during the week.Photograph: Ahn Young-joon/APIt is a familiar fear; but in its twice-yearly Global Financial Stability Review, the IMF laid out in detail the rising levels of debt being used to finance the AI boom; the intricate financial linkages between the companies involved; and the increasingly leveraged position of the investors – including hedge funds – backing them up.As far back as the Wall Street crash of almost a century ago, the economist JK Galbraith was highlighting the fact that leverage – betting with borrowed money, effectively – tends to amplify booms and busts.And as ministers met in the Thai capital, elsewhere in Asia there were tremors that may suggest Georgieva’s fear of “near-term disappointment” may already be gripping some investors.South Korea’s Kospi share index recorded its biggest weekly loss since October 2008, at the height of the financial crisis, tumbling by 14.5% during the week, as traders ditched chip manufacturerssuch as Samsung and SK Hynix.Tech market sell-off deepens amid fears over US inflation and AI debtRead moreAnalysts reported that questions around the borrowing, spending commitments and future profitability of AI companies unsettled the markets.Bondsissued by the datacentre CoreWeave slumped almost to distressed levels as these worries swirled.Expectations of future increases in US interest rates also rose, after data showing that consumer price inflation rose in September, as did inflation at the US factory gate. US tech stocks were also hit, knocking 2% off the Nasdaq index between Monday and Thursday.It was just the latest of a series of market wobbles of late, and finance ministers and central bankers probably gave it little thought as they were whisked in air-conditioned comfort back to their capitals this weekend.But if the boom does turn to bust, sending shock waves through the global economy, they won’t be able to say they weren’t warned that the “resilience” we have been enjoying rests on shaky foundations.Explore more on these topicsGlobal economyInternational Monetary Fund (IMF)World BankEconomicsMarket turmoilBudget deficitInterest ratesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: UK sees growing demand for help bridging gap between end of work and start of pension | Pensions | The Guardian
description: Fixed-term annuities give income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Fixed-term annuities give income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end
Content: After falling out of fashion, annuities have become more popular with those planning their retirement.Photograph: Halfpoint/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenAfter falling out of fashion, annuities have become more popular with those planning their retirement.Photograph: Halfpoint/Getty Images/iStockphotoPensionsUK sees growing demand for help bridging gap between end of work and start of pensionFixed-term annuities give income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the endRupert JonesSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinancial firms are reporting growing demand for a product that helps bridge the gap between stopping work and getting your pension.Sales of retirement annuitieshave risen sharplyduring the last couple of years, and now advisers are seeing a fresh surge of interest in what they say is one of the market’s “lesser-known” options.An annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income. The vast majority of people opt for one that provides an income for the rest of their life, called a lifetime annuity.But more individuals are now buying a version that gives them an income for a set period – such as five or 10 years – and an agreed lump sum at the end. They can then decide what to do with that cash based on their circumstances at the time.View image in fullscreenMore people are interested in fixed-term annuities.Photograph: De Visu/AlamyThis type of product is called a fixed-term annuity, and the retirement specialist Standard Life says it can be a way to secure a guaranteed income for a set period while giving you the flexibility to review your options later.After falling out of fashion, annuities have become more popular partly because of higher annuity rates and tax changes, but also because they offer some financial certainty during turbulent times.On top of that, a fixed-term annuity can give some breathing space if, say, you don’t feel quite ready to sign up to a lifetime annuity or go into drawdown (where you withdraw a portion of your pension savings every year and leave the rest invested).Standard Life says its data reveals there has been growing customer interest in fixed-term annuities this year, while its rival Canada Life said recently it had experienced a “significant rise in demand” for its version of this product.So how much income might you get from a fixed-term annuity?This week Standard Life said a 62-year-old with a £100,000 pension pot could currently get a guaranteed income of about £13,800 a year for five years, and would get a £50,000 lump sum at the end of the term.View image in fullscreenAn annuity is a product that turns an individual’s pension pot into a regular, guaranteed income.Photograph: Ascannio/AlamyThis level of income is higher than the full new state pension of £12,548 a year. You get that when you reach state pension age, which has started to rise from 66 and will hit 67 in April 2028.According to the latest Standard Life research, 62 is, on average, the age when people would like to retire. So someone could use a fixed-term annuity to fund the period between stopping work and getting their state pension, providing some financial certainty.Nick Flynn at Canada Life says these types of products are resonating with retirees “because they solve real challenges, helping retirees buy time before committing to drawdown or purchasing a lifetime annuity”.He adds: “Customers are choosing the product to bridge the gap to state pension or defined benefit pension start dates, help fund specific commitments such as mortgage payments or school fees, or stabilise income in the earlier years of retirement.”Changes to the inheritance tax (IHT) treatment of pensions, announced by Rachel Reeves in the 2024 autumn budget, have helped give annuities a new lease of life.View image in fullscreenLegal & General found that misconceptions and confusion about annuities were widespread.Photograph: Alessia Pierdomenico/ReutersThe then chancellor announced that from April 2027, money left in a defined contribution (AKA money purchase) pension after someone’s death will no longer be exempt from IHT. All private pensions and most workplace schemes are defined contribution.The changes mean “unused” pension savings could be taxed as part of someone’s estate if they exceed the IHT threshold. Unused funds are money in a pension pot that has not been used to claim an income, such as buying an annuity.However, the insurer Legal & General says it surveyed 2,000 UK adults aged 50-plus earlier this year, and found misconceptions and confusion about annuities remained “widespread”.For example, only 35% of respondents correctly identified a lifetime annuity as the retirement option that guaranteed an income for life. Meanwhile, 30% felt that annuities were too difficult to understand.But L&G says: “Annuities are actually quite simple. They let you exchange some or all of your pension savings for a guaranteed income.”However, it adds: “They are not right for everyone. Annuities generally cannot be changed once set up or cancelled after the cooling-off period.”L&G hasa myth-busting guide on its website.Explore more on these topicsPensionsAnnuitiesRetirement planningState pensionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Poldark’s resilience helped me turn round my business | Culture | The Guardian
description: Staffing issues, financial woes, equipment failure and a thousand other things made it seem as if being the boss of a dental practice wasn’t for me, but TV’s burly hero inspired me to push on
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Staffing issues, financial woes, equipment failure and a thousand other things made it seem as if being the boss of a dental practice wasn’t for me, but TV’s burly hero inspired me to push on
Content: ‘The mine became my odd internal shorthand for my practice.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillView image in fullscreen‘The mine became my odd internal shorthand for my practice.’Illustration: Martin O’NeillMy cultural awakeningCulturePoldark’s resilience helped me turn round my businessStaffing issues, financial woes, equipment failure and a thousand other things made it seem as if being the boss of a dental practice wasn’t for me, but TV’s burly hero inspired me to push onMaysa HattabSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIdiscovered the TV seriesPoldarkabout a year into a new business, an ill-fitting professional identity, and life in a new city. Having worked for others since dental school, I’d taken possession of a practice the year I turned 30.The practice needed serious refurbishment. I bought it despite dire warnings that my plans for the building, and the way I wanted to treat patients, couldn’t keep a practice in the black. After months of frigid rooms (the building barely had central heating) and frantic clinics, being constantly reminded I hadn’t yet accrued years of trust like the previous owner, I found myself in the upstairs office at 8pm on a Monday, weeping over a spreadsheet.I approached Poldark with low expectations, seeking an old-fashioned escapist release. I could retreat into romantic landscapes, candlelit longing, or stakes much higher than any I’d taken on: shipwrecks, deadly outbreaks (when those were still the stuff of fiction), injustice and heartbreak. Debbie Horsfield’s glowing 2015 adaptation of the novels turned the melodrama dials high enough to engage a frazzled end-of-day brain which couldn’t grasp a plot for much longer than 20 minutes.At first, it didn’t disappoint on the escapism front: operatic passions, shimmering violins, tumbling curls and terrible choices abounded. But later, and with no small sense of ridiculousness, I saw parallels to my business everywhere. In Ross Poldark’s stubborn refusal to accept defeat, reopening his family’s derelict copper mine and rebuilding his home despite a chorus advising him to walk away. I saw them in his cousin and rival Francis’s jaundiced self-pity, both men brought low by market forces. Rocks fall, mines flood and people falter, and even doing all you should can’t mitigate failure.While Ross sublimated his regrets into sweaty labour, I poured my own into trying to be the most accommodating boss I could. Soon, “the mine” became my odd internal shorthand for the practice: for a recruitment rollercoaster, endless building work and countless small disasters. My academic and professional life (plus my middle-daughter status) trained me to expect that if I worked hard enough, the right outcomes would follow. The practice dismantled that idea with ruthless efficiency.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markIt is about claiming the uglier feelings, accepting that hard work can’t fix everythingFor someone who negotiates other people’s intimate boundaries and anxieties daily, I was shockingly unprepared for how visceral the reality felt. I was still less prepared for rage. Worse, I felt being a good boss and good dentist meant I should never burden those around me with my frustration and fear. This backfired more than once, making me seem remote to my colleagues. Others felt distance when they needed humanity.The roiling Cornwall seas took on a weird, hallucinatory quality while my life contracted to nothing but equipment woes, shortages and tense payroll cycles. Peak unreality hit during a hellish period of several staff changes in succession, with costs mounting, waiting lists expanding despite more hours and every reason to believe all of it was a horrible mistake.Raye’s I Know You’re Hurting urged me to confront a lifetime of depressionRead moreThen came the moments I couldn’t muscle through: a missed target with serious financial consequences; a bruising clash that, in retrospect, was my own fault. It wasn’t quite Poldark (no one almost drowned!). Nor was it the catastrophe I feared, but the beginning of learning how to be boss without tamping down every human feeling.Though the worries around what I “should” have been doing didn’t vanish, the practice survived: one day, one patient, one system and one decision at a time. Still, I needed help. That came through someone who grew into an extraordinary business manager, co-conspirator and friend. Paring back my hours, not having my fingerprints on every single process, and letting people see me, helped the practice grow beyond survival.As the 10th anniversary of the practice approached, and in a perverse fit of nostalgia, I decided to rewatch Poldark. While wonderful, it didn’t hold quite the same charge, for reasons besides Aidan Turner’s (very lovely) bare chest. Back then, it was more about claiming the uglier feelings, accepting that hard work can’t fix everything and that sometimes, the mine just floods.Share your cultural awakeningsYou can tell us how a cultural moment has prompted you to make a major life change by filling in the form below or emailing us on cultural.awakening@theguardian.com.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
