title: TV tonight: the return of hit mystery thriller Dark Winds  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Cops Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee are back looking for a killer. Plus, Celine Dion and David Bowie inspire Strictly’s icons week! Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Cops Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee are back looking for a killer. Plus, Celine Dion and David Bowie inspire Strictly’s icons week! Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Grim discovery … Dark Winds on U&Alibi.Photograph: UKTVView image in fullscreenGrim discovery … Dark Winds on U&Alibi.Photograph: UKTVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: the return of hit mystery thriller Dark WindsCops Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee are back looking for a killer. Plus, Celine Dion and David Bowie inspire Strictly’s icons week! Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Alexi Duggins,Priya Elan,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesSat 17 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDark Winds9pm, U&AlibiA shootout in a diner marks a thrilling start to the fourth season of this mystery thriller, which has quietly earned quite a fanbase over the years. Set in the 70s, Zahn McClarnon and Kiowa Gordon return as Navajo police team Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee. This time, they’re looking for a runaway school student, while a killer is also on a search of her own.Hollie RichardsonStrictly Come Dancing: Icons Week6.15pm, BBC OneCeline Dion! Shania Twain! Ricky Martin! David Bowie! It can only be icons week. Poor Melanie and Aljaž won’t be around to take on Bonnie Tyler as planned, and Delta is sitting it out with an injury. But Cach and Maddie will take on the foxtrot, while Lacey and Vito glide to the American Smooth and John and Katya get serious with a paso.HRTalking Pictures: World Cinema Classics9pm, BBC FourCelia Imrie returns to celebrate international films, starting with Akira Kurosawa’s Ran, which Christopher Nolan showed to his team when making blockbuster The Odyssey. Imrie also looks at the works of directors Agnès Varda, Francois Truffaut, Luis Buñuel and Ingmar Bergman.HRMarble Hall Murders9.20pm, BBC OneCan Lesley Manville do any wrong? It’s certainly hard to believe – unless you’re a character in her literary mystery show. In episode four, book editor Susan (Manville) is woken by police to be informed that she’s the prime suspect for a hit and run on her author Eliot (Jamie Blackley). Can she prove her innocence?Alexi DugginsSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneNot exactly a noted gag merchant (considering his roles in Happy Valley and A Little Life), James Norton takes the hosting roulette this week. But unlike its US counterpart, SNL UK has not misfired yet thanks to stunningly sharp writing, so expectations are high. The Streets will be the musical guest.Priya ElanKrapopolis11.45pm, BBC ThreeRichard Ayoade voices a fusspot king trying to modernise his ancient Greek city in this daft but zinger-packed animated comedy from Rick and Morty co-creator Dan Harmon. This marathon of six episodes includes a trip to Hades, a melancholy hydra and divine voice cameos from Susan Sarandon and Steve Buscemi.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceTenzing, out now, Apple TVView image in fullscreenTwice as ice … Tenzing on Apple TV.Photograph: AppleTo Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston) and British expedition leader Col John Hunt (Willem Dafoe), it was ‘Mount Everest’, named to honour a 19th-century British Raj official. But Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), the Tibetan-Indian mountaineer who joined them on that historic 1953 trek to the summit, called the peak by its Sherpa name Chomolungma, meaning “holy mother”. To Tenzing, the mountain is not so much somewhere to conquer but someone to connect with. As director Jennifer Peedom’s film tells his story, it scales the heights of the adventure biopic, discovering new angles from which to view old themes of ambition, colonialism and class.Ellen E JonesCléo from 5 to 7Saturday, 9.45pm, BBC FourThe plot of this 1962, Agnès Varda-directed classic is deceptively simple: as she awaits the results of a cancer biopsy, Florence (Corinne Marchand), a singer known professionally as ‘Cléo Victoire’, wanders around Paris, meeting old friends and strangers, getting tarot readings or going to the cinema; alternating between despair, resignation and a kind of ecstasy. Yet each encounter, and even the apparent longueurs in between, vibrates with the life-affirming energy of the French New Wave, a movement busily reinventing the form before our very eyes.EEJGoodfellas, 11.40pm, Sky Cinema GreatsView image in fullscreenPlease hold … Goodfellas on Sky Cinema Greats.Photograph: ScreenProd/Photononstop/AlamyIt’s the greatest mafia film of all time. The Sopranos’ archetype. Martin Scorsese’s masterpiece of masterpieces, and a film you should rewatch every few years just to recalibrate your cinematic senses. Ray Liotta stars as Henry Hill, an Irish-Italian kid from round the way, and an “average nobody”, according to his iconic voiceover. That is, until he gets mixed up with wiseguys Jimmy Conway (Robert De Niro), Tommy DeVito (Joe Pesci) and Paulie (Paul Sorvino), who teach him their code and show him the only way to live.EEJLive sportTrack Cycling : World Championships 2026, 10.15am, BBC TwoWith the women’s madison and individual pursuit.Racing: Ascot, 12.45pm, ITV1All seven races on Champions Day.Premier League Football: Everton v Chelsea, 11am, TNT Sports 1Newcastle play Aston Villa at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacy
Author: David Smith
Headline: The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacy
Content: Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenNathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24Documentary films‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesThe entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacyDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Agus’s first encounter withElizabeth Holmesat a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different.“The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,”Agus, a medical oncologist, recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.”You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreHolmes is not like you or me. She was still a teenager when she founded Theranos, touting technology capable of performing medical tests using only a few drops of blood. She cultivated a distinctive persona: blond hair, an unblinking gaze, a husky voice and a black turtleneck worn in homage to Apple co-founderSteve Jobs.Holmes mesmerised investors and board members including Rupert Murdoch, Larry Ellison, Carlos Slim and former secretaries of stateHenry Kissingerand George Shultz. She became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. But it was all an illusion, a confidence trick built on a scam. Holmes’s shining career ended in disgrace and imprisonment.Margaret O’Mara, a history professor at the University of Washington in Seattle and author of The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, says: “You can’t make this stuff up. If some screenwriter had tried to manufacture this out of whole cloth people would be like, no, this is an unbelievable story. Yet it’s real. Who’s the real Elizabeth Holmes? That’s a question that still hasn’t been answered.”Perhaps the answer lies inYou Can See Everything, a reality-bending documentary, released in the US on Friday, in which Holmes goes eyeball-to-eyeball with the absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder, who directs along with Lance Oppenheim. It was filmed in the 34 days before she was due to report to federal prison camp Bryan in Texas to begin her 11-year sentence for wire fraud and conspiracy.That fate seemed unthinkable in 2003 when, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford University and establishedTheranos, promising to revolutionise the multibillion-dollar blood-testing industry by using microfluidics to run hundreds of tests on just a few drops of blood.She found a receptive audience among investors who wantedSilicon Valleyto deliver more than Facebook friends. O’Mara explains:“She stands out in her ascent as a female entrepreneur at a time when men were dominating the scene and she was doing something that was in tech but seemed to be change-the-world-tech.“The techlash wasn’t brewing yet but, where there was criticism of Silicon Valley, it was like: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people and all you’re doing is building apps? Why don’t you do something a little more meaningful?’ And: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people, but they all seem to be men.’”O’Mara adds: “She was going against gendered expectations but also, to become the female Steve Jobs, she made herself less feminine and also made herself less young.”Holmes ran the company with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, a businessman 19 years her senior, while keeping their romantic relationship a secret. Together they raised $945m.Theranoshad published no peer-reviewed data but Holmes was a charismatic and persuasive presence in boardrooms.Agus, a professor of medicine who is chief executive of theEllison Medical Institute, comments: “You know how you go into a room and there could be 10 people at a table and everyone’s having a discussion? All of a sudden one person speaks and the entire room goes: ‘Yeah, I’ll go that direction.’ She had that ability.“I saw how she was able to sway people. That characteristic is great if you’re a Steve Jobs. That characteristic is very difficult in health because we should be data-driven, not swayed by personalities.”By 2014 Theranos was valued at $9bn. Holmes was named the youngest female self-made billionaire in the US with a net worth of $4.5bn by the time she was 30. She was celebrated on magazine covers and in power lists.The New Yorker wrote: “Although she can quote Jane Austen by heart, she no longer devotes time to novels or friends, doesn’t date, doesn’t own a television, and hasn’t taken a vacation in ten years. Her refrigerator is all but empty, as she eats most of her meals at the office. She is a vegan, and several times a day she drinks a pulverized concoction of cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes in 2015.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersThe heady atmosphere seduced elder statesmen such as Shultz, who had served as a bridge between Washington and Silicon Valley during theRonald Reaganera. Despite no specialist expertise in laboratory diagnostics, he joined the Theranos board in 2011, when he was in his 90s. O’Mara says: “He was drawn in by the idea that here is a bright young person trying to do something more meaningful than building an app. But there wasn’t enough due diligence.”In his biography,In the Nation’s Service, journalist Philip Taubman describes how people around Shultz worried that his enthusiasm had become entangled with personal affection for Holmes. Shultz spoke to her by phone almost daily and invited her to family Christmas dinners. Holmes encouraged his attention, leaning in close when they sat together.Shultz even encouraged his grandson,Tyler Shultz, to take a summer internship at Theranos before joining the company full-time. Tyler eventually became convinced that Holmes was exaggerating what her technology could do. He took his concerns to the Wall Street Journal, whose investigation into the company was crucial to unravelling its web of deceit.Holmes suspected Tyler was behind the disclosures. Her lawyers pursued him and he was placed under surveillance, leaving him afraid and looking to his grandfather for protection. But George Shultz declined to break with Holmes. According to Taubman, he tried unsuccessfully to mediate between the two rather than stand by his grandson. George Shultz died in 2021 at the age of 100.Scientists also had their doubts about Holmes’s grand promises. Agus recalls: “The problem with blood is it clots and, when you do these small fluidics, it clogs. She wouldn’t give me an answer of why that wasn’t a problem for her. To me, that was the initial red flag. The emperor with no clothes was evident in that she was either ultra-secretive, or the way she was trying to explain things didn’t make sense.”John Ioannidis, a professor of medicine and health research at Stanford University, happened to work in a building that had previously served as Theranos’s headquarters. In 2015, he published a Journal of the American Medical Association (Jama) commentary highlighting the striking absence of peer-reviewed evidence supporting Theranos’s claims.He says: “They wanted me to recant and meet withElizabeth Holmes, and maybe write together some new Jama piece saying that I had seen the light.” When Ioannidis urged them to publish validation data, Theranos cited 100-plus patent filings. “I looked at these patents and they were mostly nonsensical. One had a title close to ‘How to do clinical research’ – vague and non-specific. None of that covered the gap of what was being done.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes at federal prison camp Bryan in 2025.Photograph: Adrees Latif/ReutersBut in assessing Holmes’s motivations, Ioannidis offers a nuanced view. “I don’t think anyone can be in her mind. My most likely interpretation is that she believed she would start that wave – attract capital, funds, talent, expertise – and make this real.“I don’t think she was purely a charlatan. She was power-driven, but in Silicon Valley so many people are power-driven. She saw that the way to do this was to get power first, and then attract the people and technology to materialise it.”‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest filmsRead moreHolmes quit as chief executive in 2018 and the company collapsed that year. The trial of Holmes resulted in her 2022 sentencing to more than 11 years in prison for fraud and conspiracy. The scandal was chronicled in a book, multiple podcasts and the biographical mini-seriesThe Dropoutthat starred Amanda Seyfried.You Can See Everything offers an intimate, often bewildering glimpse into Holmes’s domestic life with her partner,Billy Evans, and their two young children during the 34 days before she reported to prison in May 2023.Lavalier’s microphones capture Holmes’s every breath as she reads bedtime stories to the children, sometimes for 12 hours a day. Evans, meanwhile, is filmed naked in the shower and whisking eggs as he corrects her cooking. They fixate on past media profiles, arguing that journalists fabricated her persona.The biggest revelation occurs off-camera. Even as she prepared to enter prison, Holmes and Evans were actively planning a new medical tech startup. In 2025, two years into her sentence, Evans sought $18.5m for Haemanthus – a company allegedly holding patents for a device claiming to scan blood, urine and saliva samples using lasers.Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me? As Silicon Valleypours unprecedented sumsinto artificial intelligence, O’Mara believes the lessons of Theranos extend well beyond Holmes herself.“The cautionary tale is resonant to a broader Silicon Valley morality tale in putting so much faith and power in the hands of one young person or a small circle of people.“The founder culture and obsession of Silicon Valley that helped Elizabeth Holmes become who she was is still alive and well and stronger than ever. We’ve never seen power and wealth more concentrated in so few hands. Not even inAmerica’s Gilded Agehave we seen this.”You Can See Everything is out in the US now, in Australia on 12 November and in the UK on 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderTheranosBiotechnology industryScamsSilicon ValleyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Audacity: this witty tech-bro takedown from a Succession writer is packed with glorious one-liners | Television | The Guardian
description: Jonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call Saul
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Jonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call Saul
Content: Screamer … Billy Magnussen stars as tech billionaire Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOView image in fullscreenScreamer … Billy Magnussen stars as tech billionaire Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOThe watcherTelevisionThe Audacity: this witty tech-bro takedown from a Succession writer is packed with glorious one-linersJonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call SaulRhik SamadderSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany of us yearn for the return of an analogue world, but it’s never coming back. You can’t buy potato waffles without a QR code. I had to arrange an IRL bank appointment for my mother to check her balance, and it took, I don’t know, 100 days? A friend of mine has boycotted WhatsApp, but I can’t tell you how that’s going because we haven’t spoken in a year.Watching The Audacity (from Thursday, HBO Max) this week, I was shaken by how much of our dystopia can be traced to a small number of men in Silicon Valley. Their products and platforms, an expression of their shortfalls as much as their skills, have reshaped our world more seismically than any political party. Their power-brokering has turned a small collection of towns and villages south of San Francisco into a modern-day Camelot.The Audacity is interested in the perverse psychology of pioneers. Our hero is Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen), founder of data analytics company Hypergnosis (ugh). They’re on the verge of being bought out by Cupertino, an Apple-coded corporate big dog, until greedy Dunc leaks the news to jack up the price. When the deal falls through, he’s desperate to regain his reputation as a power player, and morally bankrupt enough to break any law to do it. His plan involves blackmailing his therapist, for reasons I won’t spoil. His hobbies include using the privacy-hacking algorithm created for him by an exploited employee, to spy on his wife’s boyfriend – a result of the open marriage Duncan himself suggested. This show’s title is on the money.In a valley, everyone is shady. Therapist JoAnne Felder spends her days massaging the fraught egos of her billionaire clientele, yet has her own game going. There are rival startup CEOs, all vying for top spot on the podium of douchiness. The inane trappings of untethered wealth are satirised, from orthorexic diets to ayahuasca ceremonies, performative spending and pool parties. High-budget shows are a bit like a kebab shop, mind you: through the skewering of these things, we also get to enjoy them.View image in fullscreenIngenious … Simon Helberg plays geeky inventor Martin Phister in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOSo far, so Succession. But there are stranger, more melancholy strands. An eccentric inventor, developing a digital ‘friend’ for alienated teenagers. A teenage misfit who starts to live in wall cavities, his surveillance of others an eerie mirror of the adult world that has forsaken him. A reclusive CEO called Carl Bardolph, played by Zach Galifianakis. Retired into generational wealth, he misses the spotlight. Bardolph has a ‘law’ named after him, an ethos of infinite profit he once wrote on a napkin, while on speed. “It was based on the logic of the cancer cell,” he explains to Dr Felder.The Audacity excels at one liners. When Duncan’s daughter expresses qualms about her “admissions consultant”, who games the system and guarantees her spot at a top-tier university, Duncan reassures her with a Trump-y aphorism. “Cheaters never lose. And losers – they never cheat.” When the Veterans Association comes to Silicon Valley, looking for partnership, an executive dismisses them with relish. Cupertino helping the charity would be “like France helping your mother to set up a printer. Only we have much, much more money than France”.Wit is a drug The Audacity mainlines, but the show is interested in longevity. Creator Jonathan Glatzer has written on Succession and Better Call Saul. Like the latter, this is a show content to work its hand slowly, building intrigue within a complex plot. I can’t say yet whether it lands all the pieces. Still, I’m enjoying the wild-eyed performance from Magnussen. In real life, the actor is absurdly handsome. Here, his fair curls are piled atop his head (possibly inspired by the way Zuckerberg grew his hair out?). The effect makes him resemble a young Jerry Stiller, or a fried doughnut.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn irony strikes me – if these tech bros do bring about the apocalypse, burning up the planet and making most of humanity extinct, those who survive will actually be living an analogue lifestyle; sucking runoff from a storm drain by an abandoned shopping centre. Something to look forward to. I might even have my mother’s bank appointment by then!Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #265: Your favourite record labels, from Motown to Flying Nun | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Record labels always push music forward into interesting new places. Here’s a celebration of their power by readers and Guardian music writers
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Record labels always push music forward into interesting new places. Here’s a celebration of their power by readers and Guardian music writers
Content: You can’t beat a classic label …  Motown.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYou can’t beat a classic label …  Motown.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #265: Your favourite record labels, from Motown to Flying NunIn this week’s newsletter: Record labels always push music forward into interesting new places. Here’s a celebration of their power by readers and Guardian music writersDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast week we asked Guide subscribers to tell us about their favourite record labels, and the response was enthusiastic. Clearly, even in this age of streaming services that flatten albums, singles, EPs and mixtapes into one single “feed”, the lure of a label – and its role in identifying, nurturing and developing musical talents – remains.So this week, a celebration of the record label: along with some readers’ favourites, we’ve asked music writers to share their personal picks. They’ve put together a great list of familiar and off-the-beaten-track labels that might just help you discover your next favourite album (I can already tell I’ll be spinning the Verlaines record recommended by reader James a fair bit!).‘Record labels throb with thrill and romance’“As a stream of AI slop joins the torrent of content that arcs across popular culture, well-curated labels become more important than ever for time-poor and garbage-resistant listeners. One of today’s best isAD93, founded by Londoner Nic Tasker. It manages to be totally open-minded, while its signees nevertheless have a shared spirit: experimentalism used to dig out beauty and originality. Moin’s avant-rock is unmissable, as is Joanne Robertson’s ambient balladry, and inJames Kthey have a genuine possible pop star. They’re also cannily hoovering up artists out of contract, bringing back the likes of untameable singer-songwriter Ryley Walker. Their catalogue might evoke everything from sweaty dancefloor to empty moorland, but it’s all under the same sky.” –Ben Beaumont-Thomas, Guardian music editor“My favourite record label has to beCBS Recordsin all its manifestations. They recorded so many of the greats, including Miles Davis, Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen etc. They also released the first sampler album in 1969,The Rock Machine Turns You On. At less than half the price of most albums, it contained tracks by established artists like Dylan, Simon and Garfunkel and the Byrds and introduced lesser-known artists like Spirit, The Zombies and the best psychedelic band of the 60s, The United States of America. They followed it a year later with Rock Machine I Love You, which had a similar great selection of artists.” –Millard Parkinson“I don’t think anyone has shaped my taste in music quite like AG Cook, founder ofPC Music. Running from 2014 to 2024, the label and the artists that orbited it – including SOPHIE, Hannah Diamond and GFOTY – injected pop with haunting, glitchy garage and happy hardcore-adjacent sounds, at a time when dance-pop meant Clean Bandit and Jess Glynne. Charli xcx has repeatedly credited the collective with shaping her now generation-defining alt-pop. (Cook was a producer on both Brat and Rock Music.) My favourite release?Danny L Harle’s Broken Flowers EP, from 2015. It sounds like the future, being underwater, and a northern town centre super-club all at the same time.” –Kate Lloyd, Guardian commissioning editor and music journalist“My favourite record label is easily Manchester’sGondwana Records, led by the brilliant jazz trumpeter Matthew Halsall. Alongside a super-cool graphic design aesthetic, the label has also curated a fantastic range of artists, across 85 album releases since 2008. As well as Matthew Halsall’s own albums, they’ve released work by GoGo Penguin, Mammal Hands, Portico Quartet, Hania Rani and Jasmine Myra. The consistency of quality is astounding, and it’s so hard to single out one release, but if pushed it would probably beGoGo Penguin’s brilliant v2.0.” –Ian Oxley“So many record labels throb with thrill and romance, but none better thanRough Trade. They’ve been with me since my teenage love of The Smiths, to the day I picked up a new EP by a band called the Strokes, through my discoveries of Arcade Fire and Arthur Russell, through to the staggering folk talents they release today, likeLisa O’Neill, LankumandRadie Peat. The warm, welcoming Geoff Travis and Jeannette Lee only release stuff they really love, from any genre, and it shows. Also: what a logo. The best label ever.” –Jude Rogers, music journalist and broadcasterView image in fullscreenSincere … PC Music’s Hannah Diamond.Photograph: Burak Çıngı/Redferns“My favourite record label would have to be the now defunctSlash Records. I started out with Los Lobos, but moved on to The Blasters, The Del Fuegos, Bo Deans, L7 and Violent Femmes. Favourite amongst these (based purely on replays) has to bethe Del Fuegos’ Stand Up, a drunken blues rock album, and their final album on Slash.” –Matt PudduckFor the eclecticism of its artists and the many bonkers stories of its hard-partying ways, my favourite label has to beLondon Records. I prided myself on my ‘edgy’ teenage musical allegiances and London’s books reflected these nicely – they too shunned Take That in favour of East 17, and signed All Saints (clearly far cooler than the Spice Girls). My favourite release though was The Raw & the Cooked byFine Young Cannibals, which my dad introduced me to and which became a staple on long summer drives. –Lucia CavendishAn independent record label specialising in hip-hop and UK rap primarily from Nottingham shouldn’t have been this good. ButSon Recordswas. Yes, there was the daftness of MC Pitman, who did novelty records taking cues from Roots Manuva (Witness the Pitness, anyone?), but their releases byCappoandScorzayzeeform part of an overlooked part of British MC culture. The thick Notts accent and attitude give the whole thing a flavour that chimes with UK drill’s contemporary regional heroes like Esdeekid. –Lanre Bakare, Guardian arts and culture correspondentskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I came of age in the 2000s, when it was cool to have racoon tails at the back of your hair and wear pink eyeliner. I don’t look back on my style decisions during that time fondly, but the music still has a special place in my heart. On that point:Fueled by Ramenhas to be one of the most iconic labels ever. title: ‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisis | Elif Shafak | The Guardian
description: The Turkish writer talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novel
Author: Lisa Allardice
Headline: The Turkish writer talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novel
Content: Elif Shafak.Photograph: Alice Zoo/The GuardianView image in fullscreenElif Shafak.Photograph: Alice Zoo/The GuardianElif ShafakInterview‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisisLisa AllardiceThe author talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novelSat 17 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers.There Are Rivers in the Sky, which follows a single raindrop from ancient Nineveh to the River Tigris in 2018, was one of the UK’s bestselling literary novels last year.The Island of Missing Trees, a love story set in post-colonial Cyprus and contemporary London, was shortlisted for the Women’s prize in 2022, and10 Minutes 38 seconds in This Strange World, narrated by a murdered sex worker in Istanbul, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2019. Last December she waselectedpresident of the Royal Society of Literature. It would be tempting to say she is on a roll, but Shafak’s reputation and readership have been steadily growing for more than 20 years and spanning as many books, of which 14 are novels.In a 2017Ted Talk, which has been viewed more than 6.4m times, she describes herself as an Istanbulite, “a European by birth and by choice” and a Londoner for many years. “I like to think of myself as a global soul, as a world citizen, a nomad and an itinerant storyteller.” Her novels sweep confidently across centuries and continents, taking in politics, history, feminism and ecology, typically with a dash of magic realism or mysticism.Her latest, In One Brief Moment All Eternity, is a stylistically inventive fictionalised life of Gustave Flaubert. “This book is really my love letter to literature,” Shafak says over coffee in west London, where the 54-year-old author has lived with her husband and two children for the past 18 years. While Flaubert is now considered the godfather of the modern novel – as Nabokov said, without Flaubert there would have been no Marcel Proust or James Joyce – most of his life was spent toiling in obscurity. It is this that interests Shafak. “The book is about a lonely boy who was misunderstood by almost everyone around him, including his own family members. He was regarded as a failure, as a disappointment, treated as ‘the other’.” The novel is dedicated to anyone who may have felt similarly treated. “I wanted to be able to say, ‘you’re my brother, you’re my sister’. That was the beginning,” she says.double quotation markMaybe I’m in self-imposed exile, but as a writer, I need freedom – the freedom of imagination, the freedom of speechShafak talks with the same fluency and lyrical intensity as she writes, in long, far-reaching sentences. In person, she also listens intently and smiles often, despite the seriousness of her words. We last met when she was part of thepanelto discuss theGuardian’s 100 best novels of all timelist earlier this year: Madame Bovary was in her top 10, but, like Flaubert himself, she is a huge fan of Don Quixote. On stage, she had the softest voice, but when she speaks, everyone listens. She has recently enjoyed renewed popularity with younger readers on BookTok. It is no wonder there are snaking queues of readers of all ages and nationalities for the signings after her literary events.In One Brief Moment All Eternity arose out of our own historical moment, which Shafak has dubbed “The age of three As: Angst, Anger and AI”. Yet it also started from “a very personal place”, she says, when she was struggling with depression and anxiety, or hüzün in Turkish, meaning a deep melancholy. “In the middle of a world shaped by wars and violence, division, climate crisis, technological uncertainties, you find yourself asking, ‘What is the meaning of shutting yourself in a small room and worrying about the perfect synonym?’” she says. “Is there any value in writing a short story, a poem, a novel in a time of crisis and chaos, such as the one we’re going through? I wanted to take a closer look at this question – creativity in a time of crisis.”This led her back to the 19th century, another era of change and confusion, in which “there lived a beloved novelist who dedicated his entire life to literature in a very passionate way”. While Flaubert set out to inhabit the female mind – then a radical proposition for a male novelist – Shafak upends the premise of Madame Bovary to tell his story through multiple women whose paths may have crossed with his. “I wanted to bring together the European canon of the novel with the Middle Eastern oral tradition of storytelling,” she explains. “You open a box and inside there’s another box, under this story, there’s another story. There’s a polyphony of voices.”And so Flaubert’s life is told not just through the eyes of his beloved nursemaid, Julie; his maman; his long-term mistress, Louise Colet; and his confidant George Sand, but also an acrobat he encounters as a boy, a camel called Jamilah and Emma Bovary herself. We meet an Egyptian dancer and courtesan, Kuchuck Hanem, with whom Flaubert becomes enraptured on his travels in the Middle East, passingly mentioned in biographies. “I wanted to remember this woman and say, ‘Maybe this is the woman who inspired Madame Bovary,’” Shafak says. “I want to claim that at the heart of this iconic French European literary heroine, there is an Egyptian belly dancer.” Opium, syphilis and Istanbul (Shafak always thinks of the city as “she”) are also given their own chapters.“Every time I start writing a book, I say to myself, ‘This time I’m going to keep it minimalist,’” she laughs. “I think because of who I am, my upbringing, all these cultural influences are like tributaries that flow into it. We are all interconnected, not only with each other as fellow human beings, but with nature. For me, the long narrative form is about honouring those connections.”View image in fullscreenPoster from the 1934 film adaptation of Madame Bovary.Photograph: Apic/Getty ImagesThey may be separated by nearly two centuries, by nationality and by gender, but once she started looking, the connections between Flaubert’s story and her own were striking, “starting with that lonely childhood, with that feeling of being the other,” she says.Although her parents were Turkish, Shafak was born in Strasbourg, France, in 1971, where her father was studying for a PhD. Her parents divorced five years later and the young Elif and her mother returned to live with her maternal grandmother in Ankara. Like Flaubert, Shafak grew up with two maternal figures. Although her grandmother was uneducated, she insisted her mother return to university, which she had left when she married. Shafak called her mother “big sister”, her grandmother “mother”: “From one I got my love for written culture, from the other I got my love for oral storytelling,” she says. She remembers her grandmother’s flat as a place full of magic, lefty students and Gauloises cigarette smoke.For all the love in her childhood, Shafak felt abandoned by her father, an academic who remarried. Like the celebrated Doctor Flaubert, Gustave’s father, he was “very detached, very aloof”. She didn’t see him for most of her childhood, and for a long time was very angry that he was such a good father to her half-brothers. “I felt like I was the forgotten child. There was a void. There was an absence of love,” she says. “And I think absences also shape us. Silences also shape us.”After she finally graduated, her mother became a teacher and then a diplomat. When Shafak was 10, they moved to Madrid, where she was the only Turkish pupil in the international school. As a teenager, she lived in Jordan and Germany. “Throughout all those years when I was really very lonely, books were my friends.” Shafak returned to Ankara to take a degree in international relations, followed by a PhD in political science. In her 20s, after teaching in Istanbul, she “escaped” to study in the US. Her first novel, Pinhan (The Sufi), was met with acclaim when it was published inTurkeyin 1997. But her decision to write her fifth novel, The Saint of Incipient Insanities, in English was considered a betrayal by many at home.The most significant parallel between Flaubert and Shafak is that they have both had their work put on trial: Madame Bovary for obscenity charges in 1857 and Shafak’sThe Bastard of Istanbulin 2006,for “the public denigration” of Turkishness, due to her having written about the Armenian genocide. Shafak had to live with a bodyguard for a year and a half. Her picture was burned and spat on. She was acquitted, but in 2019 her novel 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World was investigated by Turkish authorities for“crimes of obscenity”along with two earlier books, The Gaze and Three Daughters of Eve, which dealt with material such as child brides and sexual harassment. Her husband, Eyüp Can, a Turkish journalist and former editor of the Turkish liberal newspaper, Radikal, was put on a wanted list as part of President Erdoğan’s crackdown on intellectuals after the failed coup in Turkey in 2016.View image in fullscreenShafak in London.Photograph: Alice Zoo/The GuardianShe has described being a writer in Turkey as “a bit like being kissed on one cheek and slapped on the other”, with the kiss from the readers and the slap from the government. She is keen to stress how much her books are loved back home. “In countries like Turkey, a book is not a personal item. If you like a novel, you can’t just put it back on the shelf. You give it to your auntie, the auntie gives it to her neighbour. It’s incredibly heartwarming.”But she again found herself at the centre of a storm back home after her 2017 Ted talk, titled “The revolutionary power of diverse thought”, in which she came out as bisexual. “I don’t know if it’s brave,” she says now. “I wish I could have done it before. But the abuse that I received from my own motherland for weeks uninterrupted was quite, quite bruising.”She hasn’t been back to Turkey for 11 years. “There’s a melancholy to it. Maybe I’m in self-imposed exile,” she says. “But as a writer, I need freedom. I need the freedom of imagination, the freedom of speech. I felt like I first migrated into the English language and then into the UK. London became home. And I now feel rooted here, and I say this as someone who has led a very nomadic life.”Her daughter and son, who have just left home for the new university term, have grown up speaking English. Her elderly mother often stays with them for long periods. “I hope I’m not offending, but I think only a few male authors above a certain age have precise writing schedules,” she says wryly. “Everyone else just juggles multiple roles.” She often writes at night, whilelistening to heavy metal, melodic death metal in particular, on her headphones. She plays the same song on a loop, often 80 or 90 times. She is a fan of the Armenian-American band System of a Down, who have also been very vocal about the Armenian genocide. “I love it. It gives me such energy,” she says. And somehow this makes her fiction “calmer”.double quotation markYou sit at your desk and there’s a lot of self-doubt, but that, too, is part of the creative processBut it doesn’t make her calm. Writing doesn’t come any easier as you get older, she says. “It doesn’t matter whether it’s your first book, fifth book, tenth book, you suffer. You sit at your desk and there’s a lot of self-doubt. There’s a lot of anxiety, panic attacks. That, too, is part of the creative process.” When she is finished, she is not filled with satisfaction or pride, but grief. “I feel a sense of loss,” she says. “I find it so difficult to let go of the characters.”Then she goes back out into the world. She thinks it is really important for women to have a voice in public life, and surprises herself by how much she loves literary festivals. “I really am an introvert by nature, so my natural habitat is just a small room full of books,” she says. “But when I’m on stage doing a literary event, it is not a chore. It’s not a burden. It is an immense treat for the mind or the soul.” As someone for whom speaking out has led to threats of imprisonment, she is frustrated by the cynicism towards intellectualism in the UK and the US.“It’s regarded as a sign of arrogance, hubris,” she says. “I’m not claiming to be an intellectual. What I am claiming is I have a lot of respect for the intellect.”For Shafak, literature is “one of our last remaining democratic spaces where we’re not rushing from one thing to the next, we’re not just being fed snippets of information, but we slow down and we listen to each other again,” she says. “The ancient art of storytelling is so universal. It’s so timeless. It really doesn’t belong to a single ethnicity, region or religion. It belongs to all humanity. When I’m writing and in my books, I try to remember that kind of … ” For a moment she is lost for words. “I don’t know what to call it other than shared humanity.”In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak is published by Viking. title: ‘I know I can do anything’: new archive of AS Byatt’s papers looks inside the writer’s extraordinary mind | AS Byatt | The Guardian
description: The Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fiction
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fiction
Content: ‘Her prominence cannot be overstated’ … AS Byatt at Newnham College, Cambridge, her alma mater, during a visit.Photograph: Ian Cook/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Her prominence cannot be overstated’ … AS Byatt at Newnham College, Cambridge, her alma mater, during a visit.Photograph: Ian Cook/Getty ImagesAS Byatt‘I know I can do anything’: new archive of AS Byatt’s papers looks inside the writer’s extraordinary mindThe Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fictionEmma LoffhagenSat 17 Oct 2026 03.24 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 03.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 20, Antonia Susan Byatt was not yet sure she could write. “Do I take myself seriously as a writer?” she asked herself in her diary in September 1956. “No, I think not.”The young Byatt – who would go on to become one of Britain’s most celebrated writers, best known for her 1990 novel Possession: A Romance – was troubled by the possibility that her mind might not be equal to her ambitions. Yet her determination was already evident. On her 20th birthday, she wrote: “Today, I know I can do anything. But not yet.”These intimate reflections can be found among the material in a major new archive of Byatt’s work, acquired by the British Library. It offers an insight into the development of the Booker prize-winning writer, whodied aged 87in 2023, and whose intricate, intellectually ambitious fiction earned her international acclaim.View image in fullscreen‘The other side of the tapestry’ … a draft of Possession.Photograph: Copyright Antonia Susan Duffy Literary Trust/courtesy of the British LibraryThe collection comprises 68 boxes of working notebooks, manuscripts, correspondence, personal diaries and documents from Byatt’s early life. It includes handwritten drafts of Possession, which won the 1990 Booker prize, and material relating to her 1978 novel The Virgin in the Garden and The Children’s Book, which was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2009. According to the British Library’s curators, it is one of the most significant contemporary literary acquisitions the library has made in recent years.“It’s the other side of the tapestry,” says Jenny Uglow, Byatt’s editor, who worked closely with her on Possession. “In her books, you have these extremely elaborate plots, very complicated characters with their extraordinary names. And then when you actually look behind it, there are hundreds, thousands of little threads.”Born in Sheffield in 1936, Byatt studied English at Cambridge before continuing her education at Bryn Mawr College, Philadelphia, and at Oxford. She spent more than two decades teaching in universities and art schools, before leaving academia in 1983 to write full-time. She was known for her voracious research and her ability to weave apparently disparate fields of knowledge into her fiction. The archive allows researchers to follow Byatt as she assembles the raw material of her fiction, tests ideas and repeatedly questions whether they will work.The documents “reveal the way her mind works”, Uglow says. “She thought extremely fast and she had one of those racing minds, almost like a three o’clock in the morning mind, everything whirling around. She’ll say things like: ‘This is fascinating, but it doesn’t fit. I can’t go on, this is not working out.’“She got very cross if she was interrupted, or had to travel or wasn’t feeling well,” Uglow adds. “I think what the archive does is allow you to follow an extremely distinctive writer in the way that they create their work.”The handwritten drafts of Possession are particularly illuminating. The novel, which interweaves the story of two contemporary academics investigating the lives of fictional Victorian poets, is a feat of elaborate plotting. The hundreds of pages of notebooks drafting the book show Byatt diligently working through questions of chronology and the relationships between the characters before the narrative took its final shape.“Once she had decided on a book, it would take two, three or four years [to write it],” Uglow says. “She worked everything out scene by scene before she wrote the scene itself. She would really think it through, so when you get to the manuscript there aren’t many corrections.”View image in fullscreenAS Byatt’s school report card – with a distinction in English literature.Photograph: the British LibraryByatt continued to write by hand well into the 2000s and 2010s. “It’s rather like craft work,” Uglow says. “There’s a connection between the brain, the imagination and the hand.”The diaries show that Byatt’s intellectual confidence coexisted with flecks of self-doubt. At a young age, she described herself as an “intellectually slow developer” and wondered whether she had a “second rate mind”.In another entry, she wondered whether her abstract way of thinking would prevent her from creating convincing characters – “characters with blood in them”.The collection also contains correspondence with other writers, including the novelist Iris Murdoch, with whom Byatt had a friendly relationship, and letters documenting her exchanges with younger writers.“If she saw a promising young writer, she was excited,” Uglow says. “She took great pleasure in seeing their books come out, and was loyal to them.”The papers also capture Byatt’s wry observations of the people she encountered. During her time in the United States as a young woman, she offered a tart assessment of the women around her. “American women – curiously, stuntedly efficient & childlike,” she wrote. “Most of these are 26, 27 – one would imagine them less. Friendly though, and not unintelligent.”The library estimates that cataloguing the 68 boxes will take up to two years. Once complete, the archive will sit alongside its holdings of the literary papers of writers including Angela Carter, Beryl Bainbridge, Hanif Kureishi and Graham Swift.Where to start with: AS ByattRead more“The British Library is thrilled to have acquired the archive ofAS Byatt,” says Helen Melody, the library’s lead curator of contemporary literary and creative archives. “Byatt sits at the heart of the British literary establishment and her prominence within postwar British literature cannot be overstated. This collection will be a hugely significant resource for researchers seeking to learn more about her life and work.”Uglow thinks Byatt would have welcomed the acquisition. “I think she would be very happy to see her work taken seriously,” she said. “And she would have enjoyed the fact that people wanted to see it and that it was being looked after so carefully.”Explore more on these topicsAS ByattBritish LibraryLibrariesPossessionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Penelopiad review – move over, Odysseus! Margaret Atwood lets Penelope’s maids run riot | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Atwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threads
Author: Catherine Love
Headline: Atwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threads
Content: Unused comic gifts … Amelia Bullmore in The Penelopiad at York Theatre Royal.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenUnused comic gifts … Amelia Bullmore in The Penelopiad at York Theatre Royal.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewThe Penelopiad review – move over, Odysseus! Margaret Atwood lets Penelope’s maids run riotYork Theatre RoyalAtwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threadsCatherine LoveSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a summer of Odysseus hogging the spotlight thanks to Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster take on Homer, it’s time for the women to have their say. The Penelopiad is, as its title declares, the story of Odysseus’s famously faithful wife. But in Margaret Atwood’s play, adapted for the stage from her own novella, it is also Penelope’s brutally slain maids whose perspective is reclaimed. If Penelope’s voice has been sidelined, theirs have been silenced altogether.The backdrop for this revisionist storytelling is hades. In Sara Perks’s minimal design, it’s a sterile, featureless place, deliberately drained of the passion and mess of life. Thick, blood-red ropes suggest the strands – literal and narrative – woven by Penelope and the cords used to hang the maids. These wronged figures form a chorus, acting out episodes from Penelope’s life as well as interrupting with their own bitter take on events. We hear of Penelope and Odysseus’s marriage, his departure to Troy, and the long, long years that followed.View image in fullscreenRaucous contrast … the maids in The Penelopiad.Photograph: Pamela RaithThe success of any production rests on the central role of Penelope, who carries so much of the narrative, and on the treatment of the multi-roling maids. In director Juliet Forster’s version, Amelia Bullmore captures Penelope’s wry reserve and her trepidation when married off to Odysseus, but at times there’s a stiffness and lack of texture to her performance. Given Bullmore’s comic gifts as a performer, it’s surprising that much of the grim humour in Atwood’s lines feels underpowered.Balloon Girl review – tech tycoon swirls with tragic teen parachutist in a crackling, time-travelling climate rompRead moreThe maids, on the other hand, offer a raucous contrast to Penelope’s restraint. The energetic eight-strong chorus sing, dance and skip their way through the story, pulling on different outfits like kids playing dress-up, only to puncture the silliness with reminders of their deadly fate. At its best there’s a hint here of the sort of theatrical mischievousness of Kneehigh and Wise Children, though with not quite the same dazzle or bite. Welcome as this feminist retelling is, it has the potential for a greater punch than it ultimately delivers.AtYork Theatre Royaluntil 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMargaret AtwoodreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It feels like the light is pushing the darkness apart’: Gellért Gombai’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: The photographer was holidaying with his family when two shadows became a plaything for his young son
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: The photographer was holidaying with his family when two shadows became a plaything for his young son
Content: Lóci in a Grip, 2023, shot on iPhone 8.Photograph: Gellért GombaiView image in fullscreenLóci in a Grip, 2023, shot on iPhone 8.Photograph: Gellért GombaiSmart shotPhotography‘It feels like the light is pushing the darkness apart’: Gellért Gombai’s best phone pictureThe photographer was holidaying with his family when two shadows became a plaything for his young sonGrace HollidaySat 17 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGellért Gombai, his wife and two children spend much of the year at their home in Budapest, Hungary, but most of their summers in Alsóörs. “It’s a small holiday village on Lake Balaton, the largest in central Europe, so it’s often referred to as the Hungarian sea,” Gombai, a freelance photographer, says. “We go to the playground and beach most days, swim, and eat beach food, but even when I’m enjoying my holiday, I’m looking out for interesting moments to capture.”‘It struck me as a minimalist tableau’: Henk Stam’s best phone pictureRead moreOn this particular day, the family had eaten hotdogs for lunch, before Gombai had taken the kids, Lóci and Janka, to the playground. “Lóci, who was five at the time, was jumping between two shadows – one from a changing room, and the other from a building’s roof,” he says. “I asked him to stay still for a few minutes while I got the shot, and he lay like this on the ground. He’s a big-hearted little clown; I’m so glad he’s my son.” When he showed the children, “Janka immediately asked me to take the same shot of her, which often happens. Lóci said it looked like he was among mountains, or as though a monster was about to eat him.”Gombai applied his phone’s “dramatic cool” filter, and made some minor adjustments. “I really liked the slightly metaphysical spaces created by light and shadow,” he says. “If I forget for a moment it’s my son, I see a carefree form lying in the light while the darkness has bitten a large piece out of the space. Even still, it doesn’t feel sad to me. I have the feeling that the light is pushing the darkness apart.”Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Alexandra Shulman: ‘Which book am I ashamed not to have read? Literally the whole canon of classic English literature’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The former British Vogue editor-in-chief and author on a romantic kiss on a traffic island, her school-run regrets, and a very expensive nude
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The former British Vogue editor-in-chief and author on a romantic kiss on a traffic island, her school-run regrets, and a very expensive nude
Content: Alexandra Shulman: ‘I have no jokes, I have no sense of humour.’Photograph: Mark Harrison/Camera PressView image in fullscreenAlexandra Shulman: ‘I have no jokes, I have no sense of humour.’Photograph: Mark Harrison/Camera PressThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewAlexandra Shulman: ‘Which book am I ashamed not to have read? Literally the whole canon of classic English literature’Rosanna GreenstreetThe former British Vogue editor-in-chief and author on a romantic kiss on a traffic island, her school-run regrets, and a very expensive nudeSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in London, Alexandra Shulman, 68, studied social anthropology at the University of Sussex. She was a secretary at Over 21 magazine and, in the early 80s, became a journalist at Tatler. In 1990, she was made editor of British GQ and, from 1992 to 2017, she was editor‑in‑chief of British Vogue. For her contribution to fashion journalism, she was awarded both an OBE and a CBE. Her books include novels and the bestselling memoir, Clothes … and Other Things That Matter. A collection of essays,Black Coffee and Red Lipstick: Notes on Living, is out now. She is married for the second time, has a son and lives in London.When were you happiest?Anytime that I’m lying in the sun next to a swimming pool with a good book.Which living person do you most admire, and why?The king, for the amount of work he’s doing while going through cancer treatment.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?Impatience.What is the trait you most deplore in others?Insincerity.Aside fromproperty, what’s the most expensive thing you’vebought?A Roger Hilton gouache of a nude.What is your most treasured possession?Probably my laptop.Describe yourself in three wordsStubborn, emotional, reliable.What would your superpower be?To teleport myself to places so I didn’t have to go on a plane.What makes you unhappy?Anxiety about the future.What do you most dislike about your appearance?My short legs.If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?A human voice on the phone.What is your most unappealing habit?Not closing cupboards and drawers.What scares you about getting older?Becoming infirm.Who is your celebrity crush?I don’t have crushes.Which book are you ashamed not to have read?Literally the whole canon of classic English literature.Would you choose fame or anonymity?Fame.What is your guiltiest pleasure?Drinking a bottle of wine while binge‑watching something for hours.What was the best kiss of your life?A kiss on a traffic island in Paddington – I was 28.Fashion designer Henry Holland: ‘I’ve thought about a nose job but everyone says I’ll look different. That’s the point!’Read moreIf you could edit your past, what would you change?I wish I’d been able to pick my son up more often from school. When I see parents at the school gates now it nearly makes me cry.How often do you have sex?It’s unpredictable.What single thing would improve the quality of your life?Having a more sunny disposition.Would you rather have more sex, money or fame?Money.What is the most important lesson life has taught you?That, basically, if a thing’s worth doing, it’s worth doing any old how. Perfection is the enemy of achievement.What happens when we die?I don’t really want to know.Tell us a jokeI have no jokes, I have no sense of humour.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&AAlexandra ShulmanMagazinesNewspapers & magazinesVoguefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts | Food | The Guardian
description: ‘Ethereal sigh’ or ‘slimy hopelessness’? Respect this demanding veg and it will reward you
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Ethereal sigh’ or ‘slimy hopelessness’? Respect this demanding veg and it will reward you
Content: Jackson Boxer’s poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenJackson Boxer’s poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.FoodJackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnutsPoach your leeks to perfection, then pair with pickled pears and nutty misoJackson BoxerSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave a great respect for the leek, which is possibly the most demanding vegetable in its need to be freshly cooked before consumption. A warm leek, fresh from the pot, is an ethereal, collapsing sigh of diaphanous veils, whereas cold it can all too easily become a slippery and almost slimy mess of hopelessness.Poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnutsAll the various elements can be made ahead of time except the leeks, which should be just warm from their poaching, and the dressing, which should be made at the last minute. Vegetable bouillon may seem a bit of a faff to make just to poach some leeks (if you prefer, simply cook them in two litres of seasoned water with a dash of white wine instead), but a good, light vegetable broth is a useful thing to have around, and a batch will keep happily in the fridge for three or four days. To toast nuts successfully, cook them on a tray in an even layer in a 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½oven for 15-20 minutes, which will toast them evenly to the core without scorching.Prep25 minSoak and chillOvernightCook1 hr, plus coolingServes4For the hazelnut miso250g hazelnuts40g white miso paste25ml olive oil5gflaky sea salt(about 1 tsp)For the vegetable bouillon (optional; see recipe introduction)1medium carrot, peeled and quartered1 medium onion, peeled and quartered1 medium shallot, peeled and left whole2 garlic cloves, peeled4 leek tops(from trimming the leeks below)1 bay leaf5 thyme sprigs2 parsley sprigs1 star anise150ml white wine2 litres filtered water40g flaky sea saltFor the pickled pears2 conference pears150ml white-wine vinegar50g sugarFor the leeks4 leeks, trimmed, roots removed and thoroughly cleaned, then cut in half across the middle2 litres vegetable bouillon(see above and method)Minced chives and chopped chervil, to finish (optional)For the dressing200g pear pickling liquor(see above and method)100ml extra-virgin olive oil5gflaky sea salt(about 1 tsp)2g ground black pepper(about ½ tsp)50g minced shallot10g minced garlic100g toasted hazelnuts, choppedThe day before, put the nuts in a container or bowl, add a litre of water and leave overnight to soften. Next day, strain the nuts, reserving the soaking liquid.Put all the bouillon ingredients in a large pot (again, you can do this a day before), bring to a low simmer and cook gently on a medium heat for 25 minutes. Take off the heat, leave to rest and cool for four hours, then strain.Peel, quarter and core the pears, then cut each quarter in half lengthwaysand put in a container, for which you have a lid. Put the vinegar, sugar and 75ml water in a saucepan, bring to a simmer, then pour the pickling liquor over the pears, cover and chill for 12 hours.Put the drained nuts, miso, olive oil and salt in a food processor, dribble in just enough of the soaking liquid to lubricate, then blitz to a smooth, rich puree the consistency of mayonnaise; add a drop more liquid to loosen, if need be.Submerge the leeks in the bouillon, bring it to a low simmer and cook for 15 minutes, until the leeks show only gentle resistance to the tip of a sharp knife. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature for about half an hour.Meanwhile, make the dressing. In a stainless-steel bowl, whisk the pickling liquor and oil to a smooth and coherent emulsion, then stir in all the other dressing ingredients.Lift the just-warm leeks out of the poaching liquid and cut lengthways into quarters. Spoon some hazelnut miso on each plate, then arrange the leeks on top. Dot pieces of pickled pear between them, spoon over the dressing and garnish with minced chives and, if you’re lucky enough to have some, chopped chervil.Jackson Boxer is chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham andthe Henriettain LondonExplore more on these topicsFoodVegetarian food and drinkNuts and seedsVegetablesFruitHerbs and spicesStarterrecipesShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: For Valentine’s Day he gave me a heart covered in fake blood. I was appalled – and thrilled | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: Will Huxley thought Garrett looked like a Heathcliff type; they bonded over their shared love of Kate Bush. Then one day Garrett handed over an ornate gift box
Author: Doosie Morris
Headline: Will Huxley thought Garrett looked like a Heathcliff type; they bonded over their shared love of Kate Bush. Then one day Garrett handed over an ornate gift box
Content: Will and Garrett Huxley in Granada, Spain, in 2008View image in fullscreenWill and Garrett Huxley in Granada, Spain, in 2008The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: For Valentine’s Day he gave me a heart covered in fake blood. I was appalled – and thrilledWill Huxleythought Garrett looked like a Heathcliff type. They bonded over their shared love of Kate Bush. Then one day Garrett handed over an ornate gift boxFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesWill Huxley, as told toDoosie MorrisSat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 17.50 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2006 I’d just graduated film school at the Victorian College of the Arts and was working at the ABC in Melbourne. It was a pretty tumultuous time of my life. I had just broken up with my best friend and high school sweetheart – whom I adored – and was in the process of coming out.I was drinking too much and in breaks from the chaos I’d find myself drawn to the local video store. That’s where I first saw Garrett behind the counter. I had an instant crush on him and spent a lot of time perusing the art house section, so he would see how creative and cultured I was.I never had the guts to talk to him but one night in spring we ran into each other at a party. We hit it off and arranged a date at a cafe in the city.The moment I knew: We were babysitting my younger siblings and he wore a tutu to make them laughRead moreI was obsessed with Kate Bush and Wuthering Heights, and Garrett struck me as this sort of Heathcliff type; he was a dark, handsome artist with very dramatic, gothic vibes. That day we talked about art and the things that we love. I was so excited that he shared my passion for Kate Bush, and listening to Hounds of Love on repeat. We talked about John Waters and Cindy Sherman and all these artists that were really formative for us.But that coming-out period was really intense for me. Growing up, my father had enforced this notion that being gay was this dark, shameful, lonely experience. I was so scared of my truth and deep down I felt as if I didn’t deserve to be loved because of it.Garrett is nine years older than me, and was comfortable with himself in a way I thought was so brave and found so inspiring. Still, my coming-out summer was messy.View image in fullscreenWill and Garrett Huxley in Melbourne in 2009I’d get hideously drunk and perform these outrageous stripteases to Tina Turner’s Private Dancer, or Sade’s Smooth Operator for him. They were ridiculous and borderline grotesque – usually involving me tearing my underwear and wearing an assortment of cheap wigs. Instead of running away in fear – like most people would – Garrett would just sit there and smile and enjoy it. He encouraged the wildness.His patience and kindness during that time is something I will never forget and always be grateful for. It undid years of self-loathing and made me see that having a beautiful, loving relationship with a man was possible.The moment I knew: As a reality TV contestant, I was allowed one 15-minute call a week. Even at 3am, Chris would always pick upRead moreBy February we were celebrating our first Valentine’s Day together. As a gift, Garrett presented me with an ornate box. Inside I was shocked to discover a real life cow’s heart he’d procured from a butcher, covered in fake blood. It was so dramatic and macabre. I couldn’t believe the audacity! I felt likeDivine, in the John Waters film Pink Flamingoeswhen she receives a bowel movement in the mail – simultaneously appalled and thrilled. We both love John Waters – but we’re also lifelong vegetarians and huge animal lovers – which made it all the more potent.He told me later it was a test to see if I could deal. If this really overly wrought gesture of romance would spook me. If I was horrified, he said, he’d have known I wasn’t the right person for him.View image in fullscreenWill and Garrett Huxley in 2020View image in fullscreenGarrett and Will Huxley in Ischia, Italy, in 2025Garrett’s artwork at the time was drenched in this sort of visceral imagery of hearts beating and bodies coming together. This gruesome offering was outrageous but it perfectly captured Garrett’s theatricality, which I loved, and the intensity of that time for me. After that we began to connect even more through our art.For two decades we’ve been working, living and creating together. Our life’s work is conjuring our own queer utopia, as we call it. It’s all about queer romance and joy, because for both of us growing up, we didn’t have access to that.View image in fullscreenWhere Have All the Flowers Gone, 2021, by the HuxleysLearning about his First Nations heritage and the pride it brings him has also been a real honour. Sharing that, along with the queerness that I hid for so long, through our art is so healing and so beautiful.Like any couple we have our moments, but our fights are more likely to be about which heels are suitable for traversing our inflatable vulva sculptures and the best way to attach fake eyelashes in a windstorm than who’s doing the dishes.The Huxleys’ Bloodlines exhibitionwill show at the Brisbane Powerhouse from 21 October to 8 November as part of Melt festivalTell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? From quiet domestic scenes to dramatic revelations, Guardian Australia wants to hear about the moment you knew you were in lovePlease share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish.
