title: A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese | Greece holidays | The Guardian
description: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas
Content: Monemvasia, the Greece of the Spartans.Photograph: Jason Rambach/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMonemvasia, the Greece of the Spartans.Photograph: Jason Rambach/Getty ImagesGreece holidaysA Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the PeloponneseAn out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernasChris CotonouSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by Yiannis Ritsos, one of Greece’s greatest 20th-century poets. Ritsos lived in Monemvasia, in a house that is today a museum on a cobble-stretch by the tawny castle walls. A favourite passage goes: “The voyage is neither a leave-taking nor a home-coming – an ethereal bridge …”The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit.View image in fullscreenAutumn in the Peloponnese is another Greece. Forget the Cycladic white and blue; mountain valleys are carpeted in pine forests and wildflowers, a great stretch of green studded with rustic limestone houses. These villages, relieved by the end of a scorching summer, celebrate boisterous harvest festivals for wines, oranges and chestnuts in Laconia, figs in Messinia, and olives near Kalamata. This is the Greece the diaspora yearns for: thechorio– a word that snaps us back to our relatives and Greek rural life, villages where the air is healthy, eating depends on what is grown metres away, and tavernas are alive with locals rather than tourists. In the shoulder season, the weather is cool enough for long walks along the region’s spectacular trails but, at about 25C, is also still good for swimming.double quotation markThe Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surfaceThe two-hour drive to Monemvasia began with the Taygetus pass, winding through villages and cliffside tunnels as golden eagles soared above the firs. On the far side of the Taygetus, the road opened to Mystras, an archaeological Byzantine site stacked up its hillside. I climbed to the Paleologian Palace and its chapels, then descended, hungry, to the village of Parori, where Taverna Ores was servingsyglino, the local cured pork, and an okra stew. I practised my flimsy Greek with the waitress and her mother, who kept one eye on a television gameshow while stirring the stew pots.View image in fullscreenThe Byzantine Greek architecture of Monemvasia.Photograph: Kisa_Markiza/Getty Images/iStockphotoAfter lunch I stopped at Sparta – site of the ancient city state and modern metropolis. Beneath the Taygetus, in the spectral hush of the olive groves, there is an acropolis, an agora and little else. Yet the air carries something over the ruins, and it’s a short but necessary stop. A statue of Leonidas, hero of Thermopylae, stands facing the new city with the ruins at his back.This is still the Greece of the Spartans: locals remain fiercely attached to their ancient ancestry. Monemvasia has a thrilling connection: in AD600, a bishop is said to have led the Spartan population to the rock to fortify themselves against invading tribes. Set on to a slope inside the castle walls is a town of tight passages and medieval Orthodox churches. It is a vivid encounter with Byzantine Greek architecture, as well as traces of Venetian trade: the sweet, fortified wine malvasia was once a prized export. Even my guesthouse,Kelia(rooms from €70), began as a monks’ residence on the sea-facing Chryssafitissa Square.Leaving Monemvasia, I took a detour south for the golden sand dune beaches in Elafonisos. Reaching this island requires taking a 10-minute ferry ride from Pounta. The turquoise waters of Simos beach are deserted in the off-season – a necessary respite before my hour drive north-west to spend a night in Gythio. This working harbour town has neoclassical pastel mansions and waterfront restaurants provisioned by local fishers. Here the Mani begins.View image in fullscreenSimos beach is reached by ferry from Pounta.Photograph: Constantinos Iliopoulos/Alamy“Victory or death” reads the Maniot banner, above the Spartan motto “With the shield, or on the shield”. The region has a reputation for a conservative way of life that might seem unfashionable in modern Greece, but I find it seductive. The Mani’s beauty comes partly from its insularity. Driving an hour to Vathia, rugged mountains are crowned by labyrinthine stone tower villages that Maniot clans built to protect themselves during periods of vendetta or skirmishes with the Ottomans. Some are now ghost towns. Others have been converted into guesthouses.double quotation markThis is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the worldBut it was in Gerolimenas that a Greek friend suggested I stay for a few nights. The seaside village is an easy base for touring both western and eastern coasts. Along the latter, I hiked to mainland Greece’s southernmost point, Cape Tainaron lighthouse and went for an impromptu dip. The Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surface.TheAkroyiali hotel(doubles from €80 B&B) opened in the 1970s, before most of the region’s roads. It is built on Gerolimenas’s shore, so I dozed to the pulse of waves and chatter from the hotel’s taverna below, where owner Mr Theodorakakis and his family entertained guests.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKardamyli, a popular village on the Mani that quietens in autumn.Photograph: Stephen Hughes/Alamy“The Mani is changing at its own rhythm,” Theodorakakis told me. “This is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the world.” Most Greeks prefer to visit off-season, he said. “You can actually explore the region without burning. But be careful of the north-eastern wind. It cuts through!”Leaving Gerolimenas, I drove 30 minutes up the western coastal route, entering the busy town of Areopoli, where I shopped for hand-harvested sea salt and wild oregano. Pretty Limeni and Kardamyli – the home of British writer Patrick Leigh Fermor (who popularised the region) – get the Mani day-trip overspill from Kalamata. Regardless, it’s quieter in autumn. Every hairpin bend opens on to sea views, flowers and limestone.I was lunching over one such view of a grassy cape when the taverna owner mentioned a woman in the village who knewmiralogia. These are wailing Maniot lamentations sung at funerals, which are heard rarely these days. After two days of asking around, I found Kaiti Braimi in a small chapel where she agreed to sing. “In a way, they’re less necessary,” the octogenarian told me. “No more vendettas.”View image in fullscreenThe Polylimnio waterfalls in Messinia.Photograph: PitK/AlamyThe haunting rhythms of themiralogiawere in mind as I left the Mani to enter Messinia – cutting through Kalamata again, but this time heading west. Here, the villagers were celebrating. Clarinets hummed in taverna gardens at Sunday family parties and relatives joined hands in circles to dance thekalamatianos. Passersby stood and clapped before being dragged in.On the hour drive from Kalamata to Pylos – which would be my base – the Maniot mountains flattened into lush forests. Wildflowers bloomed on the roadside. Yet in Messinia’s expansive green are traces of ancient civilisations, including the bronze age palace of Nestor, north of Pylos.My route sidetracked to the Polylimnio waterfalls. You can sidetrack easily in Messinia; there are unspoiled beaches (like Tsapi on the south coast, where mountains tumble into the sea), as well as areas for canyoning, cycling and kayaking. After a small hike, I bathed in clear pools surrounded by pines, alone mostly, apart from an Athenian couple. “We’re here for my birthday,” the man said. “Messinia is the best place in Greece for outdoor activities.” They pointed me to a canyoning trail north of the Bay of Navarino – a tip for my next visit.That evening in Pylos’s port, only an hour from where I began my voyage in Kalamata, I paused for an ouzo at akafenion. A group of lads were watching Greece play Germany at football on the television. They wailed their ownmiralogiawith every missed shot, but when the game ended in a win the cafes along the harbour roared.I thought back on my drive through the Peloponnese’s deep south, a journey that revealed a rural Greece I’d grown up romanticising from family, and believed was slowly disappearing. But not here. In the mountains and shores of Messinia, the Mani and Laconia, I found a Greece for all seasons.Explore more on these topicsGreece holidaysRoad tripsEurope holidaysCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: a literary festival in Greece doesn’t inspire much hope – and sadly, nor do I | Life and style | The Guardian
description: In between talks on geopolitical doom, one woman says I put her off journalism, while another thanks me for doing the same for her son
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: In between talks on geopolitical doom, one woman says I put her off journalism, while another thanks me for doing the same for her son
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnLife and styleTim Dowling: a literary festival in Greece doesn’t inspire much hope – and sadly, nor do IIn between talks on geopolitical doom, one woman says I put her off journalism, while another thanks me for doing the same for her sonTim DowlingSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m at a literary festival in Greece, standing by some sort of colonnade, drink in hand, fulfilling my role as a non-luminary. Ahead of me, hands are being shaken and warm words exchanged. The sun has just set, and there is a faint glow coming off various luminaries.“Why are you just standing there?” my wife says, coming up behind me.“It’s what I do,” I say.I’ve been to lots of literary festivals without my wife, where I spend a lot of time either in my hotel room or in a dark corner of the opening drinks thing. At some point I’m usually required to give a talk, and then I go home. I do not, at any point, give off any light.double quotation markMy schedule is full: swim, rehearse, attend talks outlining different forms of geopolitical doom, lunch, swimBut I’m not even doing a talk at this festival; I’m just here to play in the band. We did it last year and we’ve been asked back. But we aren’t playing until the penultimate evening, and in the meantime my schedule is full: swim, rehearse, attend talks outlining different forms of geopolitical doom, lunch, swim.“There are people you know from last year,” my wife says. “You can’t stand behind a tree all night.”“You’re underestimating my commitment to this strategy,” I say.The next day I’m drinking a coffee between events, staring at the sea and thinking about geopolitical doom, when a woman comes up and introduces herself. She reminds me that I once gave a talk at a university where she was a journalism student. This would have been about 15 years ago. It was possibly the first time anyone had asked me to give a talk about anything, and I remember being both inept and a little graceless.“No, you were fine,” she says.“I don’t remember what I said,” I say.“Me neither,” she says.Anyway, she didn’t become a journalist as a result of my uninspiring words – she now manages cycling tours, one of which, it turns out, I’ve been on.As lunchtime approaches, my wife comes back from swimming.“How’s it going?” she says.“Fine,” I say. “We’re all doomed, but in the meantime I think I’ve signed up for a second cycling holiday.”That evening I go online and track down a contemporary student report of the university talk I gave 15 years ago. “He referred to himself as a ‘frightened little man’,” it reads. I’m struck by how long I’ve been committed to this version of myself.double quotation mark‘After spending the day with you, he decided he didn’t want to be a journalist,’ says the woman. ‘So I just wanted to thank you’I attend half a dozen more talks promising imminent extinction. The penultimate evening comes, and the band plays to a big crowd on a pier looking out to sea. The next morning people stop me in the street and at the talks to express their appreciation. For a moment I get a faint idea of what it must be like to give off a little light.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAt the end of the final lunch a woman introduces herself and tells me I once gave her stepson a day’s work experience on a journalistic assignment exploring urban wildlife. This would have been 25 years ago.“I remember him,” I say. “I remember the whole day.”Tim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guideRead moreI had contacted various guides and arranged to meet them in different parts of London where secret and exotic wildlife could be found: rare birds, insects, plants and bats. I did research, made lists and planned a route.The day before, I received a parcel containing a full safari outfit, which I was to wear in all the photographs. That, it turns out, was the assignment.When the appointed morning arrived, it was raining and freakishly cold for July. I feared the safari outfit would mean the guides wouldn’t take me seriously, but it was worse than that: they thought I wasn’t takingthemseriously. They were not happy. I was not happy. The photographer was not happy, and my work experience person was miserable.“There wasn’t really much for him to do,” I tell the woman. “But I made him carry my pith helmet because I refused to wear it on the tube.”On the wall of my office there is a framed photograph of me dressed in that stupid safari outfit, rain dripping off the pith helmet, pretending to look through binoculars. The caption reads: “Anyone Seen My Dignity?”Every time I look at it I think of the poor work experience person, standing off to the side, shivering in the drizzle and holding my butterfly net.“Anyway, after spending the day with you, he decided he didn’t want to be a journalist,” says the woman. “So I just wanted to thank you.”At the end of that day I decided I didn’t want to be a journalist either, but it was too late.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Tim Dowling columnLiterary festivalsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: The challenge of making a thatched roof pine-marten proof | Animals | The Guardian
description: Glenisla, Angus: Damage by squirrels is common; the mustelid less so. Still, as a local told me, ‘you cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live’
Author: Tom Allan
Headline: Glenisla, Angus: Damage by squirrels is common; the mustelid less so. Still, as a local told me, ‘you cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live’
Content: A pine marten, which can chew through reed, netting and even lead flashing.Photograph: Mark Hamblin/2020VISION/Devon Wildlife Trust/PAView image in fullscreenA pine marten, which can chew through reed, netting and even lead flashing.Photograph: Mark Hamblin/2020VISION/Devon Wildlife Trust/PACountry diaryAnimalsCountry diary: The challenge of making a thatched roof pine-marten proofGlenisla, Angus:Damage by squirrels is common; the mustelid less so. Still, as a local told me, ‘you cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live’Tom AllanSat 17 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 00.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThat the thatch is thick with moss and crusted with the brittle fronds of lichen is not unusual for a roof of this age. What’s puzzling me is the hole in its centre. It is about 10in wide – a dark scoop, as if someone has taken a giant ladle to the roof.When I climb the ladder for a closer look, I can see toothmarks on the reed. I also see that the hole does not go all the way through – the animal obviously gave up after an exploratory burrow.“It was probably the pine marten,” says Pam Aitchison, the owner of this thatched roundhouse in a glen just south of the Cairngorms, which I am here to re-thatch. She fed it peanut butter and jam sandwiches for a while, but stopped when she became concerned that it might be damaging the roof.This is a first for me in 14 years working on thatched roofs. Damage by squirrels is fairly common. They can chew through reed, wire netting, roof battens and even lead chimney flashings. Rats and jackdaws are familiar culprits too, but pine martens – less so.View image in fullscreenThe damaged roof looked as if someone had taken a giant ladle to it.Photograph: Tom AllanThey are a regular presence in this glen, though. Bruce, a semi-retired plumber who lives up the track, had a pair of martens nesting in the roof of his garage for a few summers. Initially,  he tried various ways of keeping them out, but in the end he decided to live with them. “They’ll squeeze through anything,” he said. “You cannae blame them wanting somewhere to live.”The tightly packed new thatch I am laying should, I hope, be less inviting to the mustelids than the soft surface of the old reed.I set to work fixing in place the bundles of water reed, which has come from just down the road, in Tayside (unlike the majority of thatching reed in the UK, which is imported from overseas). It was harvested from Britain’s largest continuous reedbed – an 11-mile-long arc ofPhragmitesplanted in the early 19th century.Originally intended as a flood defence, it is now managed by the RSPB, and contains a quarter of Britain’s population of bearded tits, as well as marsh harriers and water rails. Thatch can be a home for wildlife before it goes on the roof, too.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024 is published by Guardian Faber; order atguardianbookshop.comand get a 15% discountExplore more on these topicsAnimalsCountry diaryRural affairsScotlandHousingCommunitiesBirdsWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​ | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja California in 2024
Author: Kat Wong
Headline: Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja California in 2024
Content: Perth siblings Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33. The three men found guilty of their murders have been sentenced to 158 years in prison each.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEView image in fullscreenPerth siblings Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33. The three men found guilty of their murders have been sentenced to 158 years in prison each.Photograph: SUPPLIED/PR IMAGEMexicoMexican judge sentences three men to 158 years in prison for murders of Australian and US surfers​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend Carter Rhoad, were killed while on a surf trip in Baja California in 2024Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKat Wongwith agenciesFri 16 Oct 2026 22.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 00.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Mexican ⁠judge ⁠has sentenced ​three men to 158 years ⁠and nine months in prison each for ⁠the murder of ​two Australian ‌brothers ‌and their American friend during ‌a 2024 surf trip to the state of Baja California.The ‌defendantswere declared guilty a week ​agoof homicide, aggravated robbery, robbery with violence and vehicle theft ⁠with violence, crimes committed against ​Australian ​brothers Jake ​and Callum Robinson, and ​their ‌American friend ​Carter Rhoad.Rhoad and the Robinsons were shot dead in a suspected robbery while travelling throughMexico.They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked on 27 April 2024.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailTheir bodies were found days later in a clifftop well with gunshot wounds to the heads.Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons.Two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were also found guilty and have been sentenced.The families of the victims followed the sentencing hearing via video link.View image in fullscreenDebra and Martin Robinson, parents of Australian brothers Callum and Jake Robinson, during a news conference outside court after the verdict.Photograph: Karen Castaneda/APProsecutors had requested damages of more than $100,000 but the judge ruled against it and said any compensation would have to be pursued through civil proceedings.The brothers’ parents, Martin and Debra Robinson, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.They have established a foundation in their sons’ names to carry on their legacy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.Callum, the older of the two brothers, moved to the US as a professional lacrosse player and has been remembered for his loving nature and passion for the environment, having been involved in coastal cleanups.Jake, a doctor, was set to take up a position at Geelong hospital after returning to Australia.He has been remembered for his academic success, his passion for sport, particularly cricket and surfing, and his compassion.Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.Explore more on these topicsMexicoAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Ebike rider, 13, charged with sexual touching after girls and women allegedly harassed on northern beaches | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: Sydney teenager charged with offensive beahviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54
Author: Penry Buckley
Headline: Sydney teenager charged with offensive beahviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54
Content: A 13-year-old has been charged after girls and women were allegedly harassed in the Narrabeen area of Sydney in recent weeks.Photograph: Lee Hulsman/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA 13-year-old has been charged after girls and women were allegedly harassed in the Narrabeen area of Sydney in recent weeks.Photograph: Lee Hulsman/Getty ImagesNew South WalesEbike rider, 13, charged with sexual touching after girls and women allegedly harassed on northern beachesSydney teenager charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent in relation to incidents involving females aged 13 to 54Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastPenry BuckleySat 17 Oct 2026 19.53 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn ebike riding 13-year-old boy has been charged with multiple sexual offences allegedly committed against women on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches.New South Wales police said the boy was arrested on Saturday evening after a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area in the first weeks of October.“Following a public appeal, a 13-year-old boy was arrested after attending Mona Vale police station about 7.30pm yesterday,” police said on Sunday.The teenager was taken to Manly police station and charged with three counts of behaving in an offensive manner in or near a public place, and eight counts of sexually touching another person without consent.On Saturday, police had released CCTV images of a male they believed could assist with inquiries.Police allege that 11 separate incidents occurred against girls and women aged between 13 and 54.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe investigation was initially launched after three separate alleged incidents on 7 and 8 October.“In each incident, a male allegedly approached women on walking trails, sexually touched them and then rode away on an ebike,” police said on Saturday. In one of the incidents, the offender allegedly made “inappropriate sexual comments”.At Narrabeen lagoon about 4.30pm on 1 October the suspect “allegedly sexually touched [a] woman before riding away on an ebike,” police said.Last Monday, police received a further report that between 5pm and 5.30pm that day, two women walking along the Narrabeen lagoon near Bilarong reserve had been sexually touched by a male riding an ebike.Strike Force Mexvo was established to investigate the incidents with assistance from state crime command’s sex crimes quad.Speaking in Narrabeen before Saturday’s arrest, Supt John Duncan urged members of the public to come forward with any information about the alleged incidents.“It’s a bushland park that runs 8km, a large amount of which … runs through bushland, obviously there’s not a great deal of CCTV and cameras.”The 13-year-old was granted conditional bail to appear at children’s court on 4 November.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesSydneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Plover, not a fighter: protected bird 12th man on Tasmanian cricket ground as staff mow around nest | Tasmania | The Guardian
description: While masked lapwings have a reputation for swooping during nesting season, Windsor Park oval’s resident plover just wants a good innings
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: While masked lapwings have a reputation for swooping during nesting season, Windsor Park oval’s resident plover just wants a good innings
Content: A masked lapwing, commonly known as a plover, pictured in a suburban garden.Photograph: Tahlia Franklin/Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (NRE Tas).View image in fullscreenA masked lapwing, commonly known as a plover, pictured in a suburban garden.Photograph: Tahlia Franklin/Department of Natural Resources and Environment Tasmania (NRE Tas).TasmaniaPlover, not a fighter: protected bird 12th man on Tasmanian cricket ground as staff mow around nestWhile masked lapwings have a reputation for swooping during nesting season, Windsor Park oval’s resident plover just wants a good inningsIma CaldwellSat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt Windsor Park in Riverside, just outside Launceston in northernTasmania, a masked lapwing has claimed prime real estate in the middle of a community sports ground, showing complete indifference to the weekend cricket matches taking place around it.Warming a nest of eggs, the bird has been affectionately dubbed “Faf Swoop Plessis” by locals – a play on former South African cricket captain Faf du Plessis.Because the species is protectedunder state law, carrying fines of up to $21,300 for disturbing nests, ground staff have had to mow around the site, while players steer clear.During a match early in the season, Great Northern Raiders player Caleb Brewer drew the short straw and was stationed directly beside the nest.“At the start it was pretty weird, but towards the middle we kind of got used to it and the plover wasn’t too bad at the end,” Brewertold local paper The Examiner.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailThe next weekend, Riverside first-grade opener Josh Partridge was tasked with fielding near the plover, but reached a peaceful “mutual understanding”, according to The Examiner.“It was like the plover knew there was a game of cricket going on,” he said. “We weren’t interfering with what was going on in its life, so it didn’t want to interfere with what was going on in ours.”That kind of sporting truce is common, according to Mark Holdsworth from BirdLife Tasmania.“Lapwings will often become accustomed to the local patterns of people using a site and in many situations people modify their behaviour to avoid the core nesting area,” Holdsworth said. Everyone has learned to live with each other.”While masked lapwings – widely known across Australia as plovers – have an intimidating call and reputation forswoopingduring spring nesting season, choosing a wide-open lawn is actually a calculated survival tactic.Sports ovals are a “fantastic place” for them to nest, Holdsworth said, because unobstructed views mean parent birds can spot threats early.I saw pedestrians swear at plovers when they swooped. But I admired the birdsRead moreSean Dooley from BirdLife Australia also said that what looks like eccentric behaviour to humans makes sense for plovers.“The places they choose to nest can seem crazy from our perspective, but there is logic to it,” Dooley said. “They like to nest out in the open so they can see danger coming and they rely on camouflage to hide their eggs and their chicks. So by nesting on an oval, they have a clear view in all directions.”He said that when people give the bird a wide berth, lapwings generally realise they are not under threat.“They definitely aren’t out to get us by nature, they really only care about making sure their chicks aren’t being threatened …“Swooping isn’t their only tactic; they also put on a display that mimics having a broken wing to lure potential threats away. They’re just being good parents and doing all they can to protect their young.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLapwing eggs hatch after 28 to 30 days of shared incubation by both parents. If a clutch is infertile, incubation can continue for several weeks, while birds will often nest again at the same site if their eggs are destroyed.Once hatched, the chicks quickly leave the nest. Dooley said parent birds carry stray egg fragments away to avoid attracting predators, before guiding their offspring across the turf.“If we can just give them their space, they can move away from the nest area once they are walking,” he said.The West Tamar mayor, Christina Holmdahl, said council maintenance teams look after dozens of parks and sporting grounds across the municipality, encountering at least 10 nesting sites every year.“Given the protected listing of the masked lapwings in Tasmania, our staff take their responsibility of looking after these birds very seriously and take extra precautions to protect the birds and any nests they find,” Holmdahl said.Council workers maintain strict buffer zones around the birds and their nests when conducting maintenance.“The plovers never act aggressively towards our staff on the ground,” she said.The standoff coincides with the annualAussie Bird Countwhich runs from Monday 19 October.Now in its 13th year, the national citizen science project invites the public to record bird sightings to help researchers track how native species are coping with urban development and a changing climate. Last year, the Australian magpie was the most commonly spotted species, while the rainbow lorikeet recorded the highest overall tally.“The count is a great opportunity to discover the birds that share your neighbourhood and understand more about them,” BirdLife Australia’s James Johnson said.” For many of us, that’s likely to include the amazing masked lapwing.”Register for the 2026 counthere.Explore more on these topicsTasmaniaCricketBirdsWildlifenewsShareReuse this content

title: Most NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of vegetation | Bushfires | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafe
Author: Graham Readfearn
Headline: Exclusive: Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafe
Content: House on the NSW north coast destroyed by bushfire in 2019. Research has found 94% of homes destroyed in the black summer fires were within the 100m buffer zone to identify at-risk properties.Photograph: Christine Tondorf/The GuardianView image in fullscreenHouse on the NSW north coast destroyed by bushfire in 2019. Research has found 94% of homes destroyed in the black summer fires were within the 100m buffer zone to identify at-risk properties.Photograph: Christine Tondorf/The GuardianBushfiresMost NSW homes destroyed in black summer bushfires were within 100 metres of vegetationExclusive: Research confirms official advice about high-risk properties and warns worsening conditions will make more homes unsafeSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter hereGraham ReadfearnClimate and environment correspondentSat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlmost every home destroyed inNew South Walesduring the black summer bushfires of 2019-20 was inside the 100 metre buffer zone used to identify properties most at risk, new research has found.The findings are an endorsement of the risk maps used by authorities, but the research warns that as global heating generates ever-worsening fire conditions, firefighters may have to extend the recommended distances between homes and vegetation to keep properties safe.The NSW rural fire service said the findings reinforced how homes in high risk areas should be built to higher fire standards as it prepared for a potentially “challenging” fire season.More than 3,000 homes were lost across the country during the unprecedented fires six years ago that took 33 lives and killed or displaced almost 3 billion native animals.Of the 2,475 homes lost in NSW, the research,published in the International Journal of Wildland Fire, found 94% were less than 100 metres away from flammable vegetation such as trees.The 100 metre buffer is a key part of the widely used maps ofbushfire prone landthat firefighters use to plan local outreach activities, and planning authorities use to assess how bushfire-resistant new homes and renovations should be.‘Catastrophic wildfire loop’ after colonisation left parts of Australia more at risk from bushfires, study findsRead moreAssociate Prof Owen Price, an expert in bushfire risk at the University of Wollongong who led the research, said the findings showed a key aspect of the method to identify buildings at risk from bushfires was “more or less spot on”.“That’s reassuring. Distance to vegetation is really important and that 100 metre rule that they apply is pretty good,” he said.But the research also examined fire danger ratings – an index that combines temperature, wind, humidity and the dryness of fuel – on the days when each home was lost.When the fire danger ratings – known technically as the forest fire danger index – reached extreme or catastrophic conditions, “houses further away [than 100 metres] were burning,” Price said.“That’s a warning sign, because we know that index is going to get worse [from global heating]. We know the direction of travel.”Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterHe said wildfire researchers were alarmed by the increasing number of fires around the world hitting and moving through urban areas,including the 2025 Los Angeles Eaton firethat killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged thousands of homes and businesses.Part of his own research was aimed at understanding if similar events could be replicated in Australia.“Being very close to another house [that is on fire] is another risk factor, which is why it’s important we stop houses from burning,” he said.The research warned that the “current regulation may become less useful over time” as the climate crisis increased the risk of homes being lost.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMelissa O’Halloran, responsible for work on bushfire planning at the NSW rural fire service, said the research showed that “houses in that [bushfire prone] area should be built to a higher construction standard”.“The conditions in 2019 were extreme and outside what we would usually prepare for and, even under those conditions, our policy has stood up pretty well.“This reinforces why we want people to have bushfire protection measures in place.”O’Halloran said investigations carried out after previous fires had shown that not all residents knew they were actually living in a bushfire prone area.Homes within bushfire prone land in the state are allowed toremove trees within 10 metres of a house and clear understory within 50 metres.She said the service was reviewing its main bushfire protection policy that would consider the increasing climate risk.“We’re seeing the impacts of climate change already. It isn’t just temperatures, it’s also about how quickly the landscape dries out, as wellas extreme pyroconvectivefires,” she said.Insp James Morris, of the NSW rural fire service, said there was already heightened risk this year for fires in northern parts of the state, in the central west and the far south coast.“They’ve had high rainfall, and it does not take long for those fuels to dry out. It is important residents do their bit and prepare,” he said.“We could be in for a challenging fire season.”Explore more on these topicsBushfiresNatural disastersNew South WalesWildfiresClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warns | Cost of living crisis | The Guardian
description: Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment
Author: Kat Wong
Headline: Former minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employment
Content: Mathias Cormann, pictured in 2022, will deliver a speech warning against the dangers of populism at the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night.Photograph: Éric Piermont/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMathias Cormann, pictured in 2022, will deliver a speech warning against the dangers of populism at the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night.Photograph: Éric Piermont/AFP/Getty ImagesCost of living crisisMimicking populists will not ease cost of living or boost productivity, Mathias Cormann warnsFormer minister and OECD head urges Australia not to adopt migration caps, with research showing migrants boost employmentGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKat WongFri 16 Oct 2026 21.49 EDTLast modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 22.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralia’s mainstream political parties are being warned not to adopt populist policies such as migration caps to address voters’ grievances over the cost of living.Instead, Australia’s longest-serving finance minister,Mathias Cormann, is urging politicians to deliver housing, real wage growth and lower energy costs by boosting productivity.Australia has never driven migration into reverse by design. Would slamming on the brakes be calamitous?Read moreNow the secretary general for the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), Cormann will deliver an address to the Centre for Independent Studies on Saturday night spruiking productivity as the only way to reliably lower the cost of living over the long term.Though not directly named in his address, One Nation – which largely runs on an anti-immigration platform – has surged in popularity since the 2025 federal election, with itsprimary vote reaching 25%, according to the latest Guardian Essential poll, rising above the Coalition’s 22%.While populist parties may have gained traction by speaking to real grievances about rising energy bills, home ownership and real incomes going backwards, Cormann is expected to warn Labor and the Coalition not to follow suit.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email“Mainstream parties that respond to a populist surge by adopting its economics do not recover their voters. They lose twice: once to the original, which the electorate will always prefer to the copy, and once to the centre, which has nowhere else to go,” he will say in his address.“The lesson is consistent: deliver homes, lower energy costs, real wage growth and a credible budget, and the populist tide recedes.“Mimic the populists, and you simply confirm that they were right all along. The way to defeat populism is to solve the problems it feeds on.”Cormann will point to “arbitrary migration caps” imposed regardless of their effect on business, hospitals, aged care or universities.He will acknowledge more Australians now than any time in the past 20 years say the migration intake is too high and may support such policies, with many attributing their concerns to housing.But the answer is to address housing supply, infrastructure, services and the composition of the migration intake, he will say.According to OECD research across Australia’s regions, in places where more migrants arrived, employment among Australian-born workers grew faster, not slower, with no measurable effect on their wages.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSydney travelled, learned a trade and found love in Australia. It might have been a different story under Labor’s migration planRead moreWithout migration, Australia’s working-age population would decrease as the number of older people grows.“An ageing country that chooses to shrink its working-age population while promising to spend more on health, care and defence has not developed a plan – it has put forward a contradiction,” Cormann will say.Tariffs, which have been imposed by US president Donald Trump and proposed byOne Nation, would also fail to address the cost of living and could instead raise costs for farmers, miners and builders, Cormann will say.He believes Australia can only grow its way out of the issue through productivity.“There is no shortcut to a lower cost of living. There is no populist shortcut, through tariffs and caps and state banks,” he will say.“There is only the long way round: an economy that produces more, competes harder and grows faster than its costs … anyone offering you a quicker route is offering you a poorer country.”Explore more on these topicsCost of living crisisOne NationOECDAustralian politicsBusinessMathias CormannAustralian immigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Revealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protesters | France | The Guardian
description: French government investigating why cars funded by UK to prevent asylum seekers crossing Channel were used in school protests
Author: Diane Taylor
Headline: French government investigating why cars funded by UK to prevent asylum seekers crossing Channel were used in school protests
Content: The incident involved a UK-funded land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention) such as this one.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe incident involved a UK-funded land cruiser known as Masstech VEZI (Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention) such as this one.Photograph: Sameer Al-Doumy/AFP/Getty ImagesFranceRevealed: French police used UK-funded 4x4 vehicles to charge student protestersFrench government investigating why cars funded by UK to prevent asylum seekers crossing Channel were used in school protestsDiane TaylorSat 17 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 18.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench police have used 4x4 vehicles paid for by British taxpayers to charge at student protesters during the school protests that have swept the country.The French government has confirmed that an investigation has been launched into why the cars, funded by the UK government specifically to prevent asylum seekers crossing the Channel, were used during a protest involving school students in Dunkirk.School protestshave been taking place across France for a third week with an estimated 160,000 people involved, with protesters raising concerns about crumbling schools and teacher shortages. Demonstrators have criticised policing tactics after teargas was fired at protesters in two areas.The incident involving the UK-funded 4x4, a land cruiser known asMasstech VEZI(Vehicule d’Eclairage de Zone d’Intervention), wasreportedby French media outlet BFM TV on 10 October.The report included footage of the VEZI driving at speed, reversing then driving forwards again with a bin caught under a front wheel being dragged along. Students can be heard screaming as they scatter from the path of the vehicle.French police use UK funded 4x4 vehicle during student protest in DunkirkAccording to reports, a 14-year-old girl was injured by the vehicle and was taken to hospital, sustaining a haematoma. She was later discharged from hospital. She is now recovering, but she told reporters that what happened to her was “unacceptable”.The VEZI was earmarked for UK-funded operations on French beaches to stop asylum seekers boarding dinghies, part of an Anglo-French border agreement signed in January 2018 and known as the Sandhurst treaty.This treaty specifies cooperation betweenFranceand the UK in combatting irregular immigration and secures UK financial support for French efforts through the “Sandhurst funds”.These funds enable France’s national gendarmerie (police service) to acquire additional resources such as all-terrain vehicles suited to dunes and beaches, including the VEZIs, which are reinforced with grilles.According to a recent French parliamentary cross-party inquiry into Anglo-French border agreements, nine of these specialised VEZI vehicles have been bought under the terms of the Sandhurst treaty. The inquiry report states that to be eligible for Sandhurst funding, the equipment must contribute directly to combatting illegal migration in the UK.A spokesperson from the office of Laurent Nuñez, France’s minister of the interior, when asked why a vehicle funded by the UK and specifically earmarked for border control was used to counter a schools protest, said: “We can confirm the opening of an investigation into this.”Sources close to the investigation said: “I don’t think the British are aware that their money is being used to beat French kids.”Another expressed concern about the expanding militarisation of French policing to support authoritarian policies.A spokesperson for Utopia 56, a French association that provides support to asylum seekers in northern France, said: “In Dunkirk, the 4x4 that ploughed into high school students during the protests is a vehicle funded by the British Sandhurst fund – money earmarked for combatting Channel crossings.“The practice of using 4x4s to chase people in the student protest is the same one used on the beaches.“Disproportionate force is employed to silence, intimidate and deter. The repressive tactics being tested at the border to prevent crossings should serve as a warning to everyone.“These are surveillance, control and repression methods that will be replicated in other contexts. The incident involving the vehicle in the student protest is proof of this.”The UK Home Office declined to comment.Explore more on these topicsFranceEuropeImmigration and asylumProtestnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy says | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Ukrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plants
Author: Andrew Roth
Headline: Ukrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plants
Content: ‘The lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the “diesel deal” is the first step,’ said Zelenskyy.Photograph: Thierry Monasse/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘The lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the “diesel deal” is the first step,’ said Zelenskyy.Photograph: Thierry Monasse/Getty ImagesUkraineTrump’s pause on Russia sanctions is ‘reward’ for Putin, Zelenskyy saysUkrainian president warns it will embolden Russian leader and intensify war as Moscow hits country’s power plantsPower plant attacks reflect Russian blueprint to make Ukrainian cities unlivableAndrew Rothin KyivSat 17 Oct 2026 11.38 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVolodymyr Zelenskyy has describedDonald Trump’s decision to roll back sanctions on Russiaas a “reward” for Vladimir Putin and warned it will embolden the Russian leader and intensify the Kremlin’s war, as Moscow launched one of its worst strikes yet on Ukraine’s power plants in an attempt to black out the country’s cities before winter.The Ukrainian president also said he expected theTrump administrationto lift more sanctions against Russia in the future and called for Europe to establish its own negotiations with Moscow as the US has sought better ties and business deals with the Kremlin.“Unfortunately, the lifting of sanctions will continue, and I believe that the ‘diesel deal’ is the first step,” said Zelenskyy on Saturday. “Unfortunately, it seems to me that this cannot stop Putin; on the contrary, he feels joy and happiness that he has such support.”In a social media message, Zelenskyy wrote: “A US ⁠sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground.“We must keep trying to end the ‌war. To end it, not give Putin every reason to continue it indefinitely.”View image in fullscreenA policeman helps an elderly woman to walk out from a residential building damaged by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia, Ukraine.Photograph: Kateryna Klochko/APIn the Trump administration’s latest effort to reduce tensions withRussia, the US president announced on Friday that he would put a hold on a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause on the legislation passed by both chambers was in the national interest.The act, named after the late senator Lindsey Graham,who championed the legislation, would have introduced tough new sanctions on Russia including a 100% tariff on major importers of Russian oil such as China and India, as well as sanctions on Russia’s energy sector, financial institutions and shadow fleet of oil tankers.On Saturday, Zelenskyy said the decision to waive the sanctions would encourageVladimir Putinto intensify the war in Ukraine and called for support in the US to resurrect the bill.“At the time when the Russians launched such a massive strike against our energy sector, in America, regrettably, a decision was made to completely ignore the Lindsey Graham law, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to end this war,” he wrote in a statement. “This law could have – and still can! – help a great deal. But the law needs to actually work, and every voice in support of it matters.”US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Saturday said Trump’s sanctions waiver would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy.“The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia.View image in fullscreenA car burns after a Russian airstrike on a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Kateryna Klochko/APThe move was greeted by the Russian presidential envoy, Kirill Dmitriev, who wrote on social media: “The Trump administration’s suspension of the Graham Act is an important and truly historic moment.”The legislation, which sanctions Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps the country’s energy supplies moving, was due to be implemented in two days.It also directs Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.Zelenskyy also said themilitary-grade Starlink terminals used by Ukrainian forcesstill had limited functionality, and would disconnect from the network when travelling at more than 161km/h (100mph), interfering with drone operations.The service was throttled insideUkrainewithout warning on Tuesday, and Zelenskyy said his government had determined that the restrictions were a “deliberate operation … to prevent us from defending ourselves”.By sending vehicles with the terminals into EU countries, the Ukrainians found they operated at speeds of more than 180km/h, in effect proving that the terminals were only experiencing restrictions in Ukraine.“The conclusion is clear: the restrictions are in effect within Ukraine but do not apply within the European Union,” he said. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTrump’s announcement that he would pause US sanctions came a week after he said Washington hadagreed to purchase diesel from Russiato try to bring down global energy prices, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.Trump said last week that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tonnes in November and 1m tonnes “immediately thereafter”. Russia would deliver an additional 3m tonnes “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote.View image in fullscreenA protest calling for the resignation of Kyiv mayor Vitaly Klitschko, amid anger over increasing cost of  public transport, the destruction of Kyiv’s green spaces and handing them over for development, and insufficient funding for the Ukrainian army from the city budget.Photograph: Sergey Dolzhenko/EPAThe Trump administration’s decision to waive the sanctions is the latest consequence of a brutal quarrel between Trump and Zelenskyy. Several times this week, the US did not provide intelligence of impending ballistic missile attacks to Ukraine, in addition to the White House reportedly ordering the Pentagon to throttle the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet network used by Ukraine’s armed forces.“We very much hope – and I personally hope – that the president of the United States of America will do everything so that Putin stops the killings, stops the strikes on our energy infrastructure, and stops this war,” Zelenskyy said. “But once again, you cannot achieve this by restricting Ukraine’s responses to Russia for killing our people. And even less so by lifting sanctions.”Trump has demanded that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he has blamed the war in Ukraine, rather than the closure of the strait of Hormuz, for the worldwide spike in diesel prices. Ukraine unilaterally halted the strikes after Trump declared an “energy ceasefire” last week, but resumed them when it became clear that Russia was stepping up its attacks on Ukrainian power plants and substations.View image in fullscreenA mobile blast shelter installed in Kyiv for emergency protection during air raid alerts.Photograph: Danylo Antoniuk/Anadolu/Getty ImagesZelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia had launched one of its worst strikes yet against the country’s energy infrastructure, hitting more than 15 critical power generation and transmission facilities and causing “severe consequences”.He also indicated that Ukraine’s dwindling stock of anti-air weapons made it difficult to shoot down many of the loitering munitions, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles being launched each night at Ukraine.“Although our warriors are shooting down a significant number of them,” he said, the “sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences.”Explore more on these topicsUkraineVolodymyr ZelenskyyDonald TrumpRussiaVladimir PutinUS foreign policyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Pope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operation | Pope Leo XIV | The Guardian
description: Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung
Author: Angela Giuffrida
Headline: Doctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lung
Content: Pope Leo XIV leaves the Gemelli hospital, Rome, four days after lung surgery.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAView image in fullscreenPope Leo XIV leaves the Gemelli hospital, Rome, four days after lung surgery.Photograph: Massimo Percossi/EPAPope Leo XIVPope Leo discharged from hospital after cancer operationDoctors say pontiff is ‘fit for discharge’ after operation to remove cancerous tumour from his lungPope Leo lung cancer surgery: what kind of operation did he have and what happens next?Angela Giuffridain RomeSat 17 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 12.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePope Leo has been discharged from hospital in Rome afterundergoing an operation to remove a cancerous tumour from his lung.Leo, 71, was deemed “fit for discharge”, his doctors, Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora, said in a statement published by the Vatican.He walked unaided from the hospital on Saturday afternoon, to cheers from well-wishers.Leo, who in May last year became the first US-born leader of the Roman Catholic church, has been in the Gemelli hospital since Tuesday, when doctors removed part of his right lung in order to extract the tumour.“Considering the blood tests, the chest X-ray done this morning, and evaluating the clinical picture, the Holy Father has been deemed fit for discharge,” the statement said.View image in fullscreenLeo celebrating Mass at the Agostino Gemelli Polyclinic in Rome.Photograph: Vatican Media/APDoctors said on Wednesday that Leo’s recovery from the operation was progressing normally. They are waiting for the results of tests to determine whether the cancer has spread and if more treatment will be needed.Leo was diagnosed with the most common kind of lung cancer – adenocarcinoma.The pontiff celebrated mass in his room on the 10th-floor of the Gemelli hospital in the north-west of the Italian capital before being discharged.The Vatican said he would recite the Angelus prayer on Sunday “from the window of the papal apartment”. It was during his angelus last week, in a rare moment of Vatican transparency, thatLeo made the shock announcement to the crowd gathered in St Peter’s Squarethat a small nodule on his lung had been detected during a check-up.The pope has worked from hospital, including making a phone call on Friday to Vladimir Putin, during which he urged the Russian president to call a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.The Vatican had originally estimated a week-long stay in hospital. The pope’s appointments had been cancelled until 20 October.However, the pope’s surgeon told Vatican media on Saturday that there were “no clinical reasons” to prevent him from traveling to Latin America as scheduled from 6 to 17 November.Dr Stefano Margaritora said that “the Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery” and that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so”.View image in fullscreenThe Gemelli hospital in Rome.Photograph: Alessandra Tarantino/AP“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” he told Vatican News.Before the cancer diagnosis, Leo, who enjoys sports, especially playing tennis, was generally believed to be in good health. He often makes use of the papal retreat in Castel Gandolfo, close to Rome.The Gemelli, located in the north-west of the Italian capital, is renowned for treating reigning popes. Pope John Paul II stayed there so many times that the Vatican worked with the hospital to establish a high-security papal suite.Explore more on these topicsPope Leo XIVThe papacyReligionCatholicismItalyEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym | Isabel Allende | The Guardian
description: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits
Content: Allende on stage with King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain at the award ceremony in Barcelona.Photograph: Pau de la Calle/GTRES/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAllende on stage with King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain at the award ceremony in Barcelona.Photograph: Pau de la Calle/GTRES/ShutterstockIsabel AllendeIsabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonymChilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the SpiritsEmma LoffhagenandElla CreamerSat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Chilean-American authorIsabel Allendehas won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday withLa hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired byChile.The newstory follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional titleLos que faltan.However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”Isabel Allende: ‘I have been displaced most of my life’Read moreThe prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded toLa bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Molawas in fact three male writers– Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.Explore more on these topicsIsabel AllendeFictionAwards and prizesSpainChileEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli settlers attack European diplomats in West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: French mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olives
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: French mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olives
Content: Footage shows attacked French mayor in occupied West BankWest BankIsraeli settlers attack European diplomats in West BankFrench mayor and archbishop also attacked during violent attempt to stop Palestinians harvesting olivesEmma Graham-Harrisonin TaybehSat 17 Oct 2026 14.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 14.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli settler militants have attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and the archbishop of Cambrai in Taybeh, in the occupiedWest Bank, injuring three people and damaging a car, in the latest violent attempt to prevent Palestinians from harvesting olives on their own land.Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries, was wearing his red, white and blue sash of office and attempting to enter a vehicle with diplomatic plates when he was assaulted and knocked to the ground on Saturday.The masked militant shouted “Vive la France” as he launched the attack, a witness said. Badoux’s wife, and Vincent Dollmann, archbishop of Cambrai, were also threatened by the group of seven men, some armed with clubs.The group had joined the olive harvest on lands belonging to the Christian town of Taybeh, along with the French consul general in Jerusalem, his wife and other diplomats, and the Belgian and Polish consuls.Settlers first attacked a group working on the lower slopes of hills near Taybeh. As well as stealing olives, they kicked, abused and assaulted a Palestinian woman in her 70s and beat a man so badly he needed six stitches for a head injury.Then they approached the diplomats and Badoux, who was in Taybeh for the launch of a twinning agreement with his town in northern France. During the attack, the militants smashed the window of an armoured car belonging to the Belgian mission.View image in fullscreenThe smashed window of mayor Badoux’s car.Photograph: Emma Graham-Harrison/The GuardianMaxime Prévot, Belgium’s deputy prime minister and minister of foreign affairs, condemned the violence against Palestinians, foreign diplomats and journalists, and said his country would continue to push for European Union sanctions on settlers.“Harvesting olives, reporting the news or carrying out diplomatic duties should never put anyone at risk of attack,” he said. “This violence cannot be separated from Israel’s illegal settlement policy … the occupation of the Palestinian territory must end.”Palestinian residents of Taybeh have lived with years of escalating attacks from Israeli militants, but settlers had never targeted foreign diplomats there, said Father Bashar Fawadleh, the town’s parish priest.“What happened today is not an isolated incident. It represents a deeply disturbing escalation in settler violence,” Fawadleh said.Since the start of the annual olive harvest in late September,Israeli militants have used violenceto stop Palestinians bringing in a crop that is economically and culturally vital to their communities.Since 27 September, settlers have launched more than 170 attacks, Israeli rights group Yesh Din said. They killed at least four people, injured more than 100 and damaged thousands of trees, according to Palestinian authorities.Even the presence of Israeli activists, diplomats, senior clergy and journalists no longer serves as a deterrence to extreme violence.“If such violence can take place before international witnesses, one must ask what protection remains for local families and farmers when those witnesses are no longer present,” Fawadleh said. “No individual should have to risk physical assault simply to harvest olives from their own land.”On Friday, Israeli militantsattacked and severely injured Washington Post photographer Heidi Levineas she reported on the harvest in the town of Abu Falah. She required surgery on Saturday morning and is now in “moderate” condition, according to a spokesperson for Israel’s Beilinson hospital where she is being treated.US Secretary ⁠of ​State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that America wants Israel ⁠to do more to deter attacks committed by settlers. “We’re very disturbed by those images and ⁠what we’re seeing,” Rubio said. “We’ve asked the Israelis and continue to ask them to crack ⁠down on that stuff.”Israel had already severely restricted the harvest this year by imposing new rules barring Palestinians from trees located in Area C, an area under the Israeli military’s control, which comprises most of the West Bank’s agricultural land.Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, condemned the attacks and said police had opened an investigation. He said foreign diplomats risked attacks from Israeli civilians if they travelled in the occupied West Bank without military coordination.Demanding diplomats give advance notification of travel violates both diplomatic conventions and international law, said one western diplomatic source who asked not to be named.“Israel is in charge of security in Area B and C (the majority of the West Bank), so is obliged to assure safety there for all,” the source said.A culture of near total impunity for Israeli violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank has prompted former prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the international criminal court to intervene.Gadi Eisenkot, an opposition politician and former general hoping to unseat prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu in elections to be held later this month described the attack as “Jewish terror under the auspices of the Israeli government”.Eisenkot backs Jewish Israeli expansion in occupiedPalestinebut wants militant violence brought under control because the attackers are “harming the settlement enterprise in [the West Bank] and national security”.Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: UAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gains | Yemen | The Guardian
description: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: United Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulers
Content: Fighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a rally to recruit more fighters in Sana’a.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFighters loyal to the Houthis take part in a rally to recruit more fighters in Sana’a.Photograph: Mohammed Huwais/AFP/Getty ImagesYemenUAE agrees with Saudi Arabia to re-enter Yemen conflict amid Houthi gainsUnited Arab Emirates will reportedly resume payments to Yemeni forces as gains by Iran-backed Houthi fighters alarm Gulf state rulersYemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Patrick WintourDiplomatic editorSat 17 Oct 2026 07.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe United Arab Emirates has agreed to re-enter theYemenconflict by resuming payments to some government forces fighting Iran-aligned Houthis in the south, according to sources in Yemen. In return, Saudi Arabia has agreed to provide air cover for the anti-Houthi force.The new cooperation agreement is the first tangible sign thatthe deep rift between the UAE and Saudi Arabia over Yemen’s future is starting to be healed– if only because the advance by Houthi forces across Yemen has alarmed all the rival Gulf state rulers.Saudi Arabia is facing daily drone and missile attacks and is struggling to maintain an atmosphere of normality, as Houthi strikes immobilise its airports and some of its energy infrastructure.Southern forces – mainly in the Giant Brigades – were previously trained and funded by the UAE, and are regarded as some of the most effective in the disjointed anti-Houthi military coalition. But the UAE quit operations insideYemenin January, cutting off its funding supply line.Neither Saudi Arabia nor the UAE have responded to a demand this week by southern Yemen separatists for a referendum on secession, a move that would restore the 1967-1990 borders, when Yemen was two separate states.View image in fullscreenYemeni Southern Giants Brigades fighters celebrate and wave their weapons.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe separatist Southern Transition Council has also not yet agreed for its troops to fight outside the borders of the old Southern Yemen, but an explicit agreement by Saudi Arabia to allow a referendum would be likely to lead to the lifting of that restriction.Yemen’s UN-recognised government, based in Aden, declared last week a counteroffensive to drive Houthi forces from the capital Sana’a, but so far the military drive has met with limited success around Majzar near Marib and the Bab al-Mandab strait.There is also no direct contact between the STC leader, Aidarous al-Zubaidi, and Saudi officials. Zubaidi fled to Abu Dhabi in January after a failed STC attempt to take charge across the south and announce a referendum on separation in two years’ time. In response, the Saudis bombed UAE arms shipments for STC forces.TheUAE then announced it was quitting all involvement in Yemen, and the Saudi-backed government said it would seek to try Zubaidi for treason.Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthroughRead moreUAE officials are deeply concerned by the state of the conflict. Despite massive losses, theHouthisare determined eventually to capture Taiz and Marib, the two remaining cities outside the boundaries of the old Southern Yemen.On Friday two missiles fired by the Houthis struck the airport of Aden while a passenger plane was preparing to take off. No casualties were reported.The missiles landed about 500 metres from the Yemenia Airways aircraft, and approximately 100 metres from the midpoint of the runway, said Yemen’s information minister, Moammar Al-Eryani.The strike came a day after at least five people were killed and 16 injured in a Houthi attack on a presidential palace in Aden.Egypt’s president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said he was convening an emergency session of parliament to grant his country’s military the powers to take action in defence of Saudi Arabia. He stressed Egypt would not be taking any offensive action, and would only defend Saudi Arabia.In the UK, discussions are continuing about a Saudi request for further military aid. The UK has sent an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft, but regional diplomats are pressing for the UK to do more. Some concern is being expressed over whether Riyadh should be engaging more closely with other Gulf States, including Oman and Qatar, on the issue.The legal implications of a blanket UK backing for the largely Saudi air campaign is also being considered, since the court of appeal in 2019 found the UK had acted unlawfully in issuing arms export licences during a previous Saudi bombing campaign of Yemen in 2015-16. The Campaign Against Arms Trade said the UK had made no proper assessment of potential Saudi breaches of international humanitarian law, forcing the UK to revise its procedures.Saudi Arabia claims to have revised its methods substantially since then, and certainly argues that it is acting in self-defence in line with the UN charter.
