The UN security council on 15 October adopted a UN presidential statement on 15 October asserting Saudi Arabia’s right to act in self-defence in line with international law.No accurate death toll in the war since August is available, but more than 200,000 people have been displaced, according to the UN, which is placing increasing pressure on Aden-based humanitarian groups.Explore more on these topicsYemenHouthisUnited Arab EmiratesSaudi ArabiaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in Gaza | Gaza | The Guardian
description: Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marry
Author: Aseel Mousa
Headline: Families have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marry
Content: Wijdan Abu Matar, front, has managed to bring her children together in Cairo, Egypt, but her husband, Hatem, remains in Gaza.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The GuardianView image in fullscreenWijdan Abu Matar, front, has managed to bring her children together in Cairo, Egypt, but her husband, Hatem, remains in Gaza.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The GuardianGaza‘I cannot carry all of this alone’: the couples kept apart by the war in GazaFamilies have been scattered, fathers separated from their children, and couples unable to reunite and marryAseel MousaSat 17 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWijdan Abu Matar, 43, was forced to leaveGazain November 2023 with her eight children for medical treatment, while her injured husband, Hatem, remained behind.Wijdan and her family were living in the Nuseirat refugee camp when the Gaza war began with the 7 October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel. Ten days later, on 17 October that year, an Israeli strike hit the al-Muhandseen tower, near their home, injuring Wijdan and every member of her family.“We were sitting together, just about to start lunch when the bombing happened,” Wijdan recalled. “The ceiling collapsed over our heads. Everything went dark. I couldn’t see anything. I just started screaming the names of my sons and daughters.”Her daughter Nour, 15, suffered the most serious injuries, including a fractured skull and bleeding in the brain. Five-year-old Amna suffered severe burns to her chest. The family was initially separated after the strike.Nour spent about 33 days in intensive care, with Wijdan by her side. Amna and Aysel, three and a half, were at a different hospital for 15 days.View image in fullscreenAysel, who incurred severe burns in the bombing, holds up a photograph of her father.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The GuardianOn 30 November 2023, Wijdan travelled with Nour to a hospital inEgyptfor treatment. For months, the family remained scattered across Egypt, receiving medical treatment and staying with other relatives.“I felt completely helpless,” Wijdan said. “There was a fire in my heart because I was away from my husband and my family was scattered.”Eventually, Wijdan managed to bring her children together in an apartment in Egypt. Three years on, however, she is still separated from her husband, who remains in Gaza. “I have become both the mother and the father to my children,” she said. “The responsibility is exhausting me, and I am constantly worried about my husband.”Hatem suffered a serious leg injury that limits his mobility and is now displaced in a tent in Nuseirat. Even speaking to him is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection. “When he manages to get online, he calls me and the children. He tells me, ‘I am counting the days until I can see you again.’ I can see the tears in his eyes,” Wijdan says.View image in fullscreenSpeaking to Hatem is difficult because of Gaza’s unreliable internet connection, Wijdan says.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The GuardianWijdan has no regular source of income and relies on donations. Hatem stopped receiving a salary 10 months ago and his injury prevents him from working.In Egypt, life is difficult for Wijdan and her family. She says she cannot afford transportation to send five of her children to school. “I see my children’s future slipping away in front of me, and there is nothing I can do.”Nour still requires medical treatment, but Wijdan often cannot afford her medication. She sometimes considers returning to Gaza to be with Hatem, but fears exposing her children to further suffering.“I dream of getting my children the treatment they need, and I hope we can reunite with my husband as soon as possible so he can also receive treatment,” Wijdan said. “I cannot carry all of this alone. Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war.”View image in fullscreen‘Psychologically, I am exhausted. I have lost 35 members of my family in this war,’ says Wijdan Abu Matar.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The GuardianSince the war beganwith Hamas’s attack on Israelthat killed 1,200 people, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the health ministry. Earlier this yearan independent UN inquiryfound that Israel continues to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children in Gaza.‘All I want to do is cry’: trauma of 7 October survivors three years after the attacksRead moreSami Abu Tabaq, a 29-year-old Palestinian photojournalist, was forced to leave the Gaza Strip in April 2024, leaving behind his family and his fiancee, Ola.“Loneliness kills me every day,” he said. “Life away from the woman I love and my family is incredibly hard. I’m desperately waiting for the day God brings us together again.”Sami became engaged to Ola five months before the war began. They had met by chance when he chose her family’s home as a location for a photoshoot. Before the war, they saw each other constantly. They went to the sea, had dinner at restaurants in Gaza, and spent months preparing the house where they planned to live after their wedding, which was scheduled for November 2023.Sami and his family fled their home in Tal al-Zaatar, Jabaliya, early on in the war. Their home was badly damaged and later destroyed, along with the house Sami and Ola had been planning to move into once they got married.When his sister decided to flee south with her children, Sami accompanied her but he could not reach Ola to say goodbye.The separation became unbearable. Days, sometimes weeks, passed without Sami knowing whether Ola was alive. Once, he saw reports that an entire residential block near her home in Gaza City had been bombed. “I almost lost my mind. I had never felt so helpless,” he said. Unable to return north, he asked his brother to check on her. Eventually, his brother confirmed that she and her family were alive.‘I couldn’t cry over my children like everyone else’: the tragedy of Palestinian journalist Wael al-DahdouhRead moreSami continued working as a photojournalist from southern Gaza. Four journalists who had shared his tent were later killed, including Hamza al-Dahdouh, a son ofthe Al Jazeera journalist Wael al-Dahdouh.As Israel threatened a ground invasion of Rafah in 2024, Ola began urging Sami to leave Gaza, fearing he would be killed. Sami paid a company coordinating exits at the time for both of them to cross into Egypt. But Ola could not reach southern Gaza to travel through Rafah. “She told me, ‘You go, and I’ll follow you,’” Sami said. “And here we are, still waiting, nearly two and a half years later.” They still have not managed to get married.By his second day in Egypt, Sami was overwhelmed by guilt. “The overthinking kills me,” he said. “I felt ashamed to turn on the lights or eat proper food while my fiancee and my family were struggling to find the most basic things.”In Egypt, his life has become dominated by loneliness and sleeplessness. “There is safety in Egypt and there are beautiful places, but I stay home. Happiness has no meaning without her. I cannot enjoy anything while she is not here,” he said.View image in fullscreenSami Abu Tabaq sits alone in his apartment in Cairo, while his fiancee, Ola, remains in Gaza. Images of Gaza are shown on the television.Photograph: Mohammed Salem/The GuardianDespite the war, Ola completed her bachelor’s degree in nursing at the Islamic University of Gaza. She has also endured enormous loss: her cousin, the journalistAyat Khadoura, was killed, along with about 50 other members of her extended family.From Egypt, Sami tries to create moments of happiness for her. For her latest birthday, he contacted her brother in Gaza and secretly arranged a cake, gift and flowers. “When she woke up and saw everything, she was so happy. I love her reaction when she’s happy.” The only problem was the flowers. “They were artificial,” he said. “I wasn’t happy with them, but natural flowers can’t get into Gaza because Israel does not allow them in.”Sami says he has tried every possible way to get Ola out, without success. She is now applying for scholarships abroad, hoping education might provide a route to evacuation and, eventually, to him.Sami recently travelled to Mecca for Umrah, where one prayer remained constantly on his mind. “I prayed, ‘God, please bring us together soon,’” he said. “But one thing I know for sure: I will wait for her for the rest of my life, until God brings us together.”Explore more on these topicsGazaMiddle East and north AfricaPalestineEgyptnewsShareReuse this content

title: No action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action post | Jonathan Powell | The Guardian
description: Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Tweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’
Content: Sarah Helm pictured in 2011. She posted on X on Thursday: ‘God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.’Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSarah Helm pictured in 2011. She posted on X on Thursday: ‘God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.’Photograph: Martin Argles/The GuardianJonathan PowellNo action to be taken against wife of PM’s aide over Palestine Action postTweet by Sarah Helm, wife of national security adviser Jonathan Powell, ‘does not meet criminal threshold’Nadeem BadshahSat 17 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 16.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNo further action will be taken against Sarah Helm, the wife of the prime minister’s national security adviser, after she was accused of supporting the banned protest groupPalestine Action.Helm, a journalist and author who is married to Jonathan Powell, posted on X on Thursday: “God help us authors who support Palestine and Palestine Action.”The Metropolitan police said on Friday the post was “in the process of being assessed to determine whether any further police investigation may be required”.In an update on Saturday, a force spokesperson said: “On Thursday 15 October, we were made aware of a post on X relating to Palestine Action.“The post was assessed by specialist officers and it was determined that it did not meet the criminal threshold. No further police action will be taken.”Helm was responding on X to a discussion about the Irish authorSally Rooney, who has said she can no longer sell her books in the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.It is understood there was insufficient evidence that the post was capable of encouraging support for a proscribed organisation.The ban, which began in July 2025, made membership or support of the direct action group a criminal offence punishable by up to 14 years in prison.Downing Street has distanced itself from Helm’s remarks.The Campaign Against Antisemitism (CAA) had called on the police to investigate.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe group acknowledged that “spouses are entitled to independent views”, but said Helm’s post “raises extremely serious questions forJonathan Powelland the government.“Clearly, the police need to investigate and Sarah Helm must face the full force of the law, just like others who appear to express support for any proscribed terrorist organisation.”Earlier, a government spokesperson said: “These views are held by an individual who does not represent the government in any capacity.”Explore more on these topicsJonathan PowellPalestine ActionSally RooneynewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’ | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be British
Content: Speaking earlier in the week, Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, said that while his party carries out vetting, ‘you can’t vet people for what they say in the future’.Photograph: SOPA Images Limited/AlamyView image in fullscreenSpeaking earlier in the week, Reform UK’s leader, Nigel Farage, said that while his party carries out vetting, ‘you can’t vet people for what they say in the future’.Photograph: SOPA Images Limited/AlamyReform UKReform candidate filmed saying asylum seekers should be put in ‘concentration camps’Would-be MP recorded telling undercover reporter in ITV investigation that Muslims could not be BritishNadeem Badshahand agencySat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 16.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA would-beReform UKMP told an undercover reporter that Muslims could not be British and asylum seekers should be put in “concentration camps”.The comments were recorded as part of the undercover investigation byITVthat has already seen Reform accused of “appalling behaviour” and “extreme racism”.Reform has said it had opened investigations where activists or members had “clearly behaved inappropriately”, adding there was “no room for racism” in the party.In footage due to be broadcast on Sunday, a Reform activist and aspiring MP, who has yet to be publicly identified, described himself as “pretty hardline about Islam”.He said: “If a Muslim’s prepared to de-convert, I’m happy.View image in fullscreenZia Yusuf, Reform UK’s home affairs spokesperson has described himself as a ‘British Muslim patriot’.Photograph: Guy Corbishley/Alamy“But if they want to remain faithful to Islam, then this would be, I would have disagreements, especially with, um, I mean, as far as I understand, [Reform home affairs spokesperson] Zia Yusuf is a Muslim … to me … you cannot be a Muslim and British … it’s like oil and water.”Discussing people crossing the Channel in small boats, the same activist said: “In the first week of election, build concentration camps, and everyone who comes across on the Channel, you’re in there.”Excerpts from the investigation released earlier in the week included councillors and candidates within Reform using racist language.In one excerpt, black children were referred to as “animals”, while in another a Reform member said his area had become “infested” with Asian families.Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said Nigel Farage’s response to the revelations showed he was “completely unfit to lead”.She said: “Bad apples don’t fall far from the tree. The sleaze, scandals and appalling revelations of racism and rank misogyny piling up by the day go right to the top of Reform UK.“Nigel Farage is incapable of taking responsibility and getting his house in order because he himself shares culpability.”Speaking earlier in the week, Farage said that while Reform carries out vetting, “you can’t vet people for what they say in the future”.In a statement to ITV, the party said: “Reform UK has improved and prioritised its vetting procedures, but from time to time a handful of individuals who do not share our values will initially make it through vetting.“This is the same for all organisations. However good the vetting, one cannot vet a future comment.“There is no room for racism in Reform UK. We always respect due process of investigations and whilst these are ongoing it would not be appropriate to comment on individual cases.”On Friday,Alan Feeney resigned as a Reform councillorfor Solihull and Birmingham after racist comments he had made were uncovered in the investigation.View image in fullscreenAlan Feeney resigned as Reform councillor on Friday.Photograph: ITVITV revealed secretly recorded footage of Feeney making racist comments about Asian homeowners, calling them “parasites”, and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”, during a local election campaign.In a subsequent Facebook post, Feeney wrote: “There is no excuse for my comments. With responsibility comes accountability, and it is for that reason that I have resigned every post I hold on both Solihull borough council and Birmingham city council.”He added: “My remarks were wrong, offensive and completely unacceptable. They do not reflect the standards that the public rightly expects from an elected representative, and I take full responsibility for what I said.”Explore more on these topicsReform UKIslamophobiaITVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Plaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within days | UK news | The Guardian
description: Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’
Author: Natricia Duncan
Headline: Descendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’
Content: The plaque being unveiled on 9 October.Photograph: English HeritageThe plaque being unveiled on 9 October.Photograph: English HeritageUK newsPlaque telling story of African-Caribbean prisoners in Britain stolen within daysDescendants say theft from Portchester Castle reflects racism that has haunted ‘generation after generation’Natricia DuncanCaribbean correspondentSat 17 Oct 2026 11.57 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe theft of a plaque in Hampshire that told the little-known story of African-Caribbean prisoners in 18th-century Britain reflects the enduring racism that has fuelled centuries of atrocities against Black and IndigenousCaribbeanpeople, their descendants say.Ronald Raymond McDonald, a professional drummer, was part of a delegation that travelled from Belize and elsewhere to Portchester Castle near Portsmouth last week to honour their ancestors: 2,500 men, women and children transported to Britain as prisoners of war in 1796.McDonald, whose Garifuna ancestors fromSt Vincent and the Grenadineswere among the prisoners, said he was heartbroken to learn that the plaque had been stolen and a nearby bench vandalised with hateful graffiti.“Why would somebody do something like that when people are simply honouring their ancestors … it’s very sad,” he said.The plaque, installed at the castle, commemorated the more than 2,000 prisoners held there, marking an extraordinary chapter of Black British history: one of the largest known arrivals of African-Caribbean people in Britain before the Windrush era.The unveiling was part of a ceremony organised by theSt Vincent and the Grenadines 2nd Generation (SV2G), in partnership with the University of Warwick and English Heritage, and was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.View image in fullscreenThe unveiling was attended by Caribbean communities, diplomats, researchers and heritage organisations.Photograph: English HeritageBut days later, English Heritage staff discovered the plaque was missing. They said a padlock to one of the castle gates had been removed and the incident had been reported to police.Garifuna advocate Princess Eulogia Gorden said the theft reflected “a spirit of racism that haunts generation after generation and hides in plain sight”. It was time, she said, to recognise that “we are all connected” and to end the hate.Queen Mother Chief Freda Paulino-Sideroff, who is Garifuna and had travelled to the UK for the ceremony, was returning home to the US when she learned of the theft.“Hate will never define who we are as a people. We are resilient survivors of our ancestors who have endured,” she said.In the 1700s, her Garifuna ancestors were expelled from St Vincent by British forces and left to perish on the barren island of Baliceaux as Britain sought to crush decades of resistance to colonisation.Emilio “Sásamu” Thomas, a Garifuna cultural ambassador who also travelled from Belize for the ceremony, echoed Paulino-Sideroff’s sentiments, saying Garifuna people would not allow themselves to be victimised.His message to the perpetrators, he said, was: “Whatever pain that they are experiencing, we’re here to help them to relieve that pain.”Once a site of horror, a tiny Caribbean island could become a Garifuna shrineRead moreThe missing plaque was meant to honour the prisoners, whose story, researchers say, had been largely lost to history. They came from a coalition that included formerly enslaved Africans, Caribbean-born people, Indigenous people and French soldiers who fought against British control of St Lucia, St Vincent and the Grenadines and Grenada. Their defeat and removal helped strengthen British rule in the region.It was unveiled on 9 October, exactly 230 years after one of the ships carrying the prisoners was wrecked at Rapparee Cove in Devon, with many of those onboard losing their lives.Iona Keen of English Heritage called the removal an act of vandalism, while University of Warwick professor Katherine Astbury said the plaque was intended to provide a visible memorial of the prisoners, and a reminder of “an important, forgotten part of Caribbean history”.The vandalism came duringBlack History Monthand amid renewed debate over slavery reparations. Campaigner and author Sir Patrick Vernon said vandalism of memorials representing Black British history had occurred repeatedly over decades, citing damage to other memorials.He described the theft as symbolic of an “ongoing battle and the legacy of enslavement”.Jacqueline Roberts, SV2G chief executive, said the theft could not erase history, and stressed the importance of continuing research to uncover more hidden stories.“Our history is intertwined with British history,” she said. “It’s important to understand that part of our journey, because it is part of the complexity of our identity, and affects our sense of belonging.”Anthony Severin, St Lucia’s high commissioner and chair of the Caribbean community diplomatic caucus in the UK, described the theft as a “desecration of the memory and spirit of our commemorated ancestors”.He pledged that the plaque “whether returned or replaced, will remain affixed to the walls of Portchester Castle”.Explore more on these topicsUK newsRaceSt Vincent and the GrenadinesCaribbeanBlack History MonthCrimenewsShareReuse this content

title: SNP says campaign for next referendum on independence ‘has already begun’ | Scottish National party (SNP) | The Guardian
description: John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK
Author: Patrick Greenfield
Headline: John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UK
Content: John Swinney after delivering his keynote speech at the Scottish National party conference on Saturday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAView image in fullscreenJohn Swinney after delivering his keynote speech at the Scottish National party conference on Saturday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAScottish National party (SNP)SNP says campaign for next referendum on independence ‘has already begun’John Swinney tells party conference SNP will use ‘six-figure war chest’ to renew argument for leaving UKPatrick GreenfieldSat 17 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Swinney has said that the second referendum campaign for Scottish independence “has already begun”, revealing a nationwide effort to renew the argument for leaving the UK in his keynote address to the SNP party conference.On Saturday, the Scottish first minister said the SNP would launch its “most sophisticated campaign in history” to convince Scottish voters of the benefits of independence, backed by “a six-figure war chest”.Called ChooseScotland, the campaign will aim to build the consensus for leaving the union.Swinney told the SNP party conference in Aberdeen that the “stars were aligning” for the pro-independence cause, arguing that nationalist first ministers of Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland had panicked pro-union parties.“For centuries, people in the Celtic nations have been told that we are not good enough. Our languages were derided, our cultures suppressed, our histories rewritten,” he said.“When I stood on a stage recently with pro-independence leaders from Wales and Ireland, it certainly upset some of our opponents.“From their point of view, they are right to be worried. Watching us pledge to work together and seeing the love and respect we feel for each other’s nations. Never again can they portray us as separatists.”At the conference, leading SNP figures said a hung Westminster parliament is the most realistic path to securing a second independence referendum in Scotland as the nationalists would probably “hold the balance of power” in forming a future progressive government.The party has just eight MPs in parliament, but recent polling indicates that if a vote was held today, that number would surge at the Labour party’s expense in Scotland, although there is uncertainty surrounding how many seats it would gain.Deputy first minister Jenny Gilruth said her party would welcome an early general election to reenergise the push for independence.“The polling, of course, suggests the SNP would hold the balance of power in a hung parliament and really strong support for the SNP across the country allowing us to regain a number of seats,” she said.The sentiment was echoed by Lara Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, whotold a podcastby the pro-independence newspaper the National that they could negotiate another poll if the overall results were tight.“We have a really great opportunity at the next general election to be in a position where that negotiation can seriously start with the next iteration of the Westminster government, whether we have a hung parliament, which is looking very likely, or different coalitions,” she said.“Perhaps now we are talking about a Lib Dem-Labour coalition. The SNP are polled at getting somewhere between 40 and 50 MPs at the general election. That’s huge.“Let’s put it to Westminster and put the onus on them to meet us at the table and set that plan out for us.”The latest MRP polling by Electoral Calculus this weekpredicted a narrow Labour victory, with the SNP winning 28 seats, although previous polls have indicated they could win even more.In a visit to Lanarkshire on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the Scottish government needed to “move beyond” the question of independence while offering to work more closely on devolving power from Holyrood with Swinney’s administration. The Westminster government would have to grant a second vote on Scottish independence.“I just feel we all have to move beyond the constitutional questions. In my view, people in Scotland are suffering the cost of living crisis, like they are in England and everywhere else. And I think our job is to focus on the practicalities, to focus on solutions for people. Right now, too much time is wasted on those dramas. It consumes too much energy,” he said, when asked about the issue.Although it is not in Swinney’s power to call a second independence referendum, he told the conference that another vote could happen sooner than expected.“Our independence is very close,” he said. “Our nearest neighbours will always be our closest friends and our strongest allies. I will always want the very best for the people living in England, Wales and across Ireland.“But friends, in the long arc of history, nothing is static. And those that try to hold on to the past fail to grasp the opportunities of the future.“In this period of history, the nations of the United Kingdom are evolving into a new relationship. That is something to welcome.”Explore more on these topicsScottish National party (SNP)John SwinneyScottish politicsScotlandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-off | Devon | The Guardian
description: School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: School looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishments
Content: The Friends of Lower Field protesting against the sale of playing fields in Totnes, South Devon.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Friends of Lower Field protesting against the sale of playing fields in Totnes, South Devon.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianDevon‘We’re not playing games’: Parents launch playground protests to fight school field sell-offSchool looking to sell piece of open land beloved by people in Devon town to fund refurbishmentsSteven MorrisSat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn Saturdays throughout autumn, residents of Totnes have met at a field on the banks of the River Dart to play ballgames, fly kites or simply sit on the grass and chat.But it hasn’t just been about having fun – this has been a “play protest” aimed at trying to save a beloved piece of open land in the historicDevonmarket town.The local comprehensive,King Edward VI Community College (KEVICC),has been given the go-ahead by the UK government to sell the 1.5-hectare plot – Lower Field– and it is likely houses will be built on it.School leaders say they desperately need funds to revamp neglected buildings but campaigners claim the sell-off is an example of land that has been used by communities for decades being whisked away – a modern “enclosure” of public space.View image in fullscreenAnna Ali said there was ‘hidden impoverishment’ in the area.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian“It’s devastating,” said Becca Robinson, who uses the field for women’s and girls’ fitness classes. “I’m trying to get women and girls to be more active and to get outdoors. The great thing about the field is it’s an open space, so it feels safe. It really worries me that, if we lost it, fewer women and girls will exercise.“It’s also a spot people go just to do their own thing rather than take part in structured sport. You can just make an ad hoc decision to go and play a game or just to sit and read.”Earlier this year, the anti-poverty charity Trussell published research revealingalmost half of UK residents (45%) had lost access to at least one community space – such as a park, social club, library or post office – since 2023.Danielle McIlven, who has been organising games of rounders on the field, attended the school and said Lower Field had been part of her life for years. “It’s about the unstructured play that can take place there. In the summer you see swarms of teenagers playing there or heading down to the river.”Anna Ali, the organiser of a women’s football “kickabout” and a member of the campaign groupFriends of Lower Field, said the town had a reputation for being middle class and affluent. “But there is quite a lot of hidden impoverishment. Public green spaces are vital. I was speaking to a woman who brings her grandchildren here. They can’t afford to join sports clubs, so kicking a ball around on the field is a lifeline.”Lewis Winks, a leading member of theRight to Roamgroup, said Lower Field had been shared by the school and the wider Totnes community since it was gifted by the Elmhirst family, known forprogressive farming, forestry and educational projects on the nearby Dartington Estate, about a century ago.View image in fullscreenCampaigner Lewis Winks said Lower Field had been shared by the school and community for about a century.Photograph: Jim Wileman/The GuardianA key issue the Friends group is digging into is the details of the Elmhirst gift – and whether it may have been legally given to the community or permanently protected for community use.Winks said: “Lower Field is a vital place for young people and families to play, exercise and spend time together. Losing it would undermine the town’s vitality and wellbeing.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Friends group wants Education South West, the trust the school is part of, to explore whether the field could be sold to the community. Winks said: “We are asking for a realistic window to raise the money. A community purchase could help fund improvements at KEVICC while safeguarding the field for its pupils and the wider community.”But it is a race against time. The land is expected to be put on the market in January, giving little time to raise funds. Campaigners also highlight that measures under the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026aimed at giving communities greater influence over the places and assets that matter to themare unlikely to come into force in time. “We’re falling through the gap regarding a right to buy,” Winks said.Matthew Shanks, chief executive ofEducation South West, said it understood how important the site was to the Totnes community and wanted to have an open and constructive conversation with people.He said money raised would support significant refurbishment and modernisation across the school estate, including improvements to buildings and facilities. Shanks said the school would retain playing fields which would remain available for public use.School principal Alan Salt said he understood the future of the field mattered hugely to the community. “We want to be open and transparent about what is proposed.” The trust and school have organised an open meeting to discuss the field.Salt argued that selling it made sound financial sense. There had been little capital investment in the school for six years and it had “temporary” classrooms more than half a century old.“So we’ve got a really acute set of challenges within a very difficult national context,” he said. “At the end of the day, we are a comprehensive school trying to get the best for the students in a really difficult national picture.”Explore more on these topicsDevonAccess to green spaceSchoolsSchool fundingLand rightsCommunitiesPublic landsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Arizona joins Nevada to fight proposed cuts to their shares of Colorado River | Colorado river crisis | The Guardian
description: Move comes after Trump administration announced restrictions that could slash water supplies
Author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
Headline: Move comes after Trump administration announced restrictions that could slash water supplies
Content: Water flows from the Glen Canyon Dam down the Colorado River on 8 June in Page, Arizona.Photograph: George Frey/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWater flows from the Glen Canyon Dam down the Colorado River on 8 June in Page, Arizona.Photograph: George Frey/Getty ImagesColorado river crisisArizona joins Nevada to fight proposed cuts to their shares of Colorado RiverMove comes after Trump administration announced restrictions that could slash water suppliesUwa Ede-OsifoSat 17 Oct 2026 19.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArizona has joined Nevada in its legal battle against the Trump administration’s proposed cuts to their shares of the shrinking Colorado River.The move comes after the interior departmentannouncedrestrictions this summer that could slash the water supplied to lower basin states – Arizona, California and Nevada – over the next two years depending on the river’s condition.The river’s major reservoirs, Lake Mead and Lake Powell, have plummeted to historically low levels, due to overuse and a changing climate.The states sharing the waterway were at an impasse with the upper basin states arguing that their downstream counterparts were responsible for the reservoir’s water shortages and should thus face the largest cuts.The federal government’s intervention came after the states missed several deadlines for a consensus.The fear looming over the state of the river is that if reservoir levels plunged far enough, the waterway wouldeffectivelynot be able to flow downstream, a so-called deadpool.The upper basin states – Wyoming, Colorado, Utah and New Mexico – were spared from the water cuts, an exemption that has drawn sharp rebuke from the leaders of the lower basin states.“We are drawing a line in the sand,” Arizona governor Katie Hobbs said in a Fridaystatement.“I am taking this legal action alongside Nevada because the federal government refuses to hold the Upper Basin accountable for the water deliveries they oweArizona, and is threatening to force draconian cuts that go well beyond the Lower Basin Agreement,” Hobbs continued, referring to a two-year-voluntary water conservation pact among her state, California and Nevada.Tom Buschatzke, the director of Arizona’s water department, said “intervention in theNevadalawsuit is necessary at this time for Arizona to protect its legal rights to Colorado River water while preserving a path forward to achieving a collaborative outcome with California and Nevada to protect the Colorado River system”.An interior department spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the joint litigation.Explore more on these topicsColorado river crisisArizonaNevadaRiversUS politicsTrump administrationWaternewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Trudy strengthens to category 2 as it heads toward Mexico | Mexico | The Guardian
description: Hurricane warning in effect from Manzanillo to Cabo Corrientes as storm moves toward Pacific coast
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hurricane warning in effect from Manzanillo to Cabo Corrientes as storm moves toward Pacific coast
Content: Clouds loom over the Pacific Ocean in Boca de Apiza, Michoacán state, Mexico, on Saturday.Photograph: Gustavo Vilchis/ReutersView image in fullscreenClouds loom over the Pacific Ocean in Boca de Apiza, Michoacán state, Mexico, on Saturday.Photograph: Gustavo Vilchis/ReutersMexicoHurricane Trudy strengthens to category 2 as it heads toward MexicoHurricane warning in effect from Manzanillo to Cabo Corrientes as storm moves toward Pacific coastAssociated PressSat 17 Oct 2026 19.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrudy strengthened to a category 2 hurricane as it moved toward Mexico’s south-western and west-central Pacific coast on Saturday, the US National Hurricane Center said.A hurricane warning was in effect from Manzanillo in Colima state to Cabo Corrientes in Jalisco. The latest NHC data showed Trudy with maximum sustained winds of 100mph (155km/h) and about 205 miles (330km) south/south-east of Cabo Corrientes and 115 miles (180km) south/south-west of Manzanillo, moving north-west at 10mph (17km/h).Meanwhile, Typhoon Champi strengthened into a category 4 weather system as it moved toward Guam.Trudy’s center was expected to approach the Mexican coast on Saturday and pass near it into Sunday. After the latest warning, Mexico’s government issued a tropical storm warning for Las Islas Marias and discontinued a similar warning for its coast south of Lazaro Cardenas.The Mexican navy urged mariners and coastal residents to exercise extreme caution because of high waves, heavy rain and the risk of rising rivers, flooding and landslides in vulnerable areas.Colima authorities said the risks remained low, but warned that heavy rainfall could cause damage because the ground was already saturated by successive storms along the Pacific coast.Trudy was expected to bring 4-8in (10-20cm) of rain through the weekend, with isolated totals of about 15in (38cm).Also in the Pacific, Champi strengthened into a category 4 storm as it moved west toward Guam at 15mph (24km/h).By Saturday night local time, Champi was about 25 miles (40km) south-east of Guam, with maximum sustained winds of 140mph (225km/h), according to the US National Weather Service.The storm was forecast to pass south of Guam early Sunday local time and continue intensifying through the day. Guam and Rota remained under a typhoon warning, while Tinian and Saipan were under a tropical storm warning and typhoon watch.The governors of Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands both requested emergency disaster declarations on Friday. Approval by Donald Trump would authorize federal support and funding for emergency protective measures.Airports, harbors and some health facilities in the territories were closed. Resources were unlikely to reach the islands for three to five days, according to Saturday updates from the Federal Emergency Management Agency.The territories are still recovering from Super Typhoons Sinlaku and Bavi, which struck in April and July, respectively.Explore more on these topicsMexicoUS weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Two people, including child, killed after person drives through soccer game in Kansas | Kansas | The Guardian
description: The driver of the vehicle is in custody, and two juveniles were in the vehicle, according to Wichita police department
Author: Diana Ramirez-Simon
Headline: The driver of the vehicle is in custody, and two juveniles were in the vehicle, according to Wichita police department
Content: Police on the scene where a person drove a vehicle through a soccer field during a game in Wichita, Kansas.Photograph: Wyatt Glosson/KAKE-TV/APView image in fullscreenPolice on the scene where a person drove a vehicle through a soccer field during a game in Wichita, Kansas.Photograph: Wyatt Glosson/KAKE-TV/APKansasTwo people, including child, killed after person drives through soccer game in KansasThe driver of the vehicle is in custody, and two juveniles were in the vehicle, according to Wichita police departmentDiana Ramirez-SimonSat 17 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTFirst published on Sat 17 Oct 2026 19.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people, including a child, were killed during a soccer game in Wichita,Kansas, when a person drove a vehicle through the field at Stryker soccer complex, police have confirmed. Multiple other people were injured.The driver of the vehicle is in custody, Aaron Moses of the Wichita police department said Saturday in anews conference. There were two juveniles in the vehicle, he said.Police confirmed that one child was killed at the scene and one adult was killed, but did not release any names or ages until family could be notified. “This is a tragedy,” Moses said. Those injured were taken to hospitals but the extent of their injuries is unknown.Moses said he did not know how fast the vehicle was traveling or how it got onto the field.Officials are still investigating and the city has said all events at the soccer complex are canceled until further notice. Wichita police have set up aportalfor anyone to submit video evidence of the incident.A witness told local news station KWCH that a black pickup truck was seen “plowing through the youth soccer fields”. The truck hit multiple people before stopping 100-200 yards down the fields, the witness said. They reported seeing dozens of emergency responders giving aid and CPR to the victims.Lily Wu, the mayor of Wichita, posted a message on social media: “I’m heartbroken by reports of a tragic incident at Stryker Sports Complex. My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved.”Explore more on these topicsKansasUS crimeChildrennewsShareReuse this content

title: New York City police seek suspect in fatal subway station shooting | New York | The Guardian
description: Suspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPD
Author: Keely Aouga
Headline: Suspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPD
Content: The 7th Avenue-West 53rd Street subway station in Manhattan, New York City, on Saturday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe 7th Avenue-West 53rd Street subway station in Manhattan, New York City, on Saturday.Photograph: Kyle Mazza/NurPhoto/ShutterstockNew YorkNew York City police seek suspect in fatal subway station shootingSuspect shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to NYPDKeely AougaSat 17 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleView image in fullscreenAn image of the suspect provided by the NYPD.Photograph: Courtesy of NYPDView image in fullscreenAn image of the suspect provided by the NYPD.Photograph: Courtesy of NYPDA man was shot and killed in aNew YorkCity subway station Saturday afternoon, and the New York police department is searching for the suspect.The suspect fatally shot a man in his 30s on the E train platform of the 53rd Street-7th Avenue subway station, according to astatement from the NYPD.“On Saturday, October 17, 2026, at approximately 12:21 PM, on the northbound E train platform of the 53rd Street–7th Avenue subway station in Manhattan, this individual shot and killed a man in his 30s,” the NYPD’s statement said.According to the NYPD, the suspect displayed a firearm and discharged it, striking the victim once in the chest. EMS responded and transported the victim to NYC health + hospitals/Bellevue, where he was pronounced deceased.The identity of the victim is not known at this time.The suspect is wanted for homicide within the confines of the Midtown North Precinct/Transit District 1.The NYPD released surveillance photos of the suspect, who fled on foot and headed northbound on 7th Avenue.The images show the suspect dressed in a red tracksuit, a black vest and a black face mask and carrying a backpack.Authorities are urging individuals with information regarding the incident to reach out to itstip lineat 1-800-577-TIPS (8477), or submit tips online at theCrime Stoppers websiteor via X @NYPDTips.The investigation remains ongoing.Explore more on these topicsNew YorkGun crimeUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: ICE agent who crashed into man in Texas was targeting suspect who died years ago, family says | ICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement) | The Guardian
description: Federal officer slammed vehicle into a construction worker while pursuing a man who died in similar circumstances
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Federal officer slammed vehicle into a construction worker while pursuing a man who died in similar circumstances
Content: Carmen, sister of Miguel Parra Hernandez, at a news conference in Houston, Texas, on 14 October.Photograph: Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle/APView image in fullscreenCarmen, sister of Miguel Parra Hernandez, at a news conference in Houston, Texas, on 14 October.Photograph: Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle/APICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)ICE agent who crashed into man in Texas was targeting suspect who died years ago, family saysFederal officer slammed vehicle into a construction worker while pursuing a man who died in similar circumstancesAssociated PressSat 17 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA federal officer slammeda vehicle into a Houston construction worker andbroke his leg, believing him to be a man who apparently died years ago, the dead man’s family said on Friday, further calling into question the account given by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).The worker, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures and needs reconstructive ankle surgery, according to FIEL, a Houston-based immigration advocacy group. At a news conference on Friday, the group said the alleged suspect’s family had shared documentation proving his death.After the episode on 10 October,ICEsaid in a statement that officers had observed a suspect they were targeting, identified as Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, enter a vehicle with Parra Hernandez.But on Friday, Rafael Lemaitre, spokesperson with the Harris county district attorney’s office, told the Associated Press that Mendoza-Cervantes was not in that vehicle.ICE did not respond to requests for comment on Friday.“ICE is lying,” said Cesar Espinosa, FIEL’s executive director. “Either somebody is not telling the truth or all of a sudden these two ICE agents have developed a sixth sense and are able to see dead people.”ICE released a photo of a man it identified as Mendoza-Cervantes. But the man in the photo is actually Jose Hector Jimenez, who died years ago while being pursued by federal immigration authorities as he was trying to re-enter the US, according to FIEL.The man’s daughter provided his death certificate from the Mexican government, which has been turned over to the district attorney, Espinosa told the AP. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not respond to a request for comment.Jimenez’s daughter, Jamie Jimenez, did not respond to requests for comment from the AP. Her husband, Andres Rendon, confirmed to the AP that Jimenez was his wife’s deceased father.Criminal charges against the ICE officer who drove the vehicle are being considered by Harris county district attorney Sean Teare, who has said surveillance footage contradicts ICE’s claim that Parra Hernandez stepped in front of the vehicle.The video shows a black SUV speeding over a median and driving toward a man who is running away. The video does not show the car hitting him – that view is blocked by another vehicle – but it shows the SUV inches from the fleeing man. The video then shows him on the ground.US House member Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat who represents Houston, said that ICE appears to be lying about what happened.“If ICE was pursuing a man who died years ago, it raises serious questions about how these operations are being carried out and whether agents are even verifying who they’re looking for before putting people’s lives at risk,” Garcia said in a statement to the AP. “It’s outrageous – but frankly, not surprising.”ICE has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.Just in 2026, the second year since Trump returned to the White House, more than 30 people have died during interactions with immigration officials,the Guardian reportedin late September.Parra Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, told reporters that her client was suffering from depression in federal custody, especially after learning that he was not the target of the operation.“This never should have happened in the first place,” Bruno said.Miguel’s brother, Roberto Parra, said the two would work construction all day together and he just wants his brother treated with humanity. He said Parra Hernandez has a family to support, and his only crime was coming to a country out of necessity.FIEL is seeking Parra Hernandez’s release before he is moved from a hospital to a federal detention center.Nidia Delfín, the sister of Luis Enrique Delfín, who was detained in the ICE vehicle that hit Parra Hernandez, called for her brother’s release from federal custody so he could serve as a witness.“He’s still very concerned, still very afraid,” she said. “He’s not the same guy that was out” before Parra Hernandez was struck on 10 October.Guardian staff contributedExplore more on these topicsICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)HoustonUS immigrationTrump administrationUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report finds | Deforestation | The Guardian
description: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation
Author: Jonathan Watts
Headline: Environmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation Regulation
Content: Deforestation from illegal mining in the Tambopata national reserve near Puerto Maldonado, Peru, in August 2026.Photograph: Angela Ponce/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeforestation from illegal mining in the Tambopata national reserve near Puerto Maldonado, Peru, in August 2026.Photograph: Angela Ponce/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesDeforestationUS corporate lobbyists mounted ‘blitz’ to dilute landmark EU deforestation law, report findsEnvironmental watchdog Mighty Earth reveals two-year effort to postpone and weaken EU Deforestation RegulationJonathan WattsSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUS corporate lobbyists launched a two-year “blitz” to postpone and weaken the world’s most progressive legislation to protect forests, according to a new investigation by the environmental watchdog Mighty Earth.Major US firms and trade associations, including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz and the US Soybean Export Council, as well as numerous other US firms and organizations, sought to influence the EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) in more than 350 meetings, the advocacy groupfound.US company representatives and industry groups deny there was a concerted campaign to derail the deforestation rules, saying their meetings with EU officials raised legitimate concerns around implementation.The EUDR prohibits imports of commodities such as cattle, cocoa, coffee, oil palm, rubber,soyaand wood from deforested land. When the ban was put forward in 2003, the then European environment commissioner, Virginijus Sinkevičius,describedit as “the most ambitious legislative attempt to tackle these issues worldwide ever” and some US lawmakers said it should be a model for similar rules in the United States.In the years since, its official implementation has been delayed twice and the original goal to rigorously trace the origin of commodities has been revised so much that some of its initial supporters claimed the policy has beenin effect “dismantled”. The law will come into effect in December.Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous landsRead moreLobbyists from many countries, including Brazil and several EU nations, are known to have contributed to this dilution. Mighty Earth has provided the most detailed analysis yet of the role of organisations from the United States.It found 24 major US companies, trade associations and industry organizations discussed the EUDR in at least 173 meetings with members of the European parliament and 178 meetings with senior European Commission officials between July 2024 and July 2026.The US organisations with the highest number of meetings with the European Commission were the National Alliance of Forest Owners, Advanced Woody Biomass Alliance, the US Soybean Export Council, Bunge, the American Chamber of Commerce to theEuropean Unionand Cargill.Cargill had two meetings, Bunge one meeting and Mondlēz eight meetings.Mighty Earth said lobbying was also conducted through the US Congress, the US Department of Agriculture, the Office of the US Trade Representative and the White House.Two weeks after a July 2025 meeting at a Scottish golf course between Trump and the president of the European Commission,Ursula von der Leyen, the two sides released a jointstatementthatpromised the US special treatmentwith regard to the EUDR.The commission stated the US “poses negligible risk to global deforestation” (even though many of its biggestfinancialandtradingcompanies have been repeatedly implicated in destruction of the Amazon and similar biomes). The statement also talked about the EU working “to address the concerns of US producers and exporters regarding EUDR, with a view to avoiding undue impact on US-EU trade”.Mighty Earth said its investigation highlighted the need for the EU to adopt greater transparency about lobbying activities and to give more access to civil society to ensure balance.“Our analysis found a relentless and aggressive campaign by major US businesses, trade bodies and government officials, going all the way to President Trump, who offered to personally intervene, to further pressure EU policymakers,” Isabel Fernandez, senior adviser for Mighty Earth, said. “Some of the companies lobbying the EU, include the most egregious who are still linked to the illegal clearing of forests for commodities, such as soy that make their way into European markets.”Earlier this year a delegation of Trump administration officials went to EU capitalsarguing the law would put the US off exporting to the European marketbecause it would raise costs for US producers. In anopinion piecepublished in Agence France, Andrew Puzder, the US ambassador to the EU, said the law was: “… sold as a bold strike against global forest loss. In reality it will impose significant regulatory compliance costs while producing inconsequential environmental benefit when enforced against countries that pose no deforestation risk.”US corporate organisations said their engagement was designed to better understand and enhance the EUDR.Brazilian Amazon deforestation falls to lowest on record as pivotal vote loomsRead moreThe American Chamber of Commerce to the EU said it had raised concerns about EUDR implementation challenges, such as IT system shortcomings and a lack of clarity around the obligations of companies. But a spokesperson said its role had been constructive: “AmCham EU has consistently supported the EUDR’s objective of tackling global deforestation and promoting sustainable supply chains ... We have asked to allow sufficient time for companies and authorities to prepare and ensure the regulation can be effectively enforced without undermining its environmental objectives.”The US Soybean Export Council said it was focused on ways to support industry compliance with the EU’s rules. “USSEC does not seek delay or exemption; rather we favour a transition period as the Regulation comes into force. This would allow companies, control authorities, the European Commission, and the entire value chain to gain experience and learnings on how compliance works in practice, allowing for greater understanding and adaptations to implementation if needed moving forwards,” a spokesperson said.The agribusiness company Bunge said it was committed to deforestation-free supply chains and was investing in monitoring and traceability that had, it said, achieved 100% traceability to farm for both direct and indirect soy sourcing in priority areas of Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. A spokesperson said: “Bunge supports the objectives of the European UnionDeforestationRegulation while observing our own non-deforestation commitment and strengthening responsible sourcing. We are also in contact with relevant EU bodies and national competent authorities via sector organizations and directly to request clarification on certain specific complex scenarios regarding the practical implementation requirements of the EUDR.”Cargill and Mondelēz did not send an on-the-record response to the Guardian’s request for a comment.Explore more on these topicsDeforestationEuropean UnionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Gabby Williams lifts Valkyries past Dream in defensive slugfest to open WNBA finals | WNBA | The Guardian
description: Gabby Williams scored 26 points, including four crucial late free throws, as Golden State edged Atlanta 68-64 in a bruising WNBA finals opener
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Gabby Williams scored 26 points, including four crucial late free throws, as Golden State edged Atlanta 68-64 in a bruising WNBA finals opener
Content: Golden State’s Gabby Williams scored a game-high 26 points in Game 1 of the WNBA finals on Saturday in San Francisco.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenGolden State’s Gabby Williams scored a game-high 26 points in Game 1 of the WNBA finals on Saturday in San Francisco.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesWNBAGabby Williams lifts Valkyries past Dream in defensive slugfest to open WNBA finalsWilliams scores 26 as Golden State prevail 68-64Hosts overcome 32% shooting to take 1-0 series leadGray scores 19 in return as Atlanta fall short lateAgenciesSat 17 Oct 2026 18.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 20.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGabby Williams made two free throws with 1:18 remaining to put Golden State ahead, then added two more with 4.1 seconds left to seal a 68-64 victory over theAtlanta Dreamin Game 1 of the WNBA finals on Saturday.Williams finished with 26 points despite constant pressure from Atlanta’s stingy defense, scoring 16 in the second quarter as the Valkyries overcame a miserable shooting performance to take an early lead in the best-of-seven series.No other Golden State player reached double figures as the Valkyries shot just 32.1% from the field and went seven of 33 from three-point range.Quick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times Eastern.Sat 17 OctGame 1:Golden State 68, Atlanta 64Mon 19 OctGame 2: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Wed 21 OctGame 3: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Sat 24 OctGame 4: Golden State at Atlanta, 1pm (NBC)Mon 26 OctGame 5: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)Thu 29 OctGame 6: Golden State at Atlanta, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)Sat 31 OctGame 7: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)*-if necessaryHow to watchIn the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“We always knew we were going to find a way somehow,” Williams said in a postgame interview as fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!”Gabby Williams believes so strongly in Golden State’s poise in crunch time because of the way the Valkyries have won all season with their defense.Atlanta Dream 64-68 Golden State Valkyries: WNBA finals 2026 Game 1 – live reactionRead moreThey trust each other to make plays in the biggest moments.Williams converted two free throws with 1:18 left to put Golden State ahead and two more with 4.1 seconds remaining, finishing with 26 points despite constant pressure from Atlanta’s stingy defense as the Valkyries held off the Dream 68-64 in Game 1 of theWNBAfinals on Saturday.“Even though we were down with a few minutes left, I think we had the game right where we wanted it because it just came down to getting stops,” Williams said. “That’s been our bread and butter all season. That’s why we harp on it so much because we’ve built great defensive habits for these moments.”It was the first loss of the postseason for Atlanta, snapping a 10-game winning streak overall. Coach Karl Smesko was ready to get right back to work watching film to figure out what to do better in Game 2. The Dream have yet to win a finals game, having been swept in each of their previous three appearances.“We were right there, right there, so that’s why it hurts a little bit but it also motivates us,” he said. “We know what we’re capable of doing so we’ll have one day to get ourselves as ready as possible and then I think we’ll play even better.”Finding a way to slow down Williams – and her capable supporting cast – is going to be a challenge.After a quiet first quarter, she scored 16 of her points in the second. No other Valkyries player finished in double figures as Golden State shot 32.1% from the field and went seven of 33 from three-point range.“We always knew we were going to find a way somehow,” Williams said on the microphone after the game as fans chanted “Gabby! Gabby!”Rhyne Howard missed a three-point attempt with 1:09 left, butAngel Reesemade a steal moments later. Naz Hillmon also missed from deep. Kiah Stokes gave the Dream another chance when she missed the first of two free throws with 23.8 seconds left. Then Allisha Gray couldn’t knock down a three-pointer with nine seconds remaining.Williams converted two free throws with just over four seconds left to seal the win.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionGame 2 of the best-of-seven series is Monday night back at Chase Center, where the ear-piercing noise from a raucous “Ballhalla” crowd made for exactly the hostile environment Valkyries coach Natalie Nakase had requested from the home fans.One of these two franchises will capture their first championship, and if the opening game is any indication, it’s going to be an all-out defensive fight.Gray returned from injury to score 19 points, while Reese added 14 points and 12 rebounds. Jordin Canada contributed eight points, seven assists and five rebounds for the Dream, hitting a timely 13-foot jumper with 4:23 remaining.View image in fullscreenGolden State’s Gabby Williams drives to the basket against Atlanta’s Jordin Canada during Game 1 of the WNBA finals at Chase Center in San Francisco on Saturday.Photograph: Ezra Shaw/Getty ImagesWilliams made a driving layup with 3:22 to play that pulled Golden State within 62-61. Canada banged awkwardly into Williams’ knee on a box-out during the latter’s late free throws, and the Valkyries star was being attended to by an athletic trainer on the bench in the waning moments.“I’m OK, it was a long, physical game,” she said afterward.Gray was in the starting lineup after going through a light practice on Friday. She had missed the final two games of Atlanta’s sweep of the New York Liberty in the best-of-three semi-final series with an injury to the ring finger on her left, shooting hand.Golden State guard Tiffany Hayes hit her face hard on the floor while trying to make a steal in the closing minutes and was down with 2:38 remaining before walking off the court on her own to the locker room.Nakase said “so far” her indication was that Hayes would be available for Game 2, “so I’ll know when the medical tells me”. Hayes was undergoing her normal treatment.The 37-year-old Hayes spent her first 10 WNBA seasons with Atlanta.“It was a physical game, we understand, it’s playoffs, that’s just part of it. Tip’s OK, I just gave her a little hug,” Nakase said. “I’ll tell you what, she’s a fighter. I don’t think there’s someone more, maybe our whole team, but she wants this. And I can I say I’m going to put a little bit more energy tonight in film because I want to win this for Tip.”Explore more on these topicsWNBAGolden State ValkyriesAtlanta DreamAngel ReeseShareReuse this content

title: Jalen Hurts placed on injured reserve after Eagles quarterback diagnosed with blood clot | Philadelphia Eagles | The Guardian
description: Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts has been placed on injured reserve after doctors discovered a superficial blood clot in his calf
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Philadelphia quarterback Jalen Hurts has been placed on injured reserve after doctors discovered a superficial blood clot in his calf
Content: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts speaks to reporters after last Sunday’s game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APView image in fullscreenPhiladelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts speaks to reporters after last Sunday’s game against the Jacksonville Jaguars in London.Photograph: Alastair Grant/APPhiladelphia EaglesJalen Hurts placed on injured reserve after Eagles quarterback diagnosed with blood clotEagles star sidelined by blood clot in his calfHurts sustained injury against Rams on 4 OctoberSuper Bowl MVP must miss at least four gamesAgenciesSat 17 Oct 2026 18.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleQuarterback Jalen Hurts was placed on injured reserve on Saturday, two days after thePhiladelphia Eaglesrevealed he had a blood clot in his calf.Hurts was initially ruled out on Thursday for the Eagles’ upcoming game against Carolina. The Eagles said at the time that Hurts had been injured when he took a cleat to his calf during their game against the Los Angeles Rams on 4 October.Hurts informed the team’s medical staff of the injury after practice on 8 October. The Super Bowl LIX MVP returned to practice the following day before the team departed for London to face Jacksonville.“Out of an abundance of caution, an ultrasound was performed on Saturday (Oct. 10) following the team’s flight to London and walk-through,” the Eagles said in Thursday’s statement.“The ultrasound revealed a superficial blood clot. Our medical staff and doctors in London reviewed the results and concluded that activity and mobility were important and that Jalen could safely play. Doctors recommended a follow-up ultrasound within 72 hours of the game and the return flight to Philadelphia.”Explore more on these topicsPhiladelphia EaglesNFLUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: The ESPN producer who quit over gambling – and the stories she says went untold | US sports media | The Guardian
description: Nicole Noren says ESPN sidelined investigations into sports betting companies as gambling partnerships reshaped the network’s priorities
Author: Jane McManus
Headline: Nicole Noren says ESPN sidelined investigations into sports betting companies as gambling partnerships reshaped the network’s priorities
Content: The ESPN BET sports betting app displayed on a smartphone. ESPN launched the platform in 2023 as part of a partnership with Penn Entertainment.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe ESPN BET sports betting app displayed on a smartphone. ESPN launched the platform in 2023 as part of a partnership with Penn Entertainment.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesUS sports mediaThe ESPN producer who quit over gambling – and the stories she says went untoldNicole Noren says ESPN sidelined investigations into sports betting companies as gambling partnerships reshaped the network’s prioritiesJane McManusSat 17 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 04.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier this week, investigative journalist Nicole Noren did something almost impossible for someone who has spent her career behind the scenes.She made herself the story.The longtime producer for ESPN’s Outside the Linesused her own experience to shed lighton the way sports betting partnerships are warping sports media coverage. The issue wasn’t how ESPN was covering sports gambling, but that it was doing so less and less.Noren was used to pitching hard-hitting stories around leagues, owners and athletes. As a producer for the investigative reporting arm of the sports network, her team had traditionally been insulated from the business concerns atESPN, but she started to notice a change about seven years ago.Gambling is easy, right? Wrong: it turns out betting on sport is designed to disturb you | Barney RonayRead more“What was telling to me was that I had pitched numerous stories that would take a harder look at some of the gambling companies and addiction, and none of those stories was greenlit,” Noren told the Columbia Journalism Review in an interview with journalist Danny Funt. “They ended up doing a show on it around that time, but it became very neutered. Some of the people involved intended to make it much more hard-hitting and hold the gambling companies accountable. Let’s just say the final product didn’t end up doing that.”Noren, who detailed a family history that included seeing her grandfather, father and brother’s lives unspool due to gambling addiction, left the network in 2023 after ESPN announced the debut of ESPN BET, a partnership with Penn Entertainment.“I’m not going to work for a gambling company and have blood on my hands,” Noren bluntly told Funt.When reached for this story, Noren declined to comment further.ESPN released a statement in response: “ESPN remains committed to journalism that serves sports fans, holds powerful interests accountable and earns our audience’s trust. Our editorial decisions are guided by news judgment and journalistic integrity, and we demonstrate this every day through the award-winningcontent we produce across our platforms.”Before he retired in 2019, Bob Ley was the venerable face of Outside the Lines, which included a daily network show with deeply reported TV packages and roundtable discussions on the biggest issues in sports. (Full disclosure: I was a contributor to that show from 2010 to 2017 while working at ESPN.)“The greatest luxury in television is time and investigative reporting is the feature of a mature news organization,” said Ley, one of the most respected anchors in sports. “It’s not just the box score, it’s the financial pages and the police report.”View image in fullscreenFormer ESPN producer Nicole Noren has spoken out about the influence of sports betting partnerships on journalism, saying the network declined to pursue investigations into gambling companies and addiction.Photograph: Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for Santa Barbara International Film FestivalHe describes Noren as “passionate, honest and indefatigable”. During his tenure at the Worldwide Leader, Ley said, reporters had the leeway to cover entities that had a business relationship with ESPN. If that meant uncovering something unsavory, reporters would have editorial support and ask the subjects of those stories for comment. Sometimes, Ley said, the access even improved those stories.The network canceled Outside the Lines as a regular show in 2023, although some content is still produced under the brand. A former reporter at the network, who didn’t want to be named since they still work in media, said that the brand is obviously pulling back from investigative journalism, although there are still excellent journalists producing quality work, as ESPN pivots toward entertainment.MeanwhileMike Foss, an ESPN executive vice-president, told a conference last week that popular sports personality Pat McAfee “might be a journalist at heart”. “This is a dam-breaking moment,” said Brian Moritz, an associate professor at the Jandoli School of Communication at St Bonaventure University. “What stood out to me: everything that people assumed was happening around sports media is actually happening. To have a former producer at ESPN say it is eye-opening.”US gambling addiction is ‘out of control’ as betting markets boom, policy expert warnsRead moreIn 2018, the US supreme court overturned the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, allowing states to regulate sports betting markets within their boundaries. Since then,39 states and Washington DC have established some form of sports betting, although there is wide variation in what is allowed state-to-state. Last April, St Bonaventure and Siena College released theresults of a pollshowing that 27% of Americans and 52% of men ages 18 to 49 now have an account with a sportsbook.That’s the same demographic traditionally associated with sports viewership.“ESPN makes a lot of money from promoting sports gambling,” Moritz said. “And there’s interest in it – a lot of young men want to gamble. But that really makes you ask, what is the mission of ESPN?”Moritz noted that the rise in sports betting isn’t without cost to those consumers. According to the National Council on Problem Gambling, there has not been a nationwide survey on how addictive sports betting is since the activity became more widely legalized, but theNCPG cited researchin recent congressional testimony showing New Jersey, Ohio and Indiana have experienced a rise in problem gambling that tracks with adoption.“The young, male population that engages in sports fan activity is a Venn diagram with the demographic at risk for a gambling problem,” said Cait Huble, director of public affairs for the NCPG, which is a nonpartisan organization that advocates for harm reduction.The group is lobbying for the Points Act, which would require a percentage of the federal excise tax on sports bets to be allocated back to the states for prevention, treatment and research into of problem betting.View image in fullscreenAn ESPN BET advertisement is displayed during a Stanley Cup playoff game between Nashville and Vancouver in 2024. Sports betting partnerships have become an increasingly prominent feature of live sports broadcasts.Photograph: Brett Carlsen/Getty Images“What troubles me most is the disconnect at the ESPN executive level between making money and caring about the human impact of constantly bombarding fans with betting odds and talk,” Noren said. “It’s become impossible to escape.”DraftKings has been ESPN’s official sportsbook and odds provider since 2025. Thepress release announcing the partnershipsaid the content would be “integrated across ESPN’s ecosystem”. Many ESPN shows and live broadcasts now contain features on betting strategy and updated odds.“Game coverage is now framed by betting coverage,” said Ley, who now spends his time working with the Seton Hall Center for Sports Media, which he founded. “It’s bigger than just sports, the whole media landscape is being overturned. Even companies as big as ESPN are facing substantial pressures and having to change their business models.”Being a vocal opponent of a revenue stream is not a route to job security. The Pew Research Center, utilizing Bureau of Labor Statistics data,reportedthat newsroom jobs declined by 26% between 2008 and 2020. Even the industry giants aren’t immune. The Washington Post, one of the few outlets where sports reporters were still critically covering the betting industry,eliminatedits sports department in February.ESPN has had regular and wide-reaching layoffs every two years or so for the last decade.“I empathize with people who work at large media companies,” Noren said in the Q&A. “It’s really risky in this landscape to speak out.”It may seem almost impossible to curtail sports betting’s pull on the sports media landscape given the current White House’s disinterest in regulating business. Congress has madethe Protect College Sports Actthe legislative priority in the sports space, meaning sports betting and sports prediction markets seem to be on the back burner.However, theWashington Sun reportedthis week that the Federal Trade Commission is looking into sports betting, including deceptive advertising by sportsbooks such as FanDuel and DraftKings.Even if regulation is on the horizon, journalists are under a more immediate constraint: working in an industry that relies on sports betting for a good part of the operating budget.“These jobs are hard to come by especially if you are younger,” said Moritz, referencing in particular the students he teaches who want to make a name in this industry. “Do you even feel like you can take a stand?”Explore more on these topicsUS sports mediaGamblingESPNUS sportsTelevision industryUS television industryfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Haaland helps Maresca achieve record start as Manchester City defeat Ipswich  | Premier League | The Guardian
