title: The right is pushing its anti-trans fury on the WNBA. Players and fans are loudly pushing back | WNBA | The Guardian
description: As the WNBA finals kick off Saturday in San Francisco, the pro-LGBTQ+ sports fanbase push a message of inclusion in the face of anti-trans attacks
Author: Lex McMenamin
Headline: As the WNBA finals kick off Saturday in San Francisco, the pro-LGBTQ+ sports fanbase push a message of inclusion in the face of anti-trans attacks
Content: Fans hold up trans rights signs as Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever plays near them at ScotiaBank Arena in Toronto on 18 August 2026.Photograph: Steve Russell/Toronto Star/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFans hold up trans rights signs as Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever plays near them at ScotiaBank Arena in Toronto on 18 August 2026.Photograph: Steve Russell/Toronto Star/Getty ImagesBuilding powerWNBAThe right is pushing its anti-trans fury on the WNBA. Players and fans are loudly pushing backAs the WNBA finals kick off Saturday in San Francisco, the pro-LGBTQ+ sports fanbase push a message of inclusion in the face of anti-trans attacksSign up for WNBA 30: a free women’s basketball newsletterBuilding power is supported byAbout this contentLex McMenaminin New YorkSat 17 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTShareAt Wilka’s Sports Bar in lower Manhattan, a crowd of mostly LGBTQ+ fans was fired up during aWNBAplayoff game between the New York Liberty and the Atlanta Dream. When the Liberty’s Jonquel Jones blocked the Dream’s star forward Angel Reese at the basket, then chest-bumped her – leading teammates to separate them – the bar erupted in cheers. One fan quietly joked: “Now kiss!”“I love strong women, and I love supporting strong women,” said August, a trans organizer and Liberty fan who asked to go by their first name for privacy reasons.The scene at Wilka’s, where a sign reading “trans people belong in sports” hangs prominently behind the bar, exemplifies much of the WNBA fanbase, which,like the league itself,is heavily queer. But many wouldn’t know that from reading recent headlines about the league. Since the summer, the WNBA has become the target of rightwing activists pushing their agenda to ban trans women and girls from sports. The league has no explicit rule barring or permitting trans women and there are no trans women in the WNBA.In response, many of the league’s players and fans have made clear they don’t align with anti-trans rhetoric. Several players, like the Chicago Sky’sNatasha Cloudand the Golden State Valkyries’ Gabby Williams, have voiced their support for the trans community;Williams said in Maythat she would “welcome” a trans teammate anytime.Fans, too, have loudly pushed back – holding rallies, bringing signs into the games and even defending their sports bars, meant as a safe space for women and LGBTQ+ fans, from aggression. As the WNBA finals between the Dream and the Golden State Valkyries tip off Saturday, the pro-trans, pro-Black, pro-queer fanbase wants to remind others of the original ethos of women’s sports: inclusion and community.“It’s not about protecting women’s sports,” Allie, another Liberty fan at Wilka’s who asked to go by their first name, said about the anti-trans backlash facing the WNBA. ”And I feel better knowing the fact that the majority of the fanbase is standing up, saying: ‘No, this isn’t right.’”Why the anti-trans backlash took offThe anti-trans fury surrounding the WNBA took off in July, when Sophie Cunningham, a backup guard for the Indiana Fever,said in an interview with ESPNthat she wanted to “protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men” – an anti-trans dog-whistle used to misgender trans women. Soon after, two former NBA players declared their intention to enter the WNBA draft. (The league said they were ineligible and condemned the behavior.) It resulted in a media frenzy, withFox News airing more than 200 segmentsabout the league in July, the majority of which were about Cunningham’s comments.The sportswear company XX-XY, which lobbies women’s sports leagues and state legislatures to exclude players based on their assigned biological sex at birth, also rode the Cunningham media wave. Its shirts bearing the brand’s name – referencing biological sex chromosomes – have become recognizable by players and fans as an anti-trans statement at games and events. In August, thecompany’s founder was photographed courtside in XX-XY merchwith Cunningham and the conservative anti-trans commentator Riley Gaines. XX-XY supporters and influencers have also gathered outside Fever games with signs calling to “protect girls sports”. XX-XY did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.“We know that this is really about trying to rile up a base of folks who already show some sort of anti-gender ideology,” meaning those who oppose the rights of women and LGBTQ+ people, said Anna Castro, deputy communications director at theTransgenderLaw Center.What’s happening in the WNBA is representative of a broader rightwing push to roll back rights, healthcare and protections for trans people across the US. In June, the conservative-majority supreme court upheld the constitutionality of states banning trans girls’ participation in school sports. This November, several state ballot initiatives claim to be about “protecting girls” from “biological males” in sports but effectively bar trans students from playing. A ballot measure in Washington, for example, would require all girls to “verify” their identity by a doctor.And yet these policies don’t align with public opinion. A June poll from theNational Women’s Law Centerfound that voters do not support the supreme court setting official policy for trans athletes’ participation in sports, nor are they in favor of reversing state protections for trans student athletes.Resistance has played out at basketball arenas. When the Fever played the Seattle Storm in late July,Storm co-owner Celeste Keatonconfronted two XX-XY-sponsored courtside attendees and, according to one, told them “Jesus loves everyone” and “stop pulling this shit”. The WNBA then fined and suspended Keaton.View image in fullscreenPeople rally to support Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham after her comments on trans athletes in women’s sports before a WNBA game in Portland, Oregon, on 31 July 2026.Photograph: Craig Mitchelldyer/APWhen a group in XX-XY shirts arrived at the women’s sports bar Sports Bra in Portland, Oregon, in September,management asked them to leavebased on its policy of removing anyone wearing messaging targeting the community. “At The Sports Bra, our mission is simple: support, promote, and empower ALL girls and women in sports,” the bar’s ownersposted on Instagram. “To be clear: trans girls are girls, and trans women are women.”When a different group of rightwing anti-trans protesters arrived at the Sports Bra two weeks later,a group of neighborhood residents showed up in defense of the bar and its patrons; the rightwing protesters eventually sprayed the counter-protesters withbear spray.The anti-trans harassment creates an environment where some fans said they are scared to go to games alone, but feel safer knowing other queer and trans fans are organizing to take a stand.Similarly, WNBA players are struggling to feel protected against increased racism and harassment from viewers. Last season, men started a trend of throwing dildos on the court during games, instigated bycryptocurrency investors;this season, it continued,with crypto influencers citing the conversation around trans women and the WNBA as their motivation. Black players like the Fever’s Kelsey Mitchell report facingconstant racist invective on social media. Players and viewers have criticized the league for not doing more to combat the environment. The WNBA did not return the Guardian’s request for comment.Racist and anti-trans harassment are often intertwined, Castro said: “The trans youth and cis youth that get targeted with sports bans are trans girls of color, and particularly Black girls. I think that it’s incredible that there have been fans that have said so vehemently: ‘This is not what we’re about.’”How fans are pushing backIn August, Turning Point USA planned a pro-Cunningham rally outside the Fever game against the Liberty at Barclays Center in Brooklyn. So a group of organizers planned a rally of their own to show support for women’s sports and trans rights. Before the game, they distributed signs and T-shirts made by the Transgender Law Center that said:“Trans people belong here”. They also danced and held a party.In the Bay Area over the last three months, parents of trans kids have organized poster distributions outside Valkyries games, handing out signs thanking Williams and coach Natalie Nakase for their outspoken support for trans people. They’ve also used the signs to surround anti-trans protesters who show up.According to Arne Johnson of Rainbow Families Action, the group’s efforts to support trans youth in sports started with transhigh school track star AB Hernandez, who was subjected to an intense harassment campaign – and is a hero to his own trans daughter. Holding rallies at games has been much more joyful than testifying at state hearings against anti-trans advocates who speak cruelly to their children’s faces, he said. He didn’t need to organize fans to take a stand.View image in fullscreenTrans athlete supporters hold signs and flags outside the main entrance before a game between the New York Liberty and the Indiana Fever at Barclays Center on 22 August 2026 in New York City.Photograph: Elsa/Getty Images“They have a visceral understanding of what this is about,” he said. “That really crystallized what this WNBA fandom means: they were out there to protect each other.”He was especially touched by how the fans saw trans youth as part of their community. The group has since set up Minnesota Lynx fans with signs and merch; for the Lynx’s game against the Fever in August, head coach Cheryl Reevewore a “Trans Kids Belong” shirt.On Saturday, organizers from California and Washington will host a rally outside the finals game between the Valkyries and the Dream in San Francisco and at women’s sports bars in both states. They’re using the opportunity to call attention to a ballot measure in Washington barring transgender girls from K-12 girls’ sports teams.High schooler Jules, a trans athlete, said that during rallies outside the Valkyries game, passersby would ask her for signs and shirts, or even to take a picture with her, wearing her cape of a trans flag. It reminds her of what she loves most about sports: community.“If we got completely destroyed in a game, I would not care,” said Jules. “But if someone was being mean or being unsportsmanlike or something like that, it breaks the community of it.”

title: Premier League today: How to watch Brentford v Liverpool, TV channels & live stream Saturday 17 October | Liverpool | The Guardian
description: How will Brentford and Liverpool fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Graham Ruthven
Headline: How will Brentford and Liverpool fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Bradley Barcola are coming off a big win over Lask.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APView image in fullscreenBradley Barcola are coming off a big win over Lask.Photograph: Dénes Erdős/APSoccer watching and streaming guideLiverpoolPremier League today: How to watch Brentford v Liverpool, TV channels & live stream Saturday 17 OctoberHow will Brentford and Liverpool fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsGraham RuthvenSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrentford are flying high in the Premier League as one of just three teams still to suffer defeat this season, although Keith Andrews surely wants his team to convert some of their draws into wins.Liverpool, on the other hand, return to league action after last weekend’s humbling home defeat to Manchester City. Andoni Iraola’s side responded by putting six goals past Lask in the Champions League, but the Reds are lacking balance.The last five meetings between Brentford and Liverpool at the Gtech Community Stadium have produced no fewer than 22 goals. The recent goalscoring form of both sides suggests the pattern could continue.Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s Premier League fixture, including kick-off times, broadcast networks, and online streaming options.Brentford v LiverpoolTime (ET):3pm BST (10am ET)Stadium:Gtech Community Stadium (London)How to watchUnited States:Peacock,Stream on FuboCanada:Stream on FuboUnited Kingdom:Watch on TNT Sports 1What to watch forOnly Arsenal and Manchester City have claimed more points at home than Brentford this season. Chelsea and Tottenham Hotspur have both been stung badly by the Bees whose threat in transition and potency from set pieces will be a problem for Liverpool this weekend.Defensively, Liverpool remain as vulnerable as they were under Arne Slot last season. Iraola has struggled to find the right formula in the centre of the pitch with Hugo Ekitike, Cody Gakpo and Alexander Isak all expected to miss Saturday’s game through injury. Ryan Gravenberch is also unavailable through suspension.Liverpool have conceded six goals in their last two games. Brentford will take encouragement from this, as well as the fact they won their last home meeting with the Merseyside outfit last October. This promises to be a compelling clash.Player to watch:Bradley Barcola, Liverpool - The French winger scored a hat-trick in Liverpool’s mid-week win over LASK, highlighting how the €125m summer signing is bedding in. Barcola will be a threat down the left side and in behind the Brentford backline.Explore more on these topicsLiverpoolSoccer watching and streaming guideBrentfordUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England  | Palantir | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use
Author: Robert Booth
Headline: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in use
Content: A protest against the US tech company Palantir outside their UK headquarters in London on 1 October.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA protest against the US tech company Palantir outside their UK headquarters in London on 1 October.Photograph: Henry Nicholls/AFP/Getty ImagesPalantirPalantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in EnglandExclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in useRobert BoothUK technology editorSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.Some health bodies said the £330m federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and has improved surgery scheduling. But, from Gateshead to Truro, others said they were declining to use it or had carried out trials and reverted to old systems. A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”.The responses come as Andy Burnham’s government faces a crunch decision about whether to exercise a break clause in the seven-year NHS-Palantir deal, which was intended to better integrate the health system’s data to improve clinical accuracy and efficiency. Protests against the US firm’s role have also focused on its other contracts with the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s homeland security forces. There is also dispute over evidence for the system’s effectiveness and public concern about the involvement in theNHSof a company cofounded by the tech billionaire Peter Thiel, who said in 2023: “The NHS makes people sick.”Palantir is worming its way into the British state – it’s time to curb this controversial US company’s influence | George MonbiotRead moreAccording to more than two dozen FOI responses reviewed by the Guardian, 16 trusts and health boards declared they do not use it, following its introduction in March 2024. They include the University hospitals of North Midlands NHS trust, which said it will not use it primarily because “it does not appear to provide functionality over and above what we have already” and Dorset HealthCare university trust said it “will not be adopting or going live with the FDP”. Humber Teaching NHS foundation trust said: “We have no plans to use it.”Cambridgeshire and Peterborough NHS foundation trust said it has used the system but it has “not offered significant improvements on local systems”. Avon and Wiltshire mental health partnership NHS trust said it had yet to find an FDP tool that offered significantly more than its existing capabilities and University hospitals Birmingham NHS foundation trust, which cares for more than 2 million people, said it had no plans to use it, citing “limited expected benefit over existing solutions”. The FOIs were gathered by Medact, a health campaign that opposes Palantir’s role in the NHS, and posted to a public transparency website, WhatDoTheyKnow.Palantir has previously challenged claims that other software could be just as effective, with its senior vice-president, the former Labour MP Tom Watson,saying last week: “If there are companies that can do it, they would have taken part in free and open competition” to run the FDP.Watson, a Labour peer and former minister alongside Burnham, was appointed as Palantir’s chief lobbyist last month amid a wave of opposition to the Palantir deal. He warned his former colleagues in Labour not to let “mob rule … lead procurement practices”.But two parliamentary select committees haveurgedthe government to end Palantir’s contract, including the Commons’ science and technology committee. Martin Wrigley, a Liberal Democrat member of the committee, said the NHS boards’ responses “justify what I have been saying for the last year, which is that Palantir’s system is just not that good”.“Once again we have proven that centrally dictating a solution to the NHS can’t work,” he said. “We have to get back to developing interoperability so each trust has its own software but with a set of standards for how they interact. Palantir are great sales people but they over-promise and under-deliver.”Dr Rhiannon Mihranian Osborne, a spokesperson for Medact, said the FOIs showed alternatives existed, a safe transition away from Palantir was possible and “the government has no excuse to extend the contract”.“Instead of outsourcing key NHS functions to big tech companies, the government must back NHS innovation and the highly skilled NHS data professionals who work alongside doctors and nurses to deliver care in the public interest,” she said.View image in fullscreenA protest against Palantir’s role in the National Health Service at St Thomas’ hospital in London.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/ReutersPalantir accused Medact of “slanted analysis” and of “misleading the public”.“The FDP is, objectively, a successful programme,” a spokesperson said, adding that its purpose was to provide trusts with tools to draw on depending on their existing capabilities and needs. “It is one of just 20% of major government programmes with a green delivery rating, with ministersstatingthat it ‘is significantly exceeding its benefits forecast and has exceeded every target’.”It said NHS trusts, including Chelsea and Westminster, Leicester, Northampton, Bath, North Cumbria, Croydon, Great Western, Dorset, Chesterfield, Ashford and St Peters and Norfolk have publicly praised the FDP.Palantir also points to NHS data that shows trusts using the FDP have carried out 117,000 additional operations and a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients. NHSEnglandhas, however, had to add a caveat to its statistics, making clear it cannot draw conclusions about cause and effect as other variables have not been controlled for.The government’s national data guardian for health and social care, Dr Nicola Byrne, this weekurgedministers to give substantial weight to the “trust factor” when deciding on Palantir’s fate. More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the FDP. Byrne, a government-appointed watchdog, said there was evidence “a significant number of local organisations” were reluctant to adopt the FDP including due to concerns about Palantir and “a preference for other solutions”.Sophie Don, the chief executive of Voror, a patient data company that bid unsuccessfully against Palantir, said: “Of course Palantir isn’t the only company that can do this. It doesn’t surprise me that it is making things harder … If NHS staff are choosing not to use it, it’s a clear sign it’s not creating value. There are many home-grown systems that would release much more value to the NHS than the [Palantir] platform.”A spokesperson for NHS England said: “137 NHS trusts have now reported benefits from the wide range of tools available on the platform – helping staff join-up and improve care for patients, and work more efficiently.”Explore more on these topicsPalantirNHSEnglandHealthHospitalsShareReuse this content

title: Fake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my byline | Cybercrime | The Guardian
description: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators
Author: Linda Geddes
Headline: How a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonators
Content: Linda Geddes: ‘Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me.’Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLinda Geddes: ‘Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me.’Photograph: Adrian Sherratt/The GuardianCybercrimeFake Linda and me: the Agatha Christie-worthy mystery of the fraudster who stole my bylineHow a string of bizarre events led writer Linda Geddes to don her sleuthing cap and dig into a world of shadowy impersonatorsLinda GeddesSat 17 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 13.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt started with an entirely ordinary interaction on LinkedIn. Someone had tagged me in a post, saying how much they’d enjoyed contributing to a New York Post article I’d written about “chronoworking”. As the author of a book about circadian rhythms, it was exactly the sort of subject I might write about. Except I’d never heard of this person, let alone interviewed them.I clicked on the link and my stomach dropped. There, above an article about people who organise their working lives around their biological clocks, was my name: Linda Geddes.It was the latest in a string of increasingly bizarre events that had begun three weeks earlier, when a friend who works as an editor at the scientific journal Nature texted to ask whether I’d been pitching stories to one of her colleagues. I hadn’t.It turned out that someone had been approaching Nature editors using my name and an email address that wasn’t mine, referencing articles I’d previously written to make their pitches more convincing. Worse, the journal had recently encountered another impersonator posing asCaroline Williams, a former colleague of mine. That person had convinced an editor at Science to commission and publish an article under Caroline’s name, receiving about $1,000 for it.Further digging revealed that Fake Linda had also pitched a story to Science, unsuccessfully. Then, last week, an editor at Nature Medicinecontacted me to ask whetherI’d been pitching to them and Nature Health as well.I donned my sleuthing cap and discovered a potential link between Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Entering my impersonator’s email address into Outlook.com’s account recovery system revealed a partially obscured Gmail recovery address. An editor at Science had independently discovered the same address pattern associated with Fake Caroline’s email.View image in fullscreenLinda Geddes: ‘As someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling.’Photograph: Haybooks-May/AlamyAs someone whose livelihood depends on the reputation I’ve spent decades building, I find this deeply unsettling. Someone is potentially making money by passing themselves off as me, while putting my professional credibility at risk. Apart from one interview conducted by email, the quotes in the New York Post article were lifted from previously published features, without attribution. Many of Fake Linda’s pitches also bear the hallmarks of AI-assisted writing. Even unsuccessful pitches could damage relationships with editors.The New York Post has since removed the article, conducted an internal review and referred the matter to the appropriate authorities, a spokesperson said.What I find particularly baffling is the motive. Freelance science journalism is hardly a lucrative profession, and is quite niche. My best guess is that a struggling freelancer is impersonating more established peers to boost their earnings, perhaps using AI to make the process more efficient. But how would they receive payment without revealing their identity?Other possibilities have crossed my mind. Could it be a PR professional trying to secure coverage for a client, or someone testing how easily publishers can be fooled? Perhaps it is someone with a personal grudge. But as Caroline put it: “Why us? We’re nice!”Dr Simon Miller, the director of policy, strategy and communications at the UK fraud prevention service Cifas, is equally bemused. “Ordinarily, if you’re seeking to defraud, you’re seeking to do it at scale, in a relatively light-touch way, using mechanised, industrialised processes,” he said. “This is tantalisingly unusual. It’s almost the stuff of Agatha Christie, but with 21st-century technology.”Journalists are far from the only people finding their names attached to work they didn’t produce. In April, Prof Eric Topol, of the Scripps Institute in California, discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about.Four of his five supposed co-authors were similarly unaware of the paper, while the fifth could not be identified. Within hours of Topol flagging the incident on X, the journal’s website had disappeared.View image in fullscreenIn April, Prof Eric Topol discovered his name on a scientific paper he knew nothing about.Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty ImagesTopol, who is a bestselling author, said he has discovered at least 12 books on Amazon with his name on that he didn’t write, including several cookbooks. “I don’t even know how to cook,” he said. Particularly upsetting was when a patient told him he’d read his supposed memoir. “They said: ‘I was reading it, and a lot of those things don’t seem to be accurate.’ That’s how I found out about it.”Dr Leslie McIntosh, a vice-president of research integrity and security at Digital Science, said someone might add a respected name to a scientific paper without permission to make the work appear more credible. Fraudsters also sometimes added respected researchers as editors to make bogus journals appear legitimate and attract publication fees.Even more nightmarish would be someone deliberately publishing misleading information under someone else’s name to damage their reputation. “If their name ended up on a retracted paper, they would then have to explain that retraction,” she said.Employers are encountering yet another form of impersonation. Jamie Collier, a researcher at Google Threat Intelligence, said criminals had used stolen personal information to secure remote jobs under other people’s names, sometimes without the victim’s knowledge.Generative AI is making such deception easier, “mainly by stripping away the usual tell-tale red flags that hiring managers relied on to spot fraud,” Collier said. Large language models can generate convincing CVs, tailored cover letters and fabricated evidence of professional experience.“Real-time video filters and voice-cloning tools are the next step. While live deepfakes are still relatively nascent … threat actors are already testing them to bypass quick video screenings and mask regional accents,” Collier said.TheSociety of Authors and the Writers’ Guild of Great Britainhave warned of increasingly sophisticated scams involving people impersonating literary agents and publishers, in an attempt to get writers to part with money or sign away their rights.The Society of Authors’ chief executive, Anna Ganley, said she personally received between five and 10 scam emails a day, supposedly from book festivals, literary agents, publishers and others. Some writers had lost thousands of pounds after responding to genuine-sounding offers. “It’s incredibly difficult for writers, because you are often looking for opportunities to market your books,” she said.Unlike those scams, Fake Linda’s activities seem like a lot of work for relatively small financial gain. But the latest technology could make such impersonations easier. Miller said: “AI is allowing criminals to create sophisticated impersonations at unprecedented speed and scale.”Or multiple impersonations. I’ve since identified a third science journalist,Sara Novak, with a potential link to Fake Linda and Fake Caroline. Fake Sara apparently pitched a story to Chemical and Engineering News in August, which was declined. When Real Sara shared her impersonator’s email address with me, I discovered it links to the same masked recovery address.View image in fullscreenThe real Sara Novak.The consequences extend beyond those being impersonated. “The risk for journals and publishers is huge,” said Dr Ben Johnson, the chief editor at Nature Health,who turned down a pitch by Fake Linda. “People trust the Nature brand as a source of evidence-based quality information. If an AI-generated story from a fake journalist is submitted then I will likely spend hours editing it from AI slop into Nature prose, including all the fake quotes from people never interviewed.”All of this raises uncomfortable questions about how you can be sure you know who you’re dealing with when communicating online. When I emailed the New York Post about my impersonator, it agreed to help rectify the situation, then asked: “I see that you’re emailing me from a Guardian email address. Is there any other info you can provide to verify who you are?”After discovering that Science had inadvertently published a news story by Fake Caroline, its managing news editor, John Travis, said his team had started running all pitches and drafts through AI detectors, “though they are not perfect”. “We also require Zoom calls for any new writers,” he said.The experience has also put editors at Nature on higher alert. “Sadly, for early career freelancers, this makes me less likely to commission news stories from journalists that I haven’t worked with before,” Johnson said. “I will also have to try to find the time to have a call with new freelancers before they write, to check they are who they say they are.”Even video calls are no guarantee of identity. Google Threat Intelligence recently documentedNorth Korea-linked hackersusing real-time deepfakes to lure executives into Zoom calls with trusted peers. “They faked video and audio glitches to get the target to download a ‘troubleshooting tool’ that wiped out their credentials and wallets,” Collier said.Miller advises independently checking unexpected approaches through an established email address or telephone number. McIntosh advocates several layers of verification, like the multiple identity checks at airports. “You have to have multiple ways to ensure and triangulate that you’re speaking to the person you think you’re speaking to,” she said.For people whose identities have been hijacked, Miller advises warning professional networks and monitoring for further impersonation attempts.There may also be legal remedies. Rupert Earle, senior counsel at the London law firm Bates Wells, said that under UK law, impersonating someone to secure paid work could constitute fraud. Victims could also have civil claims for “passing off” – misleading people into believing that work or services come from an established person or business – or false attribution, if work they didn’t create was published under their name.However, identifying the perpetrator and taking legal action can be difficult, particularly when the publications are overseas and the impersonator’s location is unknown. Despite uncovering several clues linking Fake Linda and Fake Caroline, we still don’t know who is behind the accounts.But the hunt for Fake Linda continues. I’ll be reporting the incident to the UK’sReport Fraudservice. I’ve also sent a cease-and-desist email to my impersonator, demanding they stop.For such a prolific writer, they’ve gone surprisingly quiet.Explore more on these topicsCybercrimeIdentity fraudDeepfakeAI (artificial intelligence)The GuardianNewspapers & magazinesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’  | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actors
Content: It is not so much ‘killer robots’ keeping one cabinet minister awake as the idea of concentrated, super-intelligent power ending up in the hands of bad actors.Photograph: Master/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIt is not so much ‘killer robots’ keeping one cabinet minister awake as the idea of concentrated, super-intelligent power ending up in the hands of bad actors.Photograph: Master/Getty ImagesAI (artificial intelligence)The power of AI is worrying senior Labour figures – as is the fear of ‘falling behind the public’Westminster appears to be waking up to warnings over AI safety, with concerns over its use by extremist groups and bad actorsRowena MasonandDan MilmoSat 17 Oct 2026 07.33 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” said one cabinet minister, with an ominous stare.It wasLabourconference, with everyone from ministers to activists jubilant at Andy Burnham’s takeover and a bounce in the polls after the change of leader.But a number of senior Labour figures were privately starting to name the power of AI as the thing worrying them most, alongside the immediate pressures on the cost of living and fragile economy.One cabinet minister – with a brief unrelated to technology – told the Guardian that dangerous, out-of-control AI was the issue keeping them up at night, fretting about the threat to humanity. It was “not killer robots” causing the worry, they explained, but the idea of a huge amount of concentrated, super-intelligent power potentially ending up in the hands of bad actors.Another expressed concern that the government was “falling behind the public” in terms of dealing with worries about AI safety – and that it needed to catch up fast.View image in fullscreenEd Miliband was strident about the dangers of AI at the Labour party conference.Photograph: Wiktor Szymanowicz/Future Publishing/Getty ImagesIn his conference speech,Ed Milibandwas the most strident about the “daunting” dangers of AI, making the case that politicians could not and would not allow the profits of tech companies “to come at the expense of our children or indeed humanity”.And it has not taken long for these alarm bells to ring even louder, with the last seven days looking like the week Westminster fully woke up to the warnings.A flurry of activity started on Monday with Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, stating it was“likely, if not inevitable”that rogue agents would hack the British state, and saying the UK was looking to strengthen its forthcoming cybersecurity legislation.View image in fullscreenKanishka Narayan said it was ‘likely, if not inevitable’ that rogue agents would hack the British state.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/AFP/Getty ImagesIt was the main topic of discussion at cabinet on Tuesday, and that was followed by the MI5 chief Ken McCallum warning AI was “supercharging the cybersecurity contest between attackers and defenders”. He saidthe biggest threat was extremist groupsusing the technology to unleash bioweapons – toxins used to cause death and disease.Liam Byrne, the chair of the business, innovation, science and trade committee, said the change of government from Keir Starmer to Burnham was partly behind the increased focus on protecting the UK from AI threats but more still had to be done. “The reality is that the Starmer administration was much too close to the big tech companies,” Byrne said. “And Burnham is not, frankly, so there has been a change of posture. Those things, plus the security services issuing their warning, that is what has changed the weather on this.”One senior Labour government figure agreed that Burnham’s government was taking AI safety warnings more seriously. “I do feel there has been a shift. Under the last lot, too many of them had drunk the tech-bro Kool-Aid,” he said.View image in fullscreenKen McCallum, the director general of MI5, warned of extremist groups using AI to unleash bioweapons.Photograph: Jonathan Brady/WPA/Getty ImagesByrne’s committee held an evidence session this week with civil service leaders in charge of AI security and executives from the key companies –Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepMind and Meta – with a split between them about whether government testing of new models should be mandatory.He said his committee was “lighting up” the issue, particularly in terms of working with the US to regulate and monitor new models. It had been reported that Donald Trump’s administration had asked AI companies not to share their latest models with the UK’s cutting-edge AI Security Institute for testing, though Narayan confirmed this week that they had managed to retain cooperation.But Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation, particularly if Trump’s Republicans lost control of Congress in the midterm elections to the Democrats.“I think the government is still caught in a dilemma between how to keep model access, given a capricious US president, and the safeguards that the industry itself now says are essential. It’s make-your-mind-up time, I would say,” Byrne said.“The companies want to cooperate … It’s not in their commercial interest to issue models which are lethal. Now they too have got to navigate the White House. So I just think this is a moment when the government has actually got to do what is right for the country because Congress is about to change the dynamics on this in the US.”View image in fullscreenLiam Byrne said the government now needed to seize the moment and take the lead on new regulation.Photograph: House of CommonsThe UK’s upcoming G20 presidency will be the key moment to push for international action to rein in AI. Geoffrey Irving, the former chief scientist at AISI whospoke at this week’s parliamentary hearing, believes Whitehall concerns are justified. OpenAI and Anthropic’s technology has already shown its hacking capabilities but their models are released with safety guardrails in place that at least mitigate against the threat of malicious behaviour.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHowever, so-called open source AI models are freely available and can be adapted. Typically, they caught up with the paid-for models such as OpenAI’s within less than a year, said Irving, although they could cause disruption already.“It’s very likely that open source models are alreadypowerful enough to do serious damage,” Irving told the Guardian, adding that he expected open source technology to reach the capabilities of OpenAI and Anthropic products “soon”. Safety guardrails “either don’t exist or can be trivially removed” from open source models, he added.Could AI ‘change the stakes’ in the development of bioweapons?Read moreThe business committee heard this week thatAI-enabled bioweaponscould become the next serious threat to manifest itself, in the wake of cybersecurity, as models become more powerful and therefore capable of designing novel bio-harms – although experts suggest there is a gap between designing dangerous pathogens and weaponising them.Concerns over cybersecurity and bioweapons can escalate rapidly to fears about AI wiping out humanity in a variety of scenarios – a concern that is widespread within the AI community, and is shared by Irving.However, some experts argue that the government should focus on immediate risks from AI. Prof Elena Simperl, a co-director of the Institute for Artificial Intelligence at King’s College London, said the existential risk argument had “no evidence” and was a “theory” rather than a credible threat.“There are bigger, more immediate risks that AI technology is posing now and are actually evidenced, like hacking and signs that AI can be as addictive as social media,” Simperl said.View image in fullscreenThere is said to be concern over the cancellation last year of the AI programme at Porton Down.Photograph: Jack Taylor/Getty ImagesIn the absence of international AI regulation, there are some in Whitehall worried about whether the UK is doing enough preparation to defend against AI warfare and attacks.Defence sources said there was concern about the cancellation last year of the AI programme at the government’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), based at Porton Down, with worries that this was shortsighted given the need for cutting-edge research on advancing the nation’s capabilities and defending against its risks.This was countered by an MoD spokesperson who said AI was “transforming defence from industry to the battlefield and will play a decisive role in how we fight and defend” and that it must be “integrated across all workstreams, rather than a standalone programme”. They pointed to a £400m investment in AI-focused capabilities over the next four years to “prepare the UK for the future of warfare”.Others in Whitehall have the opposite concern: that worries about safety could become too dominant – and end up holding back the government’s adoption of tools that could be transformative for productivity and solving longstanding problems in public services, from medical care to reducing waiting lists.The former cabinet secretary Gus O’Donnell told the Guardian that ministers needed to be as aware of “the risk of being left behind” when it came to AI as being aware of the need for guardrails.Launching a Global Government Forum report on AI with the tech firm Cognizant, O’Donnell told the Guardian: “There is a big need to get it better and to really push on. I’m really optimistic, but the challenge for us, obviously, is managing the risks along the way, making sure that we don’t make mistakes, which reduce people’s trust, which means that that sets us back.”Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)UK security and counter-terrorismDefence policyData and computer securityComputingLabourEd MilibandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Why Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and  scary – Chinese AI | Phillip Inman | The Guardian
description: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China
Author: Phillip Inman
Headline: In the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from China
Content: Models such as DeepSeek  allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.Photograph: GK Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenModels such as DeepSeek  allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.Photograph: GK Images/AlamyViewpoint columnInternational tradeWhy Britain should reject the lure of cheap – and  scary – Chinese AIPhillip InmanIn the west the technology comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent – not so from ChinaSat 17 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 11.02 EDTShareThere is much to fear from artificial intelligence developed inChinaand handed to businesses and governments in the west almost free of charge.Every month Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi dispatch the latest versions of their “open-weight” models that allow users to take the core software and use it without paying an expensive ongoing licence.In Britain, we love cheap Chinese kit, usually setting aside any concerns about how it was made and who by.The row over whether to allow Chinese electric cars unfettered access to British retail forecourts is a case in point. They arecheaper than other EVs sold in the UKand, consumers ask: What is not to like? These same consumers might consider how Chinese EVs are subsidised by Beijing deliberately to boost exports and, in so doing, undermine foreign domestic car industries.Cheap AI takes this export threat to a higher level.It’s scary because Beijing is entering a new phase in the long march of economic development, taking the world’s second largest economy closer to making China great again.Go back 10 years and Xi Jinping’s close supporters were alert to the internal contradictions of a totalitarian, command and control state apparatus and how it could trigger social unrest, much as it did in the last centuryin Tiananmen Square.A property crash that still acts as a drag on the economy, rising unemployment, poor health services in many regions, a mismatch of men and women, an ageing population – they could all be the spark that threatens Communist party rule.Then came AI and the state discovered complete control.Now Beijing has huge surveillance capabilities, using AI to capture images of its citizens and monitor their activities if they need to.Don’t think it means Chinese people are under virtual house arrest. They can go about their daily lives, gathering in the street for an impromptu dance or to discuss how their local region might be better run. But serious dissidents? They are rooted out and sidelined, re-educated or punished.For the central committee, AI is a blessing. While the financial constraints from having to please a domestic audience have not entirely disappeared, Beijing’s leaders can concentrate on the threats they face from the rest of the world.Not that it wants to invade countries in the same manner as Russia. China’s reinvigoratedbelt and road initiativecreates permanent channels for trade less obviously than the previous iteration, allowing Beijing to turn states into clients who depend for the basics of life on Chinese technology.Where Russia is using AI to enhance cyber-attacks on European government agencies and businesses to create chaos, China wants merely to widen the circle of friends that consume its goods without asking awkward questions.Military force is also being contemplated. Now that Beijing can redirect precious resources previously needed to subsidise Chinese consumers, it is building a fleet of warships to challenge the US in the Pacific, much as Japan did in the 1930s. Taiwan, the engine of semiconductor development, is in its sights.Meanwhile, Chinese developers are launching AI models by the dozen each month at a fraction of the cost of US equivalents.There are tech analysts who say Chinese models add to the rich tapestry of AI, supplementing the closed, proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic. And they say there are European and Indian versions in development. Adding to that tapestry, Meta is fast developing open AI models, but like the other challengers, lags in the race to win over customers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn practice, an AI user has the choice between a cheap Chinese open system they can tweak for their own ends or expensive US software that comes with bells and whistles they probably don’t need.Both types have the potential to destroy humanity, asmany AI experts have documented. But on a more mundane level, in day-to-day use, only one comes with at least some effort to provide security and a benign intent, and it’s not the Chinese option.As Ross Burley says, Chinese AI comes with extra baggage. Burley is director of theCentre for Information Resilience(CIR), an independent, non-profit group dedicated to, among other things, exposing human rights abuses and countering disinformation.He says DeepSeek cannot access the properly isolated use of its software, “but that addresses just part of the risk. Running a model on your own servers doesn’t automatically remove any political censorship. Or indeed repair weaknesses in any security defences.”Anevaluation reportby the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (Nist) found political censorship in downloaded DeepSeek models running on its own infrastructure, which means that hosting those models in the UK wouldn’t, by itself, remove censorship.“We should be deeply concerned about embedding Beijing’s political restrictions into systems that businesses and public services rely on for information and decisions,” he says.The policy governing DeepSeek’s online chatbot says it collects prompts and uploaded material, processes and stores personal data in China, and permits disclosure to Chinese authorities.Michael Wooldridge, a professor of AI at the University of Oxford, says it is not unreasonable to assumedata inputted into the chatbot could be shared with the Chinese state.The consequences for policymaking are profound. The UK should reject the lure of cheap Chinese AI and seek to better tame US AI while supporting domestic and EU suppliers.Relying on Chinese tech, from cars to AI, is going to hollow out industry and undermine the security of our data.Explore more on these topicsInternational tradeViewpoint columnAI (artificial intelligence)EconomicsChinaAsia PacificAutomotive industryUK security and counter-terrorismcommentShareReuse this content

title: Ministers must be honest about Russian threat to UK, says former Foreign Office head | Cyberwar | The Guardian
description: Peter Ricketts calls for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaults
Author: Harry Taylor
Headline: Peter Ricketts calls for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaults
Content: Lord Ricketts said Vladimir Putin was ‘trying to undermine morale in European countries’.Photograph: Parliament TVLord Ricketts said Vladimir Putin was ‘trying to undermine morale in European countries’.Photograph: Parliament TVCyberwarMinisters must be honest about Russian threat to UK, says former Foreign Office headPeter Ricketts calls for more resilience in protecting banking, energy and water systems from cyber-assaultsHarry TaylorSat 17 Oct 2026 06.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMinisters need to be honest with the British public about the immediate threat posed byRussia, which could soon lead to lives being lost, a former national security adviser has said.Peter Ricketts, who advised David Cameron when he was prime minister, became the latest figure to warn about the scale of the threat posed by “hybrid attacks” from Vladimir Putin’s forces.The peer, who is the former top civil servant in the Foreign Office, said banking systems, energy or water supplies could be targeted by Kremlin cyber-assaults. He called for further investment in resilience for key sectors.It comes in a week where the heads ofMI5and the British army have warned about the danger posed by Moscow.Lord Ricketts also dismissed Andy Burnham’s claim he wanted to be a “bridge” between the US and Ukraine.Relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorated sharply this week after Donald Trumpwaived a number of economic sanctions on Russiaand suggested Ukraineneeded a new leader.Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Ricketts said: “I think they’ve really got to start a conversation with the British people about what may be coming, because not only is Putin trying to break morale in Ukraine, he’s also trying to undermine morale in European countries.”In response to a question over the impact of disruption by Russia, he added: “I’m not saying there’s going to be industrial war with tanks rolling across the north German plain.“But these hybrid attacks are getting more reckless, more dangerous. One day, people are going to land up being killed somewhere, and so we are going to have to look at responding in that sense and finding the money to do it.”Speaking about Burnham’s comments at prime minister’s questions this week saying he wanted to be a bridge between Washington and Kyiv, Ricketts said: “I don’t really go on this bridge business. I mean, I don’t think in Trump’s current mood there’s any influence that Britain can have in the short term.”Ricketts’s comments join those by the director general of MI5, Sir Ken McCallum, and the chief of the general staff, Gen Sir Roly Walker, in the last few days about Russia.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStarlink access still not fully restored for Ukraine’s military, says ZelenskyyRead moreOn Tuesday, McCallum said MI5 was devoting more resources to combating threats from hostile states than it did during the cold war and described Russia as the “number one aggressor”.And on Friday, Walker told 700 troops at Catterick garrison in North Yorkshire that politicians would soon need to have a “frank conversation” about the “sacrifices” that would be needed to prioritise defence and security.Walker, a former special forces commander, said soldiers wouldprobably need to fight in a war, given the “extreme jeopardy in the world at the moment”.The warnings come after a difficult week for Kyiv, with the US appearing to withdraw support.Trump said the decision to pause sanctions was in the US “national interest”, despite previously signing them into law in September.Last week, he lifted restrictions on Russian diesel amid spiralling fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections.He also suggested Ukraine needed a new president. Volodymyr Zelenskyy hit back this week during an EU summit, saying it was nice to be among “real leaders”.There are also concerns that the US has withdrawn intelligence sharing with Ukraine, leaving towns and cities across the country vulnerable to attack.Ricketts said the government should spend more money on protections for key infrastructure in Britain, including energy, transport, air traffic control and defence.He said: “They all need better protection, and that’s an argument that needs to be had with the British people because we need to find the money to do it.”Explore more on these topicsCyberwarRussiaVladimir PutinUK security and counter-terrorismCybercrimeMI5Donald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges? | France | The Guardian
description: Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers
Author: Kim Willsher
Headline: Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers
Content: Packages of perished goods piled outside an Intermarché store in Paris the day after a cyber-attack targeted refrigeration and freezer systems.Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersView image in fullscreenPackages of perished goods piled outside an Intermarché store in Paris the day after a cyber-attack targeted refrigeration and freezer systems.Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersFranceNot cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges?Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezersKim Willsherin ParisSat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles acrossFrancebegan to flicker and rise.In a“bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack,hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F).Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook.Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage.“It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux inParis. “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.”View image in fullscreenSupermarket staff had to remove tons of spoiled food and work late to reorder and restock shelves.Photograph: Lucien Libert/ReutersAfter removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.”If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack.Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio.The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country inEurope.Gérôme Billois, a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage.“The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said.View image in fullscreenA woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France.Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty“As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear.“Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.”The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms.Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centreANSSI confirmedsupermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted.Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated.1:05French supermarket director apologises after cyber-attack spoils fresh and frozen food - video“Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said.“The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.”She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.”The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went intounscheduled defrost cycles overnightcausing massive food loss.France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management companyUpguard.In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks.View image in fullscreenSupermarket employees restock goods in Nancy, north-east France.Photograph: Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu/GettyBillois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices.“It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said.In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry.Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio.As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time.“It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said.The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case | EditorialRead moreRybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.”The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance.“It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers.“But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured. And that must be a wake-up call to everyone.”Explore more on these topicsFranceCybercrimeSupermarketsFoodRetail industryEuropeParisnewsShareReuse this content
