title: If Trump becomes a lame duck, surely countries like Australia can say what we really think?  | Zoe Daniel | The Guardian
description: For years everyone has been dancing around Trump’s unpredictability, his bullying and his threats. It’s past time to reassert our values
Author: Zoe Daniel
Headline: For years everyone has been dancing around Trump’s unpredictability, his bullying and his threats. It’s past time to reassert our values
Content: ‘Trump is all about attention grabbing climaxes that both rate and divert attention from his failures.’Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersView image in fullscreen‘Trump is all about attention grabbing climaxes that both rate and divert attention from his failures.’Photograph: Evan Vucci/ReutersOpinionAustralian foreign policyIf Trump becomes a lame duck, surely countries like Australia can say what we really think?Zoe DanielFor years everyone has been dancing around Trump’s unpredictability, his bullying and his threats. It’s past time to reassert our valuesSat 17 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 21.23 EDTShareIn two weeks,Donald Trumpfaces his moment of truth; transformational midterm elections that will drastically influence the rest of his presidency, for better or for worse.Assuming that he cannot find a way around the constitutional ban on him running for a third time in 2028, he now has a limited time left to make sure he leaves office the most consequential president ever. Again, for better, or worse.Motivated deeply by fame, that could make for an (even more) volatile ride than we’ve seen so far as his administration enters its final stages.Whatever happens in the House and Senate elections, he remains commander in chief of the US armed forces with the power to unleash conflict, perhaps with even less restraint than he’s shown in his intemperate and economically reckless decision to go to war against Iran.So, if in many ways this era has resembled reality TV, the finale is yet to come, and Trump is all about attention grabbing climaxes that both rate and divert attention from his failures.His administration’s threats to livestream an execution – plans he’s now had to walk back – to shift the focus from Iran, andhis betrayal of Ukrainewhile doing deals with Russia is a new low.Such barbaric politically motivated “entertainment”, usually confined to the most gruesome of autocracies, announced by former Fox News host, now Secretary of War, Pete Hegseth, may be a sign of things to come.During Trump’s second term, although arguably better organised and deliberate than the first, there have been few limits on his behaviour, surrounded as he has been by yes people.Having increased his vote in 2024, winning the trifecta of the White House, with majorities in the House of Representatives and the Senate, the president has been truly off the leash.The 3 November midterms, in which all 435 seats in the House and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are up for election, represent a likely turning point.As in Australia, the issues motivating voters are predominantly hip pocket; cost of living and inflation, along with immigration, datacentres and AI.And unlike his last presidency, when Trump’s economic performance was viewed positively at a similar point in the term, this time,voters blame his tariffs and war in Iranfor high fuel prices and cost of living.All of this means that the House is highly likely to swing to the Democrats in what may beless a “blue wave” than a “red undertow” and the Senate, while more borderline,may be lostas well. This is less an endorsement of the Democrats than a referendum on Trump, with hispopularity at historic lows.Should it play out that way, Trump will be faced with the prospect of spending his final two years of ultimate power with both hands tied behind his back.When Obama lost the House amid economic woes in 2010, in what he described as a “shellacking”, and only narrowly held the Senate, it sharply limited his agenda for the rest of his term.There was legislative gridlock that led to increased use of executive orders that in turn led to a deep split between Congress and the White House with threats of legal action over executive overreach.Much the same happened after the 2018 midterms when Republicans lost control of the house in the largest Democrat gain since the 1970s but held the Senate.Having followed Obama’s agenda of hope with his own agenda of disruption, Trump will strongly resist his final years in the White House being thwarted in the same way. And theoretically with no chance of a third term, there’s a high likelihood he will simply bulldoze his way through it with a sense of impunity.Democrats will need to resist the urge to martyr him a second time with legal action and impeachment if, or when, he starts further stretching the system.Meanwhile, these changed dynamics have implications for Australia and the rest of the world.For years, everyone has been dancing around Trump’s unpredictability, his bullying and his threats.Tariffs have been used as a weapon, war has breached international law, humanitarian aid has been decimated, inclusion and equality have been called “woke”, immigration has been weaponised, human rights have been eroded, and national sovereignty has been ignored.Australia’s moves to regulate the US tech firms, to take back some control of our own information landscape, are a perfect case study, with concerns that asserting our own data sovereignty could lead to trade retaliation.Here is an opportunity to reassert our values.If Trump is a lame duck, surely we can say what we really think?Since he was first elected in 2016, boundaries have shifted, and that’s enabled some scary behaviour that’s seeped into communities, communication and politics around the world.Even here, where we have had longstanding bipartisan agreement against the death penalty, the ascendant One Nation supports bringing it back.Only we can reset the boundaries of political populism.Perhaps threatening to livestream an execution in front of a firing squad is a red line, or maybe we’ve already crossed it.Zoe Daniel is a three-time ABC foreign correspondent and former independent member for GoldsteinExplore more on these topicsAustralian foreign policyOpinionDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Move over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogroping | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women
Content: This photo provided by police in Cologne, Germany, shows a robot that was seized as evidence, on 11 October.Photograph: Polizei Koeln/Cologne Police/APView image in fullscreenThis photo provided by police in Cologne, Germany, shows a robot that was seized as evidence, on 11 October.Photograph: Polizei Koeln/Cologne Police/APThe Week in PatriarchyRobotsMove over, pervert glasses – the latest toxic trend is robogropingArwa MahdawiWhenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and womenSat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTShareYou may be familiar withrule 34of the internet, which states that if something exists or can be imagined, there will almost certainly be online porn of it. Now let me introduce my rule 35: whenever a new technology is created, it will, without exception, immediately be used to harass girls and women.See, for example, Meta’s “pervert glasses”. As anyone could have foreseen, putting a tiny camera and microphone into smartglasses would immediately lead to people using them to record and harass women. Lo and behold, that is exactly what happened. So-called manfluencers havefilmed themselvestrying to flirt with women in public spaces and then uploaded the footage to TikTok. The women in these videos are often not aware they’ve been recorded until their identities are shared online and they areharassedby strangers. And what’s Meta doing about this? It’s instituted a few bans and made some privacy updates, but doesn’t seem to have an appetite to properly solve the problem. Indeed, at the Meta Connect 2026 keynote, Mark Zuckerberg didnot feel the needto apologize to the women whose lives have been upended by his technology.Then there is the Flock license plate tracking system, which has been abused by anextraordinary numberof law enforcement officers totrack the locationsof their exes or other women they are sexually interested in. And, of course, there are the AI image generators, which have been used to create deepfake pornography of women and girls. According to a2023 report, “deepfake pornography made up 98 per cent of all deepfake videos online, and 99 per cent depicted women”.Now, there’s a new toxic tech trend to worry about: livestreamed robogroping. Police in Cologne, Germany, are currentlyinvestigating an incidentin which a humanoid robot controlled by two teenage males touched a 16-year-old girl’s buttocks and made sexually suggestive gestures toward her. Footage of the groping robot, which was wearing human clothes and a fake mustache, was reportedly livestreamed by the two males online.The robot in question has now been confiscated by the local police, who seem a little befuddled by the whole thing. “We have not been aware of this phenomenon so far,” a police spokesperson told the Associated Press, adding it was “new territory for us”.It may be new territory but I can guarantee you that this won’t be the last time we hear about an incident like this. Getting your hands on an AI-powered humanoid robot is still a lot more expensive than buying a pair of smartglasses, but the technology is rapidly becoming a lot more accessible. Earlier this year, a school in New York made headlines after announcing its new teaching assistant would be ahumanoid robotcalled Sally, made by a company that makes realistic sex dolls. Outrage over the announcement forced the school district tohalt its plans, but it’s only a matter of time before we see humanoid robots in schools. Indeed, in a report published last year,Bank of Americapredicted that, as costs go down, we will see mass adoption of humanoid robots from 2035 onwards. By 2060, they expect there to be 3bn humanoid robots, which will replace 20% of the workforce in the industrial sector and 50% of the workforce in the service sector.As the industry develops, expect corporations to ensure that their profit-maximizing robots have more legal protections than the humans they may harm. This week in Philadelphia, for example, awoman was arrestedafter allegedly blocking the path of one of the annoying Uber delivery robots that are now ubiquitous in the city. (The fact the police intervened is absolutely wild to me as a Philadelphia resident, considering they rarely seem interested in doing their jobs.) A growing body of case law has found that police officers arenot under anylegal obligation to protect citizens who are not in their custody. Yet they seem surprisingly keen on protecting robots.Our brave new world, everyone! I’m afraid pervert glasses are just a small glimpse of what’s to come. By 2060, robogroping may be as commonplace as catcalling is today.You can pay $7,500 to take dating lessons from a man accused of rapeBraden Eric Peters, who goes by the nom-de-influencer Clavicular, shot to fame for smashing his facewith a hammerin order to beautify himself. Bonesmashing, as it’s called, is part of a toxic trend calledlooksmaxxing, which involves people (largely young men) going to extremes to increase their “sexual market value”. When not bonesmashing, Peters gets into regular trouble with the law. Most lately, he was charged withrape and drug offensesin Massachusetts last month; his attorneys have denied the allegations. Nevertheless, it seems that there are people out therewilling to pay $7,500for a week at Camp Looksmax, a new venture in which Peters coaches attendees on confidence and dating.Katie Miller blames the fall of the Roman Empire on women“If more women put the same energy into their marriages and into finding a spouse that they do into their careers, you would see society have a lot more babies because, ultimately, that’s what led to the downfall of Rome – when women stopped having babies, and you started putting energy elsewhere,” Stephen Miller’s influential wife said onFox News this week. Someone buy the Millers a history book please.Tradwife influencer Nara Smith says she is ‘getting her tubes tied’Smith, 25, and her husband, 28, havefour kidscalled Slim Easy, Rumble Honey, Whimsy Lou and Fawnie Golden. Speaking on theAspire podcastrecently, Smith said she didn’t think she could handle having another kid. Sounds sensible to me, but I’m not sure Katie Miller’s going to approve of that decision.Women up to 74% more likely than men to be told autoimmune condition symptoms are psychological“The damage caused to women by these types of misdiagnosis can be very long lasting in terms of trusting doctors and their own self-esteem,” the lead author of theUK-based study said.A Palestinian toddler watched her mother get burned alive in Gaza CityReem Asaad Awad was killed when an Israeli airstrike hit her home. Her young daughter, Maryam Ahmed Ghanem, was pulledout of the burning building. Maryam’s father was reportedlykilled earlierin the ongoing genocide, and it’s unclear whether she has surviving family or will become one of Gaza’smany WCNSFs: wounded child, no surviving family.Sally Rooney is unable to sell her books in the UK because of Palestine Action supportThe bestselling author said last July that royalties from her book would be used to support direct action group Palestine Action, which has been proscribed as a terrorist organization in the UK, despite the fact that it hasnever killed anyoneor attempted to do so. Rooney has now said she canno longer sell her workin the UK and can’t visit because she risks imprisonment. A round of applause, please, for the brave British government for arresting thousands of people, many ofwhom are pensioners, for their Palestine Action support and protecting us from dangerous people like Rooney. Meanwhile, the British Museum is rolling out the red carpet forIgor Tulchinsky, a billionaire who reportedly funded an illegal Israeli settlement in the West Bank.Iranian woman given death sentence for ‘blasphemy’ in social media postTwenty-three-year-old Najmeh Amini has beensentenced to deathon charges of “sab ol-nabi” (insulting the prophet). Death sentences for blasphemy are relatively rare, but rights groups have warned that Iranian authorities are increasingly using capital punishment to quash dissent.Katie Zacharia is out as press secretary after five daysOh, dear!She didn’t even get her 15 minutes of fame; her disastrous first press briefing only lasted 14 minutes. Maybe Trump should replace her with a humanoid robot.The week in pawtriarchyIf you desperately need a palate cleanser now, I recommend the Guardian’s week inwildlife photographs. I particularly enjoyed the photo of the black crested gibbon and its thousand-yard stare, which pretty much mirrors my expression all week. Hope you ape-preciate it.Explore more on these topicsRobotsThe Week in PatriarchyWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on time | Jeffrey Ingold | The Guardian
description: If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …, says culture writer Jeffrey Ingold
Author: Jeffrey Ingold
Headline: If cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …, says culture writer Jeffrey Ingold
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesThe hill I will die onMoviesThe hill I will die on: Cinemas have been getting away with lies. Films should begin on timeJeffrey IngoldIf cinemas must run 20 minutes of adverts before a feature, they could at least be honest about it. Or, I have a better solution …Sat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 15.43 EDTShareDo you remember the last time you were lied to? I certainly do. I was tricked by the North Finchley Vue, which sold me and my boyfriend tickets to a 7.15pm showing of The Odyssey. Guess what was playing at 7.15pm? A car advert. Ten minutes later, it was a trailer for the horror film Werwulf. Then there was an advert for Vue – as if I wasn’t already there. The film was half an hour late to its own showing when it finally started at 7.45pm.I am sick and tired of cinemas getting away with such treachery. I don’t want to follow in the footsteps of my friend, who knows that the ads at her local run for 22 minutes so slinks in at just the right time. I shouldn’t have to do mental maths because I am being lied to by cinemas. We are all the victims of their predatory time-wasting system.If you went to see a play and the ticket said the show started at 7.30pm, you’d rightly be annoyed if after 20 minutes the performance still hadn’t started. Yet when it comes to watching movies, we’ve collectively accepted that it’s fine for them to start later than advertised. Which also means we all put up with people coming in late, shining their phone torches and bumping into you because they tried to show up when the film actually starts.Now thatalmost a third of wide releases run over two hoursand pre-show advertising and trailers last for 20-30 minutes, something’s gotta give. I say films should start on time. I know a better moviegoing experience is possible. I grew up in Canada, where our cinemas played their films at the ticketed time and the ads started earlier. When my family showed up 10 minutes late to The Fellowship of the Ring, we missed the entire opening sequence explaining the history of the rings of power. We deserved that!A brave senator in Connecticut tried to tackle this injustice in 2025 with a bill that would “require the disclosure of accurate movie start times in advertisements and listings”. However, it was watered down to a mere “working group” after pushback from cinema operators. They warned they’d lose vital revenue if advertisers pulled back because people started skipping the pre-show entirely. Erin Brockovich wouldn’t have given in so easily.How can we succeed where the Connecticut senator failed? Simple: we also get rid of assigned seating. Say goodbye to paying£26 for an Ultra Lux reclinerif you want the best view. It’s a flat fee no matter where you sit. Welcome to the Hunger Games of cinema seating.If you want a “good” seat for a film, you have to earn it by showing up early. Exactly like when I was young, the ads and trailers will play before the start time so the film can begin promptly. Arrive on time, after the trailers, and you might be stuck in the front row, but that’s on you for avoiding the ads.I’m just a cinephile, standing in front of a movie theatre, asking it to respect me and my time. Why is that so hard?Jeffrey Ingold is a freelance journalist covering LGBTQ+ issues, music and cultureExplore more on these topicsFilmThe hill I will die onAdvertisingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Letby public inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safe | Mark McDonald | The Guardian
description: I fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyone, says Lucy Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald
Author: Mark McDonald
Headline: I fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyone, says Lucy Letby’s barrister, Mark McDonald
Content: ‘The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAView image in fullscreen‘The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions.’Photograph: Jeff Moore/PAOpinionLucy LetbyThe Letby public inquiry will lead to more blame and suspicion in the NHS – and patients will be less safeMark McDonaldI fear for what comes next because medics must be able to ask questions, raise concerns and admit mistakes. A defensive staff is dangerous for everyoneMark McDonald is a barrister representing Lucy LetbySat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 03.31 EDTShareIhave been Lucy Letby’s barrister for the past two years. I have spent thousands of hours going through the evidence, speaking to experts and examining what happened to the babies who died or became seriously unwell on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester hospital. I have worked with nearly 30 experts, including internationally recognised specialists in neonatology, pathology, insulin, statistics and other fields. It may be to some an inconvenient truth, but I am convinced that Letby is innocent, and her convictions represent one of the most serious miscarriages of justice in modern British legal history. That means she was failed by the police, the NHS, the criminal justice system and, importantly, a plethora of experts who simply got it wrong.My work on the case has also raised wider concerns about the evidence and conclusions surrounding the deaths on the neonatal unit, and what the lessons being drawn fromthis casewill mean for doctors and nurses in neonatal medicine.Neonatal units are among the most demanding environments in theNHS. These are tiny, desperately ill babies. Their condition can change within minutes, and doctors and nurses make difficult decisions under enormous pressure, often with incomplete information.Sometimes, despite the best care, babies die. That is an uncomfortable truth, but any serious discussion about neonatal safety has to acknowledge it. What worries me is that we risk creating a culture in which clinicians become frightened to work in these environments.Imagine being a doctor working a night shift in a neonatal unit. A baby’s condition suddenly deteriorates and you have to make decisions quickly, but despite your efforts they die. Then, years later, the circumstances of those decisions are reconstructed with the benefit of hindsight. Every action is examined. Every decision is questioned. And the possibility of a criminal investigation hangs over the process. Who would still want to work in neonatal medicine?This is not only atheoretical question. The NHS already faces enormous challenges in recruiting and retaining staff. We need people who do take on this challenging work to feel confident enough to make decisions. We need them to be able to say: “I don’t know”. We need them to admit mistakes, report near misses and challenge colleagues and managers. Above all, we need them to tell the truth.For many years, the NHS has tried to develop what is often described as a learning or “no-blame” culture. The idea behind this was never that there should be no accountability. What it means is that when something goes wrong, the first questions should be: what happened? Why did it happen? And what can we learn?A public inquiry set up after Letby’s convictions, chaired by Lady Justice Thirlwall,delivered its reportin mid-September. The report placed great emphasis on monitoring and surveillance, and specifically stated a needto move away from the no-blame culture. These recommendations risk creating a surveillance society within the NHS, where clinicians fear that every adverse outcome may lead to scrutiny and blame. Patient safety depends on openness, trust and learning from mistakes, not a culture of suspicion in which clinical error, systemic failure and deliberate criminal conduct become dangerously blurred.That would be a terrible unintended consequence. The safest NHS is not one in which staff are frightened of making mistakes and practise defensively. It is one in which staff feel safe enough to admit mistakes.Thirlwall’s is not the first major inquiry into failures in maternity and neonatal care. Over the past two decades, there have been major investigations into trusts inMorecambe Bay,Shrewsbury and Telford,East KentandNottingham, among others. Again and again, inquiries have found problems with leadership, communication, escalation, teamwork and listening. Again and again, recommendations have been made and promises given that the NHS will learn. So perhaps we need to ask a more difficult question: why hasn’t it?The answer cannot simply be that we need another set of rules, another layer of monitoring, or another system for identifying individual responsibility. We need to listen to the people who actually work in these units. This is where I am particularly critical of the government, of successive governments.Who is asking what these changes will feel like to a nurse working a 12-hour shift in an understaffed neonatal intensive care unit? Who is asking what it will feel like to a doctor knowing that an unexpected clinical outcome could result in years of scrutiny? The government has a responsibility to protect patients. But it also has a responsibility to protect the workforce on whom patient safety depends. The two things are inseparable.I think trade unions also have a responsibility here. They should defend patients, but they should also defend their members. This does not mean defending wrongdoing. It means defending fairness, and making sure that a doctor or nurse is judged in the circumstances in which they actually made a decision, rather than simply with the benefit of hindsight. It means recognising that an adverse clinical outcome is not evidence of criminal conduct.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThere has been remarkably little public debate about the possibility that the response to Thirlwall’s inquiry could create fear among NHS workers. Furthermore, no Labour MP has spoken up, and that silence matters.The Thirlwall recommendations risk creating an environment in which a disgruntled healthcare professional can point the finger at another, triggering investigations that can quickly become criminal investigations.The doctors and nurses caring for vulnerable newborns deserve protection from unfair hindsight, disproportionate suspicion and a culture in which every adverse outcome becomes a potential question of individual blame. Because if the lesson we take from the Thirlwall inquiry is that we need more blame, more surveillance and more fear, then I worry that we will have learned the wrong lesson.We will not have made the NHS safer. We will simply have made it harder for the NHS to care for the babies who need it most.Mark McDonald is a criminal defence and human rights barrister specialising in miscarriages of justiceDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: French schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truth | Rokhaya Diallo | The Guardian
description: To protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not, says Guardian Europe columnist Rokhaya Diallo
Author: Rokhaya Diallo
Headline: To protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is not, says Guardian Europe columnist Rokhaya Diallo
Content: Police preparing to charge against pupils and students in Paris, France, on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Tonny Linke/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPolice preparing to charge against pupils and students in Paris, France, on 13 October 2026.Photograph: Tonny Linke/NurPhoto/ShutterstockOpinionFranceFrench schoolchildren have been treated like enemies to be crushed – for telling the truthRokhaya DialloTo protest against shameful conditions in schools is entirely legitimate. The government’s response is notSat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 04.53 EDTShareAs a secondary school pupil in 1994, I took part inprotestsagainst a reform that would have allowed French employers to pay young people below the minimum wage. Our campaign was successful, but if we had had to face the terrifying police responseunleashed on student protestersin France over recent weeks, I would have stayed at home.A 14-year-old boy, Eden, suffered a fractured jaw and had teeth knocked out after a police teargas grenade struck him in the face. Sixteen-year-old Maëllostthe sight in one eye allegedly after being struck by a shot from an LBD, a form of rubber-bullet launcher. Evan, 15, had his hand blown off in an explosion involving a police stun grenade. And in Dunkirk, a police SUV is alleged to have driven repeatedlyat groupsof secondary school pupils, as an officer could be heard saying: “Come closer, we’ll smash their fucking faces in.”Accountsfrom children left terrified by brutal treatment in police custody describe traumatic experiences with severe psychological and physical consequences.France, the self-styled home of human rights, is now attracting the kind of international legal scrutiny you would expect if this were an authoritarian regime gone mad. The human rights organisation Ligue des droits de l’Hommehas condemnedthe alarming “brutalisation of young people”, and the threat to their freedom of expression.A UN special rapporteurhas calledon the French authorities to respect the physical safety of protesters. The UN human rights officesaysit is following incidents surrounding the protests in France “with concern”. Amnesty International hascalled for the suspensionof rubber-bullet launchers at school protests, condemned the disproportionate use of force and reminded the authorities of their duty to protect children. The Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg, whose activism increasingly encompasses struggles against oppression and state violence,travelled to Francethis week to support school pupils.View image in fullscreenA student checks her smartphone in front of the Helene Boucher high school during a protest in Paris, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026. (AP Photo/Teresa Suarez)Photograph: Teresa Suárez/APIt is often argued that France is broke, and that crippling debt levels make the student demand for€10bn of investmentto improve their learning conditions a non-starter. But even in our difficult fiscal position, public spending is a political choice: to reduce debt you can cut public spending or you can raise revenue.Economists Élise Huillery and Romane Paris have come up with acredible proposalfor investing an additional €11.8bn a year in education, funded through tax reform targeting large inheritances, raising €12.7bn in 2026 and increasing taxes only for the wealthiest 1% of heirs. This would make money available to raise teachers’ pay, improve support for pupils, student grants and housing, and expand university places.But the debate about public spending does not invalidate the legitimate grievances of pupils, teachers and parents, which are not new. Nor does it justify a vicious law and order response. Learning conditions in some of the most disadvantaged schools have been deteriorating to shockingly poor levels for a long time. I highlighted school conditions in France in the Guardianthree years ago, arguing then that the state education system was among the most unequal in the developed world. The lack of resources assigned to such basic things as teaching vacancies has been glaringly apparent for years, with jobs in some districts sometimes left unfilled for months.More than 20m teaching hours were lost in state secondary schools in 2024-25, equivalent to almost one in 10 lessons. More than 15m of those hours were lost because no replacement teachers were provided. Schools in designated priority education areas, which serve disadvantaged communities, have been particularly affected,according to France’s National Audit Office.In Seine-Saint-Denis, the poorest part of mainland France, two-thirds of school doctor posts were vacant in 2023. As early as 2022, the Créteil education authorityreporteda shortfall of 60 school nurses and 20 social workers, with 90% of the unfilled posts in Seine-Saint-Denis. In 2025,49 suicideswere recorded among staff in the national education system. While these deaths cannot all be attributed to work, it is hard to avoid thinking of the severe deterioration in working conditions across the sector.Then there are the schools that are physicallyfalling apart: water that isunsafe to drinkbecause of bacterial contamination, pupilsreporting ratsandcockroaches,filthy toilets, and in one case, a septic tank that overflows when it rains. There are power cuts, missing furniture and some classrooms are sopoorly insulatedthat temperatures fall below 14C in winter and hit 40C during heatwaves.In Mayotte, where protests began, a secondary school built for 900 pupils is accommodating 2,300. The protests then spread to mainlandFrancethrough a school in Créteil that began the academic year short of 13 teachers and other staff, as well as a deputy headteacher.Another issue at the core of pupils’ anger is Parcoursup, the system through which school leavers apply for higher education. Seen as discriminatory, it has left 126,000 applicants – many from disadvantaged backgrounds –without a placethis year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRather than deal with this crisis as justified social protest based on legitimate demands, the government has invoked a doctrine set out in its Operational Guide to Urban Violence. It hastreated school pupils as internal enemiesto be neutralised. This sets up a coercive response, disregarding the possibility of resolving the conflict through constructive measures.By 8 October,6,877 people had been taken into police custody, about 80% of them children. On 1 October alone, police made 1,949 arrests, exceeding the highest single-day total recorded since 1961,saysthe historian Éric Anceau.According tothe Syndicat de la magistrature, a French judges’ leftwing union, the numbers reflect a clear determination to crush the movement. So overwhelming has the police deployment been thatteachersandparentshave had to form human chains to protect children.The police operations are also driven by a focus on arrests, which encourages forceful confrontations and fuels the escalation. This in turn draws more people into rioting. About 700 police officers and a number of teachers have been injured since the start of the unrest.The sociologist Olivier Fillieulepoints outthat policing protests requires an assessment of risk. If the swift break-up a blockade exposes teenagers to serious injury, you have to consider alternatives. Temporarily accepting a degree of disorder when immediate intervention risks creating more of it should remain a guiding principle of policing protests, Filleule says, noting that the French authorities know how to apply restraint when farmers stage blockades.Yet while the police have opened internal investigations into 36 allegations of officer violence, the interior minister Laurent Nuñezsaidhe had given the forces “no instructions to exercise restraint”. This is a shameful and contemptuous way to respond to young people’s healthy expression of dissent. Such violence towards citizens has no place in a democracy.Rokhaya Diallo is a French journalist, film-maker, activist andGuardian EuropecolumnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsFranceOpinionProtestSchoolsEuropeStudent politicsYoung peopleChildrencommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisis | Elif Shafak | The Guardian
description: The Turkish writer talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novel
Author: Lisa Allardice
Headline: The Turkish writer talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novel
Content: Elif Shafak.Photograph: Alice Zoo/The GuardianView image in fullscreenElif Shafak.Photograph: Alice Zoo/The GuardianElif ShafakInterview‘Is there any value in writing a story in a time of chaos?’: novelist Elif Shafak on her creative crisisLisa AllardiceThe author talks about her nomadic childhood, being targeted by the Turkish government and overcoming depression to write her latest novelSat 17 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a long time Elif Shafak was referred to as Turkey’s “most widely read female author”. Today, she is surely simply its best loved. Orhan Pamuk may have won the Nobel prize in literature, but it is Shafak whose novels are fervently passed among readers.There Are Rivers in the Sky, which follows a single raindrop from ancient Nineveh to the River Tigris in 2018, was one of the UK’s bestselling literary novels last year.The Island of Missing Trees, a love story set in post-colonial Cyprus and contemporary London, was shortlisted for the Women’s prize in 2022, and10 Minutes 38 seconds in This Strange World, narrated by a murdered sex worker in Istanbul, was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2019. Last December she waselectedpresident of the Royal Society of Literature. It would be tempting to say she is on a roll, but Shafak’s reputation and readership have been steadily growing for more than 20 years and spanning as many books, of which 14 are novels.In a 2017Ted Talk, which has been viewed more than 6.4m times, she describes herself as an Istanbulite, “a European by birth and by choice” and a Londoner for many years. “I like to think of myself as a global soul, as a world citizen, a nomad and an itinerant storyteller.” Her novels sweep confidently across centuries and continents, taking in politics, history, feminism and ecology, typically with a dash of magic realism or mysticism.Her latest, In One Brief Moment All Eternity, is a stylistically inventive fictionalised life of Gustave Flaubert. “This book is really my love letter to literature,” Shafak says over coffee in west London, where the 54-year-old author has lived with her husband and two children for the past 18 years. While Flaubert is now considered the godfather of the modern novel – as Nabokov said, without Flaubert there would have been no Marcel Proust or James Joyce – most of his life was spent toiling in obscurity. It is this that interests Shafak. “The book is about a lonely boy who was misunderstood by almost everyone around him, including his own family members. He was regarded as a failure, as a disappointment, treated as ‘the other’.” The novel is dedicated to anyone who may have felt similarly treated. “I wanted to be able to say, ‘you’re my brother, you’re my sister’. That was the beginning,” she says.double quotation markMaybe I’m in self-imposed exile, but as a writer, I need freedom – the freedom of imagination, the freedom of speechShafak talks with the same fluency and lyrical intensity as she writes, in long, far-reaching sentences. In person, she also listens intently and smiles often, despite the seriousness of her words. We last met when she was part of thepanelto discuss theGuardian’s 100 best novels of all timelist earlier this year: Madame Bovary was in her top 10, but, like Flaubert himself, she is a huge fan of Don Quixote. On stage, she had the softest voice, but when she speaks, everyone listens. She has recently enjoyed renewed popularity with younger readers on BookTok. It is no wonder there are snaking queues of readers of all ages and nationalities for the signings after her literary events.In One Brief Moment All Eternity arose out of our own historical moment, which Shafak has dubbed “The age of three As: Angst, Anger and AI”. Yet it also started from “a very personal place”, she says, when she was struggling with depression and anxiety, or hüzün in Turkish, meaning a deep melancholy. “In the middle of a world shaped by wars and violence, division, climate crisis, technological uncertainties, you find yourself asking, ‘What is the meaning of shutting yourself in a small room and worrying about the perfect synonym?’” she says. “Is there any value in writing a short story, a poem, a novel in a time of crisis and chaos, such as the one we’re going through? I wanted to take a closer look at this question – creativity in a time of crisis.”This led her back to the 19th century, another era of change and confusion, in which “there lived a beloved novelist who dedicated his entire life to literature in a very passionate way”. While Flaubert set out to inhabit the female mind – then a radical proposition for a male novelist – Shafak upends the premise of Madame Bovary to tell his story through multiple women whose paths may have crossed with his. “I wanted to bring together the European canon of the novel with the Middle Eastern oral tradition of storytelling,” she explains. “You open a box and inside there’s another box, under this story, there’s another story. There’s a polyphony of voices.”And so Flaubert’s life is told not just through the eyes of his beloved nursemaid, Julie; his maman; his long-term mistress, Louise Colet; and his confidant George Sand, but also an acrobat he encounters as a boy, a camel called Jamilah and Emma Bovary herself. We meet an Egyptian dancer and courtesan, Kuchuck Hanem, with whom Flaubert becomes enraptured on his travels in the Middle East, passingly mentioned in biographies. “I wanted to remember this woman and say, ‘Maybe this is the woman who inspired Madame Bovary,’” Shafak says. “I want to claim that at the heart of this iconic French European literary heroine, there is an Egyptian belly dancer.” Opium, syphilis and Istanbul (Shafak always thinks of the city as “she”) are also given their own chapters.“Every time I start writing a book, I say to myself, ‘This time I’m going to keep it minimalist,’” she laughs. “I think because of who I am, my upbringing, all these cultural influences are like tributaries that flow into it. We are all interconnected, not only with each other as fellow human beings, but with nature. For me, the long narrative form is about honouring those connections.”View image in fullscreenPoster from the 1934 film adaptation of Madame Bovary.Photograph: Apic/Getty ImagesThey may be separated by nearly two centuries, by nationality and by gender, but once she started looking, the connections between Flaubert’s story and her own were striking, “starting with that lonely childhood, with that feeling of being the other,” she says.Although her parents were Turkish, Shafak was born in Strasbourg, France, in 1971, where her father was studying for a PhD. Her parents divorced five years later and the young Elif and her mother returned to live with her maternal grandmother in Ankara. Like Flaubert, Shafak grew up with two maternal figures. Although her grandmother was uneducated, she insisted her mother return to university, which she had left when she married. Shafak called her mother “big sister”, her grandmother “mother”: “From one I got my love for written culture, from the other I got my love for oral storytelling,” she says. She remembers her grandmother’s flat as a place full of magic, lefty students and Gauloises cigarette smoke.For all the love in her childhood, Shafak felt abandoned by her father, an academic who remarried. Like the celebrated Doctor Flaubert, Gustave’s father, he was “very detached, very aloof”. She didn’t see him for most of her childhood, and for a long time was very angry that he was such a good father to her half-brothers. “I felt like I was the forgotten child. There was a void. There was an absence of love,” she says. “And I think absences also shape us. Silences also shape us.”After she finally graduated, her mother became a teacher and then a diplomat. When Shafak was 10, they moved to Madrid, where she was the only Turkish pupil in the international school. As a teenager, she lived in Jordan and Germany. “Throughout all those years when I was really very lonely, books were my friends.” Shafak returned to Ankara to take a degree in international relations, followed by a PhD in political science. In her 20s, after teaching in Istanbul, she “escaped” to study in the US. Her first novel, Pinhan (The Sufi), was met with acclaim when it was published inTurkeyin 1997. But her decision to write her fifth novel, The Saint of Incipient Insanities, in English was considered a betrayal by many at home.The most significant parallel between Flaubert and Shafak is that they have both had their work put on trial: Madame Bovary for obscenity charges in 1857 and Shafak’sThe Bastard of Istanbulin 2006,for “the public denigration” of Turkishness, due to her having written about the Armenian genocide. Shafak had to live with a bodyguard for a year and a half. Her picture was burned and spat on. She was acquitted, but in 2019 her novel 10 Minutes 38 Seconds in This Strange World was investigated by Turkish authorities for“crimes of obscenity”along with two earlier books, The Gaze and Three Daughters of Eve, which dealt with material such as child brides and sexual harassment. Her husband, Eyüp Can, a Turkish journalist and former editor of the Turkish liberal newspaper, Radikal, was put on a wanted list as part of President Erdoğan’s crackdown on intellectuals after the failed coup in Turkey in 2016.View image in fullscreenShafak in London.Photograph: Alice Zoo/The GuardianShe has described being a writer in Turkey as “a bit like being kissed on one cheek and slapped on the other”, with the kiss from the readers and the slap from the government. She is keen to stress how much her books are loved back home. “In countries like Turkey, a book is not a personal item. If you like a novel, you can’t just put it back on the shelf. You give it to your auntie, the auntie gives it to her neighbour. It’s incredibly heartwarming.”But she again found herself at the centre of a storm back home after her 2017 Ted talk, titled “The revolutionary power of diverse thought”, in which she came out as bisexual. “I don’t know if it’s brave,” she says now. “I wish I could have done it before. But the abuse that I received from my own motherland for weeks uninterrupted was quite, quite bruising.”She hasn’t been back to Turkey for 11 years. “There’s a melancholy to it. Maybe I’m in self-imposed exile,” she says. “But as a writer, I need freedom. I need the freedom of imagination, the freedom of speech. I felt like I first migrated into the English language and then into the UK. London became home. And I now feel rooted here, and I say this as someone who has led a very nomadic life.”Her daughter and son, who have just left home for the new university term, have grown up speaking English. Her elderly mother often stays with them for long periods. “I hope I’m not offending, but I think only a few male authors above a certain age have precise writing schedules,” she says wryly. “Everyone else just juggles multiple roles.” She often writes at night, whilelistening to heavy metal, melodic death metal in particular, on her headphones. She plays the same song on a loop, often 80 or 90 times. She is a fan of the Armenian-American band System of a Down, who have also been very vocal about the Armenian genocide. “I love it. It gives me such energy,” she says. And somehow this makes her fiction “calmer”.double quotation markYou sit at your desk and there’s a lot of self-doubt, but that, too, is part of the creative processBut it doesn’t make her calm. Writing doesn’t come any easier as you get older, she says. “It doesn’t matter whether it’s your first book, fifth book, tenth book, you suffer. You sit at your desk and there’s a lot of self-doubt. There’s a lot of anxiety, panic attacks. That, too, is part of the creative process.” When she is finished, she is not filled with satisfaction or pride, but grief. “I feel a sense of loss,” she says. “I find it so difficult to let go of the characters.”Then she goes back out into the world. She thinks it is really important for women to have a voice in public life, and surprises herself by how much she loves literary festivals. “I really am an introvert by nature, so my natural habitat is just a small room full of books,” she says. “But when I’m on stage doing a literary event, it is not a chore. It’s not a burden. It is an immense treat for the mind or the soul.” As someone for whom speaking out has led to threats of imprisonment, she is frustrated by the cynicism towards intellectualism in the UK and the US.“It’s regarded as a sign of arrogance, hubris,” she says. “I’m not claiming to be an intellectual. What I am claiming is I have a lot of respect for the intellect.”For Shafak, literature is “one of our last remaining democratic spaces where we’re not rushing from one thing to the next, we’re not just being fed snippets of information, but we slow down and we listen to each other again,” she says. “The ancient art of storytelling is so universal. It’s so timeless. It really doesn’t belong to a single ethnicity, region or religion. It belongs to all humanity. When I’m writing and in my books, I try to remember that kind of … ” For a moment she is lost for words. “I don’t know what to call it other than shared humanity.”In One Brief Moment All Eternity by Elif Shafak is published by Viking.
