title: The Digger disaster: what an epic movie flop means for Tom Cruise and Hollywood | Digger | The Guardian
description: Unprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris is predicted to lose $245m. How did this happen?
Author: Catherine Shoard
Headline: Unprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris is predicted to lose $245m. How did this happen?
Content: The world premiere turned out to be the high point of Digger’s theatrical runComposite: Alex Mellon/Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe world premiere turned out to be the high point of Digger’s theatrical runComposite: Alex Mellon/Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesThe Saturday readDiggerThe Digger disaster: what an epic movie flop means for Tom Cruise and HollywoodUnprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris is predicted to lose $245m. How did this happen?Catherine ShoardSat 17 Oct 2026 04.12 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 10.30 EDTShareThe fanfare at Digger’s world premiere in London four weeks ago was literal. As the Prince and Princess of Wales took to the stage, their arrival was heralded by the band of the Irish guards’ fanfare team – bugles gleaming, epaulets shining, bearskin bonnets rippling under the lights.Given the occasion, the band were not overdressed. Joining William (velvet tux) and Kate (chiffon gown, the late Diana’s earrings) to introduce the film was cinema’s longest-reigning monarch, Tom Cruise (Armani), along with a retinue including directorAlejandro González Iñárrituand co-stars Sandra Hüller, Riz Ahmed, John Goodman, Jesse Plemons and Michael Stuhlbarg. Loyal courtiers filled the front rows: Salma Hayek, Hannah Waddingham and no fewer than three Beckhams (David, Cruz and Romeo).The film itself started two hours late, thanks to Cruise’s trademark completism with red carpet selfies and autographs. But no one minded, much. If anyone has earned the right to keep 800 people waiting as the babysitter fees mount and they lose all feeling in their legs, it is surely the one remaining unassailable movie star, that most grinning and irresistible enigma, the man who “saved Hollywood’s ass” when Top Gun: Maverick tempted people back to multiplexes after two years of Covid.View image in fullscreenPrince William, Catherine, Princess of Wales and Tom Cruise attend the Digger world premiere in London.Photograph: Chris Jackson/Getty Images for Warner BrosAt 11pm, when the lights came up, the mood was different. There was disquiet. Applause, too, of course, but also murmurings and scurries for the exit, only slightly hobbled by pins and needles. Could it be that this hottest of tickets was actually a stone cold turkey?The world premiere turned out to be the high point of Digger’s theatrical run. When the film opened worldwide a week later, reeling from almost universally horrified reviews, the box office was appalling – and things went downhill from there. Digger made $8m over its first weekend in the US, before dropping 60% for its second. Its international opening was yet worse: $12m across 74 territories, for a per country average of $162k. So far, Digger has made $37.7m. Estimates suggest a final haul of $50m.Its costs were … higher. Originally budgeted at $125m, production on the six-month shoot spiralled to about $175m. A further $100m was spent on marketing. Given that cinemas retain around half of the revenue of ticket sales, the film would appear to need to make $350m to break even (thoughWarner Brosputs the number at closer to $300m). These numbers are complicated further by Cruise’s “first-dollar” deal, which means initial takings are diverted straight to him, rather than the studio.Digger’s predicted $245m loss catapults it straight into the upper echelons of the most costly flops of all time, alongside 1995 swashbuckler Cutthroat Island ($222m loss, adjusted for inflation), 2018 steampunk dud Mortal Engines ($224m adjusted) and doomed Captain America spin-off The Marvels (whose estimated adjusted losses range between $205m and $250m). In some sense, Digger has already performed worse than all three. Pre-release, no one had high hopes for any of them – yet they still managed to make at least double the amount Digger is expected to take in. No one anticipated Cutthroat Island upending our ideas about what big swing satire could be. Or that Hugo Weaving’s turn in Mortal Engines would make him an Oscars shoo-in. But Digger is unique: an unprecedented folly of misjudgment, bad timing and spectacular hubris.View image in fullscreenDigger’s predicted loss catapults it into the upper echelons of the most costly flops of all time.Photograph: Courtesy of Warner Bros PicturesTo excavate Digger’s fatal flaw, it is helpful to return to its roots. The idea for its central character – a boorish billionaire oil magnate, whose drilling in the arctic triggers eco-catastrophe – came to Iñárritu, the Mexican film-maker who broke through with Amores Perros, in 2015. Then, he was working on The Revenant – another expensive ($165m) epic centred on a big gamey performance, in that case from Leonardo DiCaprio, who, playing a frontiersman on the run, waded through a frozen river, ate raw bison liver, climbed inside a horse’s carcass – and duly won an Oscar. At the same ceremony, Iñárritu also won best director, making him the third person ever to do so in consecutive years, having triumphed in 2014 with the splashy theatrics of Birdman.Iñárritu has said he didn’t initially pursue Digger because, despite developing an obsession with the character, he “wasn’t looking for a story” (ominous words, in hindsight). But after The Revenant’s success, he began to develop the concept with Netflix as a vehicle for DiCaprio, under the working title Blah, Blah, Blah (ominous klaxon #2). Then someone at the streamer noticed they already had a pricey eco-dramedy with Leonardo DiCaprio in the works in the form of Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up – the failure of which completes a quick ominous hat-trick – and Digger was ditched. So Iñárritu busied himself instead with Bardo, False Chronicle of a Handful of Truths: an almost three-hour, black-and-white, existential semi-autographical vanity project of the type only the most recently gilded of directors would have the indulgence to realise. Few people saw it, fewer still liked it.Meanwhile, Cruise, glowing from his recent canonisation as the saviour of cinema, was on the hunt for films to broaden his portfolio beyond action franchises such as Top Gun and Mission: Impossible. Perhaps recalling the delighted horror that met his fat-suited cameo in Tropic Thunder as repellant studio head Les Grossman, he reached out to Iñárritu, and they began work in 2022. The shoot began in late 2024, on 35mm, filmed in Vista Vision – which is, for the avoidance of doubt, magnificently expensive.This time last year, the film was in post-production, and Cruise was in Los Angeles receiving an honorary Oscar – his first ever Academy Award. His emotional speech detailed a lifetime devoted to the craft. “Making films is not what I do, it is who I am,” he told the crowd. The man to give him the statuette? Iñárritu. The auguries were obvious: if ever a movie were to win Cruise his first Oscar proper, this would be the man who would hand it to him.View image in fullscreenAlejandro González Iñárritu is only the third person ever to win the Oscar for best director in consecutive years.Photograph: Rodrigo Reyes Marin/AFLO/ShutterstockDid anyone notice during production that Digger was awful? Or that sufficient numbers of people were likely to loathe it that the film would be a fiasco? If so, they were either cowed or buoyed by the confidence of the two men at its helm. Plus, says Steven Gaydos, former executive editor of Variety, for the past decade or so, this kind of reckless endeavour has been standard industry practice: “Digger is just the latest Hollywood supertanker art film to go down.”He tracks the origins of that trend to the pre-pandemic eagerness of streamers to write blank cheques for directors who might confer credibility on them. Auteurs were quick to sign up, but the lack of oversight or guardrails – exactly the terms that sweetened the deal – meant their movies often pleased only themselves.Sometimes the strategy (sincebinnedat Netflix) sort of worked. Neither Alfonso Cuarón’s Roma nor Noah Baumbach’s Marriage Story, Jane Campion’s The Power of the Dog or David Fincher’s Mank secured Netflix that coveted best picture Oscar, but they came pretty close. Often, it was more obviously unsuccessful. Gaydos highlights the $175m Netflix sunk into Martin Scorsese’s The Irishman in 2019, and then the $200m Apple handed him in 2022 for Killers of the Flower Moon. “Again,” says Gaydos, “beaucoup Oscar nominations, no wins”.View image in fullscreenBabylon was a critical flop that ‘missed recoupment by $135m’.Photograph: Scott Garfield/APMeanwhile traditional studios, spooked by streamers’ dominance, copied the playbook – including the fallout. After awards glory with Whiplash and La La Land, Damien Chazelle saddled Paramount with Babylon, a critical flop, which, says Gaydos, “missed recoupment by $135m”. After sweeping the Oscars with Parasite, Bong Joon-ho’s Mickey 17 repeated the trick at Warner Bros, sinking $200m.That studio’s form with the Hollywood supertanker art film isn’t all bad: last year they lost $150m on another VistaVision whopper, but at least Paul Thomas Anderson’s One Battle After Another won them lots of Oscars, including best picture. And at that stage Warners could sustain the hit, with the coffers swamped from the likes of Sinners, The Minecraft Movie and F1.This time round, there was no blockbuster safety net – hence, says Gaydos, “this supertanker might have sunk the studio’s chiefs Michael de Luca and Pam Abdy.” The final release from the studio before its Paramount Skydance takeover was such an unqualified calamity that the first move of incoming owner David Ellison was to axe them both.Pre-merger, many had voiced concerns about the sorts of projects that might be greenlit by the new super-studio. Now they know: Ellison’s appetite for new ideas and original IP will have been diminished yet further. “Overspending on art has never been a winning strategy in Hollywood,” says Gaydos. “But no one’s ever seen the scale of these recent maydays and the oceans of red ink the supertanker art films have left in their wake.”View image in fullscreenTom Cruise, left, and Riz Ahmed in a scene from Digger.Photograph: Warner Bros Pictures/APOf all the injured parties emerging from the wreckage of Digger – save perhaps for De Luca and Abdy – Cruise is the most mortally wounded. He’s had misfires before: 2017’s The Mummy lost $95m, but still grossed over $400m. The only conclusions to be drawn will be chastening for a man who would have assumed he was appreciated as much as an artist as a preternaturally-youthful pensioner with a fierce commitment to near fatal stunts and taking his top off.Yet clearly, it seems, people do not go to aTom Cruisemovie to see him act. They go to see a movie star. Yes, he sported prosthetics in Tropic Thunder, but you could still see the man beneath the mask, and he wasn’t in it for long anyway. In Digger, so thick are the layers of rubber it might as well be anyone beneath them.Aside from riding a motorbike off a cliff, Cruise’s fans do not want him to take risks, nor to indulge in the level of belligerent insanity both he and his character display here, which serves as an uncomfortable reminder of the Oprah sofa-jumping years. They also want him to be the good guy. In Top Gun and, especially, Mission: Impossible, he’s a quasi-Messiah: the only man able save the world. In Digger, he plays the only man able to destroy it. That’s the opposite of what Cruise’s fanbase wants.Yet beyond Cruise’s usual acolytes, there are plenty of people who might well have been keen to see Digger if they’d known what it really was: an ambitious, meta-textual liberal satire that seeks to address collective culpability for ecological collapse. Unfortunately all of the promotion for the film has sought to suppress this – in part because explaining how necessitates revealing a key plot spoiler.Instead, the push focused on its star’s transformation, on teases and reveals of Digger’s colossal tum and obnoxious hectoring. So confident were the makers of Digger in their film’s pre-sold allure they forgot to actually sell it.By the time the reviews were out, the marketing had no choice but to scramble. A new campaign was launched quoting negative and positive reviews, before urging audiences to ignore the critics and judge for themselves. Retrospectively positioning a movie’s divisiveness as intentional isn’t necessarily a bad plan. But the strategy inevitably recalled that taken by Francis Ford Coppola’s $125m disaster Megalopolis in 2024 – which further self-sabotaged by attributing made-up quotes to real-life critics. This was an unhappy association, and within days Digger’s ads had pivoted again, suddenly telling punters they should take note of the critics after all, because although US reviewers were iffy, the French really liked it.View image in fullscreenTom Cruise attends the premiere of Mission: Impossible - The Final Reckoning, May 15, 2025.Photograph: Kate Green/Getty Images for Paramount PicturesBy then, the muddle didn’t matter. Only the morbidly curious could be tempted to the cinema. Word of mouth did its own work, too: Digger’s CinemaScore (which records exiting audience reaction on US opening night) was C+. That’s considerably less than the new Paw Patrol movie (A) and worse even than new Mark Zuckerberg drama The Social Reckoning (B+), whose own duff box office further suggests people aren’t automatically eager to spend their weekends gazing at supersized billionaires doing dreadful things.Tom Cruise’s Digger has flopped spectacularly – but I think it is a misunderstood masterpieceRead moreCruise may still discreetly campaign for an Oscar nomination – the cost of doing so would be small change compared with the losses already incurred. In a year of standout performances from the likes of Andrew Scott (Elsinore) and John Malkovich (Wild Horse Nine), victory is all but impossible, yet Cruise and co may yet calculate that some such acknowledgment from his peers might help lessen the blow – and vindicate everyone’s decision-making.And, in fact, there are early signs that the scale of Digger’s disaster may work in its favour. After all, this is no Bardo-ish damp squib, destined to be a footnote in a book no one ever reads. This is a movie whose title is already synonymous with gobsmacking folly. An apparently grassroots lobby is building a compelling case for Digger being a cult classic in the making. Celebrities have put their heads above the parapet to champion it – and not only partisan ones such as Anne Hathaway, set to star with Cruise in the upcoming Days of Thunder sequel, who gave it 10/10 on Letterboxd, or Glen Powell – whom Cruise mentored on Top Gun: Maverick – and who called it “pure cinematic joy”.Jane Fonda cheerled at length for the film on Instagram, calling Cruise “very good and very brave”. “Daring, bold and cinematically complex,” chipped in Guillermo del Toro. Neil Young named it “the best film I have ever seen”. Meanwhile, commemorative programmes from that world premiere – still less than a month ago – are already fetching considerable sums on eBay, onelistingproudly describing the “highly sought-after collectable” as “brand new and unread”. Digger, it seems, is unlikely to stay buried for ever.This article was amended on 17 October to correct the average per country first weekend take of Digger outside the US to $162k.

title: ‘Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works’: film-maker Charles Burnett on his chronicling of Black working-class life | Black US culture | The Guardian
description: A restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audience
Author: Adria R Walker
Headline: A restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audience
Content: Actors Dennis Kemper and Everette Silas on set of Charles Burnett’s My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveView image in fullscreenActors Dennis Kemper and Everette Silas on set of Charles Burnett’s My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveBlack US culture‘Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works’: film-maker Charles Burnett on his chronicling of Black working-class lifeA restored version of his 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding, set in South Central LA, brings Burnett’s vision to a new audienceAdria R WalkerSat 17 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTShareCharles Burnett had a dilemma. He had agreed to attend the wedding of a co-worker, but the wedding was scheduled for the same day and time as a funeral for a childhood friend.Initially, the film-maker – a landmark chronicler of Black working-class lives – decided he’d go to the funeral. But when he tried to break the news to the co-worker, she was so dejected that he couldn’t go through with it. He tried asking the bride to change the wedding – which was “ridiculous to think of trying to do”, he says decades later – but that didn’t work either. He decided he’d go to both events.But when the day came, he got trapped at the wedding. He “suffered through that” and, in the process, missed the funeral.This dilemma is at the heart of My Brother’s Wedding, Burnett’s tragicomic 1983 film. Like Burnett, character Pierce Mundy has committed to going to a wedding when a childhood friend suddenly dies. Like Burnett, Pierce feels an obligation to be at both places, though the wedding and funeral were scheduled for the same time. Like Burnett, Pierce even, unsuccessfully, tries to change the wedding.The Disciple: A Wu-Tang Fable review – Netflix doc on ‘secret album’ is strictly for super fansRead more“The idea was the fact that if you want to be someone’s brother’s keeper, you have to have principles and you have to be mature enough to make decisions and say, yes or no,” Burnett says. “You may have good thoughts and be a decent person, but you have to have more than that. If you’re going to be responsible for someone, you have to have a certain amount of maturity. It means making just decisions, proper decisions in your life.”View image in fullscreenEverette Silas (as Pierce Mundy) and Jessie Holmes (his mother, Mrs Mundy) in Charles Burnett’s 1983 film My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: A film by Charles Burnett/Milestone FilmsMy Brother’s Wedding was beset with production problems that limited the film’s release. The main actor disappeared from set after demanding more pay (when Burnett tracked the actor down, he had reinvented himself as a pastor).In post-production, a German broadcaster asked Burnett for a finished cut of the film. He rushed through a rough cut, which the production company accepted as the final cut against his wishes. That longer, unfinished version of the film was shown to mixed reviews at the New Directors/NewFilms festival in New York City in 1983, and was essentially impossible to view for many years.“It would have been better just to say, start all over again,” Burnett said. “The days were gone by that time. Rather than re-edit the film, I had to make terms with the material I had. That’s what film-making is about. You run into all these problems, and in each one, you have a whole set of different problems. Sometimes it’s not perfect, but it works, it works.”At 82, Burnett, once called “the nation’s least-known great film-maker” by the New York Times, is enjoying a resurgence of interest in and celebration of his career. In 2025, his 1978 debut filmKiller of Sheep, considered a masterpiece, was restored, introducing the director and his oeuvre to newer audiences. And this year, after several decades, My Brother’s Wedding, the director’s sophomore film, was digitally restored and remastered by Milestone Films, the largest Black-owned film distributor in the US, UCLA Film & Television Archive, the Berkeley Art Museum & Pacific Film Archive, and Kino Lorber.Burnett supervised the restoration of My Brother’s Keeper in consultation with Maya S Cade, president of Milestone Films, and Jillian Borders, head of preservation at the UCLA Film & Television Archive. The restored film has enjoyed sold-out screenings at New York’s Film Forum, is being shown at theatres across the country and is available to stream on the Criterion Channel. The film is also slated to be screened across the United Kingdom and Europe later this year.View image in fullscreenOn the set of My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveCade said that the restorations of both films “feel like resurrections”. Both Burnett’s debut and sophomore films are, decades after their initial release, able to be presented as originally intended. “We’re trying to use the tools available to ensure that Charles’s vision lasts not only our lifetimes, but many other lifetimes to come,” Cade said. “The goal of restoration is to use every tool in our arsenal to make the song that you may be familiar with, if you will, sing anew.”Groundbreaking director Reginald Hudlin: ‘It’s taken a lot of effort but the reward is always worth it’Read moreCade, who also runsBlack Film Archive, an online database of Black films made between 1898 and 1999, has been Burnett’s archivist for more than one and a half years. Recently, while sorting through his materials, she uncovered never-before-seen images made on the set of My Brother’s Keeper. The images, printed here, are raw and intimate. They’re testaments, Cade said, to the number of people required to make a film and “its own kind of archival repair”.They are also ways for the non-professional actors and everyday people who participated in the making of the film to be honored. For Burnett, the restorations and the images allow him to reminisce about his experiences with old friends, many of whom are now dead. It’s both a painful and joyous experience for the auteur. “It’s nice to see them again,” he said. “I do appreciate what they’ve done because most of the independent films I made were done with non-actors, and I’m always so guilty about not having the money to pay them. But I’m glad [about] the restoration because I’m sure they see it and they can see it again in a positive way. It looks good and it’s their story.”View image in fullscreenOn set of My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveBurnett wrote, directed and produced My Brother’s Wedding on location in south central Los Angeles, where he grew up. His realism frankly depicts Black life in LA, using non-professional actors who, like the director, are firmly rooted in a time and place. In his original treatment for the film, Burnett wrote that “the story communicates to all persons.”Making the film allowed Burnett to explore his feelings about class differences that he saw and experienced while growing up in Watts, a neighborhood in south LA. In the film, Pierce’s brother, Wendell, is engaged to Sonia, an upper-middle-class woman whose “sweetness”, Pierce thinks, is “about as fake as a $3 bill”.In one scene, Wendell and Sonia’s families share dinner together. Sonia’s family’s wealth is on display – “signifying”, Pierce calls it, elsewhere in the film – from their fine wine to a maid who serves the family dinner. Pierce, who “has a romantic view of the ‘have-nots’”, is over it.He lists various jobs he’s held, from driving a cement truck, working as a brakeman at the railroad and driving explosives and “all sorts of dangerous materials”. Pierce’s mother says that she wishes her sons were a doctor and lawyer, like Sonia’s parents’ children, instead. The scene culminates in a fiery exchange between Pierce, Wendell and Sonia.“When we were growing up in LA, there was this class difference. We had this romantic notion about the poor and the middle class,” Burnett says. He said that class limited the opportunities available to lower-income people in his community.Burnett, who was born in Vicksburg, Mississippi, said there was a “porch life”, when he was growing up, where people talked and told stories about their lives in the south. Like him, most of his neighbors were southerners – from Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas and Arkansas – who moved to California.“My grandmother and mother and them would always be talking about their experiences in Mississippi,” he said. “They were from Natchez and Vicksburg … It was this vision of the south. It was so mystical, in a way, because of the way they told it and their relationships with people … It was like this story of this place that had this magical quality about it.”In his films, Burnett maintains this culture of storytelling, and an intrinsic understanding of the importance of the mundane, translating it to the screen. The characters in My Brother’s Wedding are just people. They have wants and desires; they are not caricatures of good or evil, even if they are in conflict with each other. The film’s humor is found in the simple moments, much like it is in real life.View image in fullscreenOn the set of My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: Charles Burnett ArchiveMuch of the film follows Pierce as he lives his life. Burnett’s decision to focus on a narrative about a young Black man and his experiences in south central LA was revolutionary. Pierce isn’t a larger-than-life character from a Blaxploitation film, nor is he a caricature. He is just a young man with a difficult decision.Burnett was a central figure in the LA Rebellion film movement, in which several Black film-makers, including Julie Dash, Haile Gerima and others, rejected Hollywood norms and instead prioritized realism and a focus on Black life. “The whole idea was telling stories about Black experience,” Burnett said. The directors were pushing back against racist films that shaped American cinema, like DW Griffith’s 1915 filmThe Birth of a Nation, which led to a resurgence of the Ku Klux Klan and anti-Black violence. “[In the] LA Rebellion, we’re responding to the negative images of Hollywood, particularly Birth of a Nation and things like that, that really destroy who we are … We were fighting against those negative images and Blackface and things like that.”It’s worth considering how Burnett’s career might have developed differently had his sophomore film received the distribution it deserved. His first film inspired generations of artists, such as Ava DuVernay, Sean Baker, Yasiin Bey and Barry Jenkins. Though his career was not allowed to flourish as it should have, in many ways, Burnett is responsible for generations of film-makers, though he speaks about himself and his career with a humbleness that doesn’t hint at the weight of his impact. Arthur Jafa and Dash, both of whom would go on to shape cinema in their own right, first met while working as assistants on My Brother’s Wedding. Jafa was first assistant camera, on his first-ever film set, while Dash was first assistant director. Years ago, while he was casting for a professional acting crew, Burnett said that he ran into many older Black actors. When they walked into the room, he asked, “Where have you been?”View image in fullscreenEverette Silas (as Pierce Mundy) and Dennis Kemper (as Mr Mundy) in My Brother’s Wedding.Photograph: A film by Charles Burnett/Milestone Films“It’s a dumb question to ask, because you know where they’ve been,” he said. “Not given an opportunity to express themselves [even though they] are so talented. That was one of the most difficult experiences, realizing this wasted talent.”But, in some cases, their stories are preserved in the archives. They’re in photos, like the ones from the set of My Brother’s Wedding, or in other documents Cade has found in Burnett’s archive.Burnett was always focused on telling stories, on being a director – he eschewed any notion that he himself was or should be a brand. And yet, he subconsciously created an archive, allowing himself and others to step back in time and appreciate the largely under-sung work he and other Black artists did for American cinema.

title: ‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacy
Author: David Smith
Headline: The entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacy
Content: Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24View image in fullscreenNathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Courtesy of A24Documentary films‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesThe entrepreneur turned fraudster is the subject of an Oscar-tipped new documentary that takes an unusual look at her strange legacyDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 17 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 05.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDavid Agus’s first encounter withElizabeth Holmesat a health conference came as a shock. The Holmes he met in the green room was personable and pleasant. The Holmes he interviewed on stage was altogether different.“The accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,”Agus, a medical oncologist, recalls by phone from Los Angeles. “It was as if I had met a person and then interviewed a separate person. That transition from the green room to the stage – I had never experienced something like that before.”You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreHolmes is not like you or me. She was still a teenager when she founded Theranos, touting technology capable of performing medical tests using only a few drops of blood. She cultivated a distinctive persona: blond hair, an unblinking gaze, a husky voice and a black turtleneck worn in homage to Apple co-founderSteve Jobs.Holmes mesmerised investors and board members including Rupert Murdoch, Larry Ellison, Carlos Slim and former secretaries of stateHenry Kissingerand George Shultz. She became America’s youngest self-made female billionaire. But it was all an illusion, a confidence trick built on a scam. Holmes’s shining career ended in disgrace and imprisonment.Margaret O’Mara, a history professor at the University of Washington in Seattle and author of The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America, says: “You can’t make this stuff up. If some screenwriter had tried to manufacture this out of whole cloth people would be like, no, this is an unbelievable story. Yet it’s real. Who’s the real Elizabeth Holmes? That’s a question that still hasn’t been answered.”Perhaps the answer lies inYou Can See Everything, a reality-bending documentary, released in the US on Friday, in which Holmes goes eyeball-to-eyeball with the absurdist comedian Nathan Fielder, who directs along with Lance Oppenheim. It was filmed in the 34 days before she was due to report to federal prison camp Bryan in Texas to begin her 11-year sentence for wire fraud and conspiracy.That fate seemed unthinkable in 2003 when, at the age of 19, Holmes dropped out of Stanford University and establishedTheranos, promising to revolutionise the multibillion-dollar blood-testing industry by using microfluidics to run hundreds of tests on just a few drops of blood.She found a receptive audience among investors who wantedSilicon Valleyto deliver more than Facebook friends. O’Mara explains:“She stands out in her ascent as a female entrepreneur at a time when men were dominating the scene and she was doing something that was in tech but seemed to be change-the-world-tech.“The techlash wasn’t brewing yet but, where there was criticism of Silicon Valley, it was like: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people and all you’re doing is building apps? Why don’t you do something a little more meaningful?’ And: ‘Hey, you’ve got all these brilliant people, but they all seem to be men.’”O’Mara adds: “She was going against gendered expectations but also, to become the female Steve Jobs, she made herself less feminine and also made herself less young.”Holmes ran the company with Ramesh “Sunny” Balwani, a businessman 19 years her senior, while keeping their romantic relationship a secret. Together they raised $945m.Theranoshad published no peer-reviewed data but Holmes was a charismatic and persuasive presence in boardrooms.Agus, a professor of medicine who is chief executive of theEllison Medical Institute, comments: “You know how you go into a room and there could be 10 people at a table and everyone’s having a discussion? All of a sudden one person speaks and the entire room goes: ‘Yeah, I’ll go that direction.’ She had that ability.“I saw how she was able to sway people. That characteristic is great if you’re a Steve Jobs. That characteristic is very difficult in health because we should be data-driven, not swayed by personalities.”By 2014 Theranos was valued at $9bn. Holmes was named the youngest female self-made billionaire in the US with a net worth of $4.5bn by the time she was 30. She was celebrated on magazine covers and in power lists.The New Yorker wrote: “Although she can quote Jane Austen by heart, she no longer devotes time to novels or friends, doesn’t date, doesn’t own a television, and hasn’t taken a vacation in ten years. Her refrigerator is all but empty, as she eats most of her meals at the office. She is a vegan, and several times a day she drinks a pulverized concoction of cucumber, parsley, kale, spinach, romaine lettuce, and celery.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes in 2015.Photograph: Brendan McDermid/ReutersThe heady atmosphere seduced elder statesmen such as Shultz, who had served as a bridge between Washington and Silicon Valley during theRonald Reaganera. Despite no specialist expertise in laboratory diagnostics, he joined the Theranos board in 2011, when he was in his 90s. O’Mara says: “He was drawn in by the idea that here is a bright young person trying to do something more meaningful than building an app. But there wasn’t enough due diligence.”In his biography,In the Nation’s Service, journalist Philip Taubman describes how people around Shultz worried that his enthusiasm had become entangled with personal affection for Holmes. Shultz spoke to her by phone almost daily and invited her to family Christmas dinners. Holmes encouraged his attention, leaning in close when they sat together.Shultz even encouraged his grandson,Tyler Shultz, to take a summer internship at Theranos before joining the company full-time. Tyler eventually became convinced that Holmes was exaggerating what her technology could do. He took his concerns to the Wall Street Journal, whose investigation into the company was crucial to unravelling its web of deceit.Holmes suspected Tyler was behind the disclosures. Her lawyers pursued him and he was placed under surveillance, leaving him afraid and looking to his grandfather for protection. But George Shultz declined to break with Holmes. According to Taubman, he tried unsuccessfully to mediate between the two rather than stand by his grandson. George Shultz died in 2021 at the age of 100.Scientists also had their doubts about Holmes’s grand promises. Agus recalls: “The problem with blood is it clots and, when you do these small fluidics, it clogs. She wouldn’t give me an answer of why that wasn’t a problem for her. To me, that was the initial red flag. The emperor with no clothes was evident in that she was either ultra-secretive, or the way she was trying to explain things didn’t make sense.”John Ioannidis, a professor of medicine and health research at Stanford University, happened to work in a building that had previously served as Theranos’s headquarters. In 2015, he published a Journal of the American Medical Association (Jama) commentary highlighting the striking absence of peer-reviewed evidence supporting Theranos’s claims.He says: “They wanted me to recant and meet withElizabeth Holmes, and maybe write together some new Jama piece saying that I had seen the light.” When Ioannidis urged them to publish validation data, Theranos cited 100-plus patent filings. “I looked at these patents and they were mostly nonsensical. One had a title close to ‘How to do clinical research’ – vague and non-specific. None of that covered the gap of what was being done.”View image in fullscreenElizabeth Holmes at federal prison camp Bryan in 2025.Photograph: Adrees Latif/ReutersBut in assessing Holmes’s motivations, Ioannidis offers a nuanced view. “I don’t think anyone can be in her mind. My most likely interpretation is that she believed she would start that wave – attract capital, funds, talent, expertise – and make this real.“I don’t think she was purely a charlatan. She was power-driven, but in Silicon Valley so many people are power-driven. She saw that the way to do this was to get power first, and then attract the people and technology to materialise it.”‘Stranger than stranger-than-fiction’: how Lance Oppenheim made the year’s two buzziest filmsRead moreHolmes quit as chief executive in 2018 and the company collapsed that year. The trial of Holmes resulted in her 2022 sentencing to more than 11 years in prison for fraud and conspiracy. The scandal was chronicled in a book, multiple podcasts and the biographical mini-seriesThe Dropoutthat starred Amanda Seyfried.You Can See Everything offers an intimate, often bewildering glimpse into Holmes’s domestic life with her partner,Billy Evans, and their two young children during the 34 days before she reported to prison in May 2023.Lavalier’s microphones capture Holmes’s every breath as she reads bedtime stories to the children, sometimes for 12 hours a day. Evans, meanwhile, is filmed naked in the shower and whisking eggs as he corrects her cooking. They fixate on past media profiles, arguing that journalists fabricated her persona.The biggest revelation occurs off-camera. Even as she prepared to enter prison, Holmes and Evans were actively planning a new medical tech startup. In 2025, two years into her sentence, Evans sought $18.5m for Haemanthus – a company allegedly holding patents for a device claiming to scan blood, urine and saliva samples using lasers.Fool me once, shame on you; fool me twice, shame on me? As Silicon Valleypours unprecedented sumsinto artificial intelligence, O’Mara believes the lessons of Theranos extend well beyond Holmes herself.“The cautionary tale is resonant to a broader Silicon Valley morality tale in putting so much faith and power in the hands of one young person or a small circle of people.“The founder culture and obsession of Silicon Valley that helped Elizabeth Holmes become who she was is still alive and well and stronger than ever. We’ve never seen power and wealth more concentrated in so few hands. Not even inAmerica’s Gilded Agehave we seen this.”You Can See Everything is out in the US now, in Australia on 12 November and in the UK on 20 NovemberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsElizabeth HolmesNathan FielderTheranosBiotechnology industryScamsSilicon ValleyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I know I can do anything’: new archive of AS Byatt’s papers looks inside the writer’s extraordinary mind | AS Byatt | The Guardian
description: The Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fiction
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fiction
Content: ‘Her prominence cannot be overstated’ … AS Byatt at Newnham College, Cambridge, her alma mater, during a visit.Photograph: Ian Cook/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Her prominence cannot be overstated’ … AS Byatt at Newnham College, Cambridge, her alma mater, during a visit.Photograph: Ian Cook/Getty ImagesAS Byatt‘I know I can do anything’: new archive of AS Byatt’s papers looks inside the writer’s extraordinary mindThe Booker-wining author of Possession was known for her voracious research. Now, 68 boxes of her notebooks, letters and diaries acquired by the British Library reveal how she assembled the raw material of her fictionEmma LoffhagenSat 17 Oct 2026 03.24 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 03.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 20, Antonia Susan Byatt was not yet sure she could write. “Do I take myself seriously as a writer?” she asked herself in her diary in September 1956. “No, I think not.”The young Byatt – who would go on to become one of Britain’s most celebrated writers, best known for her 1990 novel Possession: A Romance – was troubled by the possibility that her mind might not be equal to her ambitions. Yet her determination was already evident. On her 20th birthday, she wrote: “Today, I know I can do anything. But not yet.”These intimate reflections can be found among the material in a major new archive of Byatt’s work, acquired by the British Library. It offers an insight into the development of the Booker prize-winning writer, whodied aged 87in 2023, and whose intricate, intellectually ambitious fiction earned her international acclaim.View image in fullscreen‘The other side of the tapestry’ … a draft of Possession.Photograph: Copyright Antonia Susan Duffy Literary Trust/courtesy of the British LibraryThe collection comprises 68 boxes of working notebooks, manuscripts, correspondence, personal diaries and documents from Byatt’s early life. It includes handwritten drafts of Possession, which won the 1990 Booker prize, and material relating to her 1978 novel The Virgin in the Garden and The Children’s Book, which was shortlisted for the Booker prize in 2009. According to the British Library’s curators, it is one of the most significant contemporary literary acquisitions the library has made in recent years.“It’s the other side of the tapestry,” says Jenny Uglow, Byatt’s editor, who worked closely with her on Possession. “In her books, you have these extremely elaborate plots, very complicated characters with their extraordinary names. And then when you actually look behind it, there are hundreds, thousands of little threads.”Born in Sheffield in 1936, Byatt studied English at Cambridge before continuing her education at Bryn Mawr College, Philadelphia, and at Oxford. She spent more than two decades teaching in universities and art schools, before leaving academia in 1983 to write full-time. She was known for her voracious research and her ability to weave apparently disparate fields of knowledge into her fiction. The archive allows researchers to follow Byatt as she assembles the raw material of her fiction, tests ideas and repeatedly questions whether they will work.The documents “reveal the way her mind works”, Uglow says. “She thought extremely fast and she had one of those racing minds, almost like a three o’clock in the morning mind, everything whirling around. She’ll say things like: ‘This is fascinating, but it doesn’t fit. I can’t go on, this is not working out.’“She got very cross if she was interrupted, or had to travel or wasn’t feeling well,” Uglow adds. “I think what the archive does is allow you to follow an extremely distinctive writer in the way that they create their work.”The handwritten drafts of Possession are particularly illuminating. The novel, which interweaves the story of two contemporary academics investigating the lives of fictional Victorian poets, is a feat of elaborate plotting. The hundreds of pages of notebooks drafting the book show Byatt diligently working through questions of chronology and the relationships between the characters before the narrative took its final shape.“Once she had decided on a book, it would take two, three or four years [to write it],” Uglow says. “She worked everything out scene by scene before she wrote the scene itself. She would really think it through, so when you get to the manuscript there aren’t many corrections.”View image in fullscreenAS Byatt’s school report card – with a distinction in English literature.Photograph: the British LibraryByatt continued to write by hand well into the 2000s and 2010s. “It’s rather like craft work,” Uglow says. “There’s a connection between the brain, the imagination and the hand.”The diaries show that Byatt’s intellectual confidence coexisted with flecks of self-doubt. At a young age, she described herself as an “intellectually slow developer” and wondered whether she had a “second rate mind”.In another entry, she wondered whether her abstract way of thinking would prevent her from creating convincing characters – “characters with blood in them”.The collection also contains correspondence with other writers, including the novelist Iris Murdoch, with whom Byatt had a friendly relationship, and letters documenting her exchanges with younger writers.“If she saw a promising young writer, she was excited,” Uglow says. “She took great pleasure in seeing their books come out, and was loyal to them.”The papers also capture Byatt’s wry observations of the people she encountered. During her time in the United States as a young woman, she offered a tart assessment of the women around her. “American women – curiously, stuntedly efficient & childlike,” she wrote. “Most of these are 26, 27 – one would imagine them less. Friendly though, and not unintelligent.”The library estimates that cataloguing the 68 boxes will take up to two years. Once complete, the archive will sit alongside its holdings of the literary papers of writers including Angela Carter, Beryl Bainbridge, Hanif Kureishi and Graham Swift.Where to start with: AS ByattRead more“The British Library is thrilled to have acquired the archive ofAS Byatt,” says Helen Melody, the library’s lead curator of contemporary literary and creative archives. “Byatt sits at the heart of the British literary establishment and her prominence within postwar British literature cannot be overstated. This collection will be a hugely significant resource for researchers seeking to learn more about her life and work.”Uglow thinks Byatt would have welcomed the acquisition. “I think she would be very happy to see her work taken seriously,” she said. “And she would have enjoyed the fact that people wanted to see it and that it was being looked after so carefully.”Explore more on these topicsAS ByattBritish LibraryLibrariesPossessionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Penelopiad review – move over, Odysseus! Margaret Atwood lets Penelope’s maids run riot | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Atwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threads
Author: Catherine Love
Headline: Atwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threads
Content: Unused comic gifts … Amelia Bullmore in The Penelopiad at York Theatre Royal.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenUnused comic gifts … Amelia Bullmore in The Penelopiad at York Theatre Royal.Photograph: Pamela RaithTheatreReviewThe Penelopiad review – move over, Odysseus! Margaret Atwood lets Penelope’s maids run riotYork Theatre RoyalAtwood’s adaptation of her own novella is revived with Amelia Bullmore as a wry Penelope but it’s the eight-strong chorus who pull the story’s threadsCatherine LoveSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAfter a summer of Odysseus hogging the spotlight thanks to Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster take on Homer, it’s time for the women to have their say. The Penelopiad is, as its title declares, the story of Odysseus’s famously faithful wife. But in Margaret Atwood’s play, adapted for the stage from her own novella, it is also Penelope’s brutally slain maids whose perspective is reclaimed. If Penelope’s voice has been sidelined, theirs have been silenced altogether.The backdrop for this revisionist storytelling is hades. In Sara Perks’s minimal design, it’s a sterile, featureless place, deliberately drained of the passion and mess of life. Thick, blood-red ropes suggest the strands – literal and narrative – woven by Penelope and the cords used to hang the maids. These wronged figures form a chorus, acting out episodes from Penelope’s life as well as interrupting with their own bitter take on events. We hear of Penelope and Odysseus’s marriage, his departure to Troy, and the long, long years that followed.View image in fullscreenRaucous contrast … the maids in The Penelopiad.Photograph: Pamela RaithThe success of any production rests on the central role of Penelope, who carries so much of the narrative, and on the treatment of the multi-roling maids. In director Juliet Forster’s version, Amelia Bullmore captures Penelope’s wry reserve and her trepidation when married off to Odysseus, but at times there’s a stiffness and lack of texture to her performance. Given Bullmore’s comic gifts as a performer, it’s surprising that much of the grim humour in Atwood’s lines feels underpowered.Balloon Girl review – tech tycoon swirls with tragic teen parachutist in a crackling, time-travelling climate rompRead moreThe maids, on the other hand, offer a raucous contrast to Penelope’s restraint. The energetic eight-strong chorus sing, dance and skip their way through the story, pulling on different outfits like kids playing dress-up, only to puncture the silliness with reminders of their deadly fate. At its best there’s a hint here of the sort of theatrical mischievousness of Kneehigh and Wise Children, though with not quite the same dazzle or bite. Welcome as this feminist retelling is, it has the potential for a greater punch than it ultimately delivers.AtYork Theatre Royaluntil 31 OctoberExplore more on these topicsTheatreMargaret AtwoodreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Influencer Project to Melanie C: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: A social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: A social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tour
Content: Doom scroll … The Influencer Project.Photograph: -View image in fullscreenDoom scroll … The Influencer Project.Photograph: -Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Going out, staying inCultureThe Influencer Project to Melanie C: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadA social media star comes a cropper in timely horror, and the Spice Girls ledge takes her disco- and indie-tinged bops out on a short tourSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaThe Influencer ProjectOut nowWhen your career involves constantly posting footage of everything you do to social media, it makes things a cakewalk for stalkers. And lo, the influencer-in-peril horror subgenre was born. British social media star Chiara King plays herself in this chilling iteration, set in Copenhagen.NazaOut nowThe ongoing genocide in Gaza has proven an urgent subject for documentaries and drama alike. Here, directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor (two of the four film-makers behind the 2025 Oscar winner No Other Land) construct a doc made up of interviews with Israeli Intelligence Corps agents, who map out the details of targeted airstrikes in civilian areas.WhalefallOut nowWhat if you were swallowed by a whale but survived? That’s the vivid premise of this – what to call it? Eco horror? Monster movie? Survival thriller? Maybe all three? – in which scuba diver Jay (Austin Abrams) has one hour to find a way to escape before his oxygen runs out. Also starring Josh Brolin (sadly not as the whale).Street FighterOut nowThis reboot marks the third live-action movie based on the hit video game to make it to the big screen, and features Jason Momoa as Blanka, 50 Cent as Balrog, and Callina Liang as Chun-Li. Ready… set… fight!Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenThe Spice of life … Melanie C.Photograph: Taylor Jewell/Invision/APMelanie C18 to 24 October; tour starts DublinThe seemingly indefatigable Melanie C, whose dancefloor-focused ninth solo album Sweat peaked at No 3 earlier in the year, takes her solo oeuvre for a spin around a collection of mid-sized venues. As well as the raft of recent bangers, there should be space for some Northern Star-era pop gems, too.Michael CraggJ Cole19 October to 2 November; tour starts LondonThe US rapper heads out on his first solo headline tour in five years in support of seventh, and apparently final album, The Fall-Off. A star-studded, 24-track behemoth, it’s quite the swansong, so chances are these arena shows will carry a similar sense of celebratory closure.MCMingus Big BandRonnie Scott’s, London, 19 to 24 OctoberCharles Mingus, one of the most soulfully creative jazz composers, died in 1979, but the powerful legacy band bearing his name has cherished his repertoire for three decades. The classy lineup includes saxists Wayne Escoffery and Craig Handy, trumpter Alex Sipiagin, and uncannily Mingus-echoing bassist Boris Kozlov.John FordhamRoyal Liverpool PhilharmonicLiverpool Philharmonic Hall, 17OctoberRising-star conductor Adam Hickox takes to the podium for the world premiere of a new clarinet concerto by Gavin Higgins, performed by outgoing RLPO artist in residence Mark Simpson. The programme culminates in Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring – still thrilling, more than a century after its own premiere provoked a riot.Flora WillsonGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenAl smiles … Sturtevant’s Haring Tag, 1986.Photograph: Fredrik Nilsen StudioSturtevantRaven Row, London, to 20 DecemberSturtevant was the ultimate appropriator, a satirical copycat who had been mimicking the work of other artists since the 1960s. This first UK institutional show since her death in 2014 is a celebration of her radical take on conceptualism.Hokusai: 36 Views of Mount FujiDulwich Picture Gallery, London, 13 October to 17 JanuaryHokusai’s iconic depiction of Mount Fuji, one of the most famous images in the history of art, wasn’t a one-off. It was part of a series, and this exhibition brings the full set together.Joy GregoryArnolfini, Bristol, 17 October to 7 FebruaryA celebration of four decades of experimental photography by this leading voice in Black and feminist art, working across historic photographic processes and digital manipulation.Larry AchiampongKarst, Plymouth, to 12 DecemberUsing the visual language of science fiction, this British Ghanaian artist tackles big ideas of colonialism, class, diaspora and displacement in this continuation of his ambitious film project.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenCruise control … Olga Koch.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianOlga KochWhere Else?, Margate, 15 October; touring to 4 DecemberNot all standups ooze confidence like Koch – and not all have such good reason to. In her meticulously crafted new show Fat Tom Cruise, the Russian-British comedian (and PhD student) explores the masculinity crisis via routines delivered with vim, vigour and flair.Rachel AroestiSome WomanNational Theatre: Dorfman, London,to 21 NovemberAnne-Marie Duff stars as an overlooked woman who, after a troubling encounter on a train platform, decides to take a stand in this new play from Helen Edmundson.Miriam GillinsonNorthern Ballet: CinderellaNottingham Theatre Royal, Friday to 24 October; touringto 15 DecemberA new Cinderella for Northern Ballet. Created by choreographer Michael Pink for Milwaukee Ballet, this is the show’s UK premiere, with all the trappings – pumpkin carriage, fairy godmother, comic stepsisters – as well as a great live Prokofiev score.Lyndsey WinshipLannyBristol Old Vic,to 7 NovemberMax Porter’s acclaimed novel is adapted for the stage by Bea Roberts, with a cast drawn largely from the south-west. It’s a blurred and beguiling tale about a young boy who goes missing: is it foul play, the work of an ancient shape-shifting figure or something else?MGskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenReich here, Reich now … It Gets Worse.Photograph: Channel 4It Gets WorseChannel 4, 15 October, 10pmLeo Reich has created the first good gen Z hangout comedy with this London-set tale of three university friends struggling to self-actualise in their mid-20s. From Lena Dunham to Zadie Smith, celebrity cameos abound – but Reich’s winningly bratty protagonist is the real star attraction.The AudacityHBO Max, 15 OctoberWriter Jonathan Glatzer (Succession, Better Call Saul) mines frantic comedy from the dark heart of Silicon Valley in a series about a megalomaniacal tech boss (Billy Magnussen). Industry’s Sarah Goldberg plays his therapist, Motherland’s Lucy Punch is his wife and Zach Galifianakis guests as another unhinged billionaire.The New Stanford Prison ExperimentNetflix, 14 OctoberThe 1971 psychological study which saw male college students randomly split into guards and prisoners in a mock jail remains one of the most fascinating and notorious of all time. Will Netflix’s new reality show version have the same results – and, crucially, the same grim appeal?Last One Laughing: HalloweenPrime Video, 16 OctoberThe spectacular success of our version of the Japanese gameshow means it’s already entered seasonal spin-off territory. Phil Wang and Reece Shearsmith (plus old faves Lou Sanders and Daisy May Cooper) are among the comics trying desperately not to laugh or – spooky twist alert! – scream in this latest edition.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenNintendo Switch Sports Resort.Photograph: NintendoNintendo Switch Sports ResortSwitch 2; out 15 OctoberTake up boxing, bowling, archery, basketball, tennis, skating and more in this latest game in the fine controller-waggling lineage of Wii Sports. Parents of competitive siblings: remember to use the controller straps to stop a Joy-Con from flying through a window.Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4PC, Switch 2, PS5, Xbox; out FridayActivision’s theatre of war goes on tour to Korea, where an invasion threatens the stability of the rest of the world. The multiplayer offers the usual cornucopia of ways to play soldiers, where the campaign follows a Korean private and returning character Captain Price, on the run after an assassination.Keza MacDonaldStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenSongs for the ages … Rachel Chinouriri.Photograph: Yana Van NuffelRachel Chinouriri – I Think I Spoke Too SoonOut nowLyrically influenced by a mid-20s existential crisis, the second album by London singer-songwriter Chinouriri sweetens those fears with vibrant musical touches. On Broken Chair and One Song Away from Crying she dabbles in bubbling 80s synthpop, while the murkier Make Believe grows slowly overcast.Angèle – InstinctOut nowFive years after her second album, Nonante-Cinq, the Belgian superstar returns with more gleaming dance-pop. With production from French knob twiddlers Justice and SebastiAn, plus assistance from Caroline Polachek on the slinky Love Triangle, it’s a play for the big leagues.Florrie – Magic for a WhileOut nowAs part of production hothouse Xenomania, Florrie played drums on hits by Kylie and Girls Aloud. Since stepping up to the mic she’s released her own collection of decadent bops, with this second album expanding into indie pop (The Times) and pensive balladry (Catch You If You Fall).Fontaines DC – Dopamine ChamberOut nowAfter hitting their creative and commercial stride on 2024’s Grammy-nominated Romance, the Irish rock experimentalists are back with this swaggering fifth album. As with Romance it’s been produced by James Ford, who peppers the undulating Tongue with twitchy electronic effects.MCStaying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreenThe LRB PodcastPodcastIntellectuals’ favourite the London Review of Books makes the big questions of our time slightly more digestible in this audio series. Writers, thinkers and experts discuss everything from the worth of criticism to the German far right.TED-Ed:Public Speaking 101YouTubeThis ongoing and insightful series of lectures on public speaking is sure to give even the shyest person confidence to talk to a crowd. The most recent episode covers succinct ways to explain complex ideas.Illuminated: FaithlessBBC Sounds, out nowJournalist May Robson’s expertly reported and deeply moving documentary follows four people who were raised in religious devotion and who have since chosen to leave their faith. Testimony comes from former Jehovah’s Witnesses, Mormons and others.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Selma Blair ‘did not intend to harm anyone’ during airplane incident, representatives say | Selma Blair | The Guardian
description: Actor experienced a ‘medical emergency’ on flight during which she allegedly injured crew members, statement says
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Actor experienced a ‘medical emergency’ on flight during which she allegedly injured crew members, statement says
Content: Selma Blair leaves court on 12 October 2026 in New York after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APView image in fullscreenSelma Blair leaves court on 12 October 2026 in New York after her arraignment on charges of injuring two flight attendants during a cross-country flight.Photograph: Ryan Murphy/APSelma BlairSelma Blair ‘did not intend to harm anyone’ during airplane incident, representatives sayActor experienced a ‘medical emergency’ on flight during which she allegedly injured crew members, statement saysRamon Antonio Vargasand agenciesSat 17 Oct 2026 09.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleActorSelma Blairdid not mean to hurt anyone during the recent flight which led to her arrest on allegations that she assaulted a pair of cabin crew members, a police officer and a nurse, her representatives said on Friday in a statement that characterized the episode as a medical emergency.The lengthy statement also dismissed prior media coverage ofBlair’s arrestafter a Delta Air Lines flight fromLos AngelestoNew Yorkas unsympathetic and inaccurate, singling out reporting from several outlets alleging that she tried to open the door of the airplane that she and her fellow passengers were on.“Selma Blair experienced a medical emergency on the flight,” her representatives’ statement contended. “There was no attempt to open the door of the aircraft. Selma did not intend to harm anyone.”Selma Blair charged with assault of police officer and nurse after allegedly attacking flight attendantsRead moreFriday’s statement from Blair’s camp added some contours to brief remarks made in the days since her arrest by her publicist and lawyer which maintained that there had been a medical emergency but did not elaborate much.Without specifying who may have done so, the statement on Friday called it “outrageous” for anyone to suggest Blair does not have multiple sclerosis (MS), a chronic neurological disorder whichshe went public about being diagnosed within 2018.“What Selma has been able to do physically in the years since is nothing short of a miracle,” said the statement, which was reported by theAssociated PressandPeople. “She still has bad days, and she lives with pain daily.”The statement said Blair has a condition secondary to her MS known as pseudobulbar affect, “which bears directly on how a medical episode presents to people who do not know her”.Blair therefore “travels with a service dog who doesn’t leave her side”.“And the authorities took her dog from her,” said the statement, which described Blair as a disability rights and MS community advocate.Blair’s statement faulted media outlets which – in covering her arrest on Sunday – referred to a 2016 incident in which she reportedly began screaming uncontrollably while on a Los Angeles-bound flight from Cancún, Mexico, before being removed on a stretcher.The actor apologized after that earlier incident, saying that she “mixed alcohol with medication”, blacking out as a result while saying and doing things that “I deeply regret”.Blair’s representatives expressed gratitude to the “handful of journalists [who] have taken the time to report on Selma as a human being rather than a headline”.“Fair reporting has been the exception,” said their statement on Friday, which accused the media of building a narrative around Blair almost solely on police allegations “and a decade-old headline”.“There is much more to this than has been reported,” the statement continued, without offering specifics. “And we ask to consider the entirety of the facts before rushing to judgment, whether in the courtroom or in the court of public opinion.”Authorities accused Blair of injuring two flight attendants while traveling from LA to the John F Kennedy airport (JFK) inNew Yorkon Sunday night. She also was alleged to have kicked a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she arrived at the facility, said a statement from the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey, which operates JFK.She pleaded not guilty on Monday to state assault charges involving the officer and the nurse, with a judge ordering Blair to stay away from them. Blair was freed on bail and tentatively scheduled to return to court in January.Meanwhile, the AP reported that Blair had gotten a notice from the FBI charging her with assault for alleged actions on Delta flight 938. The outlet cited a federal law enforcement official who spoke on the condition of anonymity for not being authorized to speak publicly about the case.Details of exactly what happened in the moments leading up to Blair’s arrest haven’t been disclosed by Delta, state authorities or the FBI. An air traffic control audio recording from the flight Blair was on captured the pilot saying: “One flight attendant and one passenger … sustained some minor injuries – a bloody nose as well as some bite marks.”“I don’t think we need an ambulance or anything like that – but we just want to get some medical personnel at the gate to look at their injuries,” the pilot said, according to the recording, a copy of which waspublishedby NBC Los Angeles.Beside that case and the incident in 2016, Blair grappled with controversy when sheapologizedin February 2024 for an Islamophobic comment on social media.Blair’s major film credits include Cruel Intentions in 1999, Legally Blonde in 2001 and Hellboy in 2004.She earned a 2011 Grammy award nomination for best spoken word album for children for her work on Anne Frank: The Diary of a Young Girl – The Definitive Edition. And she also starred in the acclaimed 2021 documentary Introducing, Selma Blair, which explores her life after her MS diagnosis.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsSelma BlairNew YorkAir transportMultiple sclerosisUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Isabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonym | Isabel Allende | The Guardian
description: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: Chilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the Spirits
Content: Allende on stage with King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain at the award ceremony in Barcelona.Photograph: Pau de la Calle/GTRES/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAllende on stage with King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia of Spain at the award ceremony in Barcelona.Photograph: Pau de la Calle/GTRES/ShutterstockIsabel AllendeIsabel Allende wins €1m Spanish literary prize under pseudonymChilean-American author awarded Premio Planeta for sequel to her 1982 debut novel, The House of the SpiritsEmma LoffhagenandElla CreamerSat 17 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Chilean-American authorIsabel Allendehas won Spain’s €1m (£843,000) Premio Planeta, one of the world’s most lucrative literary prizes, under a pseudonym, with a sequel to her celebrated debut novel, The House of the Spirits.Allende, 84, won the 75th edition of the award on Thursday withLa hora antes del alba, which returns to the characters of her 1982 novel, a multigenerational family saga set against political upheaval in a country inspired byChile.The newstory follows Alba, the granddaughter of Esteban Trueba and Clara del Valle, as she tries to recover from imprisonment and torture during Pinochet’s dictatorship, according to Reuters. Allende said the book would bring the universe of The House of the Spirits to a close. The 1982 novel is often read alongside Daughter of Fortune and Portrait in Sepia as part of a loose trilogy of interconnected family sagas.Speaking at the award ceremony in Barcelona, attended by King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia, Allende said it was “like winning the Nobel”.“I had never entered a competition because I wanted to avoid the embarrassment of coming last,” she said. “At my age, there is very little to lose.”She said she had been prompted to write the sequel by decades of readers asking what happened to Alba. She also drew parallels between the political circumstances surrounding the novel and the contemporary rise of extremism. Allende was forced into exile after the 1973 military coup led by Augusto Pinochet that overthrew the Chilean president Salvador Allende, a cousin of her father. Allende had been Latin America’s first democratically elected Marxist leader. Under Pinochet’s regime, an estimated 40,000 people were tortured and more than 3,000 killed.“Now that I see so many democracies threatened by authoritarianism, extreme nationalism and even fascism, I feel again the fear that led me to leave my country,” she said.Allende is one of the best-known writers in the Spanish-speaking world, whose books have sold more than 80m copies worldwide and been translated into more than 40 languages. The prize is open to unpublished manuscripts, with the option of submitting under a pseudonym, and Allende entered under the name Luz Ventura, with the fictional titleLos que faltan.However, the judges may have been able to pick up on Allende’s style. “I’d be very surprised if the judges did not know that it was Isabel Allende,” said Prof Duncan Wheeler, the chair of Spanish studies at Leeds University and president-elect of the Association of Hispanists of Great Britain and Ireland. “You have to bear in mind that the Planeta prize is one of the most generously remunerated in the Spanish-speaking world, but definitely not the most prestigious.”Isabel Allende: ‘I have been displaced most of my life’Read moreThe prize has at times faced criticism over the choice of winner. In 2021, the prize was awarded toLa bestia, a thriller published under the pseudonym Carmen Mola, which had been marketed as the identity of a female author. At the awards ceremony, it was revealed that Molawas in fact three male writers– Jorge Díaz, Agustín Martínez and Antonio Mercero.The prize is run by Planeta, one of the largest publishing groups in the Spanish-speaking world, and includes the condition that the winning book be published by them. Allende has been published by Plaza & Janés, an imprint of Penguin Random House, since The House of the Spirits, so this marks a significant coup for Planeta.Despite the option to submit pseudonymously, the prize has a history of favouring established writers and TV figures: past winners of the prize have included prominent Spanish-language authors such as Juan Marsé and Manuel Vázquez Montalbán, and the controversial TV personality Juan de Val.Asked about the perceived trend of awarding the prize to figures known for appearing on TV shows, José Creuheras, the president of the Planeta Group, said, according to the Spanish newspaper El País: “I’m not in a position to say whether the Planeta Prize has more or less prestige than it did in the past. We have some of contemporary literature’s biggest names among our winners and finalists. The prize’s reach, as measured by the figures, speaks for itself, and the number of people taking an interest in the Planeta is growing.”The runner-up was the Spanish writer and screenwriter Sergio Hernández, whose historical novel La añoranza won €200,000.Explore more on these topicsIsabel AllendeFictionAwards and prizesSpainChileEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Muscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad) | Men | The Guardian
description: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power
Author: Gabrielle Schwarz
Headline: From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power
Content: A Frenchman weeps as historic French battle flags are taken out of Marseille for safekeeping in 1941.Photograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA Frenchman weeps as historic French battle flags are taken out of Marseille for safekeeping in 1941.Photograph: Historical/Corbis/Getty ImagesMenMuscles, metrosexuals and male tears: the 39 pictures that changed the way we see men (for good and for bad)From a body-building Arnie to a weeping Frenchman, these 39 groundbreaking images have upended assumptions about how men behave, dress and project power. Introduction by Luke KennardCaptions byGabrielle Schwarzand Felix BazalgetteSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 04.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave an image of myself in 2011, pushing my newborn son in a big red buggy because he would only nap when in motion. As I traversed the streets of suburban Birmingham, I felt observed, glanced at, commented on in a manner that ranged from pity to reproach to disproportionate admiration. Daft that it should be a remarkable sight, I thought, but there we go. Probably I’d have felt less self-conscious if I’d followed David Bowie’s example and – as in one of the images showcased here – worn what looks like a dress.On depictions of men and women in art history, John Berger famously stated that “men act, women appear”.Menwere portrayed demonstrating their physical power and readiness for action; to assert their dominance. Just turning that gaze around and using the lens to capture masculinity feels subversive, maybe even a little undermining.It is odd that a quarter of the way through the 21st century images of men crying–see the “weeping Frenchman” during the second world war and Paul Gascoigne’s tears during the 1990 World Cup – could still be seen as remarkable. Judith Butler describes masculinity as aphantasm, a haunting fiction of invulnerability and toughness that is all the more potent because it’s such a lie. We know this, but we’ve probably all had a part in enforcing it, knowingly or obliviously. Boys are still told they shouldn’t be sensitive, that it’s somehow shameful.These photographs are proof that masculinity has strong connotations, histories and counter-histories; a lot of baggage. We stand in some relation to that baggage however we choose to express ourselves, and an image can either reinforce or challenge those associations.Anyone with half a mind must feel a certain amount of pity for a man who feels the need to be depicted in his finery, or in a manner that expresses his prowess or authority – see Karen Knorr’s photographs satirising the privileged postures of men in gentlemen’s clubs – but we’re still surrounded by them, like it or not.Despite the wonderful range here, it’s interesting how normatively hench many of the men depicted are, from Eugen Sandow, the father of bodybuilding, to Arnie to Hulk Hogan. There’s an absence of the body type enjoyed by roughly 80% of men: basically OK, a bit lumpy, sporadically hairy.
