As one mod put it to a BBC interviewer at the time: “You can’t just stand and let a load of kids take the mick out of you, can you?”GSHells Angels,1965By Bill RayView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Bill Ray/The Life Picture Collection/ShutterstockHells Angels – the motorcycle gang founded in California – haunted the US psyche in the 1960s. They modelled a rebellious, hyper-masculine image, but were also – for the time – provocatively homoerotic, frequently giving each other “a sloppy wet kiss”, in writer Hunter S Thompson’s words. “It blows their minds,” said one Hells Angel of the effect on “squares” – “especially the tongue bit”.FBRusty, 2008By Catherine OpieView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Catherine Opie/© Catherine Opie, Courtesy Regen Projects, Los Angeles; Lehmann Maupin, New York, Hong Kong, London, and Seoul; and Thomas Dane Gallery.An interest in “performing masculinity” – which she first explored in San Francisco’s butch lesbian community in the 1990s – eventually led photographer Catherine Opie to high school football. Her portraits of star players, taken just after practice, show “adolescent boys beginning to form and perform for the first time an image-ideal of manhood”, in the words of one critic.Opie also linked the series to the various wars that the US was involved in at the time. “So many young men were having to make very interesting choices between sports scholarships and becoming a soldier,” she has said. “It was actually very emotional.”FBA Scottish Pub,1968By Jürgen SchadebergView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jürgen SchadebergHistorically, pubs and other drinking places were considered a “masculine republic”, somewhere for the menfolk to gather while their wives stayed at home. The notion of the watering hole as an almost exclusively male space – with notable exceptions granted to barmaids, landladies and loose women – is summed up in this image of an establishment in the working-class Gorbals district of Glasgow in 1968.German-bornSchadeberg, best-known for his portraits oflife in South Africaunder apartheid, had been sent to the Gorbals to document an area in rapid transition: the old tenements were being pulled down and replaced by modernist housing.GSPaul Gascoigne crying at the World Cup, 1990By Billy SticklandView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Inpho Photography/Getty Images“I had let down the fans, my team-mates, the manager, everybody,” remembered Paul Gascoigne in 2020. “I cried because I thought it was the end of my career.”In 1990, 23-year-old Gazza had already captured the hearts of the public for his skill in the World Cup. When he burst into tears after receiving a yellow card for tackling a West German player, the nation erupted with a mixture of sympathy and, eventually, mockery.Today, public male tears are a relatively uncontroversial part of major sports tournaments, with everyone from Tiger Woods to Roger Federer having a good sob.FBThese 39 images are a snapshot of men’s lives – which other landmark pictures come to mind for you? Emailsaturday@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsMenPhotographyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Audacity: this witty tech-bro takedown from a Succession writer is packed with glorious one-liners | Television | The Guardian
description: Jonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call Saul
Author: Rhik Samadder
Headline: Jonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call Saul
Content: Screamer … Billy Magnussen stars as tech billionaire Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOView image in fullscreenScreamer … Billy Magnussen stars as tech billionaire Duncan Park in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOThe watcherTelevisionThe Audacity: this witty tech-bro takedown from a Succession writer is packed with glorious one-linersJonathan Glatzer’s pitch-black Silicon Valley satire exposes tech-CEO greed and billionaire egos – at the intriguing, measured pace of Better Call SaulRhik SamadderSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMany of us yearn for the return of an analogue world, but it’s never coming back. You can’t buy potato waffles without a QR code. I had to arrange an IRL bank appointment for my mother to check her balance, and it took, I don’t know, 100 days? A friend of mine has boycotted WhatsApp, but I can’t tell you how that’s going because we haven’t spoken in a year.Watching The Audacity (from Thursday, HBO Max) this week, I was shaken by how much of our dystopia can be traced to a small number of men in Silicon Valley. Their products and platforms, an expression of their shortfalls as much as their skills, have reshaped our world more seismically than any political party. Their power-brokering has turned a small collection of towns and villages south of San Francisco into a modern-day Camelot.The Audacity is interested in the perverse psychology of pioneers. Our hero is Duncan Park (Billy Magnussen), founder of data analytics company Hypergnosis (ugh). They’re on the verge of being bought out by Cupertino, an Apple-coded corporate big dog, until greedy Dunc leaks the news to jack up the price. When the deal falls through, he’s desperate to regain his reputation as a power player, and morally bankrupt enough to break any law to do it. His plan involves blackmailing his therapist, for reasons I won’t spoil. His hobbies include using the privacy-hacking algorithm created for him by an exploited employee, to spy on his wife’s boyfriend – a result of the open marriage Duncan himself suggested. This show’s title is on the money.In a valley, everyone is shady. Therapist JoAnne Felder spends her days massaging the fraught egos of her billionaire clientele, yet has her own game going. There are rival startup CEOs, all vying for top spot on the podium of douchiness. The inane trappings of untethered wealth are satirised, from orthorexic diets to ayahuasca ceremonies, performative spending and pool parties. High-budget shows are a bit like a kebab shop, mind you: through the skewering of these things, we also get to enjoy them.View image in fullscreenIngenious … Simon Helberg plays geeky inventor Martin Phister in The Audacity.Photograph: Ed Araquel / AMC/HBOSo far, so Succession. But there are stranger, more melancholy strands. An eccentric inventor, developing a digital ‘friend’ for alienated teenagers. A teenage misfit who starts to live in wall cavities, his surveillance of others an eerie mirror of the adult world that has forsaken him. A reclusive CEO called Carl Bardolph, played by Zach Galifianakis. Retired into generational wealth, he misses the spotlight. Bardolph has a ‘law’ named after him, an ethos of infinite profit he once wrote on a napkin, while on speed. “It was based on the logic of the cancer cell,” he explains to Dr Felder.The Audacity excels at one liners. When Duncan’s daughter expresses qualms about her “admissions consultant”, who games the system and guarantees her spot at a top-tier university, Duncan reassures her with a Trump-y aphorism. “Cheaters never lose. And losers – they never cheat.” When the Veterans Association comes to Silicon Valley, looking for partnership, an executive dismisses them with relish. Cupertino helping the charity would be “like France helping your mother to set up a printer. Only we have much, much more money than France”.Wit is a drug The Audacity mainlines, but the show is interested in longevity. Creator Jonathan Glatzer has written on Succession and Better Call Saul. Like the latter, this is a show content to work its hand slowly, building intrigue within a complex plot. I can’t say yet whether it lands all the pieces. Still, I’m enjoying the wild-eyed performance from Magnussen. In real life, the actor is absurdly handsome. Here, his fair curls are piled atop his head (possibly inspired by the way Zuckerberg grew his hair out?). The effect makes him resemble a young Jerry Stiller, or a fried doughnut.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWhat's OnGet the best TV reviews, news and features in your inbox every MondayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAn irony strikes me – if these tech bros do bring about the apocalypse, burning up the planet and making most of humanity extinct, those who survive will actually be living an analogue lifestyle; sucking runoff from a storm drain by an abandoned shopping centre. Something to look forward to. I might even have my mother’s bank appointment by then!Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: the return of hit mystery thriller Dark Winds  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Cops Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee are back looking for a killer. Plus, Celine Dion and David Bowie inspire Strictly’s icons week! Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Cops Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee are back looking for a killer. Plus, Celine Dion and David Bowie inspire Strictly’s icons week! Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Grim discovery … Dark Winds on U&Alibi.Photograph: UKTVView image in fullscreenGrim discovery … Dark Winds on U&Alibi.Photograph: UKTVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: the return of hit mystery thriller Dark WindsCops Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee are back looking for a killer. Plus, Celine Dion and David Bowie inspire Strictly’s icons week! Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Alexi Duggins,Priya Elan,Graeme VirtueandEllen E JonesSat 17 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDark Winds9pm, U&AlibiA shootout in a diner marks a thrilling start to the fourth season of this mystery thriller, which has quietly earned quite a fanbase over the years. Set in the 70s, Zahn McClarnon and Kiowa Gordon return as Navajo police team Joe Leaphorn and Jim Chee. This time, they’re looking for a runaway school student, while a killer is also on a search of her own.Hollie RichardsonStrictly Come Dancing: Icons Week6.15pm, BBC OneCeline Dion! Shania Twain! Ricky Martin! David Bowie! It can only be icons week. Poor Melanie and Aljaž won’t be around to take on Bonnie Tyler as planned, and Delta is sitting it out with an injury. But Cach and Maddie will take on the foxtrot, while Lacey and Vito glide to the American Smooth and John and Katya get serious with a paso.HRTalking Pictures: World Cinema Classics9pm, BBC FourCelia Imrie returns to celebrate international films, starting with Akira Kurosawa’s Ran, which Christopher Nolan showed to his team when making blockbuster The Odyssey. Imrie also looks at the works of directors Agnès Varda, Francois Truffaut, Luis Buñuel and Ingmar Bergman.HRMarble Hall Murders9.20pm, BBC OneCan Lesley Manville do any wrong? It’s certainly hard to believe – unless you’re a character in her literary mystery show. In episode four, book editor Susan (Manville) is woken by police to be informed that she’s the prime suspect for a hit and run on her author Eliot (Jamie Blackley). Can she prove her innocence?Alexi DugginsSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneNot exactly a noted gag merchant (considering his roles in Happy Valley and A Little Life), James Norton takes the hosting roulette this week. But unlike its US counterpart, SNL UK has not misfired yet thanks to stunningly sharp writing, so expectations are high. The Streets will be the musical guest.Priya ElanKrapopolis11.45pm, BBC ThreeRichard Ayoade voices a fusspot king trying to modernise his ancient Greek city in this daft but zinger-packed animated comedy from Rick and Morty co-creator Dan Harmon. This marathon of six episodes includes a trip to Hades, a melancholy hydra and divine voice cameos from Susan Sarandon and Steve Buscemi.Graeme VirtueFilm choiceTenzing, out now, Apple TVView image in fullscreenTwice as ice … Tenzing on Apple TV.Photograph: AppleTo Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston) and British expedition leader Col John Hunt (Willem Dafoe), it was ‘Mount Everest’, named to honour a 19th-century British Raj official. But Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), the Tibetan-Indian mountaineer who joined them on that historic 1953 trek to the summit, called the peak by its Sherpa name Chomolungma, meaning “holy mother”. To Tenzing, the mountain is not so much somewhere to conquer but someone to connect with. As director Jennifer Peedom’s film tells his story, it scales the heights of the adventure biopic, discovering new angles from which to view old themes of ambition, colonialism and class.Ellen E JonesCléo from 5 to 7Saturday, 9.45pm, BBC FourThe plot of this 1962, Agnès Varda-directed classic is deceptively simple: as she awaits the results of a cancer biopsy, Florence (Corinne Marchand), a singer known professionally as ‘Cléo Victoire’, wanders around Paris, meeting old friends and strangers, getting tarot readings or going to the cinema; alternating between despair, resignation and a kind of ecstasy. Yet each encounter, and even the apparent longueurs in between, vibrates with the life-affirming energy of the French New Wave, a movement busily reinventing the form before our very eyes.EEJGoodfellas, 11.40pm, Sky Cinema GreatsView image in fullscreenPlease hold … Goodfellas on Sky Cinema Greats.Photograph: ScreenProd/Photononstop/AlamyIt’s the greatest mafia film of all time. The Sopranos’ archetype. Martin Scorsese’s masterpiece of masterpieces, and a film you should rewatch every few years just to recalibrate your cinematic senses. Ray Liotta stars as Henry Hill, an Irish-Italian kid from round the way, and an “average nobody”, according to his iconic voiceover. That is, until he gets mixed up with wiseguys Jimmy Conway (Robert De Niro), Tommy DeVito (Joe Pesci) and Paulie (Paul Sorvino), who teach him their code and show him the only way to live.EEJLive sportTrack Cycling : World Championships 2026, 10.15am, BBC TwoWith the women’s madison and individual pursuit.Racing: Ascot, 12.45pm, ITV1All seven races on Champions Day.Premier League Football: Everton v Chelsea, 11am, TNT Sports 1Newcastle play Aston Villa at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #265: Your favourite record labels, from Motown to Flying Nun | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Record labels always push music forward into interesting new places. Here’s a celebration of their power by readers and Guardian music writers
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Record labels always push music forward into interesting new places. Here’s a celebration of their power by readers and Guardian music writers
Content: You can’t beat a classic label …  Motown.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenYou can’t beat a classic label …  Motown.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #265: Your favourite record labels, from Motown to Flying NunIn this week’s newsletter: Record labels always push music forward into interesting new places. Here’s a celebration of their power by readers and Guardian music writersDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 17 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLast week we asked Guide subscribers to tell us about their favourite record labels, and the response was enthusiastic. Clearly, even in this age of streaming services that flatten albums, singles, EPs and mixtapes into one single “feed”, the lure of a label – and its role in identifying, nurturing and developing musical talents – remains.So this week, a celebration of the record label: along with some readers’ favourites, we’ve asked music writers to share their personal picks. They’ve put together a great list of familiar and off-the-beaten-track labels that might just help you discover your next favourite album (I can already tell I’ll be spinning the Verlaines record recommended by reader James a fair bit!).‘Record labels throb with thrill and romance’“As a stream of AI slop joins the torrent of content that arcs across popular culture, well-curated labels become more important than ever for time-poor and garbage-resistant listeners. One of today’s best isAD93, founded by Londoner Nic Tasker. It manages to be totally open-minded, while its signees nevertheless have a shared spirit: experimentalism used to dig out beauty and originality. Moin’s avant-rock is unmissable, as is Joanne Robertson’s ambient balladry, and inJames Kthey have a genuine possible pop star. They’re also cannily hoovering up artists out of contract, bringing back the likes of untameable singer-songwriter Ryley Walker. Their catalogue might evoke everything from sweaty dancefloor to empty moorland, but it’s all under the same sky.” –Ben Beaumont-Thomas, Guardian music editor“My favourite record label has to beCBS Recordsin all its manifestations. They recorded so many of the greats, including Miles Davis, Bob Dylan, Leonard Cohen etc. They also released the first sampler album in 1969,The Rock Machine Turns You On. At less than half the price of most albums, it contained tracks by established artists like Dylan, Simon and Garfunkel and the Byrds and introduced lesser-known artists like Spirit, The Zombies and the best psychedelic band of the 60s, The United States of America. They followed it a year later with Rock Machine I Love You, which had a similar great selection of artists.” –Millard Parkinson“I don’t think anyone has shaped my taste in music quite like AG Cook, founder ofPC Music. Running from 2014 to 2024, the label and the artists that orbited it – including SOPHIE, Hannah Diamond and GFOTY – injected pop with haunting, glitchy garage and happy hardcore-adjacent sounds, at a time when dance-pop meant Clean Bandit and Jess Glynne. Charli xcx has repeatedly credited the collective with shaping her now generation-defining alt-pop. (Cook was a producer on both Brat and Rock Music.) My favourite release?Danny L Harle’s Broken Flowers EP, from 2015. It sounds like the future, being underwater, and a northern town centre super-club all at the same time.” –Kate Lloyd, Guardian commissioning editor and music journalist“My favourite record label is easily Manchester’sGondwana Records, led by the brilliant jazz trumpeter Matthew Halsall. Alongside a super-cool graphic design aesthetic, the label has also curated a fantastic range of artists, across 85 album releases since 2008. As well as Matthew Halsall’s own albums, they’ve released work by GoGo Penguin, Mammal Hands, Portico Quartet, Hania Rani and Jasmine Myra. The consistency of quality is astounding, and it’s so hard to single out one release, but if pushed it would probably beGoGo Penguin’s brilliant v2.0.” –Ian Oxley“So many record labels throb with thrill and romance, but none better thanRough Trade. They’ve been with me since my teenage love of The Smiths, to the day I picked up a new EP by a band called the Strokes, through my discoveries of Arcade Fire and Arthur Russell, through to the staggering folk talents they release today, likeLisa O’Neill, LankumandRadie Peat. The warm, welcoming Geoff Travis and Jeannette Lee only release stuff they really love, from any genre, and it shows. Also: what a logo. The best label ever.” –Jude Rogers, music journalist and broadcasterView image in fullscreenSincere … PC Music’s Hannah Diamond.Photograph: Burak Çıngı/Redferns“My favourite record label would have to be the now defunctSlash Records. I started out with Los Lobos, but moved on to The Blasters, The Del Fuegos, Bo Deans, L7 and Violent Femmes. Favourite amongst these (based purely on replays) has to bethe Del Fuegos’ Stand Up, a drunken blues rock album, and their final album on Slash.” –Matt PudduckFor the eclecticism of its artists and the many bonkers stories of its hard-partying ways, my favourite label has to beLondon Records. I prided myself on my ‘edgy’ teenage musical allegiances and London’s books reflected these nicely – they too shunned Take That in favour of East 17, and signed All Saints (clearly far cooler than the Spice Girls). My favourite release though was The Raw & the Cooked byFine Young Cannibals, which my dad introduced me to and which became a staple on long summer drives. –Lucia CavendishAn independent record label specialising in hip-hop and UK rap primarily from Nottingham shouldn’t have been this good. ButSon Recordswas. Yes, there was the daftness of MC Pitman, who did novelty records taking cues from Roots Manuva (Witness the Pitness, anyone?), but their releases byCappoandScorzayzeeform part of an overlooked part of British MC culture. The thick Notts accent and attitude give the whole thing a flavour that chimes with UK drill’s contemporary regional heroes like Esdeekid. –Lanre Bakare, Guardian arts and culture correspondentskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I came of age in the 2000s, when it was cool to have racoon tails at the back of your hair and wear pink eyeliner. I don’t look back on my style decisions during that time fondly, but the music still has a special place in my heart. On that point:Fueled by Ramenhas to be one of the most iconic labels ever. Their roster included the likes of Paramore, Panic! at the Disco, Jimmy Eat World, Fall Out Boy and my favouritesGym Class Heroes– which all went down swimmingly with the emo drink of choice: a pint of Strongbow laced with Ribena.” –Poppy Bennett“On my side of the world it has to beFlying Nun Records, the little indie label that brought us Dunedin sounds and much more. As for the album I would pick it’s Hallelujah All the Way Home bythe Verlaines. A masterpiece in songwriting by Graeme Downes that he submitted as part of his classical music master’s thesis (it received an A grade, I recall). They played the song Lying in State at breakneck speed with guitars and drums orchestrating the strains of Mahler within.” –James Mowatt“Motown Recordsis a very clear and obvious choice for me. Being introduced to them was thanks to the confluence of me being into hip-hop (like so many others), and coming of musical age at a time when dad wanted to share his albums, and every movie and television show wanted to get nostalgic. Excellent music, amazing performers, and the joy of hearing where so many of those [hip-hop] samples came from. I’ll always have the softest of spots for Marvin, Diana and the like, but at heart I’m aTemptationsfan first and foremost. Sky’s The Limit is a true no-bad-tracks album.” –Jamie GambellTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: A Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the Peloponnese | Greece holidays | The Guardian
description: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernas
Content: Monemvasia, the Greece of the Spartans.Photograph: Jason Rambach/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMonemvasia, the Greece of the Spartans.Photograph: Jason Rambach/Getty ImagesGreece holidaysA Greece for all seasons: my autumn roadtrip through the PeloponneseAn out-of-season journey through the peninsula reveals Byzantine villages, deserted beaches and friendly tavernasChris CotonouSat 17 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs I drove across the causeway which links the tiny fortress island of Monemvasia to the south-eastern coast of the Peloponnese, the Aegean sparkling on all sides, I recalled a line by Yiannis Ritsos, one of Greece’s greatest 20th-century poets. Ritsos lived in Monemvasia, in a house that is today a museum on a cobble-stretch by the tawny castle walls. A favourite passage goes: “The voyage is neither a leave-taking nor a home-coming – an ethereal bridge …”The excuse for my trip to the Peloponnese’s deep south – Messinia, the Mani, and Laconia – fell between those two ideas. My mother has roots in the Peloponnese – a sort-of homecoming that I’ve long wanted to explore – and with the summer over and greedy for an adventure to myself, I set out by car, leaving Kalamata, the leafy port city and gateway to the area, on a coastal road circuit.View image in fullscreenAutumn in the Peloponnese is another Greece. Forget the Cycladic white and blue; mountain valleys are carpeted in pine forests and wildflowers, a great stretch of green studded with rustic limestone houses. These villages, relieved by the end of a scorching summer, celebrate boisterous harvest festivals for wines, oranges and chestnuts in Laconia, figs in Messinia, and olives near Kalamata. This is the Greece the diaspora yearns for: thechorio– a word that snaps us back to our relatives and Greek rural life, villages where the air is healthy, eating depends on what is grown metres away, and tavernas are alive with locals rather than tourists. In the shoulder season, the weather is cool enough for long walks along the region’s spectacular trails but, at about 25C, is also still good for swimming.double quotation markThe Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surfaceThe two-hour drive to Monemvasia began with the Taygetus pass, winding through villages and cliffside tunnels as golden eagles soared above the firs. On the far side of the Taygetus, the road opened to Mystras, an archaeological Byzantine site stacked up its hillside. I climbed to the Paleologian Palace and its chapels, then descended, hungry, to the village of Parori, where Taverna Ores was servingsyglino, the local cured pork, and an okra stew. I practised my flimsy Greek with the waitress and her mother, who kept one eye on a television gameshow while stirring the stew pots.View image in fullscreenThe Byzantine Greek architecture of Monemvasia.Photograph: Kisa_Markiza/Getty Images/iStockphotoAfter lunch I stopped at Sparta – site of the ancient city state and modern metropolis. Beneath the Taygetus, in the spectral hush of the olive groves, there is an acropolis, an agora and little else. Yet the air carries something over the ruins, and it’s a short but necessary stop. A statue of Leonidas, hero of Thermopylae, stands facing the new city with the ruins at his back.This is still the Greece of the Spartans: locals remain fiercely attached to their ancient ancestry. Monemvasia has a thrilling connection: in AD600, a bishop is said to have led the Spartan population to the rock to fortify themselves against invading tribes. Set on to a slope inside the castle walls is a town of tight passages and medieval Orthodox churches. It is a vivid encounter with Byzantine Greek architecture, as well as traces of Venetian trade: the sweet, fortified wine malvasia was once a prized export. Even my guesthouse,Kelia(rooms from €70), began as a monks’ residence on the sea-facing Chryssafitissa Square.Leaving Monemvasia, I took a detour south for the golden sand dune beaches in Elafonisos. Reaching this island requires taking a 10-minute ferry ride from Pounta. The turquoise waters of Simos beach are deserted in the off-season – a necessary respite before my hour drive north-west to spend a night in Gythio. This working harbour town has neoclassical pastel mansions and waterfront restaurants provisioned by local fishers. Here the Mani begins.View image in fullscreenSimos beach is reached by ferry from Pounta.Photograph: Constantinos Iliopoulos/Alamy“Victory or death” reads the Maniot banner, above the Spartan motto “With the shield, or on the shield”. The region has a reputation for a conservative way of life that might seem unfashionable in modern Greece, but I find it seductive. The Mani’s beauty comes partly from its insularity. Driving an hour to Vathia, rugged mountains are crowned by labyrinthine stone tower villages that Maniot clans built to protect themselves during periods of vendetta or skirmishes with the Ottomans. Some are now ghost towns. Others have been converted into guesthouses.double quotation markThis is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the worldBut it was in Gerolimenas that a Greek friend suggested I stay for a few nights. The seaside village is an easy base for touring both western and eastern coasts. Along the latter, I hiked to mainland Greece’s southernmost point, Cape Tainaron lighthouse and went for an impromptu dip. The Mani’s water is so gin-clear the boats appear to hover above the surface.TheAkroyiali hotel(doubles from €80 B&B) opened in the 1970s, before most of the region’s roads. It is built on Gerolimenas’s shore, so I dozed to the pulse of waves and chatter from the hotel’s taverna below, where owner Mr Theodorakakis and his family entertained guests.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKardamyli, a popular village on the Mani that quietens in autumn.Photograph: Stephen Hughes/Alamy“The Mani is changing at its own rhythm,” Theodorakakis told me. “This is a special place. We can’t keep hiding from the world.” Most Greeks prefer to visit off-season, he said. “You can actually explore the region without burning. But be careful of the north-eastern wind. It cuts through!”Leaving Gerolimenas, I drove 30 minutes up the western coastal route, entering the busy town of Areopoli, where I shopped for hand-harvested sea salt and wild oregano. Pretty Limeni and Kardamyli – the home of British writer Patrick Leigh Fermor (who popularised the region) – get the Mani day-trip overspill from Kalamata. Regardless, it’s quieter in autumn. Every hairpin bend opens on to sea views, flowers and limestone.I was lunching over one such view of a grassy cape when the taverna owner mentioned a woman in the village who knewmiralogia. These are wailing Maniot lamentations sung at funerals, which are heard rarely these days. After two days of asking around, I found Kaiti Braimi in a small chapel where she agreed to sing. “In a way, they’re less necessary,” the octogenarian told me. “No more vendettas.”View image in fullscreenThe Polylimnio waterfalls in Messinia.Photograph: PitK/AlamyThe haunting rhythms of themiralogiawere in mind as I left the Mani to enter Messinia – cutting through Kalamata again, but this time heading west. Here, the villagers were celebrating. Clarinets hummed in taverna gardens at Sunday family parties and relatives joined hands in circles to dance thekalamatianos. Passersby stood and clapped before being dragged in.On the hour drive from Kalamata to Pylos – which would be my base – the Maniot mountains flattened into lush forests. Wildflowers bloomed on the roadside. Yet in Messinia’s expansive green are traces of ancient civilisations, including the bronze age palace of Nestor, north of Pylos.My route sidetracked to the Polylimnio waterfalls. You can sidetrack easily in Messinia; there are unspoiled beaches (like Tsapi on the south coast, where mountains tumble into the sea), as well as areas for canyoning, cycling and kayaking. After a small hike, I bathed in clear pools surrounded by pines, alone mostly, apart from an Athenian couple. “We’re here for my birthday,” the man said. “Messinia is the best place in Greece for outdoor activities.” They pointed me to a canyoning trail north of the Bay of Navarino – a tip for my next visit.That evening in Pylos’s port, only an hour from where I began my voyage in Kalamata, I paused for an ouzo at akafenion. A group of lads were watching Greece play Germany at football on the television. They wailed their ownmiralogiawith every missed shot, but when the game ended in a win the cafes along the harbour roared.I thought back on my drive through the Peloponnese’s deep south, a journey that revealed a rural Greece I’d grown up romanticising from family, and believed was slowly disappearing. But not here. In the mountains and shores of Messinia, the Mani and Laconia, I found a Greece for all seasons.Explore more on these topicsGreece holidaysRoad tripsEurope holidaysCultural tripsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘If AI were asked to make miso, it would taste like this’: the best (and worst) supermarket miso, tasted and rated | Food | The Guardian
description: We ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thing
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: We ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thing
Content: The least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonView image in fullscreenThe least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert BillingtonGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterFoodReview‘If AI were asked to make miso, it would taste like this’: the best (and worst) supermarket miso, tasted and ratedWe ran supermarket pastes through the ‘soup test’ to find out which ones have an authentic flavour and which are nothing like the real thingThe best supermarket kimchiTom HuntSat 17 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMiso is a simple product that’s traditionally made by fermenting pulses (usually soya beans) with salt andkoji, typically a grain (rice or barley, and more recently oats, say) inoculated withAspergillus oryzaemould. Bar one fabulous exception, however, our supermarkets seem to have flipped the “you get what you pay for” adage on its head when it comes to miso: the least authentic and most processed products in this test were also some of the most expensive, even though they’re little more than synthetic imitations cut with thickeners, colourants, acidulants and preservatives.I asked my friend Jono Hope fromSlow Sauce, a miso and shoyu brewery in Scotland, for advice, and he told me not to taste it straight from the jar; its intense, salty flavour would ruin my palate. Instead, he advised mixing a teaspoon with warm water, then drinking it – “the soup test”.The best supermarket miso pastesBest overall:Hikari Maru-Yu additive-free koji misoView image in fullscreen£5.49 for 375g at the Japan Centre (£1.46/100g)★★★★★A glossy, burnt sienna paste with a granular texture and rich, floral, sweet and earthy aroma. Soup test: fresh, sweet on the nose, with a salty, fruity flavour. Made simply.Best bargain:Yutaka organic miso pasteView image in fullscreen£3.30 for 300g at Sainsbury’s (£1.10/100g)★★★★★A very smooth, sienna-coloured caramel paste with a velvety texture and yeasty, umami aroma. The soup is mild and very sweet, with notes of barley. Great Taste two-star winner in 2024. A perfectly simple recipe formula (34% soya beans, rice, 11.9% salt) and incredible value.And the rest …Slow Sauce organic pink misoView image in fullscreen£13 for 200g at Slow Sauce (£6.50/100g)★★★★★A coarse yellow paste with a sweet and fruity aroma. Soup test: a soft, sweet lactic aroma and a clean taste. Made with Scottish oat koji, flamingo peas and sea salt, all magnified through the slow fermentation. Sweet, young, funky and alive – and this week’s best splurge.Clearspring organic brown rice misoView image in fullscreen£5 for 300g at Waitrose (£1.67/100g)£5.10 for 300g at Ocado (£1.70/100g)★★★★☆A shiny, dark chocolate brown paste with an unfathomably rich and mature soy sauce aroma. Soup test: a sweet, subtle aroma, and a deep, meaty, mushroom flavour with an underlying sour twang. Made from brown rice koji.Miso Tasty red misoView image in fullscreen£3.10 for 200g at Tesco (£1.55/100g)£3.10 for 200g at Amazon (£1.55/100g)★★★☆☆A matt, umber-violet paste with a smooth texture and deep, rich and floral aroma. Soup test: a sweet, fruity scent and a rich but mildly astringent taste. Made to a simple formula. Great Taste one star in 2025.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMarukome miso with dashiView image in fullscreen£5.99 for 375g at Japan Centre (£1.60/100g)★★★☆☆A glossy, yellow paste with a super-smooth texture and a deep, smoky, fishy aroma. Soup test: a smoked bonito and fruity, sweet sake lees aroma, perfect for instant miso soups and noodles. An ultra-processed recipe, though, including MSG, bonito, disodium inosinate and disodium guanylate.Itsu traditional Miso’easyView image in fullscreen£2 for 105g (5 x 21g sachets) at Asda (£1.90/100g)£2 for 105g (5 x 21g sachets) at Ocado (£1.90/100g)★★☆☆☆Thin, glossy, caramel-coloured paste with the aroma of ethanol, acetic acid and soy sauce. Soup test: mild, sweet and simple in flavour. Made with 53% miso cut with water, alcohol and yeast extract.Blue Dragon miso pasteView image in fullscreen£2 for 135g at Morrisons (£1.48/100g)£2.50 for 135g at Asda (£1.85/100g)★☆☆☆☆A thin, glossy, brown sugar-coloured paste with a sour but rounded umami aroma. Soup test: an acidic aroma and intensely salty taste with rich umami notes in the background. It’s 55% miso paste cut with salt, sugar, acidity regulators and preservatives.Sainsbury’s Inspired to Cook miso pasteView image in fullscreen£1.90 for 100g at Sainsbury’s (£1.90/100g)★☆☆☆☆A thin, ochre paste with an acidic umami aroma. Soup test: sour-forward with a rounded, earthy flavour. Made with 45% miso paste cut with cornflour, acidity regulator and preservative potassium sorbate.Tesco miso pasteView image in fullscreen£1.80 for 100g at Tesco (£1.80/100g)☆☆☆☆☆A thin, shiny, yellow paste with an odd sour but still umami aroma. Soup test: unexpectedly sour. If AI were asked to make miso, I expect it would taste like this synthetic impression of miso that’s nothing like the real thing. Contains citric acid, colour (plain caramel) and potassium sorbate.For more, read thebest (and worst) supermarket sushi, tasted and ratedExplore more on these topicsFoodThe FilterJapanese food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts | Food | The Guardian
description: ‘Ethereal sigh’ or ‘slimy hopelessness’? Respect this demanding veg and it will reward you
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: ‘Ethereal sigh’ or ‘slimy hopelessness’? Respect this demanding veg and it will reward you
Content: Jackson Boxer’s poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenJackson Boxer’s poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnuts.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.FoodJackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnutsPoach your leeks to perfection, then pair with pickled pears and nutty misoJackson BoxerSat 17 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIhave a great respect for the leek, which is possibly the most demanding vegetable in its need to be freshly cooked before consumption. A warm leek, fresh from the pot, is an ethereal, collapsing sigh of diaphanous veils, whereas cold it can all too easily become a slippery and almost slimy mess of hopelessness.Poached leeks with pickled pear and hazelnutsAll the various elements can be made ahead of time except the leeks, which should be just warm from their poaching, and the dressing, which should be made at the last minute. Vegetable bouillon may seem a bit of a faff to make just to poach some leeks (if you prefer, simply cook them in two litres of seasoned water with a dash of white wine instead), but a good, light vegetable broth is a useful thing to have around, and a batch will keep happily in the fridge for three or four days. To toast nuts successfully, cook them on a tray in an even layer in a 170C (150C fan)/335F/gas 3½oven for 15-20 minutes, which will toast them evenly to the core without scorching.Prep25 minSoak and chillOvernightCook1 hr, plus coolingServes4For the hazelnut miso250g hazelnuts40g white miso paste25ml olive oil5gflaky sea salt(about 1 tsp)For the vegetable bouillon (optional; see recipe introduction)1medium carrot, peeled and quartered1 medium onion, peeled and quartered1 medium shallot, peeled and left whole2 garlic cloves, peeled4 leek tops(from trimming the leeks below)1 bay leaf5 thyme sprigs2 parsley sprigs1 star anise150ml white wine2 litres filtered water40g flaky sea saltFor the pickled pears2 conference pears150ml white-wine vinegar50g sugarFor the leeks4 leeks, trimmed, roots removed and thoroughly cleaned, then cut in half across the middle2 litres vegetable bouillon(see above and method)Minced chives and chopped chervil, to finish (optional)For the dressing200g pear pickling liquor(see above and method)100ml extra-virgin olive oil5gflaky sea salt(about 1 tsp)2g ground black pepper(about ½ tsp)50g minced shallot10g minced garlic100g toasted hazelnuts, choppedThe day before, put the nuts in a container or bowl, add a litre of water and leave overnight to soften. Next day, strain the nuts, reserving the soaking liquid.Put all the bouillon ingredients in a large pot (again, you can do this a day before), bring to a low simmer and cook gently on a medium heat for 25 minutes. Take off the heat, leave to rest and cool for four hours, then strain.Peel, quarter and core the pears, then cut each quarter in half lengthwaysand put in a container, for which you have a lid. Put the vinegar, sugar and 75ml water in a saucepan, bring to a simmer, then pour the pickling liquor over the pears, cover and chill for 12 hours.Put the drained nuts, miso, olive oil and salt in a food processor, dribble in just enough of the soaking liquid to lubricate, then blitz to a smooth, rich puree the consistency of mayonnaise; add a drop more liquid to loosen, if need be.Submerge the leeks in the bouillon, bring it to a low simmer and cook for 15 minutes, until the leeks show only gentle resistance to the tip of a sharp knife. Take off the heat and leave to cool to room temperature for about half an hour.Meanwhile, make the dressing. In a stainless-steel bowl, whisk the pickling liquor and oil to a smooth and coherent emulsion, then stir in all the other dressing ingredients.Lift the just-warm leeks out of the poaching liquid and cut lengthways into quarters. Spoon some hazelnut miso on each plate, then arrange the leeks on top. Dot pieces of pickled pear between them, spoon over the dressing and garnish with minced chives and, if you’re lucky enough to have some, chopped chervil.Jackson Boxer is chef/owner ofBrunswick House,VesperandDove, all in London, and culinary director ofCowley Manornear Cheltenham andthe Henriettain LondonExplore more on these topicsFoodVegetarian food and drinkNuts and seedsVegetablesFruitHerbs and spicesStarterrecipesShareReuse this content
